en: Now, having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! regarding the Śrī-Vāmana Purāṇa.
Salutations to that Śrīdhara, who assumed the disguised form of a dwarf and, having wrested the sovereignty of the three worlds from Bali, bestowed it upon Indra.
Nārada questioned Pulastya, the best among those skilled in speech, as he sat in his hermitage, concerning the ancient account centered on Vāmana.
O Brahman, how was dwarfhood formerly assumed by the Lord Viṣṇu, the all-powerful? Tell that to me as I ask you.
And how did Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas, having become a Vaiṣṇava, fight with the gods? In this matter, there is a great doubt. (Vāmana Purāṇa 1.4)
And it is heard, O best of the twice-born, that Dakṣa’s daughter Satī,
a woman of excellent complexion, became the beloved wife of Śaṅkara.
For what purpose did that woman of beautiful countenance, having abandoned her own body,
become born in the home of Himavat, the high-souled lord of mountains?
Furthermore, that auspicious lady became the wife of the God of Gods;
resolve this doubt of mine, for you are considered by me to be all-knowing. (VamP 1.7)
O best of beings, O twice-born one, tell me the majesty of sacred fords, the nature of gifts, and the rules for various religious observances.
Having been addressed in this manner by Nārada, Pulastya,
the best of sages and foremost among speakers, replied to Nārada, the treasury of asceticism.
Pulastya said:
O best of sages, having made your attention steady, listen as I recount from the very beginning, in due order, the entire Vāmana Purāṇa.
In ancient times, having seen that the summer season had arrived, the goddess Haimavatī spoke these words to Maheśvara, who was staying on Mount Mandara.
"O Lord of the Gods, the summer season has begun, yet you have no dwelling where we two might stay during this summer heat, protected from the wind and the sun."
Thus addressed by Bhavānī, Śaṅkara spoke these words:
"O lady of beautiful teeth, O auspicious one, I am without a home and always a dweller of the forest."
Thus addressed by Śaṅkara, O Nārada,
that virtuous woman spent the summer season together with Śarva in the shade of trees.
At the end of the summer heat, he became like the ocean— wondrous, frequented by no men,
with the quarters of the sky darkened by clouds, and possessing the intense passion of the rainy season.
Seeing that the rainy season had arrived, Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, then spoke these words with affection to the Lord of Gods: VamP_1.16 //
O Maheśvara, the winds blow, rending the hearts asunder; these mountains roar;
lightning flashes amidst the masses of dark blue clouds; and the peacocks cry out with their shrill *kekā* calls.
Showers fall, descending from the sky; cranes and herons move toward the clouds;
and the kadamba, sarja, arjuna, and ketakī trees release their blossoms when struck by the gentle breeze.
Upon hearing the thunderous roar of Magha, the swans instantly abandon their lakes,
just as the host of yogis completely forsakes their dwellings, even those with deeply rooted foundations.
"O Śambhu, these herds of forest deer roam, run, and play;
likewise, O Lord, the flashes of lightning gleam intensely here amidst the dark clouds.
Surely, having seen the abundance of water, these brave ones sport among the young trees."
The rivers, whose currents were once surging, have suddenly become sluggish on the beautiful banks marked by the deer of the moon;
what wonder is there in this, that a woman, having served a man who is not radiant, becomes ill-behaved?

The sky was covered with dark clouds; the *sārja* trees were laden with flowers and buds, the *nīpa* trees with fruit, the *bilva* trees with fruit, the rivers with water, and the great lakes with lotuses and leaves.
"At this most terrible time, indeed, I tell you:
build a house here in this great and excellent ocean, O Śambhu, so that I may be completely at peace."
Having heard these words, which were as beautiful as the Vedas, the Three-eyed Lord spoke this speech:
"I have no wealth for the purpose of maintaining a household; my dear, my only covering is the skin of a lion."
O auspicious lady, the lord of serpents is my sacred thread; likewise, Padma and Piṅgala are my earrings.
Kambala is one of my armlets, and another serpent, Dhanañjaya, is the second. (Vāmana Purāṇa 1.25)
On the left side is Takṣaka, and likewise on the north;
Nīla also, with a complexion like blue collyrium, shines resplendently and firmly established upon the slope of the hips.
Pulastya said:
Having heard these harsh words from Śaṅkara—which, though true, were like a falsehood—Mṛḍānī was struck with fear.
Beholding her husband looking down at her, she spoke reproachfully out of distress; sighing with heat, she was overcome by both anger and shame.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, how indeed will this rainy season pass?
Standing at the foot of a tree, I speak thus out of great sorrow."
Śaṅkara said:
Having ascended a lofty fragment of a rain cloud, he stood together with the daughter of Dakṣa, his body firmly established upon it;
therefore, the name of that horse became renowned in heaven as Jīmūtaketu.
Thus ends the first chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Thereafter, the rainy season arrived for the three-eyed Lord atop the clouds.
O Sage, the delightful autumn season, which brings joy to the worlds, arrived.

The dark clouds abandon the expanse of the sky; herons leave the trees; rivers desert their banks; lotuses forsake their fragrance; crows abandon their nests; the ruru deer its antlers; and the reservoir its turbid water. (VamP 2.2)
The lotuses born from the mud bloom; the moonbeams shine upon the creepers laden with beautiful flowers;
the cowherd settlements rejoice in delight, and the virtuous follow the path of contentment.
In lakes there are lotuses, in the sky there are stars, and likewise there are waters in reservoirs;
for the minds of the virtuous and the splendors of the moon attain purity through the various quarters of the world.
And at such a time, Hara,
taking Satī who was dwelling upon the back of Maghavat, went to Mandara, the king of mountains.
Then, standing upon the back of Mandara on a level rocky surface,
the Lord Śambhu of great splendor took his delight together with Satī.
Then, when autumn had passed and Keśava had awakened,
Dakṣa, the best of the Prajāpatis, began to perform a sacrifice.
He summoned the twelve Ādityas, Śakra and the other foremost gods,
along with Kaśyapa, and appointed them as members of the sacrificial assembly.
He saw Vasiṣṭha, whose vows were praised, together with Arundhatī;
Atri together with Anasūyā; and Kauśika together with Dhṛti.
O Brahmin, [he saw] Gautama with Ahalyā, Bharadvāja with Amāyā,
and likewise the ṛṣi Aṅgiras together with Candrā.
Having addressed the members of the assembly in the sacrificial hall— learned men, endowed with virtue, and masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences— the skillful Dakṣa spoke.
And having summoned Dharma along with his wife Ahimsā,
he invited them and appointed them as gatekeepers of the sacrificial enclosure.
He appointed Ariṣṭanemi to the task of gathering fuel,
and Bhṛgu, who was perfectly skilled, to the performance of the mantra-rites.
Likewise, Prajāpati appointed the pure god Candra, together with Rohiṇī,
to the lordship over riches.
At the sacrifice, Prajāpati invited all his sons-in-law, daughters, and grandsons, with the exception of Sati and Śaṅkara.
Nārada said: For what reason was the Great Lord Maheśvara— the lord of the worlds, the master of wealth, the eldest, the most excellent, the most preeminent, and the primordial one— not invited?
Pulastya said: Although Lord Śiva is the eldest, the most excellent, the most preeminent, and the primordial one,
the Lord known as Kapālī was not invited by Dakṣa.
Nārada said: For what purpose did the Lord Śaṅkara—the best of the gods, the wielder of the trident, the three-eyed one, and the bearer of the skull—come into being through what action?
Listen with an attentive mind to this ancient narrative,
as it was told in the Ādipurāṇa by Brahmā, whose form is unmanifest.
In the past, however, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—was a single ocean;
the moon, sun, and stars had perished, and the wind and fire had vanished.
Inconceivable and unknowable, devoid of both existence and non-existence,
it was submerged by mountains and trees, become darkness, and extremely difficult to behold.
In that [egg], the Blessed One sleeps for a sleep lasting a thousand years;
at the end of the night, assuming a form characterized by passion (rājasa), he creates the worlds.
Rājasa was five-faced, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
the creator of this world of moving and unmoving beings, and of wondrous appearance.
In the same way, another being consisting of darkness arose, three-eyed,
with a trident in his hand and matted hair, displaying a rosary of beads.
Then the Great-Souled One indeed created a most terrible ego-principle (ahaṅkāra),
by which those two very gods, Brahmā and Śaṅkara, were both overcome.
Enveloped by egoism, Rudra replied to the Grandfather:
"Who are you that have arrived here? By whom were you created? Tell me."
Then the Grandfather, out of pride, replied: "Who are you?
Let it be told who your father is here, or who your mother."
Thus, O lover of strife, in the past there arose between those two, Brahmā and Īśa,
a mutual dispute, and from that your birth came to pass.
For you too, as soon as you were born, flew up into the sky,
holding an incomparable lute and making a "kilakila" sound.
Then Śambhu, having been utterly defeated by the proud lotus-born one,
stood dejected with his face cast down, like the moon eclipsed by Rāhu.
"I promise you this, O three-eyed one whose form is darkness:
clothed in the directions, mounted upon a bull, you are the destroyer of the worlds."
Having been addressed thus, the unborn Lord Śaṅkara, filled with rage, gazed incessantly at their face with his terrible eye, desiring to consume them.
Then, five beautiful faces of the Three-eyed One appeared:
white, red, golden-white, blue, and bright with tawny matted hair.
Having seen those faces which were like the sun, the face of Brahmā immediately spoke these words:
"When water is struck, bubbles arise; what power do they possess?"
Having heard that, the high-souled Śaṅkara, filled with wrath,
severed with the tip of his nail the head of the Brahmin who had spoken such harsh words.
Once severed, it fell upon the very palm of Śaṅkara’s left hand; that head never fell away from the hand of Śaṅkara.
Then, although overcome by anger, Brahmā performed a wondrous deed;
he created a wise man, equipped with armor, earrings, and arrows.
With bow in hand, the mighty-armed and imperishable one, bearing arrows and spears, possessed four arms and great quivers; his appearance was like that of the sun.
He said: "Go, O evil-minded one! Let me not strike you down with my trident;
for who would wish to kill one as sinful as you, already possessed of such wickedness?"
Having been addressed thus by that high-souled Puruṣa, Śaṅkara,
filled with shame, then went to Badarikāśrama.
Indeed, on the mountain that is the refuge of snow lies the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
where the holy Sarasvatī flows, the best of rivers.
Having gone there and seen him, he said to Nārāyaṇa:
"O Blessed One, give me alms; I am a great Kāpālika."
Thus addressed, the Son of Dharma spoke these words to Rudra:
"O Maheśvara, strike your left arm with your trident."
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, the three-eyed and impetuous one struck Nārāyaṇa’s left arm with his trident.
From the path struck by the trident, three streams issued forth;
one, having ascended into the sky, remained there adorned with stars.
The second fell to the ground;
the ascetic Atri caught it, and from that [seed] Durvāsas was born, a portion of Śaṅkara.
The third stream fell upon a skull of fierce appearance;
from it there arose a youth, a child clad in armor.
Dark-complexioned yet radiant, with bow and arrows in hand, roaring like a rain-cloud in the monsoon—
speaking thus, whose head shall I strike from his shoulders like a palm fruit?
Śakra approached him and spoke these words: "O Nara, strike down this man born from the arm of Nārāyaṇa—this son of Brahmā who possesses the radiance of a hundred suns—with wicked speech."
Thus addressed by Śaṅkara, that hero took up the famous primordial bow Ājagava,
as well as inexhaustible quivers, and set his mind upon battle.
Then those two of great strength, the son of Brahmā and the son of Śarva born from his arm, fought most fiercely for a thousand divine years; thereafter Hara approached Viriñci and spoke.
"O Grandfather, your powerful man has been defeated by Nara of divine and wondrous deeds;
having rushed forward, he struck him with great arrows, and that marvel has spread throughout the ten directions. (VamP 2.53)
Brahmā addressed these words to that Lord Śambhu: "There is no birth for this unconquered one here;
though he has been defeated, he shall remain yours, while that high-souled person belongs to me."
Thus addressed, the three-eyed god cast the person of Viriñci upon the Sun;
then that deity cast the person of Nara, who originates from Dharma, into the very body of Nara for the sake of the conflict.
Thus ends the second [chapter] of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then Rudra, with the terrible skull situated in the palm of his hand, spoke.
O Brahmin, his senses agitated by anxiety, he fell into a state of great distress.
Then the fierce and terrifying Brahmahatyā, possessing the luster of a mass of blue collyrium and having blood-stained hair, approached Hara.
Seeing her arrive, Hara questioned the fierce Vikarālinī: "Who are you that have come here, O terrible one? Tell me, for what purpose? (VamP 3.3)
Then the most terrible Brahman-slaughter spoke to the skull-bearer:
"I am the murder of a Brahmin; O Three-eyed One, accept me as I have come to you."
Having spoken these words, Brahman-slaughter entered Rudra,
who held a trident in his hand and whose body was intensely tormented.
Overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, Śarva went to the hermitage of Badarikāśrama,
but there he did not see the sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Not seeing the two sons of Dharma, he was overcome with anxiety and grief;
he went to the Yamunā to bathe, and its waters became dried up.
Seeing the Kālindī with its waters dried up,
Śiva went to the Plakṣajā river to bathe, and she vanished from sight.
Thereafter, having gone to the Puṣkara forest, the Māgadha forest,
and the Saindhava forest, he bathed there according to his desire.
Likewise, she bathed at Naimiṣa forest, Dharmāraṇya, and at Īśvara; yet that terrible Brahmahatyā was not released from her.
In rivers, at sacred fords, as well as in hermitages, holy places, and temples of the gods, Śarva—
though endowed with yoga and absorbed in meditation— did not grant liberation from sin to that one whose banner is the ocean.
Then, despondent, Śaṅkara went to Kurujāṅgala;
having gone there, he then beheld the wielder of the discus, whose banner bears the bird Garuda.
Having seen that lotus-eyed one bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace,
Hara joined his palms in reverence and uttered this hymn of praise.
Hara said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods; salutations to you, whose banner bears Garuḍa;
O Vāsudeva, wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace—salutations be unto you."
Salutations to you, O Nirguṇa, Ananta, the incomparable Creator; O supportless one who is the support of all, salutations be unto you, who are both knowledge and ignorance.
O Eternal One, embodiment of Brahman, salutations be unto you who are joined with *rajas*;
O Lord, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has been created by you.
O Lokeśa presiding over all beings, O Viṣṇu in form, O Adhokṣaja,
O protector of creatures, O mighty-armed Janārdana, homage be to you!
O embodiment of darkness, I am indeed this one born from a portion of your wrath;
O Lord of Gods, endowed with qualities, all-pervading one, salutations be to you! (VamP 3.18)
O Lord of the World, you are this vast earth, water, sky, and fire; you are wind, intellect, and mind, as well as the night; homage be to you!
Dharma, sacrifice, austerity, truth, non-violence, purity, straightforwardness, forgiveness, charity, compassion, prosperity, and celibacy—you are these, O Lord. (VamP 3.20)
You are the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs; you are the object of knowledge and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
You are the secondary Vedas, O Lord; you are everything—salutations be to you!
Homage, homage to you, O Acyuta, wielder of the discus; let there be homage to you, O Mādhava, in the form of the Fish!
You are considered compassionate in this world by me; protect me, O Keśava, from the bond of sin.
Destroy my impurity that resides within my body, which arose from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
I am scorched and ruined by my thoughtless deed. You are a sacred ford; purify me! Homage, homage to you! (VamP 3.23)
Pulastya said:
Thus praised by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
the Blessed Lord Cakradhara spoke these words for the destruction of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter.
Hrī said:
O Maheśvara, listen to these words of mine, uttered with a sweet voice;
they destroy the sin of killing a Brahmin, bestow auspiciousness, and increase merit.
He who was previously born from a portion of myself in the sacred Maṇḍala, that imperishable one,
dwells eternally at Prayāga, renowned as Yogaśāyin.
From his right foot issued forth the most excellent river, renowned as the Varaṇā;
she is auspicious and the remover of all sins.
The second one, from the left side, was renowned as the sword;
both of them became the best of rivers, honored by the world.
The region situated between those two is the field (*kṣetra*) of the one who lies in Yoga;
it is the foremost sacred ford (*tīrtha*) in the three worlds, which liberates one from all sins.
There is nothing like it in the sky, nor on the earth, nor in the subterranean realm (*rasātala*).
Therein lies the meritorious and auspicious city renowned as Vārāṇasī,
wherein even the lords of enjoyment, O Lord, attain dissolution into you.
Hearing the tinkling of the girdles of the playful women amidst the Vedic chants of the preeminent Brahmins,
the teachers repeatedly laughed and teased them for their pure-toned voices.
In that city, as women walked along the crossroads, the moon was struck with wonder upon seeing their footprints reddened by lac; he wondered, "Has this pond-lotus actually come to land?"
In that city, the lofty temples obstruct the moon during the delights of the night;
even by day, they likewise block the sun with their long banners fluttering in the wind.
And in that city, bees, enticed by the reflections upon walls of moonstone,
mistook the spotless lotus-faces of painted women for flowers and did not move on to any other blossoms.
Moreover, there was no exhaustion among men who were defeated by the game of enchantment,
nor was there any fatigue for women who were joined in the play of passion within the long chambers of their homes.
And no one, O Śambhu, forcibly blocks the palaces of others by means other than the eyes;
nor does anyone exert prowess with force against the weak in that city, for there is indeed delight in sexual union.
In that [time], pride and intoxication arise in men as youth approaches, just as the noose-knots of lordly elephants are severed and their rutting flow ceases when their intoxication has passed.
O Lord, in that [constellation] Kauśika, the owls alone always delight in faults and no other people;
likewise, in the host of stars there is a lack of noble birth, and in prose there is a lapse from metrical form.
In that city, O Śaṅkara, there are playful women supported by their lovers and surrounded by paramours, their bodies adorned with the moon, just like you.
O Lord of the Gods, in such a great hermitage as this Vārāṇasī, you,
the restless Sun who removes all sins, dwell.
O best of gods, go to that place which is called Daśāśvamedha, where Keśava, who is a portion of myself, resides; there you shall obtain liberation from sin.
Thus addressed by the one whose banner is Garuḍa, he whose banner is the bull bowed his head to him and departed with speed for Vārāṇasī, just as Garuḍa had done, for the sake of liberation from sin.
Having gone to the highly meritorious city of Sutīrtha and beheld the restless horse that had performed ten *aśvamedha* sacrifices,
and having bathed in its sacred fords to be freed from sin, he approached Keśava to see him.
Having seen Keśava, Śaṅkara prostrated himself and said this:
"O Hṛṣīkeśa, by your grace, the slaughter of a Brahmin has come to an end."
"O Lord of Gods, this skull does not leave my hand;
I do not know the reason for this, so you ought to tell it to me."
Pulastya said:
Having heard the words of Mahādeva, Keśava spoke these words:
"O Rudra, there is a cause for this; I shall tell you all of it."
"That divine lake before me, filled with lotuses and water-lilies,
is this most excellent and meritorious ford, worshipped by gods and gandharvas."
O Śambhu, perform your bath in this most excellent sacred ford;
as soon as you have bathed, even this very day, your skull will be liberated.
"Therefore, O Rudra, you shall become renowned in the world as Kapālī;
and this sacred bathing place (tīrtha) shall likewise be known as Kapālamocana."
Pulastya said:
O Sage, having been thus addressed by Keśava, the lord of the gods, Maheśvara bathed at Kapālamocana according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
After bathing at the sacred ford of Tripurāntaka, the skull fell from the palm of his hand;
by the grace of the Blessed One, that excellent ford thereafter became known by the name Kapālamocana.
Thus ends the third chapter in the glorious Vāma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
"O celestial sage, in this manner the blessed Lord Hara became Kapālī."
For this reason, he was not invited by Dakṣa.
Then, having learned that Satī was the daughter of Kapālin, Prajāpati [Brahmā] realized that although she was worthy of being invited to the sacrifice, she had not been invited by Dakṣa.
In the meantime, Jayā, the daughter of Gautama, went to Mount Mandara, the king of mountains with its beautiful caves, in order to see the Goddess.
Seeing her arrived there alone, he said to Jayā:
"For what reason have Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā not come? (VamP 4.4)
Having heard the words of the goddess, she said to the Supreme Goddess:
"They have all gone, invited to the sacrifice of their maternal grandfather."
"Having come together with my father Gautama and my mother Ahalyā,
I have arrived here, eager to go there to see you."
Why do you not go there, as the Lord Maheśvara has done?
Have you not been invited by your father, or will you go of your own accord?
All the ṛṣis, as well as the wives of the ṛṣis and the gods, departed;
and the Moon, together with his wife, went to the sacrifice along with his maternal aunts.
All beings, moving and unmoving, throughout the fourteen worlds have been invited to this sacrifice; why have you not been invited?
Pulastya said: O Brahmin,
having heard those words of Jayā, which were like the falling of a thunderbolt,
the virtuous woman was overwhelmed with grief and then met her death.
When Jayā saw Satī dead, overwhelmed by anger and grief,
she shed tears from her eyes and lamented aloud.
Hearing the sound of that wailing, the three-eyed wielder of the trident exclaimed, "Ah! What is this? and approached Jayā.
Having arrived, he beheld the queen fallen upon the ground like a creeper severed from a tree by an axe, her limbs relaxed and her virtue destroyed.
Seeing the goddess Jayā fallen, Śaṅkara asked her:
"Why has she fallen to the ground like a creeper that has been cut down?"
Having heard the words of Śaṅkara, Jayā spoke these words:
"Having heard that the sisters of Dakṣa, while engaged in the sacrifice, have been joined with their husbands... (VamP 4.15).
O Lord of the three worlds, together with the Ādityas and other gods such as Śakra,
this maternal aunt of yours has fallen into calamity and is being consumed by inner grief.
Pulastya said:
Having heard these terrible words, Rudra blazed forth, overwhelmed with anger;
from all his limbs, flames suddenly issued forth as he grew enraged.
Then, O Sage, from the anger of the Three-eyed One,
hosts with lion faces arose from the hair of his body, led by Vīrabhadra.
Surrounded by his hosts, he went from that Mount Mandara to the mountain called Himavat,
and from there to Kanakhala, where Dakṣa performed a sacrifice.
Then, O Sage, the mighty Vīrabhadra, the lord of the hosts and wielder of the trident,
stood in the northwestern direction.
O great sage, when Jayā, having seized her mace out of anger, stood in the southeast, Śarva, bearing his trident, stood in the center out of wrath.
Seeing the face of Maḍagāri, the gods led by Śakra, as well as the ṛṣis, yakṣas, and gandharvas, wondered, "What is this? (VamP 4.22).
Then, taking up his bow and arrows resembling venomous serpents,
Dharma, the gatekeeper, rushed toward Vīrabhadra.
Seeing Dharma suddenly rushing toward him, the Lord of the Gaṇas seized with one hand his trident, which blazed like fire.
With the second [hand] he took up a bow, with the third arrows,
and seizing a mace with the fourth, the host rushed toward Dharma.
Then, seeing the four-armed Lord of the Gaṇas, the imperishable Dharmarāja stood forth, having become eight-armed and bearing various weapons.
Armed with a sword, shield, mace, spear, battle-axe,
and excellent goad, as well as a bow and arrows, he stood there desiring to slay the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Ganeśvara, also filled with rage, rained down sharp arrows to destroy the eternal Dharma, just as a cloud pours rain during the monsoon.
O Sage, those two great-souled ones, bearing arrows and bows,
with their limbs drenched and reddened by blood, shone like two *kiṃśuka* trees in bloom.

Then, having been swiftly and forcibly defeated by the leader of the Gaṇas with his excellent weapons, that Dharma turned away dejected; O Lord of Munis, Vīrabhadra entered the sacrifice. [4.30] As Vīrabhadra, the lord of the Gaṇas, entered the sacrificial enclosure—
Upon seeing this, O Sage, the gods suddenly rose up, armed with their weapons.
The eight Vasus are highly fortunate; the nine planets are most terrible;
the twelve Ādityas, headed by Indra, and the eleven Rudras indeed exist.
The Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas;
the Yakṣas and Kimpuruṣas, as well as the birds and the inhabitants of the earth.
From the lineage of Vaivasvata came the renowned Dharmakīrti;
and from the Lunar dynasty (Soma-vaṃśa) arose the fierce Bhojakīrti, who possessed mighty arms.
The sons of Diti, the Dānavas, and others who had gathered there—
all of them, with weapons raised, rushed toward the fierce Vīrabhadra.
As they were rushing toward him, the Gaṇa, wielding his bow and arrows,
swiftly charged at them all with a multitude of shafts.
They unleashed an incomparable rain of weapons upon Gaṇeśa;
but Gaṇeśa, for his part, cut them down and shattered them with excellent missiles.
Constantly being struck by arrows and weapons by the high-souled Vīrabhadra, the gods and the others called for a retreat.
Then the leader of the Gaṇas entered the vast middle of the sacrifice,
where the seers were offering oblations and performing the ritual expansions.
Then, seeing that host with the faces of lions, the great seers were terrified; abandoning the sacrifice, they went for refuge to the Infallible One.
Seeing those great seers distressed and terrified in mind, the wielder of the discus said,
"Do not fear," and rose up with his excellent weapons.
Then, having drawn his Śārṅga bow, he released arrows resembling flames of fire—
arrows capable of rending the armor of the body— at Vīrabhadra.
Having struck his body, those arrows of Hari indeed became fruitless;
they fell to the earth with their hopes shattered, like beggars from atheists.
Seeing that his own unfailing arrows had become futile, Keśava prepared to shroud Vīrabhadra with divine weapons.
As those weapons were hurled by Vāsudeva, Gaṇanāyaka warded them off with his trident, mace, and arrows.
Seeing his weapons destroyed, Mādhava hurled a mace;
[the demon], having struck it with a trident, caused it to fall to the ground.
Halāyudha hurled a pestle at Vīrabhadra,
and Gaṇeśa likewise parried it with his mace.
Seeing the mace and the plow held back,
the one whose banner bears the sword (Kārttikeya) angrily hurled his discus at Vīrabhadra.
Seeing Sudarśana approaching, resembling a hundred suns,
the lord of the Gaṇas cast aside his trident and swallowed the discus, just as the Lord of the Gods in the form of a fish swallowed Madhu.
When his discus was swallowed by the leader of the Gaṇas, Murāri, his beautiful dark eyes flushed with extreme rage,
rushed forward, lifted the lord of the Gaṇas, and violently dashed him against the ground.
As he was crushed upon the ground by the force of Hari’s thighs,
the discus emerged from his mouth along with a gush of blood.
Then, seeing that the discus had emerged, Hṛṣīkeśa, the destroyer of Kaiṭabha, took it up and Vīrabhadra released it.
Released by Hṛṣīkeśa, Vīrabhadra went to Jaṭādhara and reported his defeat at the hands of Vāsudeva.
Then Jaṭādhara, seeing Gaṇeśa drenched in blood and hissing like a serpent, the imperishable one then gave way to wrath.
Then, overcome by anger, Śambhu stationed Vīrabhadra,
equipped with his weapons, in that place previously designated.
Then, having commanded Vīrabhadra and Bhadrakālī, Śaṅkara,
the wielder of the trident, entered the sacrificial enclosure with his eyes copper-red with rage.
Then, when the foremost of gods, the matted-haired wielder of the trident and destroyer of Tripura,
entered Dakṣa’s sacrifice to bring about its destruction, a supreme terror indeed arose among the sages.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having seen Hari wearing matted hair and with eyes bloodshot from anger, [the Lord spoke].
Departing from that place, he vanished and remained within a *kubja* mango tree.
O Sage, upon seeing Hara, the eight Vasus flowed forth with great force;
she became the most excellent of rivers, the Sarasvatī known by the name Sītā.
Likewise, the eleven Rudras, three-eyed and having the bull as their emblem,
approached Śaṅkara himself and, fleeing in all directions, met their destruction.
O great sage, the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, Anala, and Bhāskara, having approached the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), were its consumers.
The moon, together with the hosts of stars, having illuminated the night,
rose up and ascended the sky, established in its own domain.
O Sage, Kaśyapa and the other sages, reciting the Śatarudriya,
stood bowed down with their hands joined in handfuls of flowers.
Having seen Rudra superior in strength, Dakṣa’s consort repeatedly lamented piteously before Śakra and the other lords of the gods.
Then, by the high-souled Śaṅkara, who was overcome with anger,
many immortals were struck down with blows from his palms.
O Sage, some gods were destroyed by blows from his feet, others by his trident,
and likewise other deities and the like were brought to ruin by the fire of his gaze.
Then Pūṣan, seeing Hara slaughtering the gods and asuras,
stretched out his arms in anger and fled from Maheśvara.
Beholding him as he was rushing forward, the three-eyed Lord Śaṅkara received him with both arms and with one hand.
Indeed, even as Śambhu grasped the radiant sun with both hands,
streams of blood issued forth from his fingers on all sides.
Then, with great speed, he continuously whirled the sun-god Aṃśumat around, like a lion with a young deer.
Indeed, even the arms of Nārada Āṃśumān, who was whirled about with extreme velocity, became shortened as the bonds of their tendons snapped.
Beholding Maṃśumat with all his limbs drenched in blood, Maheśvara released him and departed for another place.
Then Pūṣan, laughing and baring his teeth,
said repeatedly to the Lord of the chariot, "Come here, come here, O Kāpālin!"
Then, overcome by anger, Śambhu struck Pūṣan with great force and,
hitting him with his fist, knocked out his teeth onto the surface of the earth.
With his teeth shattered and his face drenched in blood, Pūṣan fell unconscious upon the earth like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
From his two eyes, which were terrible in appearance, Bhaga beheld Pūṣan fallen and drenched in blood, even as he looked upon the bull-bannered god Śiva.
Then Tripuraghna, enraged, struck his eyes with his palm and cast them to the ground,
agitating all the gods.
Then all the sons of Diti, led by Prahlāda, placed Śatakratu at their head and fled in the ten directions out of fear, along with the Maruts and the Hutāśas (the gods of fire).
When the deities had departed, the sons of Diti, headed by Prahlāda, [remained].
Then, O Sage, having paid their respects, they all stood with palms joined in reverence.
Then Śaṅkara, with his terrible eye, beheld that sacrificial enclosure out of anger, intending to burn it along with all the gods and asuras.
Then the heroes hid themselves, others bowed down,
some fled, and others, seeing Hara, went out of fear to the abode of Vaivasvata.
The three fires gazed upon the unbearable Nairṛta with their three eyes;
as soon as they were seen by the Three-eyed One, they were reduced to ashes in an instant.
When the fire was extinguished, the sacrifice itself, having assumed a divine form as a deer,
fled through the sky with a distressed gait, accompanied by the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Bending his bow with great speed, the powerful Maheśvara, assuming the form of Time itself, took up that very Pāśupata arrow and pursued him.
With one half, he is known as Jaṭādhara at the edge of the sacrificial enclosure;
with the other half, Śarva is said to be in the sky in the form of Time (Kāla).
Nārada said:
You have described Śambhu, who moves through the sky, as being the very form of Time;
you ought to explain his characteristics and his true nature in their entirety.
Pulastya said: O best of sages, I shall describe the true form of the destroyer of Tripura, the consumer of time, by whom the sky was pervaded out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
Where Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and a portion of Kṛttikā are located,
that is the zodiac sign of Aries, the domain of Mars, which constitutes the head of the one whose form is Time.
O Brahmin, the three directions beginning with the southeast belong to Brahmā; the house of Kavi belongs to Prajāpati;
and this face, extending to the northern half, is proclaimed as that of Vṛṣan.
The three and a half degrees beginning from Ārdrā constitute this house of Mercury, Gemini;
it belongs to the trident-bearing Lord who resides in the sky upon his two arms.
The portion of Āditya is Puṣya, and Āśleṣā is the house of the Moon;

the zodiac sign is named Karkaṭaka, situated at the side of the Destroyer of Sacrifice (Rudra). The asterism of the Pitṛs (Maghā), the deity Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī), and the Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī) belong to Keśarin.
O Brahmin, the solar region is proclaimed to be the heart of the All-pervading Lord.
The three northern quarters, Pāṇi, and half of Citrā constitute this Kanyā;
it is the abode of the Son of Soma and the second stomach of the Lord.
Two portions of Citrā, three portions of Svāti, and the second three portions of Viśākhā— this second abode of Venus is declared to be the navel, Tula.
The portion of Viśākhā, Anurādhā, and Jyeṣṭhā, as well as this house of Mars—
the second sign, Scorpio— is the genitals of Kālasaravarūpin.
O sage among the immortals, it is proclaimed that the root, the eastern and northern portions, the abode of the gods, Aries, and Sagittarius constitute the two thighs of Īśa.
O Sage, the three constellations of Uttara, Śravaṇa, and half of Dhaniṣṭhā constitute the head of the Supreme Lord; Makara and Śatabhiṣā are his knees.
The half of Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, and three quarters of Pūrvabhādrapadā constitute the abode of Saturn;
this is the sign of Aquarius, and the two shanks are situated therein.
One part of Proṣṭhapadā, as well as Uttarā and Revatī, is the second abode of Jupiter; Pisces, however, constitutes both feet.

Having thus assumed the form of Time, the three-eyed Lord struck the King of the Path (Mārgarāja) with his sacrifice out of wrath. Pierced by it, he became conscious of the sensation of pain and remained suspended in the sky, his body covered with stars.
Nārada said:
"O Brahman, you have indeed described to me the twelve zodiac signs;
tell me specifically their characteristics according to their essential nature."
Pulastya said:
O Nārada, listen as I shall describe your own form regarding the zodiac signs—of what nature their movements are and in which places they dwell. *Vāmana Purāṇa* 5.45.
The ram has a form similar to that [of the sheep] among goats, sheep, cattle, and so forth;
its place of movement is indeed among grains, jewels, mines, and the like.
And he constantly roams everywhere upon the earth covered with fresh grass, as well as upon the flowering banks of lakes.
For the bull, possessing a similar form, wanders among the cow-pens and other such places;
its dwelling place, however, is the soil belonging to the cultivators.
The man and woman have equal appearance, share the same bed and seat, and hold a lute; such is the couple among singers, dancers, and artisans.
His pleasure-ground for sport is eternally established as the Vihārāvana;
there dwells the well-known pair named Mithuna, a zodiacal sign consisting of two parts.
Cancer is declared to be equal to the crab (Kulīra), residing in water,
as well as in fields, ponds, riverbanks, and secluded forest lands.
The lion, however, dwells in mountains, forests, difficult terrains, and mountain clefts;
it resides in hunters' villages, in deep ravines, and in caves. (VamP 5.52)
A maiden with ears of rice in her hand, mounted upon a goat,
wanders through the place of female delight and dwells among the reed-thickets.
And there, O Nārada, dwells a man named Tulāpāṇi, who inspects the market stalls along the streets and resides in the city's roadside rest-houses.
Moving through chasms and anthills, having the form of a scorpion, it dwells within poisonous excrement, insects, stones, and the like. (VamP 5.55)

Dhanuṣṭu has thighs like the trunk of an elephant; he is a radiant wielder of the bow, a hero skilled in weapons and brave on horseback, and one who stands firm upon elephants, chariots, and other vehicles.
O Brahmin, Makara has the face of a deer; his shoulders, eyes, and limbs are like those of a bull.
This Makara, who frequents the rivers, dwells in the great ocean.
An empty water-jar, a man carrying a burden, one drenched in water, a frequenter of gambling halls, and one who stays in the houses of tavern-keepers; VamP_5.58.
Then there are two fish joined together; one fish wanders through the oceans of sacred fords, while the other dwells in holy regions, in the abodes of gods and Brahmins.
O great sage, the characteristics of the signs beginning with Aries have been declared to you by me;
this ancient secret must not be told by you to anyone.

O celestial sage, I have thus related to you how the Three-eyed One, in ancient times, narrated this meritorious, primordial, supreme, purifying, sin-removing, and auspicious account of the destruction of the sacrifice.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
"O Sage, that Dharma who was born from the heart of Brahmā possesses a divine form."
Dākṣāyaṇī was his wife; upon her he begot sons.
O celestial sage, Hari and Kṛṣṇa likewise became Nārāyaṇa and Nara, who were constantly devoted to the practice of yoga.
And Nara and Nārāyaṇa, those two gentle and ancient best of sages, performed austerities out of a desire for the welfare of the world.
Having reached the Himalaya mountain at the sacred site of Badarikāśrama,
they both remained on the broad bank of the Gaṅgā, intent upon that Supreme Brahman.
O Brahmin, when this entire world of moving and non-moving beings was scorched by the ascetic power of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Śakra then fell into agitation.
Agitated by their asceticism, Śatakratu sent the most excellent Apsarases, beginning with Rambhā, to that great hermitage in order to cause a disturbance.
And Kandarpa, exceedingly difficult to withstand, with the sprouts of the mango tree as his great weapon,
went to the hermitage together with his companion, Vasanta.
Then Mādhava and Kandarpa, along with those excellent Apsarases,
arrived at Badarikāśrama and sported there according to their desire.
Then, when spring had arrived, the *śiṃśuka* trees, glowing with the brilliance of fire,
shone constantly with their leafless branches, beautifying the surface of the earth.
O Sage, having torn apart the elephant named Śiśira as if with its claws,
the lion of spring has arrived, adorned with palāśa flowers.
"I have conquered the mass of frost by my own splendor;
let Spring mock him indeed with its jasmine buds," [he said] loudly. (VamP 6.11)
The forests of flowering *karṇikāra* trees shone resplendently,
like the golden ornaments upon the sons of the lord of men.
Following them, the *nīpa* trees shone like reddish-brown attendants who had received their due honors from their master, or like servants before a prince.
The red Aśoka groves, suddenly ablaze with blossoms,
appear as if drenched in blood after the battle of King Spring.
Herds of deer, turned golden-brown, shine in the dense forest,
just as virtuous people, covered in horripilation, do upon the arrival of a friend.
On the banks of the river, the reeds shine with their flower-clusters, as if wishing to say with a finger: "What tree is equal to us? (VamP 6.16).
O divine sage, she is slender, with hands like red *aśoka* flowers, feet like *kiṃśuka* blossoms,
hair like blue *aśoka* flowers, dark-complexioned, and her face like a blooming lotus.
O Brahmin, she has eyes like blue lotuses, breasts like bilva fruits,
teeth like blossoming kunda flowers, and her hands are adorned with clusters of blossoms.
With lips like the bandhujīva flower, white with teeth like sinduvāra blossoms,
possessing the song of the male cuckoo, divine, and clad in auspicious aṅkola garments.
O Brahmin, she had a mass of peacock feathers for her hair-tuft, the cry of cranes for her anklets, the sacrificial hall for her tongue, and the gait of an intoxicated swan.
O Brahmin, the Goddess of Spring has arrived at Badarikāśrama, adorned with putrajīva flowers as her garments and graced by rows of hair-like bees.
Then Nārāyaṇa, having observed the faultlessness of the hermitage and having surveyed all the directions, beheld Anaṅga.
Nārada said:
"O Brahman-sage, who was that bodiless one (Anaṅga) in that Badarikāśrama whom the Lord of the World, the imperishable god Nārāyaṇa, beheld?"
Pulastya said:
He who is called Kandarpa, the son of Harṣa, known as Kāma,
was indeed consumed by Śaṅkara and thus attained the state of being bodiless (Anaṅga).
Nārada said:
For what purpose, and for what reason, was this Kāmadeva burnt by Śambhu, the God of gods? You ought to explain this to me.
Pulastya said: O Brahmin, when Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, had gone to the abode of Yama after destroying that sacrifice of Dakṣa, the Three-eyed Lord wandered about.
Then, seeing the bull-bannered god without a wife, Kandarpa, whose weapon is the flower, struck him with the missile Unmāda.
Then Hara, swiftly struck by the arrow Unmāda,
wandered about like one intoxicated through the forests and lakes.
O divine sage, remembering Satī, Mahādeva was likewise struck by madness; he found no peace, like an elephant pierced by an arrow.
Then, O sage, the Lord of Gods fell into the river Kālindī;
when Śaṅkara was submerged, the waters were consumed by fire and attained the state of being black.
From that time forth, the water of the Kālindī, resembling bumblebees or collyrium,
flowed down as that holy ford, as if it were her mass of hair falling upon the earth.
Then, in sacred rivers, in lakes and streams, on delightful sandbanks, and in ponds and lotus-pools; VamP_6.32 //
Wandering at his own will among delightful mountains, forests, and mountain peaks, Maheśvara did not find peace at all.
O divine sage, Śaṅkara sings for a moment, weeps for a moment,
and meditates for a moment upon the slender-limbed and enchanting daughter of Dakṣa.
Having meditated for a moment, Hara sleeps for a moment and then dreams;
seeing that daughter of Dakṣa in his dream, he speaks thus to her.
"Stay, you pitiless one! Why do you abandon me, O blameless fool?
O deluded woman, separated from you, I am consumed by the fire of passion. (VamP 6.36)
O virtuous one, you who are true, do not be angry;
O beautiful lady, you ought to speak to me who am bowed down, prostrating at your feet.
O beloved, you are constantly heard, seen, touched, and worshipped;
you are even perpetually embraced—why then do you not speak to me?
Seeing people lamenting, in whom would compassion not arise? Especially you, O young woman, who are so utterly merciless toward your husband!
"O slender-waisted one, these very words were spoken by you to me previously:
'I shall not live without you. That has been made false by you."
"Come, come, O fair-eyed one; embrace me, for I am tormented by desire. Otherwise, my fever shall not be quenched; I swear this to you in truth, my beloved."
Having lamented thus at the end of his dream, he was awakened at that very moment;
yet in the forest, he continued to cry out with a loud voice again and again.
Seeing Pāśa nearby crying out and lamenting,
the bull-bannered god [Śiva] swiftly bent his bow and pierced him again with an arrow named Saṃtāpana (the Tormentor).
Then, pierced by the Saṃtāpana weapon, he became even more intensely tormented;
scorching the entire world, he emitted hissing breaths again and again.
And Madana struck him yet again with the yawning-weapon (*vijṛmbhaṇāstra*), whereupon he yawned;
then, deeply pierced by the arrows of Kāma, he continued to yawn and wandered about in confusion.
He beheld the son of the lord of the Yakṣas, named Pāñcālika, the foremost in the world.
Having seen the son of the Giver of Wealth, the Three-eyed One approached his side and spoke these words:
"O nephew, speak whatever you intend to say today; perform it, for you are one of immeasurable prowess."
Pāñcālika said:

"O Lord, whatever you shall tell me, I will do it, even if it be most difficult for the hosts of gods to perform. Command me, O Śambhu of incomparable valor; I am your servant, endowed with devotion, O Lord."
Īśvara said:
"Since the boon-granting Ambikā has passed away, my body is scorched by the fire of desire.
Shattered by the arrows of longing, madness, and intoxication, I find neither fortitude, nor pleasure, nor happiness."
O son, likewise, yawning, fever, and fierce madness driven by passion—no other man is indeed capable of bearing these except for you; therefore, accept them.
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by the bull-bannered god, the Yakṣa accepted the power of yawning and the other [boons];
he quickly attained satisfaction, and then the wielder of the trident, being pleased, spoke these words.
Hara said:
"O son, because you have endured the yawning and other such acts which are so difficult to restrain,
I shall grant you a boon for your worship that shall bring laughter to the world."
When any man— whether old, young, or middle-aged, or even a woman— beholds you in the month of Caitra, or touches you, or worships you with devotion, they all then become possessed by madness.
They sing, they dance, they delight, and they play musical instruments with great effort before you; they become devoted to humorous speech in your presence, yet they remain truly engaged in yoga.
"By my very name you shall become renowned on earth as Pāñcālikeśa, worthy of worship;
through my grace, you shall be a granter of boons to men and most highly honored—go forth! VamP_6.54.
Thus addressed by the Lord, that Yakṣa went instantly to all lands—
the most meritorious region situated to the north of Kālañjara and to the south of the Himavat mountains.
Established in that most meritorious region, he was honored there by the grace of Rudra;
when he had departed, the Blessed Lord, the three-eyed god, also went to the Vindhya mountain.
Thereupon Madana went there and beheld the one who has the bull as his emblem;
and seeing him desirous of striking, Hara then spoke aloud.
Then Hara, impelled by passion, entered the formidable Dāruvana forest,
where the sages were dwelling together with their wives.
And all those sages, having seen him, bowed their heads;
then the Blessed One said to them, "Let alms be given to me."
Then all those great seers remained silent;
meanwhile, Nārada wandered through all their hermitages.
Seeing him having entered then, all the wives of Bhārgava and Ātreya,
being of weak character, became agitated on every side.
Except for Arundhatī alone and the lady Anasūyā,
whose minds were fixed upon the worship of their husbands and their concerns for them.
Then all [the women] became agitated and followed wherever Maheśvara went; afflicted by desire, their senses were overwhelmed by intoxication.
Leaving their own empty hermitages, the wives of the sages followed him like intoxicated female elephants following a rutting bull elephant.
Then, O sage, having seen this, all the seers of the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras lineages, filled with wrath, said: "Let his phallus fall to the earth! (VamP 6.65)
Then the Liṅga of the God fell, splitting the earth asunder;
thereafter, the trident-bearer Nīlalohita vanished from sight.
Then that fallen linga, having split the surface of the earth,
quickly entered Rasātala and pierced the cosmic egg from above.
Then the earth trembled, as did the mountains, rivers, and trees; all the subterranean realms, filled with both the mobile and the immobile, shook.
Seeing the worlds, beginning with the earth, thoroughly agitated, the Grandfather went to the ocean named Kṣīroda to see Mādhava.
Having seen Hṛṣīkeśa there and having prostrated with devotion, the gods of the worlds said: "O Lord, O All-pervading One, for what reason are you agitated?"
Then Hari said, "O Brahmin, the Śārva Liṅga was struck down by the great ṛṣis;
oppressed by its weight, the earth trembled."
Then, having heard that most wonderful thing, the god Brahmā, the Grandfather,
said again and again, "O Lord of Gods, let us go there."
Then the divine Grandfather and Keśava, the Lord of the World,
arrived at that place where the linga of Bhava was located.
Then, having seen that infinite linga and having mounted the lord of birds,
the omnipresent Hari entered the netherworld, filled with wonder.
Having ascended in every direction above by means of the Brahma-lotus celestial vehicle, O Brahmā, he found no end; filled with wonder, he returned once more.
Then Viṣṇu, the refuge of the seven worlds, having gone to the nether regions,
emerged with discus in hand, yet he did not find an end to them, O great sage.
Both Viṣṇu and Pitāmaha, having approached the Liṅga of Hara with their palms joined in reverence, began to praise the God.
Hari and Brahmā said:
"Homage be to you, O wielder of the trident; homage be to you, O whose banner is the bull!
O Jīmūtavāhana, O Sage, O Śarva, O Tryambaka, O Śaṅkara!"
O Maheśvara, O Maheśāna, O Suparṇākṣa, O Vṛṣākapi! O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, O you who have the form of Time, homage be to you! VamP_6.79.
You are the beginning of this world, you are the middle, O Supreme Lord;
you are the end as well, O Blessed One, you are all-pervading—homage be to you!
Pulastya said:
Thus being praised in that forest of wood, Hara,
the best among speakers, assumed his own form and spoke these words to them.
Hara said:
"O lords of the gods, for what reason do you both praise me here, when I am so utterly distressed, my body tormented by desire, and my conduct thus humiliated?"
The two gods said:
"O Śaṅkara, this *liṅga* which was cast down upon the earth by Bhakta—let it be taken up once again; then, O God, we shall offer praise."
Hara said:
"O best of gods, if the deities worship my linga, then I shall accept it; otherwise, by no means whatsoever."
Then the Blessed One Keśava said, "So be it," and he himself took up the golden-brown *liṅga* as the Brahman.

Then the Blessed One established the fourfold caste system for the worship of Hara, as well as their principal scriptures, which are known through various modes of expression. O Sage, the first is renowned as Śaiva, and the other is Pāśupata.
The third has a face like Time (Kāla), and the fourth holds a skull-cup (kapālin).
He himself was a devotee of Śiva and was known as the beloved disciple of Vasiṣṭha;
he then had a disciple known as Gopāyana.
There was a great Pāśupata ascetic named Bharadvāja, whose wealth was his austerity;
King Ṛṣabha, the lord of the Somakas, was also his disciple.
O sage, the venerable Āpastamba, whose wealth was his asceticism, lived in the Kāla age;
he had a Vaiśya disciple named Krātheśvara.
And Mahāvratī was the son of Dhanada, and his powerful disciple was known as Karṇodara; though a Śūdra by birth, he was a man of great asceticism.
Thus, having established the four stages of life for the worship of Śiva, the Blessed One returned to his own abode.
When the Brahmin had departed, Śarva then withdrew that subtle *liṅga* and, having established it in Citravana, he wandered about.
Then, as Maheśa was wandering further, the flower-armed god [Kāmadeva] approached him.
Standing at a distance in front, the archer was intent on causing torment.
Then, seeing him before him, Hara, his eyes inflamed with rage,
looked at Smara from the tip of his crest down to his feet.
O Brahmin, even the radiant Madana was consumed by the three-eyed one as he looked upon him, starting from his feet up to his armpits, just like a piece of wood.
Seeing his two feet being scorched,
that god whose weapon is the flower cast aside his excellent bow, and it then broke into five pieces.
When it was a fist-closed bundle, golden-backed and of great luster,
it became that *campaka* tree, rich in fragrance and endowed with excellent qualities.
O Sage, that place which was formerly devoid of handsomeness and adorned with vajras has become a forest of *kesara* trees known by the name Bakula.
That beautiful peak which had formerly been adorned with sapphires was born as the lovely Pāṭalā, adorned with rows of bees.
Above the fist, there was a place with the luster of a moonstone;
from it arose five clusters of jasmine flowers, radiant as the rays of the moon.
O Sage, with an upward-turned fist, the place below the two corners was adorned with coral;
from that, O Sage, various jasmine flowers were produced within the hollows of the earth.
O Nārada, the most excellent, delightful, and fragrant flowers, endowed with the *jāti* fragrance,
were personally offered by the God himself.
Smara discharged arrows upon the earth as his body burned;
thousands of trees laden with fruit appeared all at once.
Various fragrant and delicious fruits, such as mangoes and others,
which were fit even for the best of gods to eat, were produced through the grace of Hara.
Having thus consumed Smara and restrained his own body, the omnipresent and imperishable Rudra went to the Snowy Mountain for the sake of performing penance.
Thus, in ancient times, Kāma was burnt along with his arrow and his bow by Śambhu, the best of gods;
thereafter, that great archer was celebrated by the gods as Anaṅga (the Bodiless), having been worshipped by the foremost of the deities.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then, O Brahmin, the lordly sage Nārāyaṇa, having seen Anaṅga...
Laughing, Kandarpa spoke these words: "Please be seated here."
Seeing his imperturbability, Kāma was filled with wonder;
even Vasanta, O great sage, quickly fell into deep reflection. (VamP 7.2)
Then, having seen the Apsarases and honored them with a welcome, the Blessed One said to Vasanta: "Come, come; please stay."
Then, smiling, the Blessed One took a flower-cluster covered in blossoms that was golden-hued at its base and fashioned from it a young girl upon his thighs.
Seeing her, who was born from his thigh and beautiful in every limb, Kandarpa then thought: "Is she perhaps that beloved Rati, though now bodiless?"
That very same lovely face, with its beautiful eyes, curved eyebrows, and locks of hair,
with its fine nose, bridge, and lower lip, was now intent upon gazing [at him].
Her two breasts, brought forth, sparse, full,
with sunken nipples, shine like two noble men— plump and closely joined.
That very same slender belly of the fair-limbed woman, adorned with three folds,
shines forth— smooth and graced by a line of hair.
And this line of body hair, proceeding from the hips to the slope of the breasts,
shines like a swarm of bees moving from a sandbank to a bed of lotuses.
Her hips, exceedingly broad and encircled by a girdle,
shine like Mount Mandara bound by the serpent during the churning of the ocean for the sake of Lakṣmī.
With thighs resembling plantain trunks, rooted upwards,
that woman of beautiful limbs shines forth, possessing a complexion like the filaments of a lotus.
Her knees have hidden ankles, her shanks are beautiful and hairless;
likewise, her feet shine forth with a luster like that of red lac.
Reflecting thus, O Sage, that Kāma became overwhelmed by passion for her of faultless eyes; how much more so, then, would any other person?
O Nārada, upon seeing Urvaśī, Mādhava also reflected:
"Could this be the capital city of King Kāma standing here in person?"
Surely this is the splendor of the moon that has arrived at the end of the night;
terrified by the heat and oppression of the sun's rays, it has come here for refuge.
While reflecting in this manner, Mādhava stood still, having restrained the host of Apsarases, as if a sage established in meditation.
Then, O great sage, having seen all of them— Kandarpa and the others— struck with wonder, he of auspicious vows smiled and spoke these words.
"O Mādhava, let this celestial nymph of desire, produced from my thigh,
be taken to the world of the gods and given to Vāsava."
Thus addressed, they departed for heaven trembling, taking Urvaśī with them;
he gave her, endowed with beauty and youth, to the Thousand-eyed One.
O Great Sage, when the two sons born of Dharma recounted their conduct to the king of the gods, he was filled with supreme wonder at their desires and other traits.
For such a life indeed attained the highest renown;
it spread throughout the netherworlds, among mortals, and across the eight directions.
O Sage, once the fierce Hiraṇyakaśipu had been slain,
a Dānava named Prahlāda was then consecrated in that kingdom.
While that lord of the Daityas, who honored gods and Brahmins,
was ruling, kings on earth then performed sacrifices according to the prescribed rites.
The Brāhmaṇas practice austerity and dharma and undertake pilgrimages;
the Vaiśyas are established in the livelihood of cattle-keeping; and the Śūdras are devoted to service.
Then the four castes returned to their respective duties and religious practices within their own stages of life; consequently, O Sage, the gods became endowed with their proper livelihoods.
Then Cyavana, the lord of the Bhṛgus, a man of great asceticism,
went to the Narmadā river to bathe, as well as to the holy site of Akulīśvara.
Having seen Mahādeva there, he descended into the river to bathe;
once he had descended, a serpent named Kekaralohita seized him.
Seized by that serpent, he remembered Hari in his mind;
once the lotus-eyed Lord was remembered, the great serpent became free from poison.
He was carried down to the subterranean realm by that exceedingly fierce serpent;
yet, having been rendered free from poison, that best of serpents released Cyavana.
As soon as he was released by the Naga, Cyavana, the best of the Bhṛgus,
moved about while being honored on all sides by the Naga maidens.
Then, while reflecting, he entered the great city of the Dānavas;
there, being honored by the lords of the Daityas, Prahlāda beheld him.
The one of great splendor paid due honor to the son of Bhṛgu;
once he had been honored and was seated, he was questioned regarding the purpose of his arrival.
And he said, "O Great King, I have come today to bathe in this great sacred ford of great fruit, and to behold Ākulīśvara."
I descended into the river itself and was forcibly seized by a serpent;
I was brought to the netherworld (pātāla), and there you were seen by me as well.
Having heard these words of Cyavana, the lord of the Daityas,
who was skilled in speech, spoke this righteous reply.
Prahlāda said:
"O Blessed One, what sacred fords (tīrthas) are there on the earth, which ones are in the sky, and which ones might be in the netherworld (rasātala)? You ought to tell me this."
Cyavana said:
"O mighty-armed one, they know Naimiṣa to be the sacred ford on earth, Puṣkara in the intermediate space,
and Cakratīrtha in the depths of the netherworld."
Pulastya said:
O great sage, having heard those words of Bhārgava, the king of the Daityas,
desiring to go to Naimiṣa, spoke thus to the Dānavas.
Prahlāda said: "Arise! We shall go to bathe at the Naimiṣa holy ford;
there we shall behold the lotus-eyed, yellow-robed, and infallible Lord."
Pulastya said:
Having been thus addressed by the lord of the Dānavas, all those Daityas and Dānavas made incomparable preparations and emerged from the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Having approached together, those mighty Daityas and Dānavas arrived at the Naimiṣa forest and, filled with joy, performed their ritual ablutions.
Then the glorious lord of the Daityas went out on a hunt;
while hunting, he beheld the sacred Sarasvatī with its pure waters.
Not far from there, he saw a large-branching śāla tree covered with arrows;
other arrows were seen stuck together, their tips interlocked.
Then, seeing those arrows of wondrous form with serpent-bands as their slings, the lord of the Daityas indeed gave way to incomparable wrath.
Then, not far away, he saw two sages wearing black antelope skins,
bearing heavy masses of matted hair, their minds intent upon ascetic practice.
And on his two sides were two divine bows endowed with auspicious marks—
the Śārṅga and the Āgava— as well as two inexhaustible great quivers.
Seeing them, the Dānava then thought, "These are two Dāmabikās," and then he spoke these words to those two supreme men: *Vāmana Purāṇa* 7.47.
Why have you both undertaken this hypocrisy that destroys righteousness?
Where is your asceticism, where is your mass of matted hair, and where are these two excellent weapons?
Then Nara said to the Daitya: "O Lord of the Ditis, what is your anxiety?
For whatever one who possesses the necessary capability should do, that indeed shall be accomplished for him."
Then the Lord of the Daityas said to them both: "What power do you two have here while I, the lord of the Daityas and the establisher of the bridge of dharma, remain?"
Then Nara replied to him: "The power of the two of us is formidable;
no one would be able to fight Nara and Nārāyaṇa in battle."
The lord of the Daityas, dejected and enraged, made this vow:
"By whatever means possible, I shall conquer Nara and Nārāyaṇa in battle."
Having spoken these words, the high-souled lord of the Daityas stationed his army at the edge of the forest,
drew back the string of his drawn bow, and let out a most terrible sound by slapping his palms.
Then the man, having bent his bow Ājagava, released many sharp-pointed arrows;
the Daitya, however, cut them down with peerless shafts that had golden feathers.
Then, seeing his arrows severed in battle by the lord of the Daityas as if by one who was peerless, the man became enraged; bending his great bow, he released various other arrows.
A man discharged one arrow, the lord of the Daityas two, the son of Dharma three, and the lord of the Daityas four;
but Nara released five arrows, while the protector of the Dravidas loosed six sharpened shafts.

O Brahmin, seven arrows were released by the leader of the Daityas at the chief of the Seven Sages; two and four at Nara; six and three at the leader of the Daityas; and six, three, and one at Nārāyaṇa by the lord of the Ditis.
One, six, and five arrows were released by the man; eight and seven by the Dānava;
six, seven, eight, nine, and six by the man; and the lord of the Daityas discharged seventy-two.
The Daitya released one hundred arrows, Dharmaputra three hundred, and the king of the Daityas six;
yet those two discharged even more than that—countless arrows indeed—out of intense fury.
Then the man covered the earth, the quarters, and the sky with countless multitudes of arrows;
yet that foremost of Daityas also swiftly cut them down with shafts featuring golden feathers.
Then, with winged arrows and excellent weapons of terrible form, the two heroes— the man and the dānava— fought each other most fiercely in battle.
Then, as the Grandfather’s weapon was fixed upon the bow by the Daitya who held a supreme missile in his hand,
the Maheśvara weapon and Puruṣottama himself struck each other equally and both fell down.
When the Brahmāstra had been neutralized, Prahlāda, overcome with rage,
seized a mace and swiftly leaped down from his excellent chariot.
Then, seeing the Daitya approaching with mace in hand, Nārāyaṇa placed Nara at his back, intending to fight him himself.

Then Diti’s son, bearing a mace, rushed toward Nārāyaṇa, the lord of light, the storehouse of asceticism, the world-protector, the ancient ṛṣi of renowned and noble prowess, who held the Śārṅga bow in his hand; O Nārada!
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having seen the wielder of the Śārṅga bow approaching before him, the lord of the Dānavas—
Having whirled his mace with great force, he struck Sādhyamata on the head.
Then, O Nārada, when the son of Dharma was struck with the mace,
water fell from his two eyes onto the earth like a shower of fire.
O Brahmin, that mace hurled by the Dānava at the head of Nārāyaṇa shattered into a hundred pieces, like a thunderbolt upon a mountain peak.
Then, turning back, the lord of the Daityas quickly mounted his chariot;
taking up his bow, the hero drew an arrow from his quiver.
Then, his face darkened with rage, he bent his bow with force and released feathered arrows sharpened on stone, aiming them at Sādhyā.
As those arrows, resembling the crescent moon, were still approaching,
he swiftly cut them down with other shafts and pierced the Dānava.
Then the Daitya pierced Nārāyaṇa, and Nārāyaṇa pierced the Daitya,
each striking the other with straight-flying arrows that pierced the vital organs.
Then, O Sage, a gathering of gods occurred in the sky,
desiring to witness that battle, which was swift, wonderful, and well-fought.
Then, the drums of the gods resounded with a great roar,
and the Sādhyas and Daityas released an incomparable rain of flowers from the sky.
Then, while the gods stationed in the sky looked on, those two great archers fought, increasing the delight of the spectators.
Then both of them bound the sky with showers of arrows;
they covered the cardinal and intermediate directions with masses of shafts.
Then, O great sage, Nārāyaṇa drew his bow and pierced Prahlāda in all his vital organs with sharp arrows.
Likewise, the lord of the Daityas, enraged and impetuous,
bent his bow and pierced the best of men in the heart, the arms, and the face.
Then, with a single arrow having the luster of a crescent moon, he severed the bow from the fist-grip of that lord of the Daityas.
Casting aside his broken bow and taking up another,
he quickly strung it and rained down sharpened arrows.
Sādhyas, having cut down even those arrows of his with his own shafts, warded him off;
and Puruṣottama severed his bow with a razor-headed arrow.
O Sage, as each bow was cut by the Daitya, he took up another and yet another; but Sādhya, with great agility, cut down each one as it was taken up.
Then, when his bows were severed, the lord of the sons of Diti seized a formidable,
long, and solid iron club made entirely of metal.
Then, seizing a club, the Dānava whirled it around;
as it was being whirled, the great sage cut it apart with a steel arrow.
When the iron club was shattered, the glorious Prahlāda, lord of the Dānavas,
whirled a mallet with great force and hurled it at the elder brother of Nara.
O Sage, as it was falling toward him, the powerful Sādhya cut it into ten pieces with ten arrows; thus severed, it fell to the earth. (VamP 8.21)
When his mace had become useless, the impetuous one brandished a spear and hurled it at the foremost of men; but the son of Dharma cut that down as well.
When the spear was cut, the Daitya then took up a javelin and hurled it;
but the powerful one of great asceticism cut that too with a razor-edged arrow.
When those weapons were cut asunder, O Nārada, the Dānava took up another great bow and then covered [the enemy] with arrows.
Then the divine Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world and scorcher of his enemies,
struck the lord of the Daityas in the heart with an iron arrow.
O Brahmin, with his heart pierced by the god of wondrous deeds, he fell onto the seat of the chariot; the charioteer carried him away.
Having regained consciousness after a very long time,
that lord of the Daityas took up his very firm bow and once more advanced to do battle.
Seeing him arrived, the foremost of men replied:
"Go, O Lord of Daityas; we shall fight tomorrow morning; perform your daily rites."
Thus addressed by Sādhya of wondrous deeds,
the Lord of the Diti-dynasty went to the Naimiṣa forest and performed his daily rites.
While the god was thus fighting, O sage, the asura Prahlāda reflected during the night on the battle: "How shall I conquer this hypocrite?"
In this manner, O Nārada, that Daitya fought with Nārāyaṇa for a thousand divine years, yet he did not conquer the god.
Then, at the end of a thousand years, O Ajita, the Dānava approached Puruṣottama, who was dressed in yellow garments, and spoke these words.
"For what reason, O Lord of the gods, am I unable today to conquer Nārāyaṇa Hari, who is to be subdued? Tell me this cause."
The one clad in yellow garments said:
"O Prahlāda, this mighty-armed son of Dharma is difficult for you to conquer;
that wise and excellent Brahmin cannot be overcome in battle even by the gods and asuras."
Prahlāda said:
"O Lord, if he is invincible and must be overcome by me on the field of battle,
then how will that which was promised not become false?"
"O Lord of Gods, how could one like me live with such a degraded vow?
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, in your presence I shall perform the purification of my body."
Pulastya said:
Having spoken these words in the presence of the gods, the lord of the Dānavas,
having bathed his head, then stood there reciting the eternal Brahman.
Then Viṣṇu, clad in yellow garments, spoke these words to the lord of the Daityas:
"Go; you shall conquer him through devotion, by no means whatsoever through battle."
Prahlāda said:
"O God of gods, O observer of noble vows, even the three worlds have been conquered by me;
by your grace, this Śakra has been defeated, how much more so the son of Dharma?"
O Unborn One, O God of excellent vows, if even the three worlds together cannot conquer him, it is only by your grace that he can remain; what then shall I do? (VamP 8.40)
The one clad in yellow garments said:
"O tiger among Dānavas, desiring the welfare of the worlds, I have established myself in the practice of austerity in order to set the Dharma in motion."
Therefore, O Dānava, if you desire victory, propitiate him; through devotion you shall defeat him. Therefore, serve the son of Dharma.
Pulastya said:
Thus addressed by the high-souled one clad in yellow garments, the lord of the Dānavas,
being delighted, summoned Andhaka and spoke these words, O Sage.
"O Andhaka, the Daityas and Dānavas are indeed to be protected by you;
O mighty-armed one, accept this kingdom bestowed by me."
Having been addressed in this manner, Hairaṇyalocani took possession of the kingdom;
Prahlāda, for his part, then went to the holy hermitage of Badarī.
Having beheld the god Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the lord of the sons of Diti,
with palms joined in reverence, paid homage at their feet.
The imperishable Nārāyaṇa, possessed of great splendor, spoke these words to him:
"O great Asura, for what reason have you prostrated yourself here before me without having conquered me?"
Prahlāda said:
O Lord, who is capable of conquering you? What man is superior to you?
For you are indeed Nārāyaṇa, the infinite Janārdana, clad in yellow garments.
You are the lotus-eyed God; you are Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
you are the imperishable Maheśāna, the eternal Supreme Person.
Yogis contemplate you; the wise worship you;
those who have completed their studies recite your name; and the performers of sacrifice offer oblations to you.
You are Acyuta, Hṛṣīkeśa, the discus-wielder, and the upholder of the earth;
you alone are the Great Fish, the Horse-headed One, and the excellent Tortoise.
The glorious Lord, the enemy of Hiraṇyākṣa, became a boar;
and you, O Man-lion, have likewise been the one who brought about the destruction of my father.

O Lord, O Master whose banner is the king of birds, you are Brahmā, the three-eyed Śiva, the king of the immortals, the consumer of oblations, the lord of the departed, the lord of waters, the wind, the sun, the moon, and all that is stationary and moving, O All-pervading One.
Having become earth, light, space, and water in thousands of forms, you pervade the entire universe; who, O Mādhava, shall conquer you?
O Hṛṣīkeśa, Teacher of the World, if you attain satisfaction through devotion,
there is no other way for you to be conquered, O omnipresent and imperishable one.
The Blessed One said:
"I am well-pleased with you, O Daitya of noble vows, by this hymn of praise;
for by your singular devotion, O Daitya, I have been conquered by you."
O Daitya, a defeated man pays a fine;
I shall grant you a fine for this purpose—choose whatever boon you desire.
Prahlāda said:
O Nārāyaṇa, I ask for a boon which you ought to grant to me:
may my sin, both physical and mental, come to an end.
O Lord of the World, grant me this boon: that even though I fought with you, there was no verbal exchange between us. VamP_8.59.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"So be it, O lord of the Daityas; may your sin go to its destruction.
Ask for a second boon, O Asura, and I shall grant it to you."
Prahlāda said:
Whatever intellect may arise within me, O Viṣṇu, let it be dependent upon you;
let it be devoted to the worship of the gods, intent on you, and having you as its ultimate goal.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"It shall be so, O Asura; choose another boon that you desire.
O mighty-armed one, I shall grant it to you without hesitation."
Prahlāda said:
"O Adhokṣaja, by your grace I have obtained everything indeed;
may I always possess renown through your two lotus feet."
"Let it be so; furthermore, by my grace you shall always be inexhaustible, undecaying, ageless, and even immortal."
Go, O tiger among Daityas, to your own abode, devoted to your duties;
there shall be no bondage of karma for you, as my mind [is with you].
Command those Daityas and protect the kingdom eternally;
O Daitya, practice the unsurpassed dharma that is worthy of your own kind.
Pulastya said:
Thus addressed by the Lord of the World, Prahlāda spoke to the God:
"O Teacher of the World, how shall I take back the kingdom that has been renounced?"
The Lord of the World said to him: "Go to your own abode;
likewise, become a teacher of what is beneficial for the Daityas and the Dānavas."
Thus addressed by Nārāyaṇa, that leader of the Daityas then bowed down to the Lord and, being satisfied, departed for his own city.
Having been seen and honored by the Dānavas and by Andhaka,
Nārada was invited to rule the kingdom, but he did not accept it.

Having renounced his kingdom and establishing the lords of the Dānavas on the path of truth, the great lord of the Asuras remained there with his body purified by yoga, meditating upon and remembering the immeasurable Keśava.
Thus, O Nārada, in former times the lord of the Dānavas, having been defeated by Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person,
relinquished his kingdom and remained with his mind fixed upon the Creator.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O Sage, how was the blind Andhaka established in the kingdom by Prahlāda?
Though he was well-acquainted with the eternal law of kings, he was consecrated [as king].
Pulastya said:
Having regained his sight while Hiraṇyākṣa was still alive,
he was consecrated by the Daitya Prahlāda in his own position.
Nārada said:
O you of noble vows, once Andhaka was consecrated in the kingdom, what did he do?
How did he dwell together with the gods and others? Tell that to me.
Pulastya said:
Andhaka, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, was consecrated as the lord of the Daityas;
having propitiated the three-eyed Lord of Gods, the wielder of the trident, through ascetic penance.
He shall possess invincibility and immunity from being slain by gods, siddhas, ṛṣis, and pannagas;
he shall be unburnable by fire and undissoluble by water.
Thus, having obtained that boon, the Daitya Andhaka protected his kingdom; having appointed Śukra as his domestic priest, he then dwelt there in peace.
Then the Asura Andhaka made an effort against the gods;
having overrun the entire earth, he defeated the lords of men.
Having defeated the rulers of the earth and enlisting them as his allies,
he went with them to the summit of Mount Meru, which was a wondrous sight to behold.
Śakra, too, having mobilized the divine armies and mounted his great elephant,
departed from Amarāvatī after ensuring its defenses were secure.
Following Śakra, the other world-protectors of great majesty likewise mounted their respective mounts and went forth, equipped with their weapons.
And the divine army, together with Śakra of wondrous deeds, also set forth with great speed on elephants, horses, chariots, and other mounts.
In front were the twelve Ādityas, and behind were the three-eyed [Rudras];
in the middle were the eight Vasus, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Aśvins and Maruts; and the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and others, each mounted upon their own respective vehicle.
Nārada said: O Dharmaja, tell me here in full about the vehicles of Rudra and the others; I have a great curiosity regarding each one of them.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O Nārada; I shall describe to you in brief the vehicles of all [the gods], one by one in their proper order.
Born from the hand of Rudra, possessing great heroism and great speed,
the white-colored lord of elephants is the vehicle of the King of the Gods.
O Nārada, the buffalo named Pauṇḍraka, born from the thigh of Rudra, was terrifying, black in color, and as swift as thought; he was the mount of Dharmarāja.
Born from the impurity of Rudra’s karma, dark-hued and known as the ocean,
the porpoise of divine gait is the vehicle of Varuṇa.
Raudra, whose eyes are like the wheels of a cart, who has the form of a mountain, the best of men,
born from the foot of Ambikā, is the vehicle of Dhanada.
