O great sage, the vehicles of the eleven Rudras are Gandharvas of great prowess and fierce serpent-lords; they also possess white cattle, bulls of formidable speed. (Vāyu Purāṇa 9.19)
O best of sages, the chariot of the Moon has a thousand white horses as its vehicle,
and the chariots of the Ādityas are drawn by bay horses.
The Vasus were mounted on elephants, the Yakṣas had men as their vehicles,
the Kinnaras were mounted on serpents, and likewise the two Aśvins were mounted on horses.
O Brahmin, the Maruts of fearsome appearance were mounted upon deer;
the wise ones were well-mounted on horses, and the Gandharvas were on foot.
Having thus mounted their respective vehicles and donned their armor, those best of immortals, endowed with great majesty, set forth joyfully for battle.
Nārada said: "O Sage, you have described the vehicles of the gods and others;
you should likewise describe the vehicles of the Daityas exactly as they are."
Pulastya said:
Listen, O best of the twice-born, to the mounts of the Dānavas and others;
I shall describe them to you according to their true nature, as you ought to hear them.
Andhaka’s divine chariot was yoked with supreme horses of black hue; it possessed a thousand spokes and measured a hundred yojanas in circumference.
Prahlāda’s divine chariot, beautiful and made of white gold, was drawn by eight excellent horses with the hue of the moon.
Virocana’s vehicle was an elephant; Kujambha’s was a horse;
and Jambha’s was a chariot yoked with two horses resembling gold.
Śaṅkukarṇa’s mount was a horse, Hayagrīva’s an elephant,
Mayas’ a celebrated chariot, Dundubhi’s a great serpent, Śambara’s a celestial chariot, and Śaṅkhu’s a lion.
And Bala and Vṛtra, both powerful and wielding maces and clubs,
were prepared to charge at the divine armies with their feet.
Then there arose a tumultuous, chaotic, and most terrifying battle;
O Nārada, the world was enveloped in a tawny-colored dust.
O observer of noble vows, the father did not recognize his son, nor did the son likewise recognize his father; they slew their own kin, while others indeed slew those who were strangers.
Then, with great speed, one chariot-rider rushed upon another chariot-rider;
likewise, one elephant-rider charged at another elephant-rider who was mounted on a rutting lord of elephants.
Then even foot-soldiers, enraged, struck down fierce foot-soldiers; desiring victory over one another, they assailed each other.
Then, O sage, in that tumultuous battle between the gods and the asuras,
a terrible river began to flow, pacifying the dust of the battlefield.
With blood for its waters, chariots for its whirlpools, and the clashing of warriors for its current;
with the frontal globes of elephants for its turtles and arrows for its fish, that river was difficult to cross.
Carrying sharp-pointed spears as its makaras and great crocodiles,
with entrails strewn like water-moss and garlands of foam consisting of banners, [the river of battle flows].
Adorned with vultures, herons, great swans, hawks, and cakravāka birds,
it was filled with forest crows, kādamba geese, jackals, and beasts of prey.
Crowded with *piśāca* demons and sages, and difficult for ordinary people to cross,
the heroes plunged into it, crossing over by means of chariots as their rafts.
Plunging up to their ankles and submerging one another,
the warriors, desiring victory and wealth, surged forward with speed as they leapt out from the water.
Then, in that fierce and great battle which struck terror into the hearts of cowards and brought about the destruction of gods and demons,
the *rakṣasas*, *yakṣas*, and throngs of *piśācas* were exceedingly delighted and rejoiced.
Drinking the blood of the warriors more greedily, embracing their flesh and devouring it, they tear away the fat and spring about; then the birds roar at one another. (VamP 9.42)
Jackals let out shrieks, and warriors, afflicted by agony on the ground, cried out;
others, scorched by weapons, fell down, and the battle became like a cremation ground.
When that terrible and fierce clamor, which struck great fear into both gods and demons,
had set in, a battle broke out in which lives were staked as the wager— a duel like a game of dice played with lethal weapons and eyes.
The golden-eyed son Andhaka, standing in a chariot yoked with a thousand horses in the midst of battle,
encountered the Lord of the Gods, Śatakratu, who was mounted upon the back of a rutting elephant and possessed of fierce splendor.
As Yama, mounted upon a buffalo, was charging forward, the powerful Lord of the Daityas,
named Prahlāda, having ascended a chariot yoked to eight horses and having raised his weapons, received him.
Virocana also went against the Lord of Waters, while Jambha then approached the powerful Dhanada;
Śambara, having approached Vāyu, and Maya, O Lord of Sages, fought with Hutāśa.
Others, horse-faced and of great strength, sons of Diti and the foremost of the Danus,
endowed with immense power, encountered the gods— the sacrificial fire, the sun, the Vasus, and the lord of the waters— in single combat.
Then, approaching one another in battle, they roared and drew their bows with great speed;
discharging thousands of iron arrows, they cried out, "Come! Stay! Why do you speak thus?"
Scorching them with sharp arrows and striking them with unerring weapons,
they set flowing a terrifying river resembling the current of the Mandākinī.

O Nārada, in that battle, a river of blood appeared, which those gods and asuras of fierce speed— desiring the three worlds and wishing to cross over the one who nourishes and increases the hosts of piśācas and rākṣasas— were seeking to ford.
The musical instruments of the gods and asuras resound, and the hosts of sages and siddhas stationed in the sky look on;
the foremost groups of apsarases lead away those heroes who were slain in battle while facing their foes.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then, when the battle had commenced—which increased the fear of the timid—
The thousand-eyed one, taking up his great bow, discharged arrows.
Andhaka also, having drawn his great-speed, radiant bow,
discharged arrows feathered with peacock plumes at Purandara.
Both of them struck each other with arrows that had very sharp points, smooth joints,
golden feathers, and great velocity.
Then the enraged Śatamakha, brandishing his thunderbolt with his hand, hurled it at the king of the Daityas; Andhaka beheld it as it was being cast.
And Nārada struck them with floods of arrows and divine weapons;
he then reduced them to ashes, just as fire consumes mountains.
Then, seeing the extremely swift Vajra, the best among the powerful leaped down from his chariot and stood upon the ground, aided only by his arms.
Having reduced the chariot, along with its charioteer, horses, banner,
and pole, to ashes, the thunderbolt then approached Andhaka.
Striking him with his fist as he rushed forward with speed,
the powerful Andhaka cast him down to the ground and then roared.
Then, seeing him roaring, Vāsava rained down arrows forcefully, warding him off; he [the demon] advanced toward Śatakratu.
Andhaka, acting with haste, struck the elephant on the middle of its forehead with his palm,
hit it on the trunk with his foot, and having struck it with his knee, shattered its tusks;
likewise, he struck its side with his left fist.
He struck down the lordly elephant, reducing it to a state of shattered ruin with his blows.
Leaping down from the lordly elephant as he was falling, Śatakratu took up his thunderbolt with his hand and entered Amarāvatī.
When the thousand-eyed Indra turned his face away, the great host of deities was struck down by the Lord of the Daityas with his feet, fists, palms, and other blows.
Then, O best of the twice-born, Vaivasvata,
that foremost of gods, brandishing his staff, rushed toward Prahlāda, desiring to kill him.
As he was rushing forward,
the swift son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, having bent his bow, showered the son of the Sun with volleys of arrows.
Having struck down that incomparable shower of arrows with his staff and shattered them, the son of the Sun hurled his staff, which strikes terror into the worlds.
Having ascended the path of the wind and stationed himself at the hand of Dharmarāja,
he blazed like the fire of destruction at the end of time, as if to consume the three worlds.
Seeing the blazing staff approaching, the sons of Diti cried out, "Alas!
This Prahlāda is surely being slain by Yama!"
Hearing that cry of distress, Andhaka, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, said:
"Do not fear; while I am present, who is this lowest of gods?"
Having spoken these words, Nārada rushed forward with speed and, laughing, seized the staff with his left hand.
Taking him up, Andhaka then whirled him around with great speed and let out a mighty roar, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season.
Seeing Prahlāda protected by the staff from the lord of the Daityas,
the leaders of the Daitya and Dānava hosts were delighted and offered words of praise.
O Sage, seeing him brandishing his great staff, Yama, the son of the Sun,
considering it unbearable and impossible to withstand, vanished from sight.
When the King of Dharma had vanished, O great sage, the powerful Prahlāda also began to tear apart the army of the gods on all sides.
Varuṇa, stationed upon a porpoise, bound the great asuras with nooses and tore them apart with his mace; then Virocana approached him.
He struck the Lord of Waters with arrows whose touch was like a vajra, as well as with spears, shafts,
mallets, and iron clubs.
Then, having approached him with his mace and felled him to the ground,
the powerful one rushed forward and bound him with nooses like a rutting elephant.
The lord of the Danujas, by his own speed, cut those nooses into a hundred pieces;
and having approached Varuṇa, O Nārada, he seized him in the midst.
Then the imperishable Dantī hurled the lord of the waters with his two tusks and likewise trampled him along with his mount with his two feet.
Then, seeing him being crushed, the Moon, possessing cool rays,
approached and struck him with arrows that tore through his body.
Being struck by the arrows of the cool-rayed moon, that lordly elephant experienced supreme agony;
yet, being wicked, he repeatedly trampled the Lord of Waters with the soles of his feet out of sheer momentum.
O great seer, as he was being crushed, the high-souled Varuṇa seized the lordly elephant very firmly with his two feet;
touching the earth with his feet and his hands, the great being raised up the elephant's head by force.
Having seized the elephant's tail with his fingers and bound it there with the lord of serpents,
he uprooted and hurled Virocana along with the elephant, together with its driver and vehicle, into the sky.

Thrown by the Lord of Waters, Virocana fell to the surface of the earth along with his elephant, like the city of Sukeśin— complete with its palaces, gates, bolts, and towers— was cast down by Bhāskara.
Then the Lord of Waters, armed with his mace and his noose, rushed forward to slay the son of Diti;
meanwhile, an unsurpassed, tumultuous cry was let out by the Daityas, sounding like the roar of thick clouds.
"Alas, alas! That hero Virocana, the protector of the Dānava army, has been slain by Varuṇa!
O Prahlāda, O Jambha, O Kujaṃbha, and you others—come quickly and protect him along with Andhaka! VamP_10.36 //
"Oh, how mighty is the Great-Souled Lord of Waters!
Crushing the Daitya warrior along with his mount, he binds him with his noose and strikes him down with his mace, just as Mahendra slays a beast in the horse-sacrifice."
Then, having heard the sound uttered by the sons of Diti, the lords of the Daityas, with Jambha at their head,
rushed swiftly toward the Lord of Waters, like moths toward a blazing fire.
Beholding them as they approached, the god Prahlāda’s son,
the lord of the waters, cast aside his net, whirled his mace, and rushed toward those enemies with faces like Jambha.
Having likewise struck Jambha with a noose and Tāra with his palm, which was like a thunderbolt,
he swiftly felled Vṛtra with his foot and Bala with a fist, as well as Kujambha.
Afflicted by that best of gods, the Daityas fled in all directions, casting away their weapons;
then Andhaka quickly approached to fight in battle against the Lord of the Waters.
As he was rushing forward, the fierce lord of the asuras struck him with his mace after binding him with a noose;
but the daitya, having whirled that noose and seized his mace, hurled it at the Lord of the Waters.
Seeing that noose and mace falling upon him, the son of Dakṣāyaṇī entered the ocean with speed; thereafter, Andhaka crushed the army of the gods.
Then the Fire-god, fanned by the wind, consumed the army of the enemies of the gods out of rage;
at that moment, the long-armed Maya, the Viśvakarman of the Dānavas, endowed with fierce valor, rushed toward him.
O great sage, seeing him approaching together with Śambara, Agni, along with the Wind-god,
went toward Maya and Śambara, struck them on the neck with his spear, and seized them by force.
When his body-armor was pierced by that spear, his body shattered, he fell to the earth;
and Maya as well as Śambara burst into flames as the fire blazed up, clinging to their throats.
Then, being consumed by fire, that son of Diti cried out in a most terrible and loud voice,
just as a rutting elephant in the forest, seized by a lion, shrieks while afflicted by pain.
Hearing that sound, Śambara, the lord of the Daityas, his gaze clouded with anger and resentment, cried out:
"Ah! What is this? What is this? Has Maya and the Dānava Śambara been defeated by someone in battle?"
Then the Daitya warriors said to the Lord of Diti: "He is indeed being consumed by fire;
come quickly and protect him, for the fire cannot be warded off by others on the front line of battle."
Thus urged by the Daityas, O great seer, that son Hiraṇyākṣa raised a flaming iron club with speed and rushed toward Agni, crying out, "Wait! Wait!"
Having heard the words of Andhaka, the one of imperishable soul became enraged in heart and swiftly seized the Daitya;
having uprooted him from the ground, he crushed him, whereupon Andhaka approached Pāvaka.
Then, with his excellent weapon, he struck the fire-god in the middle of his noble body;
thus assailed, Agni released Śambara and Andhaka and quickly rushed toward him.
Then Andhaka struck that approaching [Agni] again on the head with his iron club;
thus struck by the lord of the Daityas, Agni fled in fear from the field of battle.

Then the valiant Andhaka, with his arrow, caused all those whom he touched— the Maruts, the Moon, the Sun, the Sādhyas, along with the Rudras, Aśvins, Vasus, and great serpents— to turn their backs and flee from the field of battle.
Then, having conquered the formidable army of the immortals— including Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Soma—
and being honored by the foremost of the Danavas, Andhaka returned to the earth.
Having reached the earth, having made the kings who pay tribute subject to his will, and having established the entire world of moving and non-moving beings under his control,
the wise one entered the foremost subterranean realm known as Aśmaka.
Even while that great asura remained there, hosts of gandharvas, vidyādharas, and siddhas,
together with apsarases, came down to Pātāla and dwelt there to attend upon him.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"Regarding that which was spoken by you, that Sukeśin descended from the sky—"
By whom was the sun cast down to the earth, and at what time, and in what places?
Who was this person named Sukeśin, by whom was he given to him previously,
and for what reason was he indeed cast down from the sky to the earth by Bhāskara?
Pulastya said: Listen attentively, O sinless one, to this ancient narrative just as the Self-born One himself told it to me, as it is being related by me.
There was a lord of the night-stalkers renowned as Vidyunmālin;
from him was born his son Sukeśin, who was preeminent in virtues.
Being pleased with him, Īśāna likewise granted him a city that moves through the sky,
as well as invincibility against enemies and immunity from being slain.
And he too, having obtained a boon from Śaṅkara, dwelt in a city that travels through the sky;
remaining ever established on the path of dharma, he took delight together with the night-stalkers.
Once, that lord of the Rākṣasas went to the Māgadha forest,
where he beheld the hermitages of sages of purified souls.
Then, having seen the great seers, he prostrated and saluted them;
once he had accepted his seat, he replied to all the seers.
Sukeśin said:
"I wish to ask you; this doubt resides in my heart.
May you explain it to me, for I do not command you."
O best of the twice-born, what is truly beneficial in the next world, and what is so in this one?
By what means is one honored among the virtuous, and by what does one increase in happiness?
Pulastya said: Having thus heard the words of Sukeśin, the supreme sages reflected and spoke for the sake of the highest good in this world and the next. *Vāyu Purāṇa* 11.11.
The sages said:
"Listen, O bull among Rākṣasas, we shall tell you that which is indeed the highest good for you, O hero, both in this world and the next, and which is imperishable. (VamP 11.12)
O night-stalker, dharma is superior in the next world and in this one as well;
by relying upon it, one is honored among the virtuous and thereby becomes happy. (VamP 11.13)
Sukeśin said:
What are the characteristics of Dharma, and what are its practices and virtuous rites? Please tell me that by relying upon which the gods and others do not fall into despair.
The sages said:
"The supreme duty of the gods is always ritual acts such as sacrifices;
it is traditionally held that their delight lies in the study of the Vedas, mastery of the Vedas, and the worship of Viṣṇu."
The Daityas' skill with their arms, their envy, their proficiency in battle,
their knowledge of the treatises on ethics, and their devotion to Hara have been described.
The dharma proclaimed by the Siddhas is the unsurpassed method of yoga;
it consists of self-study, the knowledge of Brahman, and firm devotion toward both.
One who knows [the rules] regarding dance and instrumental music should be known as a superior practitioner;
steady devotion to Sarasvatī is called the duty of the Gāndharva.
Incomparable mastery of the sciences, specialized knowledge, manly resolve, and this very dharma of the Vidyādharas, as well as devotion to Bhavānī—this is their way. (VamP 11.19)
Knowledge of the Gandharva-vidyā, steadfast devotion to the Sun,
and skill in all arts— this is remembered as the Dharma of the Kimpuruṣas.
Celibacy, freedom from pride, firm devotion to the practice of yoga,
and the ability to act according to one's will in all matters— this is remembered as the ancestral dharma.
O Rākṣasa, celibacy, moderation in eating, recitation, and knowledge—through these observances comes the understanding of Dharma; this is declared to be the Dharma pertaining to the goal (Artha).
Vedic study, celibacy, giving, and sacrifice; freedom from miserliness, freedom from exertion, compassion, non-violence, forbearance, and self-control. (VamP 11.23)
Control of the senses, purity, auspiciousness, and devotion to Acyuta, Śaṅkara, Bhāskara, and the Goddess—this is remembered as the duty of a human being. (VamP 11.24)
"Sovereignty over wealth, enjoyments, sacred study, and the worship of Śakra; pride and lack of generosity—this is the dharma among the Guhyakas. (VamP 11.25)
Violating another's wife, greed for the wealth of others, neglecting one's own Vedic study, and lack of devotion to Tryambaka— this is remembered as the Rākṣasa dharma.
Lack of discrimination, ignorance, loss of purity, untruthfulness, and a constant greed for meat—this is the nature of the Piśācas. (VamP 11.27)
O Rākṣasa, these are the twelve very sources;
within them, the twelve meritorious Dharmas, which grant the various destinies, were proclaimed by Brahmā.
Sukeśin said:
"The eternal and twelvefold imperishable duties that have been spoken of by you— among those,
you should further explain the duties pertaining to human beings."
The sages said:
"Listen, O night-walker, to the duties of men and others who dwell upon the surface of the earth in the seven continents."
In measurement of yojanas, this earth extends fifty koṭis;
indeed, it rests upon the water like a boat upon the waters of a river.
And upon that, O virtuous ones, the Lord of Gods established the supreme Śūlendra Brahmā,
exceedingly high and shaped like the pericarp of a lotus.
The divine Lord of Creatures fashioned for him this meritorious progeny in the four directions,
and he established the regions known as the continents.
It is heard that he created Jambūdvīpa in the center of that;
its measurement is said to be one hundred thousand yojanas.
Beyond that stands the formidable ocean, twice as large;
and beyond that, the Plakṣa continent is established, twice as large again.
Beyond that flows the ocean of sugarcane juice; Śālmalidvīpa is twice as large as this great ocean, and it is surrounded by a circular rim.
Suroda is twice that [in extent], and Kuśa is twice as large as that;
Ghṛtoda is likewise proclaimed to be twice the size of Kuśadvīpa.
O night-stalker, Krauñcadvīpa is said to be twice the size of the Ocean of Ghee;
the ocean known as the Ocean of Curd is likewise said to be twice the size of that island.
Twice the size of the ocean is the Śāka continent; beyond the Śāka is the excellent Ocean of Milk, twice as large, where Hari rests upon the couch of Śeṣa.
All of these are situated in a sequence that doubles in size relative to one another.
O Lord of Rākṣasas, it is recorded that from Jambūdvīpa up to the very edge of the Ocean of Milk, the distance is forty-four million, nine hundred thousand, and five [hundred] yojanas. VamP_11.40.
And beyond that, O Rākṣasa, is Puṣkaradvīpa, which has sweet water;
it measures four crores and fifty-two lakhs [of yojanas].
This Puṣkaradvīpa is of that same extent, and the ocean surrounding it is likewise filled on all sides with a shell-encrusted crust one hundred thousand yojanas thick.
In this way, these seven continents have distinct characteristics and distinct activities;
we shall describe them to you, O night-stalker, so listen!
O hero, for those eternal men who dwell among the Plakṣa trees and others at the end of the Śāka continent, there is no condition of the Yugas whatsoever.
They rejoice like gods; their dharma is declared to be divine.
O mighty-armed one, at the end of the kalpa, their dissolution is proclaimed.
Those people who dwell on Puṣkaradvīpa, which is terrible in appearance, resort to the dharma of the Piśācas; at the end of their actions, they are destroyed.
Sukeśin said:
For what purpose has Puṣkaradvīpa been described by you?
It is difficult to behold, devoid of purity, terrible, and it brings about the destruction of the fruits of one's actions.
On that island of the night-stalkers, there are dreadful hells beginning with Raurava; beyond those is the fierce Puṣkara, which is terrible to behold.
Sukeśin said:
"O ascetic rich in austerity, how many are these terrible hells?
What is their extent along the path, and what is their specific nature?"
The sages said:
"Listen, O best of Rākṣasas, to the dimensions and characteristics,
as well as the number, which is twenty-one, of all the hells beginning with Raurava."
The first hell proclaimed is named Raurava, two thousand yojanas in extent, spread with glowing embers.
The ground is made of molten copper and heated from below by fire;
because it is twice as great as the former, it is called Mahāraurava.
Beyond that, another hell situated twice as far is known as Tāmisra;
the fourth, named Andhatāmisra, is twice as great as the previous one.
Then the fifth is celebrated as Kālacakra;
Apratiṣṭhāna is the hell, and Ghaṭīyantra is the seventh.
And another, the eighth supreme hell, known as Asipatravana, is measured at seventy-two thousand yojanas in circumference.
Namaka, Taptakumbha, and the tenth, Kūṭaśālmalī;
likewise Karapatra is mentioned, as well as another called Śvānabhojana.
The pincers and the iron ball, as well as the grit of parched grain, the terrible river of caustic lye, another called Kṛmibhojana (Feast of Worms),
and likewise the eighteenth, the terrible Vaitaraṇī river, have been described.
Likewise, O Sukeśin, there is another called Saṃśoṣaṇa, who feeds on blood and pus; and there is the sharp-edged, whetted discus called Ananta—these hells have been described to you.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Sukeśin said:
"By what action do people indeed go to these hells, and in what manner?"
"O best of Brahmins, tell me this, for my curiosity is great."
The sages said:
"O Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, hear from me about those hells to which people go in this world by various actions for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their own deeds."
Those sinners who have constantly reviled the Vedas, the gods, and the twice-born, and who do not take pleasure in the meaning of the Purāṇas and Itihāsas; VamP_12.3 //
Indeed, they fall upon those who revile the Kurus, those who create obstacles for friends, and those who prevent a donor from giving;
as well as upon friends, wives, brothers, masters, servants, fathers, and sons. (12.4)
Those base individuals who, having given their daughter to one man, then give her to another,
are split in two by the servants of Yama with a saw.
Those who cause suffering to others, those who steal sandalwood and ushira root,
those who take away yak-tail fans, and those who resort to mixed grain and sand [will suffer].
If one who has been invited elsewhere eats at a *śrāddha*— whether for the gods or the ancestors—
that fool is torn asunder in two by birds with sharp beaks.
But upon him who cuts into the vital spots of the virtuous with his words,
birds stand ready to strike with their beaks.
For him who, with a perverted mind, practices slander against the virtuous,
crows with diamond-tipped beaks and claws pull out his tongue.
Those who, being arrogant, have shown contempt for their mother, father, and teachers,
sink headlong into pus, excrement, and urine, which serve as their foundation.
Those who eat while the deities, guests, living beings, servants, and visitors have not yet eaten, as well as while their children, parents, fire, and mother remain unfed; VamP_12.12 //
These lowest of beings consume the exudation of foul blood and pus;
they are born with needle-like mouths, afflicted by hunger, and possessing bodies as large as mountains.
O Lord of Rākṣasas, those who serve food unequally to those seated in a single row go to the hell called Viḍbhojana.
Those people who, seeing a seeker traveling with them as part of the same caravan,
eat without sharing, go to the world where one must consume phlegm.
O night-stalker, those whose hands have touched cows, Brahmins, or fires while they were impure are indeed cast into a most dreadful cauldron of molten lead.
Those who, while impure, have looked at the sun, the moon, or the stars out of desire—
for them, the fire within their eyes is fanned by the servants of Yama.
A friend’s wife, a mother, an elder brother, a father, a sister, female relatives, teachers, and elders—those men by whom these have been touched with their feet [must perform penance]. (VamP 12.18)
With their legs bound by iron shackles heated in fire,
they are cast into the terrible Raurava hell, where they suffer a burning sensation reaching up to their knees.
For those men by whom milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, and meat were consumed in vain,
heated iron balls are cast into their mouths as a marvel.
Those lowest of men by whom the censure of gurus, gods, the twice-born, and the Vedas has been constantly heard while they were committing such sins—[for them... VamP_12.21.
Into their ears, iron spikes, glowing like fire, are driven again and again by the servants of Dharmarāja.
Those who, having broken and destroyed water-stations, temples, the dwellings of Brahmins, assembly halls, monasteries, as well as wells, ponds, and lakes; VamP_12.23.
While they are thus lamenting, their skin is separated from the body with extremely sharp knives by the most fierce servants of Yama.
Those men who indeed urinate upon a cow, a Brahmin, the sun, or fire—
crows shall tear out their rectums and entrails.
That man who, intent only on nourishing himself, abandons his children,
servants, wife, and other circle of kinsmen when they are destitute—
even during a famine or a time of great distress— is cast into the Śvabhojya hell.
Those who abandon one who has come for refuge, and those who are prison guards,
fall into the Crushing Machine, being beaten there by the *kiṅkara* servants.
For those sinners who trouble Brahmins and others by neglecting their duties are ground upon stone-grinders and are withered away even by those who wither.
The wicked who misappropriate deposits are bound even with iron chains;
emaciated by hunger, with parched palates and lips, they are cast into the pit of scorpions.
Those sinful men who engage in sexual intercourse before their wives and those who take pleasure in the wives of others embrace the Śālmalī tree, which is heated by fire and topped with spikes.
Those lowest of the twice-born who have studied while treating their preceptor with contempt,
and he who is their teacher— let him carry a stone upon his head.
Those by whom urine, phlegm,
and excrement have been cast into the water are themselves cast down into foul-smelling excrement and urine, filled with pus.
Those foolish men on earth who have partaken of one another’s ancestral offerings and hospitality devour their own flesh among themselves.
Those who abandon the Vedas, the sacred fire, and their preceptor, as well as their wife and parents,
are cast down from the mountain peak by the servants of Yama.
Furthermore, those who are kings, those who destroy maidens, he who eats at a śrāddha for their [the aforementioned] offspring, and he who eats worms and ants—[these shall dwell there]. (VamP 12.35)
Whether from a Cāṇḍāla or even an Antyaja, he who accepts a sacrificial fee as a priest or a patron—that man is a fat worm within us. (VamP 12.36)
O night-stalker, those fools who eat the flesh of their backs and likewise live by bribery are cast into the Vṛkabhakṣa hell.
The thief of gold, the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the Guru’s bed, as well as those who seize cattle or land, and those who kill cows, women, or children; VamP_12.38.
Those men who are twice-born [brahmins] but sell cows,
as well as those who sell soma and those who sell the Vedas— these are such men.

Those who act as fraudulent members of a court, those who are impure, those who cause the destruction of obligatory and occasional rites, and those who provide false testimony— these dwell in the Mahāraurava hell.
For ten thousand years they remain in Tāmisra,
and for that same duration in Andhatāmisra, and then in the Asipatravana forest.
For that long they remain in the Ghaṭīyantra, and after that, in the Taptakumbha;
such is the downfall of those by whom this evil deed was committed.
But those fierce hells beginning with Raurava which have been mentioned by you—
all of them are said to be visited, in due order, by the ungrateful person who is censured by the world.
Just as Janārdana is the foremost among the gods, as the snowy mountain is among the mountains,
as the Sudarśana is the best among weapons, as the son of Vinatā is among birds,
as Ananta is the preeminent among great serpents, and as the earth is the principal among all beings; VamP_12.44 //
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, the lotus among water-born flowers, and devotion to the feet of Hara is foremost among the chief enemies of the gods;
just as Kurujaṅgala is the best among fields, so is Pṛthūdaka the most excellent among sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Uttaramānasa is among lakes, as Nandana is among sacred groves, as the abode of Viriñci is among the worlds, and as truth is among the performance of righteous rites; VamP_12.46.
Just as the horse-sacrifice is the most excellent among rituals, as a son is the best among those who possess touch,
and as the source of the Sumbhas is the foremost among those whose wealth is austerity, so too is the Śruti the best among the traditional scriptures here on earth.
Just as the Mātsya Purāṇa is preeminent among the Purāṇas, and the account of Svāyambhuva Manu among the Saṃhitās;
just as Manu is the foremost of the Smṛtis, and the new moon sacrifice (darśa) among the lunar days, and the gift given at the equinoxes (viṣuva) is supreme among gifts.
Just as the sun is said among luminous bodies here, the moon among the stars, and the ocean among the waters;
so are you among the best of Rākṣasas, as the binding noose is among all immobile things.
Among grains, the *śali* rice; among bipeds, the Brahmin; among quadrupeds, the cow; among beasts of prey, the lion;
among flowers, the *jāti*; among cities, Kāñcī; among women, Rambhā; and among laborers, the householder. (VamP 12.50)

Kuśasthalī is the most excellent among cities, and Madhyadeśa is the best among all regions; the mango tree is foremost among fruits, the aśoka among buds, and the myrobalan is the preeminent of all medicinal herbs.
O Lord of the Night-Rangers, just as the bulbous root is the best among roots, indigestion is the foremost among diseases;
just as milk is the best among white substances, and cotton cloth is the best among coverings.
Among the arts, proficiency in calculation is foremost; among the chief branches of knowledge, it is like the art of illusion (*indrajāla*).
Among vegetables, the *kākamācī* is preeminent, just as salt is the foremost among flavors.

As the palm tree is among tall trees, Pampā among lotus ponds, and the king of bears among forest-dwellers; as the banyan is among great trees, so is Hara the most eminent among those possessed of knowledge.
Just as the daughter of Himavat is the best among the Satīnā cows, and as the Kapilā is the most excellent among the Arjunī cows;

just as the dark-blue bull is preeminent even among bulls, and just as the Vaitaraṇī is foremost among all the difficult and terrible obstacles, O Lord of the Night-rangers, so is the Nṛpātana [the foremost].

O lord of forest-dwellers, in this world, for all other sins—even for the murder of a Brahmin or a cow—atonement may indeed be found for the most wicked; but for this man of evil conduct, there is no atonement whatsoever. There is no atonement for one who follows the way of the ungrateful, who destroys what was done by a friend, even in ten million years.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Sukeśin said:
"The terrible configuration of Puṣkaradvīpa has been described by you."
"O great seers, please describe the configuration of Jambūdvīpa."
The sages said:
Listen as the configuration of Jambūdvīpa is described—
its ninefold divisions, its vast extent, and how it bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation.
In the center is the region of Ilāvṛta; to the east is Bhadraśva, which is wonderful;
and to the northeast, O Lord of the Rākṣasas, is Hiraṇya.
To the southeast as well, the region is called Kiṃnara;
Bhārata is declared to be in the south, and Hari is in the southwest.
In the west is Kekumāla, and Ramyaka is in the north-west;
and in the north is the region of Kuru, which is filled with wish-fulfilling trees.
O Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, these nine regions— Ilāvṛta and the other eight, excluding Bhārata— are meritorious and delightful.
For them there is no state of the Yugas, nor is there any fear of old age or death;
their accomplishment is innate and consists mostly of happiness, attained without effort.
For them there is no adversity, nor are there superior, inferior, or middling states.
O night-stalker, this Bhārata-varṣa consists of nine islands;
all are separated by oceans and are inaccessible to one another.
Indrīpa, Kaserumān, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān,
Nāgadvīpa, Kaṭāha, Siṃhala, and likewise Vāruṇa.
But this ninth of those islands, surrounded by the ocean, is renowned as Kumāra; this island extends from south to north.
O hero, the Kirātas dwell at its eastern edge, the Yavanas are situated to the west,
the Āndhras to the south, and the Turuṣkas also to the north.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Sūdras dwelling therein purified themselves through their respective duties, such as sacrifice, warfare, and trade.
Their worldly transactions are held to proceed by means of these actions;
likewise, the attainment of heaven and liberation, as well as merit and demerit, [are established].
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and the Ṛkṣa mountain—
And the Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these are the seven principal mountain ranges here.
Likewise, there are other hundreds of thousands of mountain ranges dwelling in the middle region—
extensive in width and height, delightful, vast, and possessing auspicious peaks.
Kolāhala, Savaibhrāja, Mandara, Durdarācala, Vātandhama, Vaidyuta, Maināka, and likewise Sarasas.
Tuṅgaprastha, Nāgagiri, as well as Govardhana mountain,
Ujjāyana, Puṣpagiri, Arbuda, and likewise Raivata.
Ṛṣyamūka, Gomanta, Citrakūṭa, Kṛtasmara,
Śrīparvata, Koṅgaṇa, and hundreds of other mountains as well.
Interspersed with them, the regions are occupied by Mlecchas and Āryas respectively;
by them the most excellent rivers are drunk—listen attentively to which they are.
The Sarasvatī has five forms: the Kālindī, the Hiraṇvatī, the Śatadru, the Candrikā, the Nīlā, the Vitastā, the Irāvatī, and the Kuhū.
The Madhurā, the Hārarāvī, the Uśīrā, the Dhātukī, the Rasā,
the Gomatī, the Dhūtapāpā, the Bāhudā, and the Ṛṣadvatī.
The Niścirā, Gaṇḍakī, Citrā, Kauśikī, Vadhūsara,
Sarū, and Lauhityā flow forth from the foothills of the Himavat.
Vedasmṛti, Vedasinī, Vṛtraghnī, and Sindhu;
Parṇāśā, Nandinī, Pāvanī, and likewise Mahī.
The Pārā, Carmaṇvatī, Lūpī, Vidiśā, Veṇumatī,
Siprā, and Avantī are likewise remembered as the rivers that take their source from the Pāriyātra mountains.
The Śoṇa, the Mahānada, the Narmadā, the Surasā, the Kṛpā,
the Mandākinī, the Daśārṇā, and the Citrakūṭāpavāhikā.
Citrotpalā, Tamasā, Karamodā, Piśācikā, as well as Pippalaśroṇī, Vipāśā, and Vañjulāvatī.
Satsantajā, Śuktimatī, Mañjiṣṭhā, Kṛttisā, Vasu,
Ṛkṣapādaprasūtā, and likewise another, Balavāhinī.
The Śivā, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Tāpī, Niṣadhāvatī,
Veṇā, Vaitaraṇī, Sinīvāhū, and Kumudvatī.
The Toyā, the Mahāgaurī, the Durgandhā, and the Vāśilā,
as well as the rivers of auspicious, merit-bestowing waters born from the foothills of the Vindhya mountains.
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇā, Veṇā, Sarasvatī,
Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayogā, Vāhyā, and the Kāverī as well.
Dugdhodā, Nalinī, Revā, Vārisenā, and Kalasvanā—
these also are great rivers that have issued from the foothills of the Sahya mountain.
Kṛtamālā, Tāmrarṇī, Vaḍhjulā, Utpalāvatī,
Sinī, and Sudāmā— these are the rivers that originate from Śuktimat.
All the Sarasvatīs are meritorious and likewise pacifiers of sin;
all are mothers of the world, and all are the wives of the ocean.
O Rākṣasa, there are indeed thousands of other minor rivers here—
some flowing at all times and others flowing only during the rainy season— and auspicious regions arising from the northern and central lands drink [their waters] at their own will.
The Matsyas, Kuśaṭṭas, Kuṇikuṇḍalas, Pāñjālas, and Kāśis, together with the Kosalas.
These people are the Vṛkas, Śabaras, Kauvīras, and the Bhūliṅgas; these are the Śakas, the Samaśakas, and the people of the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa).
The Vāhlīkas, the Vāṭadhānas, the Ābhīras, the Kālatoyakas, the Aparāntas, as well as the Śūdras, the Pahlavas, and the Sakheṭakas; VamP_13.37 //
The Gāndhāras, the Yavanas, the Sindhus, Sauvīras, and Madrakas; the Śātadravas, the Lalitthas, and the Pārāvatas and Samūṣakas.
The Māṭharas, Udakadhārās, Cajas, Kaikayas, and likewise the Daśamas;
the Śratriyas, Prativaiśyas, and the families of Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
The Kāmbojas, the Daradas, the Barbaras, the Aṅgalaukikas,
the Cīnas, and the Tuṣāras— these various peoples dwell outside the city walls.
The Ātreyas, along with the Bharadvājas, the Prasthalas, the Daśerakas, the Lampakas, the Tāvakārāmas, and the Śūlikas together with the Taṅgaṇas; VamP_13.41.
The Aurasa, the Ālimadra, and the various tribes of Kirātas;
the Tāmasa, the Kramamāsa, the Supārśva, and likewise the Puṇḍraka.
The Kulūtas, Kuhukas, Ūrṇās, Tūṇīpādas, Sukukkuṭas,
Māṇḍavyas, and Mālavīyas are inhabitants of the Northern Region (Uttarāpatha).
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Mudgaras, Vāstus, Antargiris, Bahirgis, as well as the Pravaṅgas, Vāṅgeyas, Māṃsādas, and Baladantikas; 13.44.
The Brahmottaras, Prāvijayas, Bhārgavas, Keśavaras,
Pragjyotiṣas, Śūdras, Videhas, and Tāmraliptakas.
O Rākṣasa, these are the eastern tribes: the Mālas, Magadhas, Goṇandas, Na-japadas, Puṇḍras, Keralas, Cauḍas, and Kulyas.
The Jātuṣas, Mūṣikādās, Kumārādās, Mahāśakas, Mahārāṣṭras, Māhiṣikas, and Kāliṅgas from all sides; VamP_13.47.
The Ābhīras along with the Naiṣīkas, the forest-dwellers, and those who are Śabaras;
the Valindhyas, the Vindhyamauleyas, the Vaidarbhas, together with the Daṇḍakas.
The Paurikas, Sauśikas, Aśmakas, Bhogavardhanas,
Vaiṣikas, Kuṇḍalas, Andhras, Udbhidas, Nalakārakas,
and these southern regions, Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa; these are the southern provinces.
The Sūrpārakas, the Kārivaṇas, along with the Durgās and the Tālīkaṭas;
the Pulīyas, the Sasinīlas, as well as the Tāpasas and the Tāmasas.
The Kāraskaras, the Raminas, the Nāsikyās, those living between the Narmadā and the Mahī rivers,
the Bhārakacchas, along with the Sārasvatas, are likewise to be considered [as Mlecchas].
The Vātsyas, the Surāṣṭras, and the Āvantyas along with the Arbudas—
these are the people of the countryside situated in the western quarter.
The Kāruṣas, the Ekalavyas, and the Mekalas along with the Utkalas;
the Uttama-rṇas, the Daśārṇas, and the Bhojas together with the Kiṅkaras.
The Tośalas, the Kośalas, the Traipuras, the Aillikas, as well as the Turuṣas, the Tumbaras, the Vahanas, together with the Naiṣadhas.
The Anūpas, Tuṇḍikeras, Vītahotras, and Avantis;
Sukeśa, and Vandhyamūlastha—these are remembered as the inhabited regions (janapadas).
Now we shall describe the regions inhabited by those who dwell in the mountains:
the Nirāhāras, the Haṃsamārgas, the Kupathas, the Taṅgaṇas, and the Khaśas.
The Kuthaprāvaraṇas, the Ūrṇas, the Capuṇyas, the Sahūhukas,
the Trigarttas, the Kirātas, the Tomaras, and the Śiśirādrikas.
O Lord of the Night-rangers, these regions on the island have been described by you in great detail concerning Prince Kumāra;
now listen to the true nature of the local customs as they are proclaimed for these various lands.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
The sages said:
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-covetousness, charity, forbearance, self-restraint, and tranquility—
Freedom from miserliness, purity, and austerity, O night-stalker.
O best of Rākṣasas, this tenfold dharma is common to all castes;
even for the Brāhmaṇa, the arrangement of the four stages of life (āśramas) has been ordained.
Sukeśin said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, explain to me in detail the four stages of life for Brahmins;
as I listen, I do not reach satiety."
The sages said:
Having been initiated, one should dwell properly as a student of sacred knowledge with a guru;
listen now as we describe that dharma which pertains to him. *Vāmana Purāṇa* 14.4.
Vedic study, service to the sacred fires, ritual bathing, and likewise wandering for alms—
these should always be performed after first offering them to the teacher and then consuming them with his permission.
One should be diligent in service to the guru and properly cultivate his affection; when summoned by him, one should study with that as one's sole purpose, without a distracted mind.
Having received one, two, or even all the Vedas from the mouth of the celestial sage,
and having been granted permission and bestowed a boon upon his guru, he then gave him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One who desires the householder stage of life should dwell in the householder stage;
or he may enter the forest-dweller stage, or even the fourth, according to his own will.
In that very place, or in the house of the guru, the twice-born man should attain completion;
in the absence of the guru, he should do so with the guru’s son, or his disciple, or in the absence of those, with the guru’s grandson.
Serving [his teacher] and free from pride, he should dwell in the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya-āśrama).
In this way, O Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, that twice-born man conquers death.
Then, having returned from there with the desire for the householder stage of life,
O night-stalker, you should marry a maiden born of a family of sages who is not of the same lineage as your own.
Having acquired wealth through his own lawful labor, the twice-born man, devoted to virtuous conduct, should always properly gratify his ancestors, the gods, and guests with devotion.
"O you of excellent vows, the conduct of the virtuous has been described by you;
I wish to hear its defining characteristics—explain them to me today."
The sages said:
"O night-stalker, we have respectfully described to you what constitutes good conduct;
now listen as we explain its characteristics."
A householder must always practice the observance of proper conduct;
for one who is devoid of proper conduct, there is no well-being either in this world or the next.
In this world, sacrifice, charity, and austerity do not lead to a person's welfare if he proceeds by transgressing the conduct of the virtuous.
For a man of bad conduct does not rejoice either in this world or in the next; therefore, one should always exert effort in good conduct, for good conduct destroys inauspiciousness. (VamP 14.17)
O Rākṣasa, we shall describe the nature of that right conduct;
listen with an attentive mind to it, if you desire your own welfare. (VamP 14.18)
Dharma is its root, wealth its trunk, desire its flower, and liberation its fruit; O Sukeśin, he by whom this tree of virtuous conduct is cultivated is the enjoyer of merit.
At the first watch of Brahmā, one should awaken and call to mind the supreme gods and great sages;
one should recite the morning auspiciousness that was spoken by the three-eyed Lord of the Gods.
Sukeśin said:
What was that "Good Morning" spoken by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
by reciting which at dawn a mortal is released from the bondage of sin?
The sages said:
"Listen, O best of Rākṣasas, to this auspicious dawn proclaimed by Hara;
by hearing, remembering, and reciting it, one is liberated from all sins. (VamP 14.22)
May Brahmā, the enemy of Mura, the destroyer of Tripura, the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter,
Venus, and Saturn— all together— grant me a most auspicious dawn.
May Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Manu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Gautama,
Raibhya, Marīci, Cyavana, and Ṛbhu— all together— grant me a most auspicious dawn.
May Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, as well as Āsuri and Piṅgala,
the seven musical notes, and the seven netherworlds— all together grant me a beautiful dawn.
May the earth with its fragrance, the waters with their flavor, the wind with its touch, the fire with its brilliance,
and the sky with its sound— may all these, together with the Great One (Mahat), grant me a beautiful dawn.
May the seven oceans, the seven great mountain ranges, the seven sages, and the seven excellent islands,
beginning with the world of Bhūr and the other six realms, all together grant me a most auspicious dawn.

Thus, at dawn, one who recites, remembers, or listens with devotion to this supreme and most sacred [hymn], O sinless one, shall have evil dreams destroyed; by the grace of the Blessed One, a truly auspicious dawn shall come to pass. (VamP 14.28)
Then, having risen from his bed and reflected upon the Dharma as well as the ultimate goal, he should rise and,
uttering "Hari," go forth to perform the ritual of voiding.

One should not perform the voiding of excrement on a path to a deity, a cow, or a Brahmin, nor on a royal road, nor at a crossroads; nor should one do so here in a cow-pen, even while standing facing either the east or the west.
Then, for the purpose of purification, one should take three applications of earth on the anus, seven on the palms of the hands,
five on both [hands together], four on the thighs, one on the knees, and likewise one application of earth on the penis.

A man who knows the rules of right conduct should always take earth from within water, from the lair of a rat, from a place left over after cleaning, from a shelter, or indeed from an anthill, for the purpose of purification.
Facing either north or east, the wise man, having washed his feet and seated himself upon the ground,
should first rinse his mouth with water free from foam, and then wipe his face twice with water.
Then he should touch the cavities of his head with his hand and perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in due order;
having cleansed his hair and used a tooth-stick, he should likewise look into a mirror.
Having performed a head bath or a bath of the limbs, and having worshipped the ancestors together with the gods with water,
and having performed the fire-oblation and the auspicious touching [of the body], it is recommended to go outside.
Durvā grass, clarified butter, a water-pot, a cow with its calf, a bull, gold, clay, cow-dung, a svastika, unbroken rice, parched grain, honey, and a Brahmin girl; VamP_14.36.
Then, one should touch white and beautiful flowers, the sacrificial fire, the moon, the solar disc, and the Aśvattha tree; thereafter, one should perform the duties pertaining to one's own caste.
One should not abandon the local instructions, the supreme family dharma, nor indeed the dharma of one's own lineage;
through that, one should pursue the accomplishment of one's goals, avoiding false speech and that which is devoid of truth.

One should not speak words that are harsh or devoid of the authority of the scriptures, nor those by which one would be censured by virtuous people, nor should one ever disparage the Dharma; furthermore, one should not form associations with wicked men.
O Hero, sexual intercourse should be avoided during the twilights, during the day, with women of all castes who are the wives of others,
in empty houses, on the bare ground, with women in their menses, and in water.
A householder who has duly taken a wife must not engage in aimless wandering, nor give gifts in vain, nor slaughter animals in vain. (VamP 14.41)
From wandering aimlessly comes constant loss; from giving away wealth in vain comes the depletion of riches;
and by killing animals in vain, one incurs a sin that leads to hell. (VamP 14.42)
Through lack of praise, there is a decline in one's lineage; through the mixing of castes, there is danger;
and one should fear the world for taking up a wife in vain.
The best of men should not set their minds upon another's property or another's wife;
for another's property leads only to hell, and another's wife leads to death.
One should not look at another's wife while she is naked, nor should one converse with thieves; one should avoid looking at, touching, or conversing with a woman in her courses.
One should not sit upon the same seat with a sister, a daughter-in-law,
a mother, or even one's own daughter.
One should never bathe naked, nor should one ever sleep naked; likewise, wandering about even while naked is not desired. One should avoid from afar broken seats, vessels, and the like.

One should apply oil for anointing on the *nandā* days, undergo a haircut on the *riktā* days, eat meat on the *jayā* days, avoid women on the *pūrṇā* days, and perform all activities on the *bhadrā* days. (VamP 14.48)

One should not perform an oil massage on Sundays or on Tuesdays; one should avoid shaving on Fridays and Saturdays; and one should not approach a woman on Wednesdays. On all other days, one may always perform all these acts.
Oil, shaving, and meat should be avoided under Citrā, Hasta, Śravaṇa, Viśākhā, and Abhijit;
likewise, meat should be avoided under Mūla, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Kṛttikā, and the three Uttarās; and women should be avoided under the same asterisms.
O Lord of the Night-Rangers, one should always sleep on a worn-out bed with the head toward the north;
one should eat facing south, and never should one eat facing west, O Lord.

A wise person should circumambulate a temple, a sacred tree, a crossroads, one superior in learning, and a teacher; likewise, with diligence, he should wear garlands, food, drink, and garments that have not been worn by others.
One should always bathe with a head-bath at night, except for a specific reason;
however, one may do so during an eclipse of the planets, when one's own kinsmen have departed, or when the moon has entered one's birth asterism.

O Lord of the Night-rangers, after bathing, one should not touch a body that has been anointed with oil, nor should one shake one's hair; furthermore, having bathed, one should wipe one's limbs with a cloth or with the hand.
One should dwell in regions with good kings, where the people are always well-united,
where the farmers are free from anger, devoted to justice, and devoid of envy, and where the medicinal herbs abound.

O Lord of the Night-rangers, a wise king who is incapable yet fond of wielding the rod of punishment should never dwell in such regions; nor should he stay where the people are perpetually embroiled in strife and ever intent on conquest.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
The sages said:
"O mighty-armed one, that which is to be avoided by men who always abide in righteousness..."
We shall now describe that which has been designated as fit for consumption.
Food that has been kept overnight, food smeared with oil and stored for a long time, rice grains without oil, and likewise fine preparations made from milk. VamP_15.2 //
Manu has declared that rabbits, porcupines, monitor lizards, hedgehogs, fish, and tortoises, as well as split-pea soups and similar foods, are fit for consumption.
Likewise, [the same applies] to gems, jewels, and corals, as well as to pearls;
and also to those made of stone or wood, as well as to grasses, roots, and medicinal herbs.
The purification of winnowing baskets, grain-sacks, skins, and woven cloths, as well as all types of bark garments, is prescribed to be performed with water.
Furthermore, oily cotton cloths shall be purified with warm water mixed with sesame paste and ashes.
The purification of ivory, bone, and horn is held to be by scraping;
and for earthen vessels, purity is achieved through re-firing.
Alms-food is pure, as is that which comes from the hand of an artisan, merchandise, the mouth of a woman,
what is found on the road and is unknown, and that which has been prepared by a group of servants.
Speech that is praised, long past, or interrupted by many others is light;
the actions of children and the elderly are light, and the mouth of a child is pure.
In the charcoal-sheds of the workshops, women with infants at their breasts,
the droplets of the speech of the best of the twice-born, and drops of water were all heated.
The ground is purified by digging, burning, sweeping, and the treading of cows;
likewise, a house is purified by smearing, scraping, sprinkling, sweeping, and cleansing.
If food is contaminated by hair or insects, smelled by a cow, or infested with flies,
earth, water, ashes, and alkaline substances should be added for the sake of purification.
The purification of udumbara wood is by sour liquids; that of tin and lead is by alkaline substances; that of bell-metal is by ashes and water; and for liquids, it is by immersion.
The purification of objects smeared with impurities is by means of earth and water that remove the odor;
for other substances as well, purification occurs through the removal of the odor.
A calf is pure when discharging its mother's milk, a bird when causing fruit to fall, a donkey when carrying a load, and a dog when seizing game. (VamP 15.15)
Roads, mud, and water, boats on the path, grasses,
and structures built of baked bricks are purified by the wind alone.
If cooked food from a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* measure becomes defiled by impure substances, one should remove and discard the top portion; for the remainder, sprinkling with water is prescribed.
If one eats food that has been defiled, whether it was done unknowingly or previously known, purification is not ordained for a three-night fast or even a single day of fasting.
Having touched a woman in her courses, a dog, one who is naked, a woman who has recently given birth, an outcaste, or those who carry the dead, one should bathe for the sake of purification.
If one touches a bone that still has marrow attached to it, one should bathe with one's clothes on;
but if it is bone without marrow, one need only perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water), touch a cow, and look at the sun.
One should not step over feces, blood, spittle, or the remains of anointing ointments.
One should cast the remnants of food, excrement, urine, and the water used for washing the feet outside the house.
One should not bathe in the water of another without first removing five lumps [of earth];
one may bathe in natural pools, lakes, and rivers.
A wise person should never remain in gardens or similar places at improper times;
nor should he converse with those hated by the people, nor with women who lack heroic protectors.
Having made physical contact or engaged in conversation with those who revile the deities, ancestors, true scriptures, sacrifices, the Vedas, and so forth, one becomes pure by looking at the sun.

Those who have recently given birth, eunuchs, cats, rats, dogs, and cocks; those who have fallen from their caste, those who are outcaste, the naked, and those who are lower than Cāṇḍālas and the like—these are not to be fed.
Sukeśin said:
"Regarding those such as the *sūtikā* (women who have recently given birth) whom you have described as unfit to be fed,
I wish to hear their characteristics according to the truth."
The sages said:
A Brāhmaṇa woman who has entered into the state of being a wife to a Brāhmaṇa—
both of them are called *sūtikā* (one who has recently given birth), and their food is censured.
He who does not offer oblations at the proper time, who does not bathe, and who does not give gifts—
being devoid of worship for the ancestors and the gods, he is proclaimed a eunuch.
He who mutters prayers, performs austerities, and offers sacrifices for the sake of hypocrisy,
and does not strive for the sake of the higher world, is proclaimed to be a cat.
When wealth exists, he neither eats, nor gives, nor offers oblations;
they call him a rat, and having eaten his food, one is purified only with great difficulty. (VamP 15.30)
He who speaks as if cutting into the vital points of others, and who constantly hates the virtues of others, is said to be a dog. (VamP 15.31)
"O gods, they say that he who, being a member of an assembly, resorts to partiality is a mere cock; even his food is to be despised."
He who, having completely abandoned his own duty, resorts to the duty of another when not in times of distress, is declared by the wise to be fallen.
One who abandons the gods, one who abandons the ancestors, one who is devoid of devotion to the guru,
and one who commits the killing of cows, Brahmins, or women— he is declared to be an outcast (apaviddha).
Those families in which there is no Veda, no scripture, and no sacred vow are declared by the virtuous to be "naked"; their food is censured.
He who does not give to those afflicted by hope, who forbids another from giving, and who abandons one who has come for refuge—that man is a *caṇḍāla*, the lowest of men. (VamP 15.36)

He who has been abandoned by his kinsmen, as well as by virtuous Brahmins, and he who eats from a *kuṇḍa*—having eaten the food of such a person, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (VamP 15.37)
A man who causes the omission of obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites shall be purified by eating food after fasting for three nights.
A man who has fasted for three nights shall be purified from contact with an astrologer, a Niṣāda, a courtesan, a physician, and likewise even a miser.
Only the omission of obligatory rites (nitya-karma) occurs during death and rebirth;
however, the occasional rite (naimittika-karma) must never be discontinued under any circumstances.
"When a son is born, bathing with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father;
and when [a relative] has died, it is for all kinsmen—so said the venerable Bhṛgu."
After the cremation has been performed outside by the kinsmen, water should be offered for the deceased on the third day,
or on the fourth, or on the seventh, at which time the collection of bones takes place.
After the collection of their remains, the touching of the limbs is prescribed;
however, the rites accompanied by water-libations must be performed by the sapinda relatives once they have become purified.
And in the case of those who have died by poison, hanging, weapons, water, fire, or falling [from a height];
likewise for children, those who have entered the wandering life (pravrajyā), those who have renounced the world (saṃnyāsa), and those who have died in another country.
O Hero, immediate purification (sadyaḥ-śauca) occurs, and that is said to be of four kinds:
it is declared to be the same in the case of a miscarriage, whereas in other cases it depends on whether the full term has been reached.
A day and night for the Brahmins is three days for the Kṣatriyas;
for the Vaiśyas it is six nights, and for the Śūdras it is twelve days.
All the social classes (varṇas), according to their respective order, should perform their own ritual duties by means of those days numbered as ten, twelve, a month, and a half-month.
The ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed according to the prescribed rules for the sake of the deceased;
men should perform the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for the deceased within one year.
Then, once he has attained the status of a father, his propitiation must be performed with auspicious rites such as the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices,
according to the indications of the Śruti.
O Rākṣasa, for the sake of his ancestors, he himself should perform acts such as the gift of land, by which his ancestors become well-pleased and proceed [to their higher state]. (VamP 15.50)
Whatever is most desired and whatever is dear to one in the home,
that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that [the merit] be inexhaustible.
The triple Veda (trayī) must be studied constantly, and one should always remain devoted to the learned;
wealth should be acquired in accordance with dharma, and sacrifices should be performed according to one's ability.
And furthermore, O Rākṣasa, that which one does not feel self-reproach for while performing it should be done without hesitation, provided it is not something to be concealed from great men.
For a man living in the world who conducts himself in this manner while remaining at home,
there is the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as excellence both in this world and in the next.
This supreme stage of life, that of the householder, has been declared in brief;
now we shall proclaim the dharma of the forest-dweller’s stage—let it be attended to.
Having observed the continuity of offspring and the impermanence of the body, we shall proclaim the dharma of the forest-dweller stage of life; let it be heeded.
In that regard, there is the emaciation of the self through forest-dwelling and austerities,
sleeping on the ground, celibacy, and the performance of rites for the ancestors, the gods, and guests.
Performing oblations three times a day, bathing three times a day, wearing matted hair and bark garments,
and subsisting on forest oils— this is the rule for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
The renunciation of all attachments, the practice of celibacy, freedom from pride, mastery over the senses, and not dwelling for long in a single residence; VamP_15.59.
Absence of new undertakings, moderation in food, subsisting on alms-food, freedom from excessive anger, the desire for the awakening of self-knowledge, and likewise the realization of the Self.
The duties pertaining to the fourth stage of life have been proclaimed by us to you;
now listen, O night-stalker, to the other duties pertaining to the social classes.
The householder stage, the student stage, and the forest-dweller stage—
these three stages of life have been declared for the Kṣatriya as well, along with those very same conducts prescribed for the twice-born.
The state of a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa) and the state of a householder (gārhasthya)—these two stages of life belong to the Vaiśyas.
However, O night-walker, for the Śūdra, the state of a householder alone is the highest.
One should not neglect here the duties prescribed for one's own caste and stage of life;
the Sun becomes enraged with him who neglects them.
O night-stalker, when the sun is angry with a man, he strives for the destruction of his family and the increase of his diseases.
Therefore, one should never abandon the duty pertaining to one's own caste, nor should one neglect the lineage of one's family;
for the Sun-god indeed becomes enraged with him who abandons his own inherent dharma.
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by the sages, Sukeśin bowed down to those great seers who were treasures of Brahman and,
looking back again and again at dharma, flew up and departed for his own city.
Pulastya said: Then, O celestial sage, Sukeśin, having gone to his own excellent city,
summoned all the Rākṣasas and spoke these righteous words.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, charity, compassion, patience, celibacy, and freedom from pride. (VamP 16.2)
Speech that is auspicious, truthful, and sweet; constant performance of virtuous deeds and delight in them; and the practice of right conduct—these lead to the higher world.
Thus did the sages speak to me concerning the primordial and ancient dharma;
therefore, I command you all: let this be done without hesitation.
Pulastya said: Then, at the word of Sukeśin, all those night-stalkers,
with joyful minds, established that dharma consisting of thirteen limbs.
Thereupon, the night-stalkers attained even greater prosperity,
endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, and always accompanied by their attendants and retinues.
The splendor of that light of those great-souled Rākṣasas was such that neither the sun,
nor the stars, nor the moon were able to shine.
Thereupon, O Brahmin, he became the leader of the night-stalkers in the three worlds;
by day he was like the moon, and at night he was like the sun.
Because the movement of the sun in the sky could not be discerned,
they thought that excellent city was the moon itself, owing to its brilliance.
"Night has come," they thought, and thus they release their bloom;
for in the lotus-pools, O Brahmin, the lotuses, perceiving night as their friend, have blossomed at night, desiring to bestow their splendor.
Having perceived that it was the time of night, the owls departed;
but the crows, having learned of this, then began to kill the owls during the day.
But the *snātakas*, devoted to bathing and silent recitation (*japa*), remain immersed up to their necks in rivers at night, having ascertained that it is daytime [by the moon]. (VamP 16.12)
At that time, during the appearance of the city, the wheels did not separate;
measuring the day, they spoke loudly thus: VamP_16.13: "This is indeed the day."
Surely, by some wheel-tailed bird separated from its mate,
life was abandoned after crying out in desolation on the shore of the river.
Then, overcome by compassion, Vivasvat, scorching the entire world with his intense rays, does not set at all.
Others say that some man named Cakra must have died,
for alas, his beloved wife has performed penance, afflicted by grief for her husband.
The Lord Divākara was indeed propitiated by him through austerity;
therefore, that Sun, the conqueror of the Moon, never truly sets.
O great sage, in the sacrificial halls during the ritual, the performers of the sacrifice, together with the officiating priests, carried out their rites even at night.
The great devotees of the Bhagavān perform worship of Viṣṇu with devotion;
others [worship] the Sun and the Moon, while still others [worship] Brahmā and Hara.
And those filled with desire thought that the moon had done well,
since this delightful night was made to possess perpetual moonlight.
Others said: "The Teacher of the World, the wielder of the wheel, the self-controlled one, has been worshipped by us with sincere devotion using great fragrances and auspicious flowers."
Accompanied by Lakṣmī, the great yogi [resides] in the four months beginning with Nabhas;
this second [observance], named Aśūnyaśayana, grants all desires.
Thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, granted him an excellent bed,
which was never devoid of great riches and whose crest never set.
Having seen that the moon had performed severe and arduous penance with the desire to propitiate Rudra, they spoke thus to Rohiṇī, the queen: "The waning of the moon is certain. (VamP 16.24)
On the meritorious Akṣaya-aṣṭamī, Śambhu, being pleased, spontaneously granted her a boon according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Others said: "Hari was certainly propitiated by Candramas through this unbroken vow;
therefore, he is the unbroken (Akaṇḍa) moon in the sky."
Others said that the hare-marked moon had certainly secured protection for himself by worshipping both feet of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable.
Therefore, that radiant moon, surpassing the sun,
brings us joy and shines by day like the sun.
Indeed, it is perceived through many other signs that this is truly so;
for the sun, defeated by the hare-marked moon, does not shine as it did before.
"Just as these lotuses— smooth, covered with humming bees,
and in full bloom— appear, the rising of the sun is certainly at hand."
And since these beds of blooming night-lotuses shine so brightly,
it is therefore known that the powerful moon has risen.
O Nārada, as they were conversing there, the Sun considered their words, thinking: "What indeed is this that the world speaks of as auspicious or inauspicious?"
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the Sun, entered into meditative absorption;
he beheld the world on all sides, the three realms devoured by the night-stalkers.
Then the Blessed One, the knower of yoga, perceiving the intolerance of Teja and that increase of the night-stalker, reflected upon it.
Then he recognized them all as pure and devoted to virtuous conduct,
intent on the worship of gods and Brahmins, and endowed with righteousness.
Then the Sun, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas, the lion to the elephant of darkness, whose great rays were like claws, considered how to destroy that [obstacle].
Then the Lord of the Day (Indra) perceived a vulnerability among the Rākṣasas:
namely, their deviation from their own duty, which causes the destruction of all dharma.
Then, overcome by anger, Bhānu beheld that city of the Rākṣasas at his will with rays that pierce the enemy.
Then, seen by Bhānu with eyes swollen with rage,
he fell from the sky like a celestial body whose merit has been exhausted.
Beholding the city falling, Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa loudly uttered this: "Homage to Bhava! Homage to Śarva! (VamP 16.40).
Hearing that cry of lamentation, all the celestial *cāraṇas* wandering through the sky cried out, "Alas! Alas! This devotee of Hara is falling! (VamP 16.41).
The omnipresent and imperishable Śarva heard those words uttered by Tāraṇa;
having heard them, he reflected: "By whom shall this one be cast down to earth?"
The Lord of the Gods, the thousand-rayed one, learned of that;
then the three-eyed one became enraged at the destruction of the city of the Rākṣasas.
But being enraged, he beheld that radiant Lord;
as soon as he was seen by the Three-eyed One, he fell from the celestial realm.
He fell from the sky onto a path frequented by the wind,
landing there by chance like a stone released from a machine.
Then, released from the path of the wind, his body radiant like a *kiṃśuka* flower,
he descended from the sky, surrounded by *kinnaras* and *cāraṇas*.
Surrounded by celestial bards, the sun shines as it descends from the sky,
like a half-ripened palm fruit surrounded by monkeys.
Then the sages, having approached, replied to Bhānumālin:
"Descend into the field of Hari if you desire your own welfare."
Then, even as he was falling, Vivasvat spoke to those whose wealth is penance:
"Tell me quickly, what is that meritorious field of Hari?"
The sages said to Sūrya: "Listen to the field of great fruit belonging now to Vāsudeva, and that which will belong in the future to Śaṅkara."
From the place where he lay in yogic sleep until the sight of Keśava,
this holy field of Hari is the city named Vārāṇasī.
Having heard that, the Blessed One Bhānu, scorched by the fire of the eye of Bhava,
fell indeed into the space between Varaṇā and Asī.
Then, as the sun was sinking into her body and burning it,
he approached Varaṇā and plunged into her at his will.
Afflicted by the fire from the eye of the Three-eyed One, he repeatedly brandished his sword Varaṇā and again and again whirled it about like a circle of fire (alātacakra).
In the meantime, O Brahmin, the sages, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
nāgas, vidyādharas, as well as birds and apsarases [were present].
O Sage, as many spirits, ghosts, and other beings as were situated in the chariot of the Sun, so many went to the abode of Brahmā to report [the matter].
Then Brahmā, the lord of the gods, together with the deities,
went to the delightful Mandara, the abode of Maheśvara, for the sake of the sun.
Having gone and seen Śaṅkara, the lord of gods who holds the trident in his hand,
he propitiated him and brought [the image] to Vārāṇasī for the sake of Bhāskara.
Then Śaṅkara, taking Divākara again by the hand and giving him the name Lopa, placed him upon the chariot once more.
When the sun had been re-established, Brahmā approached Sukeśin and,
together with his kinsmen and his city, raised him once again into heaven.
Having placed Sukeśī upon his lap and embraced Śaṅkara,
he bowed to the god Keśava and went to his own home, which was like that of Virāja.
Thus, O Nārada, in ancient times the city of Sukeśin was struck down upon the earth by Bhāskara;
yet the Sun, though cast toward the surface of the ground by Bhava, was not utterly consumed by his gaze.
The Sun was raised from the surface of the earth by Bhava once again for the sake of illumination;
and the Lord of the Night-stalkers too was raised into the sky, along with his city and his kinsmen, by the Self-Existent One.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, regarding those [deities] whom you have mentioned as being directed toward the Moon by those possessed of desire—"
Speak of them for the propitiation of the two gods, Hari and Īśa.
Pulastya said: Listen, O lover of the Kali age, to the meritorious vows proclaimed by those desiring [their fulfillment],
for the propitiation of Śarva and the wise Keśava.
But when the full moon of Āṣāḍha arrives and the sun enters its northern course,
then the Lord of Gods, the husband of Śrī, sleeps upon the coils of the serpent.
When that Lord had fallen asleep, the gods, Gandharvas, and Guhyakas,
as well as the mothers of the gods, also fell asleep in succession.
Nārada said:
"Tell me the supreme ritual for the bed of Kuru and the others,
placing Janārdana at the forefront and following everything in due order."
Pulastya said:
O ascetic, when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Gemini during the bright fortnight,
on the eleventh day, the Lord of the World should prepare for his sleep.
Having made a couch of the coils of the serpent Śeṣa and worshipped Keśava,
and having likewise properly performed the investiture with the sacred thread and duly honored the twice-born, [he should proceed].
Having obtained permission from the Brahmins on the twelfth day, being self-restrained and pure, and wearing yellow garments, he should take a restful sleep with the thought, "May it be well."
Then, on the thirteenth day, Kāma sleeps upon a beautiful bed fashioned with the fragrant blossoms of Kadamba trees.
Then, on the fourteenth day, the yakṣas sleep in comfort and coolness upon golden lotuses provided with soft beds and pillows.
On the full moon day, the Lord of Umā lies down upon a bed of skins,
having bound his mass of matted hair with another skin made from a tiger.
Then the Sun enters the zodiac sign of Cancer;
thereafter, it becomes night for the immortals, marking the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
Likewise, O sinless one, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, Brahmā sleeps upon a bed made of blue lotuses,
demonstrating the supreme path to all worlds.
Viśvakarman on the second day, the Daughter of the Mountain on the third, Vināyaka on the fourth, and Dharmarāja on the fifth. (VamP 17.14)
On the sixth day Skanda sleeps; on the seventh, the Blessed Sun;
likewise Kātyāyanī on the eighth, and Kamalālayā on the ninth.
On the tenth day of the dark fortnight, the lords of the serpents, subsisting on air alone, go to sleep;
and on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, O Brahmin, the Sādhyas also go to sleep.
O Sage, this sequence has been told to you regarding the sky and so forth during sleep;
while the gods were thus asleep, the rainy season arrived.
"Kaṅka cranes ascend the best of mountains together with herons;
crows too build their nests, O bull among sages;
and these crows sleep during the season, languid from bearing their young."
On whichever lunar day Viśvakarman Prajāpati goes to sleep,
that auspicious and meritorious second day is declared to be Aśūnyaśayana (the Unempty Bed).
On that lunar day, O Sage, one should worship Hari— who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, has four arms, sits upon a couch, and is together with Lakṣmī— with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, one should gradually place fruits upon the bed for the deity;
having thus offered fragrant items, Madhusūdana should be addressed as follows.
O Trivikrama, O Infinite One, O Abode of the World, just as you are never separated from Lakṣmī,
so may your bed here always remain unforsaken by us alone through your grace.
O God, just as your bed is not empty because it is indeed equal to Lakṣmī, O Acyuta, Lord of Śrī, and giver of boons;
by that truth, O Viṣṇu of immeasurable prowess, may there be no destruction of my household life, O God.
Having uttered this and bowed to the Lord, propitiating him again and again, O divine sage, one should eat at night, avoiding oil and alkaline substances. (VamP 17.24)
On the second day, the wise man should give fruits to an eminent brahmin, offering them while reciting: "May Lakṣmīdhara be pleased with me."
By this procedure, one should observe the Cāturmāsya vow for as long as the sun remains visible while situated in the zodiac sign of Scorpio.
Then, O Sage, the gods awaken one by one in succession:
when the sun is situated in Libra, Hari awakens, then Kāma, and after that Śiva.
There, on the second image, is the form of Lakṣmīdhara,
accompanied by a bed and coverlets according to one's own means.
O great sage, this first vow has been declared to you;
when it is observed, no one here shall suffer separation.
