Likewise, that auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight which occurs in the month of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada) and is joined with the lunar mansion Mṛgaśiras is known as Kālāṣṭamī.
On that lunar day, Śaṅkara sleeps within all the liṅgas;
it is taught that when he dwells in their presence, worship there becomes inexhaustible.
There, the wise man should indeed bathe with cow urine and water;
having bathed, he should worship the Three-eyed Lord with dhattūra flowers.

O best of the twice-born, having uttered, "May Virūpākṣa be pleased with me," one should give incense made from the resin of the kesara tree, an offering of honey and clarified butter, and the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) along with gold to a Brahmin as the food-offering (naivedya). 17.33.
Likewise, in the month of Āśvayuja, one who is fasting and has conquered the senses should perform a bath with cow dung on the ninth day, offer worship with lotuses,
burn resin from the Sarja tree as incense, and present honey and sweetmeats as the food offering.
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, one should perform an ablution on the ninth;
"May Hiraṇyākṣa be pleased with me"—this is the prescribed offering, along with sesame seeds as the sacrificial fee.
In the month of Kārttika, one should perform a bath with milk, worship with Karavīra flowers,
offer incense made from the resin of the Śrīvāsa tree, and present an offering of honey and milk-rice (pāyasa).
An offering of food and silver should be given as a gift to the elder brother;
one should speak without harshness, saying, "May the Lord of Beings be pleased."
Having observed a fast on the eighth day, one should perform an ablution on the ninth;
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the worship with curd is prescribed for the goddess Bhadrā.
One should offer incense made from the resin of the *śrīvṛkṣa* tree, and as an oblation, honey with rice; red *śāli* rice is proclaimed as the appropriate sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The wise should utter the words: "Homage! May Śarva be pleased. (VamP 17.39)
In the month of Pauṣa, there should be a ritual bath and worship with sacrificial oblations and auspicious tagara;
the incense should be the resin of madhuka, and the food offering should consist of honey and śaṣkulī cakes.
A gift (dakṣiṇā) consisting of a casket is prescribed for the pleasure of the Teacher of the World;
one should say, "Homage to you, O Lord of Gods," and proclaim, "O Three-eyed One."
In the month of Māgha, one should perform a bath with water infused with *kuśa* grass, worship with *mṛgamada* (musk),
offer incense made from the resin of the *padma* tree, and present as an offering rice mixed with sesame seeds.
One should offer milk-rice together with the sacrificial oblation and gold, and utter these words:
"May Mahādeva, the Lord of Umā, be pleased with me."
In this very manner, the breaking of the fast is prescribed after six months;
at the conclusion of the fast, one should perform the ritual bathing of the Three-eyed Lord in due order.
Having anointed the deity with *gorocanā* mixed with jaggery, one should worship him, saying:
"Be pleased; I am wretched, O Lord. Perform what is fitting for the destruction of my grief."
Then, O best of the twice-born, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Phālguna, one who is firm in his vows should undertake the prescribed fast.
On the second day, one should then perform a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should worship with kunda flowers and also burn sandalwood incense.
O Sage, one should offer as an oblation rice with jaggery and ghee in a copper vessel;
and to the twice-born, one should give a sacrificial fee along with the oblation,
and please them by reciting the name of Rudra while offering a pair of garments.
In the month of Caitra, one should bathe with udumbara fruits and worship with mandāraka flowers;
a wise person should burn guggulu incense known as "buffalo-scented" (mahiṣākhya) mixed with clarified butter.
One should offer clarified butter along with water as a refreshing oblation;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), together with the food offering, is declared to consist of a deerskin.
"O Lord of Dance, salutations to you! Having uttered this, O Nārada, one should perform an act of propitiation for the Lord of the Gods, endowed with faith.
In the month of Vaiśākha, bathing with fragrant flowers and water is prescribed;
O Lord, the worship of Śaṅkara is said to be performed with mango blossoms.
The wise one offered incense mixed with resin and ghee, an oblation of food accompanied by fruit and clarified butter, and also performed the silent recitation of the Lord’s name as "Kālaghna."
One should present water-pots together with food offerings to a Brāhmaṇa who wears the sacred thread,
who possesses food and other provisions, and whose mind is fixed upon that [deity] and devoted to it.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should bathe with *āmalaka* fruits and likewise worship with *arka* flowers;
one should also incense the Three-eyed Lord, which brings about nourishment for the future.
O God, one should offer groats mixed with ghee and smeared with curd;
and being devoted, one should also give the gift of sandals, a water-vessel, and an umbrella.
"Salutations to you, O destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, O remover of Pūṣan’s teeth!
One should recite this with devotion for the pleasure of the Lord of the World. (VamP 17.57)
In the month of Āṣāḍha, bathing is prescribed, as well as worship with bilva fruits;
one should offer white dhattūra flowers and likewise burn silhaka resin as incense.
The food offerings are cakes with ghee; the sacrificial fee consists of barley with ghee.
One should loudly utter this: "Salutations to you, O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice! (VamP 17.59).
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, having performed his bath with deer-food,
he should worship Hara with śrīvṛkṣa leaves and fruits, and likewise offer incense of aguru.
One should offer as an oblation food with ghee, curd, cakes along with sweetmeats,
rice mixed with curd, rice with sesame, black gram, parched grain, and fried cakes.
One should indeed give to a Brāhmaṇa a sacrificial fee consisting of a white bull, a beautiful tawny cow, gold, and red garments;
and the wise should recite the name of Śambhu as "Gaṅgādhara."
With these other six months, he performs the excellent breaking of the fast;
thus, having fully worshipped the Six-Symbolled One for a complete year,
he obtains his desires inexhaustibly, according to the word of Maheśvara.
O divine sage, this meritorious vow, which brings about the inexhaustibility of all things and is auspicious, was spoken by Rudra himself; it is exactly so and not otherwise.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
O Brahman, when in the month of Āśvayuja the lotus of the Lord of the World [appears]...
Then, indeed, these [Vedas] emerged from his navel among the gods. 18.1.
At the tip of Kandarpa’s hand was a beautiful kadamba tree;
because of that kadamba, his supreme delight increased.
O Nārada, even for Maṇibhadra, the lord of the yakṣas,
a banyan tree appeared, and he always performed his ascetic observances there.
In the heart of Maheśvara, an auspicious *dhattūra* tree was born;
and that tree became the constant attendant of Śarva.
From the center of Brahmā’s body was born Khaḍara Kaṇṭakī, who possessed the luster of emerald; he was the most excellent son of Viśvakarman.
In the palm of Girijā’s hand, a jasmine bud appeared;
on the head of the Lord of Gaṇas, a sindhuvāraka flower resting upon his crest shone brilliantly.
On the left side of Yama is the palāśa tree;
on the south and north is the black udumbara, born from Rudra, which causes trembling and is like a bull.
For Skanda, the bandhujīva tree was [the gift] from Bandhula; for Ravi, it was the aśvattha;
for Kātyāyanī, the śamī-born tree; and for Lakṣmī, the bilva tree appeared in her hand.
O Brahman, for the lord of the Nāgas,
a clump of reeds was born upon the broad tail and back of Vāsuki, as white and black dūrvā grass.
A green sandalwood tree has grown in the hearts of those to be converted;
when all have thus been born [into the faith], through that, there shall be delight.
In that delightful and auspicious time, on whichever it may be the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Viṣṇu; by that, his [moral] deficiency is fulfilled.
With flowers, fruits, or even with roots endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor,
as well as with the most excellent medicinal herbs, [he should worship] until the arrival of autumn.
Ghee, sesame seeds, rice, barley, gold, and so forth;
jewels, pearls, corals, and various kinds of garments.
The flavors— sweet, pungent, sour, astringent, salty,
and bitter— should be offered, provided that they are indeed unbroken.
For the sake of worshipping that Great-Souled Keśava,
[these gifts] should be offered when a full year has passed without interruption in one's home.
O celestial sage, having observed the fast and remaining self-controlled on the second day,
he should bathe with that same water by which he has indeed kept his vow unbroken throughout the year.
Anointment with *siddhārthaka* seeds or sesame seeds is likewise prescribed;

one should perform the bathing of Padmanābha with clarified butter (*havis*). For the fire-oblation (*homa*), that same [substance] is declared [to be used], and for the gift (*dāna*), O twice-born, one’s own capacity is what matters.
Then one should worship Keśava with flowers, beginning from his feet;
one should offer various kinds of incense so that [the merit] may endure for a supreme year.
One should worship the Teacher of the World with gold, jewels, and garments;
one should offer meat, sugar-cane products, sweets, and sacrificial oblations.

Then, O best of sages, having fully worshipped Padmanābha, the Lord of Gods and Teacher of the World, one should make this request with the following mantra, O observer of excellent vows: (VamP 18.20)
Homage be to you, O Padmanābha, O Consort of Lakṣmī, O You of Great Splendor!
May dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa be unimpaired for me.
O Keśava, whose eyes are like blossoming lotus petals, as you are unbroken in every respect, by that truth may all my religious duties remain unimpaired today.
Thus, O Brahmin, having fasted for a full year with his senses subdued, he should indeed complete the vow without interruption regarding all matters.
When this vow has been practiced, the deities are clearly pleased;
for indeed, the inexhaustible [attainments] of dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa, and so forth, come to pass.
These vows, which have been declared by those desiring worldly rewards, have now been told to you by me;
I shall now, however, explain this auspicious Vaiṣṇava cage.
Homage, homage to you, O Govinda! Taking up your Sudarśana discus, protect me in the eastern direction, O Viṣṇu; to you I have gone for refuge.
O Viṣṇu of immeasurable luster, who has the lotus-navelled Kaumodakī mace;
protect me from the south, for I have come to you for refuge. (VamP 18.27)
Taking up the Saunanda mace, he said: "Salutations to you, O Supreme Person!
O Viṣṇu, protect me from the west; I have come to you for refuge."
O lotus-eyed one, taking up the pestle that shatters [all things], protect me!
O Lord of the World, I have gone to you for refuge in the northern quarter.
Taking up the Śārṅga bow and the Nārāyaṇa weapon, O Hari, he said:
"Salutations to you! Protect me, O slayer of Rakṣasas; I have come for refuge in the northeast."
O Viṣṇu, O Sacrificial Boar, protect me from the south-eastern quarter, holding the great conch Pāñcajanya and the lotus that is to be awakened within. (VamP 18.31)
O divine-formed man-lion, taking the hide of the sun and likewise the sword of the moon, protect me in the south-west from the Rākṣasas.
Holding the Vaijayantī garland and the Śrīvatsa as your neck-ornament, O God with the horse-head, protect me in the northwest; salutations be unto you! (VamP 18.33)
O Janārdana, having mounted Vainateya in the intermediate space, protect me always, O unconquered one; salutations to you, O invincible one! (VamP 18.34)
Having mounted Viśālākṣa, protect me in the netherworld (rasātala)!
O Akūpāra, salutations to you; O Mahāmoha, let there be salutations to you! VamP_18.35 //
Having formed a cage of eight arms upon my hands, head, feet, and sides, protect me, O God; salutations to you, O Supreme Person!
O best of the twice-born, this great Vaiṣṇava armor was spoken of long ago by the Lord for the sake of protection, together with Kātyāyanī.
There she destroyed the Dānava Mahiṣāsura,
as well as Namara, Raktabīja, and other thorns of the gods.
Nārada said:
Who was this woman named Kātyāyanī, who slew the Asura Mahiṣa,
as well as Namara, Raktabīja, and the other Kurakaṇṭakas?
Who is this one named Mahiṣa, and in whose lineage was he born?
And who is this man called Raktabīja, and whose son is he?
O dear one, you ought to tell me this in detail and exactly as it happened.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O sage, as I shall relate this sin-destroying narrative concerning this Durgā Kātyāyanī, who is always the bestower of boons.
In ancient times, there were two fierce and most powerful Asuras,
Rambha and Karambha, both of whom caused agitation to the world.
O celestial sage, those two sons of the Daityas performed austerities for the sake of obtaining sons;
for many groups of years, they remained in the water at Pañcanada.
There, one was situated in the midst of water, and the second was likewise surrounded by fire;
Karambha and Rambha were both facing the yakṣa Mālapaṭa.
Vāsava seized with his two feet one who was submerged in the water in the form of a crocodile and struck him at will.
Then, his brother having perished, the mighty Rambha, overwhelmed with anger,
desired to offer his own head into the fire after cutting it off.
Then, seizing his sword which was as radiant as the sun, he desired to cut off his own head; however, he was restrained by Agni.
And it was said: "O best of Daityas, do not destroy yourself by yourself; for though another may be difficult to kill, one's own self is even more difficult to overcome. (VamP 18.48)
"O hero, whatever you pray for, I shall grant it as you desire.
Do not die; for the story of one who has died here truly becomes lost. (VamP 18.49)
Then Rambhā spoke these words: "If you indeed grant me a boon, let there be a son for me who is a conqueror of the three worlds and superior to you in splendor."
O Purifier, he shall be invincible by all the gods, men, and Daityas;
possessing great strength like the wind, able to assume any form at will, and skilled in the knowledge of weapons.
The sage said to him, "O Brahmin, it shall be exactly as you wish;
from whichever woman you fix your mind, from her a son shall be born."
Having been addressed thus by the god Agni, the Dānava went to see the Yakṣa Mālavaṭa, who was surrounded by Yakṣas.
A lotus-treasure dwells there for them, with no other consciousness;
as do elephants, buffaloes, horses, cows, and swarming goats and sheep.
O ascetic, upon seeing them, the king of the Dānavas then conceived a desire for his queen, who was endowed with beauty and three years of age.
Desiring him, that powerful woman approached the lord of the Daityas;
and he too, impelled by destiny, went to her.
A fetus was conceived within her; then the Dānava, taking her with him, entered Pātāla and went from there to his own abode.
Seen by all the Dānavas and abandoned by his kinsmen,
being reviled as "one who commits improper acts," he went once more to Mālavaṭa.
That queen of beautiful appearance also went together with that very husband to that supreme and meritorious Yakṣa-maṇḍala.
Then, while he was dwelling there, O sage, that Śyāmā gave birth;
she brought forth a radiant son, Mahiṣa, who could assume any form at will.
Another buffalo beheld her as she had reached her season;
yet she approached the excellent Diti, guarding her own virtue.
And beholding that buffalo with its nose uplifted,
the Dānava drew his sword and swiftly rushed toward the buffalo.
By him, too, the Daitya was struck in the heart with two sharp horns;
with his heart pierced, he fell to the ground and died.
When her husband was dead, that Śyāmā sought refuge with the Yakṣas.
Then that virtuous woman, having warded off the buffalo, was protected by the Guhyakas.
Then, having been warded off by the yakṣas, the enemy of horses (Kārttikeya), afflicted by passion, fell into a divine lake; thereupon he died at the hands of the daityas.
Known by the name Namara, possessed of great strength and prowess,
he remained there relying upon the yakṣas, slaughtering beasts of prey, O Sage.
And that lord of the Daityas was placed upon the funeral pyre by the Yakṣas, led by Mālavaṭa;
and Śyāmā ascended that husband of hers.
Then, from the midst of the fire, there arose a man of fierce appearance;
terrifying with sword in hand, he put those yakṣas to flight.
Then all the buffaloes were slain by that great-souled one,
with the sole exception of the buffalo Rambha-nandana, who was protected by his guardian.
O great sage, that Daitya known by the name Raktabīja was remembered as one who had conquered all the gods, including Indra, Rudra, Arka, and the Maruts.
Though the leaders of the Danus possessed such power, the enemy of the horse (Viṣṇu) shone there with superior splendor;
and he was consecrated in the kingdom by the great lords of the Asuras, Śambara, Tāraka, and others, who had been utterly defeated.

Unable to prevail, the gods together with the world-protectors, along with the sacrificial fires and the sun, abandoned their stations; and the moon, Indra, and the sun were driven far away from Dharma.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then the gods, utterly defeated by Mahiṣa, abandoned their abodes along with their vehicles and weapons.
Placing Ṛcīka at their head, they then went to see the wielder of the discus, the Lord of Śrī.
Having gone there, they saw the two supreme gods, Śaṅkara and the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), seated together;
and having seen them and bowed down, those seekers of perfection reported the activities of Mahiṣa and the others.
O Lord, having usurped the offices of the Aśvins, Sūrya, Indra, Vāyu, Agni, and Brahmā, as well as those of Varuṇa, Śakra, and others,
Mahiṣāsura has cast us out from heaven and established us upon the earth.
Having heard these words of those who have come for refuge, you two should speak what is beneficial for the gods;
otherwise, we shall indeed go this day to the netherworld, being slaughtered in battle by the Dānava.
Having heard these words of those whose minds were agitated, and seeing them thus together with Śaṅkara, Murāri,
the imperishable-souled Hari, suddenly became as wrathful as the fire of universal destruction.
Then, due to the grace of Madhusūdana, as well as that of Pitāmaha together with Śaṅkara,
and likewise among the deities beginning with Śakra, great supernatural power and splendor issued forth from their mouths.
And that most excellent splendor, resembling a mountain peak, became one, O Sage;
for that splendor had been brought forth by that peerless great seer, Kātyāyana.
Enveloped by that splendor emitted by the Ṛṣi, she was like a thousand suns blazing with light;
and from that [splendor] was born Kātyāyanī, with tremulous, long eyes, her body purified through yoga.
Then from the face of Maheśvara there appeared three eyes with the brilliance of fire;
from the southern [face] came the hair with the splendor of Indra, and likewise eighteen arms were produced.
The pair of breasts became beautiful through the energy of Soma, while the waist was formed by the energy of Indra;
and the thighs, shanks, and hips were produced from the energy of Varuṇa.
The two feet of the Great-Grandfather of the World became like the calyxes of lotuses;
even by the splendor of the suns, his toes and the fingers of his hands were outshone by the very luster of his own arms.
The ten teeth were from the Prajāpatis; the nose and the two ears were from Yakṣa and Māruta;
and the pair of eyebrows, possessing great beauty and resembling the bow of Kandarpa, shone forth from Sādhya.
Then that supreme and great splendor of the Ṛṣi became renowned on earth by the name Kātyāyanī;
she shone forth by that very name and became famous throughout the world.
The Giver of Boons, the wielder of the trident, gave him a trident; Murāri gave him a discus; Varuṇa gave him a conch;
Hutāśa gave him a spear; Śvasana gave him a bow; and Vivasvat gave him two quivers along with inexhaustible arrows.
Vajra and Indra together with the bell; Yama and his staff; Dhanada and his mace;
Brahmā and his rosary together with the water-pot; and Kāla with his fierce sword and shield.

Soma gave him a necklace along with a chowrie; the Ocean gave him a garland; Himavat gave him the king of beasts; Vasu, the master craftsman, gave him a crest-jewel, an earring, a half-moon, and an axe.
The king of the Gandharvas [offered] a vessel filled with drink, anointed with silver and of matching beauty;
the lord of serpents [offered] a necklace of snakes; and [the gods offered] garlands of unfading flowers and nectar.
Then the three-eyed goddess, supremely delighted among the gods, let out a loud, boisterous laugh;
and the best of deities—including Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Moon, Wind, Fire, and the Sun—praised her.
Homage be to the Divine One, worshipped by the gods, whose body is purified through yoga;
who, having spread herself over the earth in the form of sleep, [manifests as] thirst, shame, hunger, fear, and beauty.
Faith, mindfulness, nourishment, and likewise forbearance, shadow, power, and she whose abode is the lotus;
conduct, compassion, delusion, and illusion—homage be to the divine one who assumes the forms of worldly existence!
Then, praised by the best of gods, the goddess mounted the king of beasts and proceeded toward the mountain;
she went to the Vindhya, that great mountain with lofty peaks, which Agastya had once caused to become low-lying.
Nārada said:
O you of pure nature and conduct, tell me why the blessed great seer Agastya made Mount Kīrṇa-matha so low-crested; for what purpose and by what cause did he do this?
Pulastya said:
In ancient times, the path of the sun moving through the sky was obstructed by the Vindhya mountain.
Thereupon, the sun, having approached the Lotus-born Brahmā at the conclusion of a fire sacrifice, spoke these words.
I have come from afar to you, O twice-born one; O lord of sages, grant me deliverance!
Bestow upon me that gift which, when practiced by a wise man, brings peace in the celestial realms.
Having thus heard the words of Divākara, which were endowed with virtue, the son of the Jar (Kumbhayoni) then spoke these words:
"I shall grant you whatever gift your heart desires; no supplicant ever departs from me disappointed. (VamP 19.25)
Having heard these nectar-like words of the Pot-born Sage, the Lord placed his hand upon [Agastya’s] head and said:
"O Blessed One, exert yourself today so that this best of mountains may yield a path for the Vindhya, by making it low."
Thus, at these words of Ravi, the one born from a jar (Agastya) then said: "Know that this is a mere pretext;
for by me the mountain with its low peaks shall be conquered by your rays. What distress can there be for you when it has taken refuge at my feet?"
Having spoken thus and having praised the Sun with devotion while bowing low,
the great seer born from a water-jar departed, leaving Daṇḍaka and increasing the size of the Vindhya mountain.
Having approached, the sage spoke these words to the mountain: "I shall go to a most meritorious and excellent great tirtha;
being old and unable to climb you, O venerable one, may you therefore immediately become lower."
Thus addressed by that supreme sage, the mountain Nīcaśṛṅga became humble;
and having traversed the Vindhya, that foremost of great seers spoke this to the mountain: VamP_19.30.
Until I have returned once more from that great hermitage with my body purified by a sacred bathing place, you must not grow here; otherwise, I shall curse you for your contempt.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One suddenly departed toward the southern direction into the intermediate space;
having ascended, he remained stationed in that quarter at the time when I, the Lord of Munis, travel there.
Having constructed there a most beautiful hermitage with gateways made of pure gold,
he then placed the daughter of Vidarbha within it and returned to his own pleasant hermitage.

During every season and at the times of the sacred festivals, that sage of immeasurable splendor always resided in that excellent hermitage; for the remainder of his time, he remained in Daṇḍaka, performing austerities.
Even Vinadhya, seeing the great hermitage in the sky, did not increase at all out of fear of the great seer;
thinking "he has not turned back," he remained with his peaks lowered even further.
Thus, O great sage, that lord of great mountains was indeed made to have low peaks by Agastya;
yet upon its high peak stands Durgā, praised by the sages, for the sake of destroying the Dānavas.
The gods, the siddhas, the great serpents, the vidyādharas, and all the hosts of spirits,
together with all the apsarases, stood around Kātyāyanī, free from sorrow and delighting her in return.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then, at that time, Kātyāyanī was dwelling there upon the peak of that best of mountains.
The two best of the Dānavas, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, beheld that ascetic woman.

Upon seeing him, the two enemies of the gods, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa—messengers of the demon Mahiṣāsura—quickly descended from Śaulā and went swiftly to their own abode; having seen the Lord of the Daityas, they spoke as follows.
"Be at ease, O Lord of Asuras; come now and let us see that Vindhya mountain there.
There dwells a goddess of great majesty, a maiden of beautiful form, more lovely than the celestial beauties."
For by her, whose locks are like clouds, the moon was conquered;
by the face of that slender lady, the three fires were conquered by her three eyes; and by her neck, the conch was conquered.

Her two breasts, well-rounded with their nipples slightly sunken, stood as if having conquered the frontal globes of an elephant; considering you to be the protector of all beings, they were made by Smara himself so difficult to overcome.
Her eighteen arms—plump, armed, and resembling the bodies of serpents—shine forth;
having recognized your prowess, they have been fashioned as if by desire itself.
And her waist, O Lord of Daityas, with its three folds like waves and its line of fine hair,
shines forth like a staircase constructed for Kama, who is terrified and anxious to ascend it out of fear.
That line of hair upon her, clinging to her swelling breasts, shone all the more;
it was like a stream of sweat from the God of Love as he trembled with fear at the ascent [of his chariot].
Her navel, deep and exceedingly radiant, turns to the right;
it is the very seal of that house of beauty, bestowed by the Queen of Love herself.
The lovely hips of the deer-eyed woman shine, adorned on all sides by her girdle;
we consider them to be the king of Kāma’s city, protected by a wall and difficult to assail.
The thighs of a maiden, hairless, smooth, and most excellent,
would shine like two regions established by the God of Love himself for the purpose of dwelling.
O Lord of the Asuras, Mahiṣa, that pair of feet of hers shines as if bent halfway;
for indeed, the Creator, having fashioned them, grew weary from the act of scrutiny and placed them upon the palm of his hand.
O Lord of the Daityas, her two well-rounded calves, free from hair, would have graced you;
for they were fashioned as if having stepped over the worlds, having indeed surpassed them through the merit of their form.
And her two feet, resembling the interior of a lotus, were indeed fashioned with great effort by the Creator; moreover, the rows of jewels upon her nails were like the garland of stars in the sky.
O Lord of the Danavas, having seen this maiden of such a form, bearing most terrible weapons,
we do not know who she is or whose daughter this young girl might be, even though we have looked at her as much as we desired.
"O Great Lord of Asuras, that unsurpassed jewel remains upon that ground;
having abandoned heaven, go yourself to the Vindhya mountains and behold it, and do whatever you deem desirable and appropriate."
Upon hearing from those two of the Goddess’s beautiful form, Mahiṣāsura set his mind upon her; there was no hesitation here, for Mahiṣa spoke thus: "She does not even exist. (VamP 20.17)
Long before, O Brahmin, auspicious and inauspicious stations have been assigned by the Creator for each man;
to whichever place he belongs, and in whatever manner, he is led there by others or goes there of his own accord.
Then the great lord of the Asuras commanded Muṇḍa, Namara, Caṇḍa, Viḍālākṣa, Piśaṅga, Vāṣkala, Ugrāyudha, Cikṣura, and Raktabīja.
Having beaten their drums, which were harsh with joy, those sons of Danu abandoned heaven and,
having arrived at the foot of the mountain and pitched their camp, they remained there.
Then, dispatched by Mahiṣāsura, there was a Daitya named Dundubhi, a leader of the Dānava hosts,
the son of Maya, who crushed the enemy armies and possessed a voice like the sound of a kettledrum.
O Brahmin, even while stationed in the sky, Dundubhi approached the goddess and spoke these words:
"O maiden, I am the messenger of the great asura, the peerless son of Rambhā in battle."
Kātyāyanī addressed Dundubhi: "Come, come, O lord of the Daityas, casting aside your fear!
Speak truly and without delusion the words which the son of Rambha has uttered."

When these words had been spoken, the son of Diti, having cast his garment upon the ground and seated himself comfortably on a supreme throne, spoke these words to the one born of Rambhā who was sitting nearby.
Dundubhī said:
"O Goddess, the Daitya Mahiṣāsura, the enemy of the gods, commands you thus:
'Since those immortals have been defeated by me in battle, they wander upon the earth deprived of their strength.'"

Heaven, the earth, and the paths of the wind are under my control, as are the netherworld and others such as Maheśvara; I am Indra, I am Rudra, I am the Sun—I am the sovereign over all worlds, O child. (VamP 20.26)
There is no one in heaven, nor on the surface of the earth, nor in the subterranean realm— whether a god, a warrior, or an asura— who,
having encountered me in battle, could survive, whether he be a bhūta, a yakṣa, or any being who wishes to live.
O charming one, O large-eyed lady, whatever jewels exist upon the earth, in heaven, or even in the depths of the netherworld—
all those have come to me today, acquired here through my prowess.
"You are a maiden who is the foremost jewel among women, and it is for your sake that I have reached this mountain.
Therefore, accept me here, the lord of the world; I am your worthy husband, powerful and sovereign."
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by the son of Diti, Durgā Kātyāyanī spoke to the son of Maya:
"It is true that you are the lord of the earth, O king of the Dānavas; it is true that the immortals have been conquered in battle."
"However, O Lord of Daityas, in our lineage there is a well-known custom called *śulka*.
If Mahiṣa grants that to me today, I shall truly accept the enemy of horses (Indra) as my husband."
Having heard these words, the son of Maya replied: "O lotus-petal-eyed one, name the bride-price;
for your sake, he would give even his own head—what indeed could the bride-price here be?"
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by the leader of the Danus, Kātyāyanī let out a loud roar and,
smiling, spoke these words for the welfare of all that is mobile and immobile.
The Goddess said:
"O Daitya, hear the bride-price established by my ancestors in our lineage:
he who shall conquer one born of my family at the front of battle, he shall indeed become her husband."
Pulastya said:
Having heard those words of the goddess, Dundubhi, the lord of the Dānavas,
went and reported them exactly as they were to Mahiṣa.
And that one of great splendor, leading all the Daityas, approached;
having reached the peak of the Vindhya mountains, he desired to fight Sarasvatī.
Then, O Nārada, the Daitya general named Cikṣura made the Dānava named Namara the leader of the army.
And he, having been appointed by him, took a portion of the powerful fourfold army and rushed swiftly toward the fortress.
Then, seeing him rushing toward them, the gods, led by Brahmā, spoke these words to the Great Goddess: "O Ambikā, bind on your armor! *VamP_20.39*
Then Durgā said to the gods: "O deities, I do not bind [you];
what lowliest of Dānavas could stand before me with armor on?"
When the goddess had not yet fashioned the armor that wards off weapons,
he then spoke the Viṣṇupañjara for her protection.
Protected by him, O Brahmin, that formidable Durgā assailed Mahiṣa, the best of the Dānavas,
who was incapable of being slain by all the gods.
Thus, in the past, that Vaiṣṇava cage was described by Śambhu, the best of gods, to the large-eyed goddess;
and indeed, by her, that lord of the Asuras, Mahiṣa, was destroyed with kicks of her feet.
O twice-born one, such is the power of the Viṣṇu-panjara, for it is sung as superior to all forms of protection;
who could inflict defeat in battle upon him in whose heart the Wielder of the Discus resides?
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
How did the goddess Kātyāyanī [slay] the mountain-dwelling Mahiṣāsura?
She likewise destroyed him along with his vehicle; such was the dispute in detail.
And this doubt, O Brahmin, revolves within my heart:
that while weapons were available, he crushed him with his feet.
Pulastya said:
Listen with an attentive mind to this ancient narrative,
which occurred at the beginning of the age of the gods— a meritorious tale that removes the fear of sin.
Thus, O Brahmin, that enraged Namuci, possessing great speed, was seen by the Goddess as she willed it, together with his elephants, horses, and chariots, as he rushed forward.
Then, bending his bow, the Daitya rained down volleys of arrows upon the mountain, just as clouds pour torrents of rain upon the sky.
Then, seeing the mountain covered by that shower of arrows,
the enraged Bhagavatī swiftly drew her excellent bow.
That bow, with its golden back, shone as it was forcibly bent by Durgā over the army of the Dānavas, like lightning among the clouds.
O observer of auspicious vows, he struck down some enemies of the gods with arrows, others with his sword,
others with his mace, and still others with his club and shield.
Though he is but one, this lion, resembling Time itself, destroys the many goddesses' enemies— the Dānavas— shaking his thick mane of hair.
The Daityas were struck by thunderbolts, their chests pierced by spears,
their necks torn by plows, and they were hacked apart by battle-axes.
With their heads split by clubs and their bonds severed by discuses,
they moved about, fell down, fainted, and others abandoned the battle.
Being struck by that fierce Durgā, those Daityas and Dānavas,
tormented by fear and thinking she was the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), fled in all directions.
Seeing the vanguard of the army broken and Durgā standing firm before him,
the demon arrived, mounted upon an intoxicated elephant.
Having approached with speed, he released a spear at the goddess;
the Dānava also hurled a trident at the lion in the battle.
As they were rushing forward, they were reduced to ashes by the goddess with a *huṃ* sound;
then Hari was seized from the middle by the lordly elephant.
Then, springing up with speed, he struck the Dānava with his palm;
the demon’s life departed, and having thrown him from the shoulder of Suñjara, he presented him to the Goddess.
O Brahmin, having seized the Dānava in the midst [of the assembly], Kātyāyanī, in her wrath,
whirled him around with her left hand and struck him like a drum.
Then, when such instruments were being played, she let out a loud, boisterous laugh;
from that laughter there arose various kinds of wondrous spirits.
Some had the faces of tigers and were fierce, while others had the forms of wolves;
some had the faces of horses, others the faces of buffaloes, and still others had the faces of boars.
Some had the faces of mice and cocks, and others had the faces of cows, goats, and sheep;
they possessed various kinds of faces, eyes, and feet, and likewise bore various types of weapons.
Some sing, others laugh, while others praise in groups;
still others play instruments there, and likewise some offer hymns of praise to Ambikā.
Together with those hosts of spirits, that goddess attacked and destroyed that Dānava army,
just as a great thunderbolt lays low the grain.
When that leader of the army had been slain, as well as the one who marched at the head of the host,
Cikṣura, the protector of the troops, then fought against the gods.
Drawing his firm bow back to his ear, that best of chariot-warriors rained down nets of arrows upon the earth, just as a cloud pours rain upon the ground.
Durgā, having cut those volleys of arrows with her own well-jointed shafts,
took up sixteen other arrows with golden feathers.
Then that beautiful woman, having slain four horses with four arrows,
struck down the charioteer with one and cut the banner with another.
Then Ambikā cut his bow, along with the arrow, with a single shaft;
when his bow was severed, the powerful one took up a sword and a shield.
As the Daitya was forcefully brandishing that sword together with his shield, [Viṣṇu] cut them apart with four arrows; thereupon, the Daitya took up a trident.
Brandishing his great trident, he then rushed toward Ambikā,
as delighted as a jackal in the forest at the sight of a lioness.
As he was charging forward, she, filled with rage, severed his feet, hands, and head with five arrows; struck down, the asura fell.
When that commander had been struck down, the great asura Tadogrāsya and the dānava Karālāsya rushed forward with speed.
Bāṣkala and Uddhata, as well as the one named Udagra who wields a formidable bow,
Durdhara, Durmukha, and another named Biḍālanayana.
These and other high-souled Dānavas, the best among the strong,
rushed toward Kātyāyanī with various weapons and missiles in their hands.
Seeing them, Durgā playfully took up a lute with her hand;
laughing, she likewise played upon an excellent hand-drum (ḍamaruka).
In whatever manner the goddess played those musical instruments,
in that very manner the hosts of spirits danced and laughed.
Then the Asuras, bearing weapons, approached Sarasvatī and struck her; but the Supreme Goddess seized them by their hair.
Having seized those great asuras by their hair and leaping from the lion onto the mountain peak,
the Mother of the World danced while playing the lute and drank the beverage of the universe.
Then, by the Goddess, the mighty great asuras had their pride shattered and their bodies torn apart by the blows of her staff-like arms;
they became disrobed and lifeless. Then, beholding those lords of the great asuras, [she acted].
The mighty Mahiṣāsura, however, put the hosts of beings to flight with the tips of his hooves;
likewise, he scattered other groups of spirits with his snout, his tail, his chest, and the wind of his breath.
And having crushed others with his thunderbolt-like roar and the tip of his horn, he rushed at the lion in battle, desiring to kill him; thereupon Ambikā fell under the sway of anger.
Then, out of anger, he whose horns were sharp quickly shattered mountains and the earth; agitating the oceans and destroying the clouds, he rushed toward the Ganges.
Then she bound the wicked one with a noose, and that lordly elephant became one with a dripping temple;
he lopped off the trunk-tip of the elephant, and he too was born again as a buffalo.
Then Amṛḍānī hurled a spear at him, and it fell to the earth with its base shattered;
she then cast a javelin given by Hutāśa, but it fell upon the sage with its tip blunted.
The discus of Hari, the destroyer of the wheel of the Daityas, was indeed hurled, yet it became as if it were no longer a discus;
and when the mace of the Lord of Wealth was brandished and thrown, it shattered and fell to the earth.
The noose of the Lord of Waters was also repelled by the great Asura with the tips of his tusks, snout, and hooves;
and the staff of Yama, hurled by him in his anger, was shattered into many fragments.
The thunderbolt hurled by the Lord of the Gods in this battle reached a state of extreme subtlety;
having abandoned the lion, it suddenly mounted the back of Mahiṣāsura’s buffalo from its difficult position.
While Mahiṣāsura was being carried on her back, he wallowed in pride due to his own prowess;
yet she, with her soft and tender feet, crushed him like a soaked hide.
Being crushed by her, he who resembled a mountain—though once powerful—became weak;
then she pierced his throat with a trident, and from it a man emerged holding a sword.

As soon as he had stepped out, [Viṣṇu] struck him in the heart with his foot, seized him by the hair in anger, and severed his head with an excellent sword; at that moment, the army of the Daityas raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (VamP 21.49).
Accompanied by Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, along with Tārā and Asiloman, the attendants of Bhavānī— whose eyes were terrified with fear—
entered Pātāla itself, afflicted by terror as they were being struck down by the Pramathas.
O great sage, seeing the victory of the goddess, the hosts of gods praise the goddess with hymns—
Nārāyaṇī, the foundation of the entire world, Kātyāyanī, who is both of terrible countenance and beautiful form.
Being praised by hosts of gods and *siddhas*, and having sat at the feet of Hara,
Durgā said to those gods, "I shall become [manifest] once more for the sake of the immortals," and having spoken thus, she entered them.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O Pulastya, let the further origin of the Goddess be told once more.
O best of those who know Brahman, I have a great curiosity today; [please explain] this in detail.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O sage; I shall tell you once more of her origin, [telling it] out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds and for the sake of slaying the demon Śumbha.
She who was the daughter of Himavat, the ascetic woman wedded by Bhava,
known by the name Umā— she became Kośāñjā, and from her was born the Kauśikī.
Having gathered together and gone to the Vindhya mountains, surrounded once more by hosts of spirits,
she will slay both Śumbha and Niśumbha with her excellent weapons.
Nārada said:
O Brahman, you have related that Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, died;
it behoves you to tell me how she was born as the daughter of Himavat.
Just as Kauśikī emerged from the treasury of Pārvatī,
so too did she slay the great Asuras Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Whose sons are these two heroes, Śumbha and Niśumbha, renowned as they are?
You should explain all of this in detail and exactly as it happened.
Pulastya said:
O sage, I shall tell you this: the origin of Pārvatī and the eternal birth of Skanda; listen with a focused mind.
When Satī had perished, Rudra remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy;
having fallen into a state of supportlessness, he resolved to perform austerities.
And he was the commander of the celestial army, the destroyer of the pride of the Daityas.
Then the gods were driven out by Śambhu, the lord of the army;
they were defeated by Mahiṣa, the lord of the Dānavas, who acted with great prowess.
Then they went to see the Lord of the Asuras, who bears the discus and the mace;
having sought refuge in Hari, the Great Swan on Śvetadvīpa.
Seeing those gods who had arrived, led by Śakra, the Supreme Person smiled and spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: VamP_22.13 //
"Have you been conquered by the evil-minded Mahiṣa, the lord of the Asuras,
that all of you have come together to my side in this manner?"
Therefore, O best of gods, do that which I tell you for the sake of your welfare,
so that by relying upon it, victory shall indeed be yours.
O gods, those who are known as the divine Pitṛs, the Agniṣvāttas and others,
have a daughter born of their mind named Menā.
O immortals, having honored that great guest with supreme faith,
you should now request Menā, the virtuous wife of Himavat, for this purpose.
In that [city], that ascetic woman will be endowed with beauty—
she by whom her dear life was cast off like a foul impurity due to Dakṣa’s wrath.
From Śaṅkara she shall give birth to a son who is a portion of his own splendor;
he shall slay the lord of the Daityas, Mahiṣa, along with his followers.
Therefore, go to that Kurukṣetra of great fruit;
there, at the sacred ford of Pṛthūdaka, let the imperishable ancestors be honored.
"If you all desire to avoid defeat by the enemy on this most auspicious and highly meritorious day, let it be done in this manner. (VamP 22.21)
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, the gods, led by Śakra,
joined their palms in reverence and questioned the Supreme Lord.
The gods said:
"What is this Kurukṣetra where the meritorious Pṛthūdaka is located? May the Blessed One tell us of the origin of that sacred ford."
What is this most meritorious lunar day (tithi), declared to be the best among all lunar days, on which the divine ancestors are indeed to be worshipped by us with great effort? (VamP 22.24)
Then, at the request of the gods, Murāri, the slayer of Kaiṭabha,
described the merit arising from Kurukṣetra as well as that specific lunar day.
The Blessed One said:
"In the beginning of the Kṛta age, there was a king named Ṛkṣa, born of the Lunar dynasty and possessed of great strength; from Ṛkṣa descended Saṃvaraṇa."
And he was consecrated by his father in his own kingdom while still a child;
even in his youth, he was devoted to righteousness and was always a devotee of mine.
His family priest was Vasiṣṭha, the son of Varuṇa;
that noble-minded sage taught him the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
Then, having entrusted all his duties to Vasiṣṭha, the treasure-house of asceticism, the prince went to the forest during a period when study was forbidden.
Then, diverted from his hunting expedition, he went alone into the lonely forest;
he proceeded to Vaibhrāja and then approached Unmādana.
Then, filled with curiosity, he wandered through the forest, which was filled with the flowers of all seasons, never satiated by the fragrance that permeated it on every side.
And he beheld the forest edge, covered with blooming red lotuses,
as well as white lotuses, night-lotuses, and blue water-lilies.
There, the apsarases and the daughters of the immortals were constantly sporting;
then, in their midst, Saṃvaraṇa beheld a maiden who was preeminent.
From the mere sight of her, that king was afflicted by the arrows of love;
and she too, upon seeing him, became distressed by the shafts of passion.
Both of them, tormented by the arrows of desire, fell into a state of delusion;
the king, his seat unsteady, fell from his horse onto the ground.
Approaching him, the high-souled Gandharvas, who can assume any form at will, sprinkled him with water; having approached, he regained consciousness in an instant.
She was then carried away by the apsarases to their own ancestral home,
and there she was comforted by them with the waters of their sweet words.
Having mounted his horse, he went to Pratiṣṭhāna, the best of cities;
having reached the summit of Mount Meru, he moved at will like an immortal.
Ever since Tapatī was seen by the descendant of Ṛkṣa on the mountain,
from that time forward she has not eaten during the day, nor does she sleep at night.
Then the son of Varuṇa, the omniscient one,
the repository of austerities, being unperturbed, understood that the heroic king was scorched by his ascetic fervor.
Leaping up, the great yogi entered the solar disc in the sky;
he beheld the god of fierce rays stationed upon his chariot.
Seeing that god Bhāskara, the best of the twice-born bowed;
and having been greeted with a bow in return by Bhāskara, he entered the chariot.
With his mass of matted locks blazing as he drew near the sun,
that glorious son of Varuṇa shone like a second sun.
Then, having been honored with the *arghya* offering by Bhāskara, that ascetic, whose wealth is his austerity,
was asked the reason for his arrival and replied to the Sun.
I have come, O Lord of Gods, O you of great splendor, to make a request of you:
for the sake of Saṃvaraṇa, you ought to grant him your daughter.
Then, O gods, that daughter Tapatī was presented by Divākara to Vasiṣṭha,
the foremost of the twice-born, who had come to his home for the sake of King Saṃvaraṇa.
Then, taking Sāvitrī with him, Vasiṣṭha returned to his own holy hermitage;
and the queen, remembering that son of the king, spoke to Vāruṇī with palms joined in reverence.
Tapatī said:

"O Brahmin, having fallen into distress, I saw in the forest a prince who was like the offspring of an immortal, accompanied by celestial nymphs as his attendants; indeed, I recognize him by his physical marks."
His auspicious feet were marked with the signs of the wheel, the mace, and the sword; his calves and thighs were like the trunks of elephants;
his hips were like those of a lion, and his waist was slender, bound by three folds.
His neck possesses the shape of a conch shell, and his arms are thick, firm, and very long;
likewise, his hands bear the marks of lotus petals, and his head shines with the form of a parasol.
His hair was dark blue and curly; his ears were symmetrical, as were his shoulders; his nose was perfectly straight;
his fingers were long with well-formed joints; and his feet, hands, and teeth were beautiful.
The prince is elevated in six respects, noble in heroism in three, deep in three, and long in three; likewise, he is red in five respects, dark in four, and bent in three.
With two white [lotuses] and four fragrant ones, ten lotuses were seen by him;
for the Blessed One, the Protector, having previously considered that prince on earth, surrounded him.
"O Lord, grant me to this ascetic who is endowed with virtue and who desires me;
for the virtuous do not say that one should give another to someone else when she has a different desire—O All-pervading One, please forgive me."
The God of Gods said:
Having been addressed thus by the daughter of Savitṛ, the Ṛṣi then became absorbed in meditation;
and perceiving that the daughter of the Sun was filled with desire, he, filled with joy, spoke these words.
"O daughter, that very son of the king whom you saw before and desire today has indeed come to my hermitage;
he is the son of Ṛkṣa, Saṃvaraṇa by name."
Then the king’s son came to that hermitage of the preeminent Brahmin;
having seen Vasiṣṭha and prostrated with his head, the lord of men stood there and beheld Tapatī.

And having seen her, whose eyes were as wide as lotuses, and thinking, "This is she whom I have seen before," he asked, "O best of the twice-born, who is this woman? Varuṇa’s son replied to that lord of men.
"O lord of men, this woman renowned on earth by the name Tapatī is the daughter of Vivasvat;
for your sake, I requested her from the Sun, and he granted her, and I brought her to my hermitage."
"Therefore, O lord of men, arise and take the hand of Queen Tapatī according to the prescribed rite.
Having been addressed thus, the king, greatly delighted, took the hand of Tapatī according to the rite.
Having obtained that husband who was pleasing to the mind, the slender Sūryāmā, whose splendor equaled that of Śakra,
took her delight in the most excellent palaces, just as the daughter of a Daitya did in heaven with the great Indra.
The God of gods said:
While she was performing penance, a son endowed with the marks of royalty was born to that best of men;
having been consecrated by the birth-rites and other ceremonies, he grew like a fire fed with clarified butter.
O gods, the tonsure ceremony was performed for this son of the Brahmin Mitrasaha by his father;
and when he was nine years old, the initiation ceremony was performed, whereby he became one who has mastered the rules of the Vedas and the Shastras.
Then, after four more years, he attained omniscience;
thus he became renowned on earth as Kuru, the son of Saṃvaraṇa, that supreme among men.
Then the king, having seen that his son was virtuous and auspicious,
made an effort to arrange a marriage alliance with a noble family.
The king gave his daughter Sodarṇinī, who was superior in beauty, to Kuru; he bestowed her upon Kuru for the sake of his son.
Having obtained that princess, he took his pleasure with that slender-waisted woman, without violating dharma or artha, just as Maghavan does with Paulomī.
Then the powerful lord of men, having recognized that his son was capable of bearing the burden of the kingdom, consecrated him as the heir apparent according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having been consecrated in his own position as king by his father,
Kuru himself protected the earth and his subjects like his own children.
He himself became the guardian of the field, and he indeed was the protector of cattle;
he was the protector of all and the mighty guardian of the subjects.
Then the thought occurred to him: "Fame is most weighty in the world;
for as long as one's fame is well-established, so long does one dwell together with the gods."
Having thus perceived the truth exactly as it is, that best of kings,
the lord of men, wandered over the entire earth for the sake of his fame.
Then the powerful Lord of the World, having reached the sacred grove named Dvaitavana,
was well-pleased and entered its interior.
There he then beheld the goddess Sarasvatī, the daughter of Brahmā born from the Plakṣa tree, the auspicious one who liberates from sin, whose tongue is like that of a lion.
Having made extensive obeisance to the mother of Sudarśana,
who stood upon the shore surrounded by millions of holy bathing places (tīrthas), the Blessed Lady.
Upon seeing that water of hers, the king bathed and became filled with joy;
he then returned once more to the northern altar of Brahmā.
The unsurpassed sacred site of Dharma named Samantapañcaka extends for five yojanas in every direction.
The gods said:
"O Puruṣottama, how many types of altars (vedis) are there for Brahmā,
by which the altar described as 'all-pentadic' (sarvapañcakā) is proclaimed as superior?"
The God of Gods said:
"The Vedas are the five bridges of Dharma for the Lord of the World;
it was upon them that the sacrifice was performed by Śambhu, the Lord of the Gods and Protector of the World."
Prayāga is the middle altar; Gayāśiras is the eastern altar;
and Virajā, which bestows infinite fruit, is the southern altar.
The western lotus-shaped altar, adorned with three sacrificial pits, is called Samantapañcaka; it is indeed the northern, imperishable altar.
The royal seer considered this field to be of great fruit, thinking:
"I shall perform agriculture; I shall produce all desires exactly as I wish."
Having thus reflected in his mind and renounced his most excellent son,
that bull among kings established an incomparable monument for the sake of his fame.
Having fashioned a golden plow and taken hold of the bull of Rudra,
the Lord himself prepared to drag Pauṇḍraka, who was like a buffalo belonging to Yama.
Approaching that best of men as he was pulling it, Takṣaka said: "O King, what is this for which you are striving here?"
Approaching that best of men as he was pulling [the bow], Śatakratu said: "O King, what is this for which you are striving here?"
The king said to the best of gods: "I cultivate austerity, truth, forgiveness, compassion, purity, charity, yoga, and the practice of celibacy."
To him Lord Hari said, "O lord of men, why have you suddenly obtained the eight-limbed seed? and having laughed, he departed from there.
Even after Śakra had departed, O King, the royal seer Sīradhṛk,
the lord of the earth, continued to plow day after day across seven krośas on all sides.
Then, having gone there, I asked, "Kuru, what is this?
and the king then fully explained that great eightfold dharma.

Then I said to him, "O King, where does this seed reside? He replied, "The seed resides within my body. I said to him, "Give it; I shall sow it. You yourself must indeed plow with the plow. (VamP 23.29)
Then the king extended his right arm;
seeing that outstretched arm, I swiftly struck it with my discus.

In the very center of that place is Pṛthūdaka, said to yield great merit, which removes sins and is auspicious;

In the beginning, this progeny was created by the Great-grandfather together with all the hosts of beings;

The gods gave Menā to the mountain Himavat;
having obtained her through the grace of the deities, Himavat was filled with joy and sported with her according to his desire.
Then Himādri, together with his daughter, bestowed the various objects of desire as she wished;
and she gave birth to three daughters who were exceedingly beautiful, like celestial nymphs.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
To Menā were born three daughters, endowed with beauty and virtuous qualities.
And the fourth son was known as Sunābha.
O Sage, the eldest daughter of Menā was born with a red body, red eyes, and adorned with red garments; she became known by the name Rāgiṇī.
Another is named Kuṭilā, who has beautiful limbs, eyes like lotus petals, and dark, curly hair;
she wears white garlands and garments.
Resembling a mass of blue sapphire, with eyes like blue lotuses, Kālī was peerless in beauty; Menakā’s daughter was inferior to her.
O Sage, when those three maidens had reached beyond six years of age, they set out to perform penance; the gods beheld those auspicious women.
Then the ascetic Kuṭilā, radiant as the rays of the moon, was led to the world of Brahmā by all the Divākaras and the Vasus.
Then all the deities said: "O Brahmin, you ought to explain what this woman will give birth to—a son who shall be the slayer of Mahiṣa?"
Then the Lord of the Gods said:
"This poor ascetic woman is not capable of bearing the splendor of Śarva; let this wretched girl be released."
Then, O Nārada, the prosperous Kuṭilā said to Brahmā:
"O Blessed One, I shall strive in such a way that the very difficult-to-withstand [weapon] of Śarva [will be neutralized]."
"I shall maintain this splendor; listen likewise, O best of beings, for I have propitiated Janārdana through well-performed austerity."
O Grandfather, just as I shall cause the head of Hara to bow down, so shall I do, O God; what I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.
Pulastya said: Then the Grandfather, the Lord Brahmā, the primordial creator and sovereign of all, being enraged, spoke these harsh and cruel words, O great sage.
Brahmā said:
"Since my word was not endured by you, O sinful and crooked one,
therefore you shall become all waters, consumed by my curse."
Thus cursed by Brahmā, O sage, the daughter of Himavat,
consisting of water, rushed with great speed and flooded the world of Brahmā.
Seeing that river with its waters overflowing,
the Grandfather bound it firmly with the bonds of speech consisting of the Ṛg, Sāman, Atharvan, and Yajus Vedas.
Bound there, O Brahmin, that daughter of the mountain remained right where she was,
consisting of water, flooding the pure matted locks of Brahmā.
She who was named Rāgavatī was also led to heaven by the gods;
having presented her to Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) spoke to her as follows: VamP_25.17.
She too, being enraged, said: "I shall surely perform such great austerity that he shall become the slayer of Mahiṣa, joined with my name."
Then Brahmā cursed her as well: "O sinful one, you shall become the twilight (sandhyā), for you have forcibly transgressed my command, which indeed cannot be violated even by the gods."
Then Brahmā cursed her as well: "O sinful one, you shall become the twilight (sandhyā), for you have forcibly transgressed my command, which is indeed unviolable even by the gods."
O best of sages, thereupon Sandhyā, becoming impassioned with desire,
assumed a firm body made of śailēya and awaited her conjunction with Kṛttikā.
Then, knowing that the two maidens had departed, the ascetic Menā tried to dissuade him from his penance, and she spoke thus: "It is Umā."
Her auspicious father and son gave her the name Mātā;
indeed, that daughter went to the penance grove under the very name Umā.
Then, fixing her mind upon the god Rudra— the trident-wielder whose banner is the bull— she performed a most difficult penance within her heart.
Then Brahmā said to the gods: "Go to the daughter of Himavat;
bring that Kālī here, who is performing austerities on the Himalayas."
Then the gods assembled and beheld the daughter of the mountain;
overcome by her splendor, they were unable to approach her.
Indra, together with the hosts of immortals, was driven away by her splendor;
having reported that her brilliance surpassed even that of Brahmā, he established himself [in his place].
Then Brahmā said: "She is surely the beloved of Śaṅkara;
it is by his splendor that you have indeed been cast down and deprived of your luster."
Therefore, O you who are free from feverish distress, go each to your own respective place;
for you have slain Mahiṣa in battle, along with his stars.
Having been addressed thus by the god Brahmā, the gods, together with Indra,
immediately departed for their own abodes, freed from their distress.
Himavat, the lord of mountains, having turned Umā away from that asceticism even as she was performing penance, brought her home together with his wife.
The high-minded god, too, having undertaken that fierce vow known as Nirāśraya,
wandered across the great mountains, including the foremost among them, Meru.
Once, he arrived at the great mountain Himavat;
honored by him with faith, the Lord dwelt there for that night.
On the second day, Mahādeva was thus addressed by Giriśa:
"O Lord, remain right here for the sake of accomplishing your ascetic penance."
Having been addressed thus by the mountain, Hara formed that resolve;
he remained, taking up residence in a hermitage, having abandoned his supportless dwelling.
Even while that trident-bearing God of gods was dwelling in the hermitage,
the auspicious Kālī, daughter of the King of Mountains, went to that place.
Seeing that his beloved Satī had returned and been born once more,
Hara honored her with a welcome and remained absorbed in yoga.
And that beautiful woman of noble form, having approached with her hands joined in reverence, together with her companions, paid homage at the feet of Śiva.
Then, after a long time, Śarva, having gazed upon the daughter of the mountain,
said, "This is not proper," and then vanished along with his attendants.
Having heard those fierce words of Śarva, Pārvatī, endowed with wisdom, burning with inner grief, spoke to her father: *VamP_25.39*
"Father, I shall go to the great forest to perform severe and mighty penance for the propitiation of the god Śaṅkara, the wielder of the Pināka bow."
Having been told "So be it" by her father, she whose name was Lalitā performed austerities upon that very outstretched foot with the desire to propitiate Hara.
Then her friends performed service for the goddess,
beginning with the gathering of sacrificial wood, *kuśa* grass, fruits, and roots.
For the sake of diversion, a clay image of Hara, the wielder of the trident, was fashioned by Pārvatī;
it became endowed with splendor, and she said, "May there be prosperity."
He performed worship unto him alone and beheld him again and again;
thereupon, the Destroyer of Tripura was filled with satisfaction toward him because of his faith.
Assuming the form of a young brahmin student, wearing a girdle of muñja grass on the month of Āṣāḍha,
he likewise carried a sacred thread, an umbrella, and a deerskin.
With his hand occupied by a water-pot and his body smeared with ashes,
he wandered from hermitage to hermitage and arrived at that hermitage of Kālī.
Then, O Nārada, Kālī rose up with her companions,
and after honoring him according to the prescribed rites, she questioned him as follows.
Umā said: "O monk, from where have you come? In what place is your hermitage?
And where will you go? Tell me quickly."
The monk said:
"O girl of pure vows, my hermitage is in Vārāṇasī;
from here, I shall go on a pilgrimage to Pṛthūdaka."
The Goddess said:
O best of Brahmins, what merit did you obtain there at Pṛthūdaka? And what fruit did you gain by bathing along the way? In which [waters] did you bathe? VamP_25.50.
The monk said:
"I indeed performed my first bath at Prayāga;
thereafter, at the holy sites of Kubjāmra, Jayanta, and Caṇḍikeśvara."
And at Bandhuvṛnda, Karkandhū, the Kanakhala Tīrtha,
as well as at the Agnikuṇḍa on the Sarasvatī, and at Bhadrā in Triviṣṭapa.
O slender-waisted one, having performed my ablutions at Konaṭa, Koṭitīrtha, and Kubjaka without any selfish desire, I have since come to your hermitage.
Having addressed you while you are staying here, I shall go to Pṛthūdaka;
since I am indeed asking you this, you ought not to be angry with me there.
O slender-waisted one, that I emaciate myself through austerity—
even though my body was already restrained in childhood— is indeed praiseworthy for the twice-born.
"For what purpose, O timid one, have you, standing in the prime of youth, undertaken such fierce asceticism? It appears to me as if there is some doubt."
O playful woman, in the first stage of life, women who enjoy excellent pleasures together with their husbands attain those enjoyments at a time when youth remains stable.
O Girijā, all beings here, including the mobile and the immobile, desire beauty, noble birth, and sovereignty through austerity; and all of that is found in great abundance in you.
Why then, having cast aside these ornaments, have you taken up matted locks?
Why, having abandoned the fine Chinese silk, do you wear garments of bark?
Pulastya said: Then, O Nārada, the friend of the goddess, Somaprabhā, who had grown old through ascetic penance, related the matter exactly as it was to the mendicant.
Somaprabha said:
O best of the twice-born, hear now the reason for which Pārvatī performed her ascetic penance; this Kālī desires Hara as her husband.
Pulastya said:
Having heard the words of Somaprabhā and shaking his head,
the mendicant laughed a great laugh and spoke these words.
The monk said:
"I tell you this word, O Pārvatī: by whom was this intellect given to you?
How shall your hand, tender as a sprout, come into contact with Śarva’s hand, which holds a serpent?"
Likewise, you are adorned with fine silk garments while Rudra is covered in the skin of a predator;
you are anointed with sandalwood paste while he is decorated with ashes—this does not appear to me to be appropriate.
Pulastya said:
O best of Brahmins, while he was speaking thus, Pārvatī said to the mendicant:
"Do not speak so, mendicant; Hara is superior in all virtues."
Whether he is auspicious or terrible, whether he possesses wealth or is destitute,
whether the Lord of Gods is adorned or likewise unadorned.
"Whether he be such or otherwise, he shall be my protector.
Let this monk, whose lips quiver with the desire to speak, be restrained.
O Śaśiprabhā, a reviler is not so sinful as one who listens [to such things]."
Pulastya said:
Having spoken thus, the giver of boons desired to rise;
then Śiva abandoned his form as a mendicant and stood in his own true form.
Having spoken thus, he said, "O beloved, go to your own father's abode;
for your sake, I shall send a great seer to the home of the Himavat."
And because they seek Rudra here with an image of the Lord made of clay,
this [Liṅga] shall become famous in the world as Bhadreśvara.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kimpuruṣas, and uragas,
as well as humans desiring auspiciousness, will constantly worship it.
O sage, having been addressed thus by the god, the daughter of the king of mountains entered the sky and went to her own father’s abode.
Śaṅkara too, endowed with great splendor, having dismissed the daughter of the mountain,
went then to Pṛthūdaka and performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
Then Maheśvara, the foremost of the gods, having bathed in Pṛthūdaka and cast off all impurity,
returned with Nandin, his attendants, and his vehicle to Mount Mandara, the great mountain.
As Tripurāntaka arrived with his hosts and the seven celestial rishis, that best of mountains, its hair standing on end in thrill, shone for a moment like a bird bristling with joy;
then, together with all the lords of the Gaṇas, the mountain performed worship for the omnipresent Three-eyed Lord with divine fruits, pure water, roots, tubers, and other offerings.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then Rudra, having been fully honored by the mountain, became filled with affection.
And then the great seer remembered Arundhatī along with him.
Once remembered by the high-souled Śaṅkara, those sages assembled on Mount Mandara, that great mountain with its beautiful caves.
Upon seeing them arrived, the god, the destroyer of Tripura,
rose up, honored them, and spoke these words:
"Blessed is this best of mountains, praiseworthy and worthy of worship by the gods;
it has likewise become cleansed of sin through the lotus-feet of you all."
"Please stay here on this broad, delightful, level, and auspicious mountain plateau,
upon rocks that are the color of lotuses, smooth, and soft."
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by the god Śaṅkara, the great ṛṣis together with Arundhatī entered upon the mountain ridge.
When the sages were seated, Nandin, the leader of the hosts of gods,
having honored them with the arghya offering and other rites, stood there with a disciplined mind.
Then the Lord of the Gods spoke these righteous and beneficial words to the seven seers, who were endowed with discipline, for the sake of increasing his own glory.
Hara said:
O Kaśyapa, O son of Atri, O son of Varuṇa, O son of Gādhi, listen, O Gautama!
Listen, O Bharadvāja, and you, O Aṅgiras, listen as well. (VamP 26.9)
In ancient times, it is said, that Satī, my beloved daughter of Dakṣa, gave up her life through the vision of yoga due to her father’s wrath.
"O best of the twice-born, Umā, the daughter of the king of mountains, has now been born once again; let the lord of mountains be entreated on my behalf."
Pulastya said:
Thus addressed, the seven ṛṣis replied, "So be it," and having uttered the words "Oṃ namaḥ śaṅkarāya," they went to Himālaya.
Then Śarva said to Arundhatī, "Go, O beautiful one;
for housewives indeed know the course of dharma among housewives."
Having been addressed in this way, Arundhatī, acknowledging the world’s custom which is difficult to transgress,
said, "Salutations to you, O Rudra," and departed with her husband.
Having gone to the peak of the Himalayas and to the medicinal plateau,
they beheld the city of the king of mountains, which was like the city of the gods.
Then they were respectfully honored by the mountain women,
while the mountains themselves, including Sunābha and others, remained composed as they paid them homage.
Accompanied by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and others led by them,
they entered the beautiful abode of the Himavat mountain, which blazed with gold.
Then all those great-souled ones, whose impurities had been washed away by austerity,
reached the great gate and stood there because of the gatekeeper.
Then the gatekeeper Adri Gandhamādana quickly approached,
carrying in his hand a great staff made of ruby.
Then the sages, having gone to the auspicious Lord of Mountains, said to him:
"Please announce that we have arrived, seeking a great purpose."
Thus addressed by the sages, Gandhamādana, the lord of mountains,
went to where the king of mountains sat, surrounded by other peaks.
Sitting on the ground on his knees, placing his hands over his mouth, and tucking his staff under his arm, the Mountain spoke these words: (VamP 26.22)
Gandhamādana said:
"O King of Mountains, these sages have arrived seeking you;
they stand at the gate as petitioners, longing for a sight of you."
Pulastya said:
Having heard the words of the gatekeeper, the Lord of Mountains rose up,
went to the door himself, and took up an excellent offering of water (arghya).
Having brought them to the assembly hall with water for their feet, the Arghya offering, and other honors, Śaila,
who was skilled in speech, addressed them once they had taken their seats.
Himavat said:
"Is this a rain without clouds, or is it a fruit without flowers?
For this arrival of yours is indeed beyond conjecture and inconceivable."
"From this day forward I am blessed, O best of beings, O King of Mountains;
today indeed my body is completely purified, since you have come to my courtyard."
The best of the twice-born have purified themselves through contact with the Self,
just as one purifies the waters of the Sarasvatī by looking at them, touching them with the foot, and treading upon the sacred ford.
"O Brahmins, I am now your slave and one who has performed meritorious deeds;
you ought to command me as to why it is that you have come as petitioners."
Together with my wife, sons, servants, and grandsons, I am yours for eternity;
standing as your servant, I await your command—please speak.
Pulastya said:
Having heard the words of the king of mountains, the sages of rigid vows spoke to the aged Aṅgiras: "Announce our purpose to the mountain."
Thus exhorted by all the sages, Kaśyapa and the others, Aṅgiras addressed these supreme words to that king of mountains: VamP_26.32.
Aṅgiras said:
"Listen, O best of mountains, to the purpose for which we have come to your abode together with Arundhatī, O mountain."
He who is that Great Soul, the Soul of All, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, Śarva, the three-eyed one, whose vehicle is the bull.
Jīmūtaketu is Śatrughna, the Lord himself who partakes in the sacrifice;
some call him Īśvara, while others call him Śiva, Sthāṇu, Bhava, or Hara.
O Lord of the Mountains, we have been sent to your presence by that Bhīma, Ugra, Maheśāna, Mahādeva, the Lord of creatures.
"This Kālī, your daughter, who is the most beautiful in all the worlds—she is being sought by the Lord of the Gods; it behoves you to grant her to him."
O best of mountains, truly blessed is that father whose daughter obtains a virtuous husband endowed with beauty and noble birth.
O Mountain, as many beings as there are— whether mobile or immobile, and of the fourfold kinds—
this goddess is their mother, since Hara has been declared their father.
Having prostrated before Śaṅkara, let the gods prostrate before your daughter;
place your foot, smeared with ashes, upon the heads of your enemies.
"We are the supplicants, Śarva is the giver of the boon, and you are Umā;
[she is] the bride, the mother of the entire world. Do that which is for your own welfare."
Pulastya said:
Having heard those words of Aṅgiras, Kālī stood with her face cast down;
having suddenly experienced joy, she once again fell into a state of dejection.
Then the Lord of Mountains spoke to Mount Gandhamādana:
"Go, having invited all the mountains, so that they may come to this great occasion."
Then the mountain Śīghratara went swiftly from house to house and summoned Merv and the other foremost mountains from all sides.
They too arrived with great haste, considering that task to be momentous;
filled with wonder, they entered and sat upon golden seats.
Udaya, Hemakūṭa, Ramyaka, Mandara,
Uddālaka, Vāruṇa, Varāha, and Garuḍāsana.
Śuktimān, Vegasānu, Dṛḍhaśṛṅga, Śṛṅgavān,
Citrakūṭa, Trikūṭa, and likewise Mount Mandara.
The Vindhya, Malaya, Pāriyātra, and Durdara;
Mount Kailāsa, Mahendra, Niṣadha, and the Añjana mountain.
These principal mountains, as well as other minor mountains,
having bowed down to those sages, were indeed seated in the assembly hall.
Then Giriśa summoned his own wife Menā;
"Come here, O auspicious and beautiful lady, together with your son."
Having paid homage to the sages and the celestial bards, that ascetic woman,
having addressed all her kinsmen, then entered [the palace] together with her son.
Then, O Nārada, when they were seated upon the great mountain,
the eloquent sage, addressing them all with a melodious voice, spoke these words.
Himavat said:
"These seven holy seers have come as suitors for my daughter;
they seek a maiden for the sake of Maheśvara, and this matter must indeed be reported to you."
"Therefore, you who are my kinsmen, speak according to your wisdom;
I shall not disregard you, so you ought to say what is appropriate."
Pulastya said:
Having heard the words of Himavat, Meru and the other foremost of stationary beings all spoke these words while remaining in their respective seats.
The sages are our suitors, and Hara, the destroyer of Tripura, is a bridegroom of choice;
O Mountain, let Kālī be given away, for she is indeed our desired son-in-law.
Then Menā also said to her husband: "Listen to my words, O Lord of Mountains;
for this very reason, the gods have bestowed her upon you after having propitiated the ancestors."
But the son who shall be born to her by the Lord of Beings will slay Mahiṣa, the lord of the Daityas, as well as Tāraka.
When Menā had spoken thus, the Lord of Mountains addressed his daughter:
"O daughter, you have now been given by me to Śarva."
She said to the sages: "O you whose wealth is asceticism, my daughter, the wife of Saṃkara, bows down before you all with devotion. (VamP 26.60)
Then Arundhatī, placing Kālī upon her lap,
consoled her as she felt ashamed with auspicious and pleasing words inspired by the joy of Śiva.
Then the Seven Sages said: "O King of Mountains, listen to this auspicious and meritorious lunar day, which is endowed with the qualities of the *jāmitra* [lunar mansion]."
On the third day, the Moon will enter the conjunction with Uttarāphālgunī; the auspicious moment (muhūrta) prescribed for that occasion is named Maitra.
"On that lunar day, Hara will take your daughter's hand in marriage with the sacred mantras; we shall go then, so you should grant us your permission."
Then, having honored those preeminent sages according to the prescribed rites with auspicious fruits, roots, and other offerings, the king of mountains slowly dismissed them.
They too arrived with great speed, having traversed the abode of the Maruts;
reaching Mount Mandara, they once again paid homage to Śaṅkara.
Having prostrated, they said to Maheśāna: "O Lord, you are the husband of the Daughter of the Mountain;
the three worlds, together with Brahmā, shall behold Ghanavāhana."
Then Maheśvara, being pleased, honored all the sages in due order according to the prescribed rite, along with Arundhatī, O Hara.
Then, having been duly honored, they departed for the deliberation of the gods;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Bhāskara also came to see Hara.
Then, O great sage, having returned to the abode of Maheśvara and offered their salutations, they entered;
and after approaching him, they paid homage to Hara and sat down, while he remembered all his attendants headed by Nandin.
Surrounded by gods and hosts, the Lord of the Mountain shines, his mass of matted locks released;
he is like a great tree in a forest, with its roots sprouting amidst *sarjaka* and *kadamba* trees.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Seeing that the gods had assembled, Nandin informed the Lord.
