Then, having risen, he embraced Hari with devotion and pressed him tightly.
Having bowed his head to Brahmā and addressed Śatakratu,
Śaṅkara looked upon the other hosts of gods and honored them.
And the hosts of Śiva’s followers, such as the Pāśupatas and others, led by Vīrabhadra, entered Mount Mandara, crying out, "Victory, O God!"
Then, together with the deities, the blessed Lord Śarva went from there to the great mountain Kailāsa to perform the marriage rites.
Then, on that great mountain, the auspicious Aditi, the mother of the gods,
Surabhi, Surasā, and others busily performed the decoration of the sacrificial ground.
Hara wears a beautiful crest of great bones, a garland of skulls, and a lion’s skin;
he has moving earrings fashioned from blue serpents.
Adorned with a great serpent as a jeweled girdle, and wearing necklaces, armlets,
and anklets, he shines resplendent, standing upon his bull with a towering mass of matted hair.
In front of him, the Gaṇas proceeded on their respective mounts,
and behind him followed the gods, led by Agni.
Janārdana, mounted upon Vainateya together with Lakṣmī, proceeds;
and the Grandfather (Brahmā), standing by the side of the gods, goes forth on his swan.
Mounted upon his elephant, the thousand-eyed Lord Indra, the sovereign, together with Śacī, held aloft a white cloth parasol spread wide.
Yamunā, the best of rivers,
holding a white fly-whisk in her hand, went along seated upon a tortoise.
Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, mounted upon an elephant, held up an excellent young-fan that resembled a swan, a jasmine flower, or the moon.
Taking up flowers endowed with fragrance of five colors, the six seasons, moving at will, went to Maheśāna.
Mounting a swift elephant resembling the intoxicated Airāvaṇa and taking an ointment with him, Pṛthūdaka went there.
The Gandharvas, headed by Tumburu, followed the Great God, singing with sweet voices,
while the Kinnaras accompanied them, playing musical instruments.
Apsarases danced and sages offered praise as they followed that Lord of the Gods, the three-eyed one who holds a trident in his hand.
Likewise, eleven crores of Rudras went there,
as did twelve crores of Adityas and eight crores of Vasus.
O best of sages, sixty-seven crores of gaṇas and twenty-four crores of rishis who have sublimated their vital energy likewise departed.
Innumerable hosts of yakṣas, kinnaras,
and rākṣasas followed the Great Lord in great excitement for the sake of the wedding.
Then, in an instant, the lords of the mountains arrived from all sides upon their elephants at the base of the king of mountains, the lord of the earth.
Then the three-eyed Blessed One bowed to the Lord of Mountains;
the mountains prostrated before Īśāna, and thereupon he became joyful.
Accompanied by the gods and his attendants,
the bull-bannered Lord entered the great city of the King of Mountains, the path to which had been shown by Nandin.
"Jīmūtakeśu has arrived!"— at these words, the women of the city abandoned their own tasks and became intent on seeing him.
Taking half of the garland with one hand and her mass of hair with the second, the beautiful woman went toward Śaṅkara.
Having placed one foot, rich with the deep red of lac-dye, while her eyes were agitated,
she approached Hara, for the other foot was indeed without lac.
Having heard that Bhīma had arrived, one woman, with only one eye still anointed,
took up another applicator-stick smeared with collyrium and ran off very fast.
Another beautiful woman, having seized her girdle and garment with her hand,
came forth naked like one intoxicated, longing for the sight of Hara.
Hearing that Īśāna had surpassed all others, the young woman, languid from the weight of her breasts and slender-waisted, reproached her own youth in anger.
Thus, causing agitation among the women of the city, Hara,
mounted upon his bull, departed for the divine residence of his father-in-law.
Then, seeing Śambhu entered the palace of the lord of mountains, the women said:
"It is only fitting that Ambikā performed such difficult penance, for this Śambhu is indeed a great god."
He is that very one by whom the body of the flower-armed god named Kandarpa was rendered bodiless;
he is the performer of the sacrifice, the destroyer of Dakṣa, the slayer of Bhaga’s eyes, the wielder of the trident, and the bearer of the Pināka bow.
Homage, homage to Śaṅkara, wielder of the trident, whose garment is the skin of the lord of beasts, enemy of Time;
homage, homage to him who has earrings marked by great serpents as necklaces, the beloved of Pārvatī.

Thus being praised, Śambhu—honored by the Siddhas and Yakṣas, encircled by serpents, and beautifully smeared with ashes—ascended the sacrificial altar, which was radiant with fire and rich in auspiciousness; he was shaded by a parasol held by the Lord of the Gods, followed by Viṣṇu, his elder brother, who stood before him with a joyful heart.
When the Destroyer of Tripura arrived with his companions and the celestial sages, the householders in the palace of the King of Mountains became busily engaged in the decoration of Kālī.

The mountains themselves fell into a state of agitation, as did the deities through their offerings and other rites; for generally, friends become anxious when they are eager for a daughter’s marriage.
Then, having adorned the goddess Girijā, whose slender limbs were covered in white silk garments,
she was led into the presence of Śaṅkara when the festival had been performed by her brother Sunābha.
Then, stationed upon a beautiful golden terrace, the gods beheld the deeds of Śaṅkara; the Lord, too, together with Kuśāṅgī, attained the station cherished by the worlds.

Where there were various sports with trees laden with flowers, where the earth was lightly strewn upon the *guṇḍikā* with drops of water and fragrant scented powders; where, for the sake of their play, the daughter of the Mountain of Hara [Pārvatī] and [Śiva] abundantly covered it with strings of pearls, and afterwards made the ground intensely red with incessantly spread heaps of vermilion.
Having thus sported together with the Daughter of the Mountain,
Hara went to the firm southern altar attended by the sages.
Then Himavat arrived, pure and clad in white garments,
with sacred grass in his hand, bringing the radiant *madhuparka* offering.
Seated there, the three-eyed lord gazed toward the direction of Śakra;
and the king of mountains, well-seated, looked upon the Seven Sages.
Seated comfortably before Śarva with his hands joined in reverence,
the illustrious Mountain spoke these words concerning the means for his own spiritual welfare.
Himavat said:
"O Blessed One, O elder brother of Pulaha, please accept this Kālī— my daughter, my granddaughter,
and the daughter of my father's daughters— who is offered by me."
Pulastya said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Mountains, joining hand with hand, gave [the gift] while uttering these words aloud: "Accept this, O Blessed One! (VamP 27.43).
He said:
"I have no mother, nor father, nor likewise kinsmen or relatives; I am without refuge, dwelling on the peak of Mount Kiri. O King of Mountains, you may accept my daughter. (VamP 27.44)
Having spoken thus, the Giver of Boons pressed his hand against the hand of the Mountain’s Daughter;
and she too, O celestial sage, having received the touch of Śambhu, attained supreme joy.
Then, having ascended the altar together with the Daughter of the Mountain and partaking of the honey-mixture, Viriñca offered white grains of parched rice; thereafter, he spoke to Girijā.
O Kālī, behold the face of your husband, radiant as the moon;
with a steady gaze and composed mind, perform the circumambulation of the fire.
Then, upon seeing Hara’s face, Ambikā attained a state of coolness,
just as the earth, scorched by the rays of the sun, does when it receives rain.
The Grandfather spoke again, saying, "Behold the face of the Lord.
Out of shame, she looked, and then she spoke softly to Brahmā.
Together with Girijā, he performed three circumambulations of the fire,
and parched grains were cast into the sacrificial fire along with the oblation.
Then Mālinī seized the foot of Hara for the sake of its sound "hā.
Hara said, "What do you ask for? I shall give it; let go! (VamP 27.51)
Mālinī said to Śaṅkara: "O Śaṅkara, grant to my friend the good fortune belonging to her own lineage; from that, you shall attain liberation."
Then Mahādeva said: "O Mālinī, I have given you; release me!
Listen as I tell you of the good fortune belonging to her own lineage. (VamP 27.53)
He who is the wearer of yellow garments, the bearer of the conch, Madhusūdana—
his very good fortune has indeed been bestowed upon our lineage.
When these words had been spoken, Mālinī, who garlanded the virtuous conduct of her own lineage, released the bull-bannered god.
When Hara was indeed seized by Mālinī by his auspicious foot,
he then beheld the face of Kālī, which was more radiant than the moon.
Seeing that, he was overcome with agitation and experienced the emission of semen;
in his terror, he caused that semen to fall upon the sand and solidify it.
Then the boon-granting Brahmā said: "O Grandfather, you ought not to slay the twice-born;
these blessed great seers, the Vālakhilyas, are worthy of honor."
Then, at the conclusion of Maheśa’s speech, eighty-eight thousand ascetics known as the Vālakhilyas rose up.
Then, when the wedding was completed, Hara entered the bridal chamber;
he enjoyed himself with Umā for the night and arose again at dawn.
Then, having obtained the daughter of the mountain, Śambhu, together with the gods and the throngs of spirits, was delighted;
honored by the king of mountains, he quickly returned to Mount Mandara.
Then, having bowed to and duly honored the gods headed by Brahmā,
Hari, and Indra, and having dismissed them, the Eight-formed Lord (Aṣṭamūrti) dwelt upon Mount Mandara together with the elemental beings.
Pulastya said: Then, O sage, while dwelling on the mountain and wandering at his own will, Rudra summoned Viśvakarman and said to him, "Construct for me a Guha."
Then he constructed for Śarva a golden abode marked with the svastika, measuring sixty-four yojanas in extent.
It had a beautiful array of ivory railings, was adorned with lattices of pearls,
possessed stairs of pure crystal, and featured balustrades made of beryl.
Then the Lord of the Gods performed a sacrifice characterized by the householder's life in a very spacious seven-chambered hall, which was endowed with all excellent qualities.
Śaṅkara followed that path of former conduct;
in this way, O Sage, a great length of time passed for the three-eyed Lord.
While the Lord of the World was sporting with Pārvatī, being mindful of dharma,
Bhava once addressed Kālī for the sake of a joke.
Overcome with indignation, Pārvatī spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
"A forest pierced by an arrow or struck down by an axe grows back again;
but a wound caused by speech, inflicted by loathsome and ill-spoken words, does not heal."
"Word-arrows fly forth from the mouth; struck by them, one grieves day and night.
A wise person indeed does not discharge them. Therefore, O knower of Dharma, you have today rendered that [Dharma] in vain."
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, I shall go to perform unsurpassed austerity;
I will strive in such a way that you will call me Kālī.
Having spoken thus and having bowed to Maheśvara, the daughter of the mountain,
permitted by him, flew up indeed toward heaven.
And having leaped up with speed toward the auspicious peak of the Himalaya mountain— which was fashioned with great effort by the Creator and cut away with a chisel— VamP_28.11.
Then, having descended, he called to mind Jayā, Vijayā,
the highly meritorious Jayantī, and fourthly, Aparājitā.
When they were thus remembered, those deities indeed assembled to see Kālī; having been granted permission by the Goddess, the auspicious ones performed service for her.
Then, while Pārvatī remained engaged in asceticism,
a tiger whose weapons were its fangs and claws came from the forest of Himavat to that place.
While the goddess stood on one foot, the tiger thought:
"When she falls, I shall surely seize her. (VamP 28.15)
Thinking thus, the lord of beasts fixed his gaze;
looking at her face, he became one-pointed in his vision.
Then, for a hundred years, the goddess, chanting the word of Brahman, practiced asceticism;
for a hundred years, the goddess, chanting the Brahman, remained there, O Lord of the Three Worlds.
Then the Grandfather, being pleased, said to the goddess: "I am gratified by your eternal austerity; you have shaken off all sin. Choose a boon according to your desire. (VamP 28.18)
Then Kālī spoke these words to the tiger, O Lotus-born One:
"Be a granter of boons; by that means I shall attain unsurpassed joy. (VamP 28.19)
Then Brahmā granted a boon to Vyāgra of wondrous deeds:
the status of a Gaṇapati before the Lord, devotion, invincibility, and righteousness.
Having thus granted the boon to the tiger, he then spoke to Śivakāntā:
"Choose a boon without hesitation; O Ambikā, I shall grant you a boon."
Then the goddess, the daughter of the mountain, spoke this boon to the Grandfather:
"Let a boon be granted to me: a complexion resembling gold."
Having said "So be it," Brahmā departed, and thereafter Pārvatī became [manifest],
casting off her dark sheath and appearing like the filaments of a lotus.
And from that treasury, O Sage, Kātyāyanī was born once more;
approaching her, the thousand-eyed god Vāsava accepted her as his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and the deity spoke these words to Girijā for his own purpose.
Indra said:
"Let this [river] be given to me; let the Kauśikī be my sister.
Since she has arisen from your treasury (kośa), she shall be called Kauśikī, and I too am Kauśika."
Having promised that he would give her to him, the thousand-eyed Indra took Kauśikī, endowed with beauty,
and departed swiftly for the Vindhya mountains.
Having gone there, he then said: "Stay here, O mighty one;
being worshipped by the gods, you shall be renowned by the name Vindhyavāsinī."
Having established the goddess there and granted her the lion as a vehicle, Hari said,
"May you be the slayer of the enemies of the gods," and departed for heaven.
O Sage, Umā too, having obtained that boon and returned again to Mandara, stood with humility before Maheśāna after bowing down to him.
Then, O Sage, the illustrious and imperishable preceptor of the gods, accompanied by Pārvatī,
remained for a thousand years in the state of great delusion.
When Rudra was established in great delusion, the worlds trembled violently;
the seven oceans surged, and the gods were seized with fear.
Then the gods, together with Indra, went to the abode of Brahmā;
having prostrated before Maheśāna, they said, "Why indeed is this world so agitated?"
Bhava said to them: "Surely [the world] stands in a state of great delusion;
overcome by that, these worlds have fallen into an insurmountable agitation."
Having spoken thus, he became silent; then the gods said to Hari:
"Come, O Śakra, let us go before this is completed."
When the destruction of delusion is completed, that imperishable child who shall be born will surely seize the station of Indra, the king of the gods.
Then, due to the words of the immortals, the isolation of the Destroyer of Strength (Balarāma) occurred;
because of that fear, his knowledge was lost through the impelling force of his future karma.
Then Śakra, the thousand-eyed one, together with the gods and Agni,
went to Mount Mandara and entered upon its peak.
"All these were indeed unable to enter that courtyard of his;
after reflecting for a very long time, they released the fire."
And that best of gods, having approached and seen Nandin at the gate,
and considering it difficult to enter, the Fire-god fell into deep anxiety.
But he, submerged in an ocean of anxiety, beheld a pure and great flight of swans emerging from the abode of Śambhu.
Having said, "This is the means," the Fire-god, in the form of a swan,
deceived the doorkeeper and entered the courtyard of Śiva.
Having entered with a subtle form into the region of the head of the one with matted hair (Kapardin), he laughed and spoke in a deep voice: "O gods, you are standing at the door."
Having heard that,
O Nārada, Śarva suddenly rose up, abandoned the daughter of the mountain, and emerged from the courtyard together with the fire.
When the Lord of the Gods had departed, the deities— along with Indra, the Sun, the Moon, and Agni— with joyful minds, touched the earth with their heads.
Then, out of affection, he said to the gods: "Tell me quickly what must be done for me;
to you who are bowed down in salutation, I shall grant a supreme boon."
The gods said: "If you are pleased with us and desire to grant a boon here,
O Lord, then let this great act of sexual union be abandoned for now."
Īśvara said:
"Let it be so; O best of immortals, this state has been renounced by me.
Let some god receive this overflowing splendor of mine."
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by Śambhu, the gods— including Indra, the Moon, and the Sun—
sat down like deities submerged in a mire.
While the gods were thus despondent, the sacrificial fire approached Śaṅkara and said: "Release your splendor; I shall receive it, O Śaṅkara. (VamP 28.49)
Then the Blessed One released that semen which had already been discharged,
just as one overcome by thirst might drink water, or as a thirsty man might drink oil.
Then, when the splendor of Śarva had indeed been drunk by the god Agni,
the gods, restored to health, took leave of Hara and went to heaven.
When the gods had departed, Hara also returned to his own abode and spoke these words to Mahādevī:
O Goddess, having arrived here with the gods, Agni was sent by them with great effort;
he was instructed and then forbidden regarding the production of a son from your womb.
Having heard her husband’s words, Śivā, enraged and with eyes red at the corners,
cursed all the deities, for she had lost the prospect of bearing a son.
Because those wicked ones do not desire my own legitimate son,
therefore they shall not give birth to sons through their own wives.
Having thus cursed the gods, Gaurī went to the purification hall;
the ascetic woman then summoned Mālinī and resolved to bathe.
Taking a fragrant, smooth unguent, the auspicious Mālinī rubbed with her two hands the golden-hued limbs of the goddess;
and Pārvatī herself wondered what kind of quality that sweat possessed.
Mālinī went quickly home for the purpose of bathing;
once she had departed, Śaileyī cleansed Gajānana of his impurities.
Having fashioned a four-armed man with a broad chest endowed with the auspicious marks,
she released him upon the earth and sat down again upon her auspicious seat.
Then Mālinī, smiling, gave him that head for bathing;
seeing Mālinī’s slight smile, Umā spoke to her, O Nārada.
"For what reason, O timid one, do you laugh so softly and yet so excessively? She replied, "I laugh thus because your son is indeed [such a being]. (Vamśastha 28.61)
"O slender-waisted one, having heard what was proclaimed by the Lord—that Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas, shall become [the attendant]—this laughter has arisen within me today. (VamP 28.62)
Since Śaṅkara had been dissuaded by the gods because he desired a son,
having heard these words, the Goddess bathed there according to the prescribed rite.
Having bathed and worshipped Śaṅkara with devotion, he returned toward his home;
then Śambhu, having arrived, sat upon that very auspicious throne.
Then, having bathed, that filthy man stood below him;
[he received] the sweat of Umā and the sweat of Bhava, combined with the water and the sacred ashes.
From contact with him, the Lord of the World, having recognized his offspring, rose up with a hiss and raised his excellent hand, filled with joy.
Taking that [garland], Hara, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, said to Nandin:
"Rudra shall bathe and worship the gods and others with words, and the ancestors with water. (VamP 28.67)
Having recited the Thousand Names, Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, approached the side of Umā; meeting the Goddess with a smile, may he be for your welfare.
"O Śaileyyā, look at your own son joined with Gumā," he said;
thus addressed, the daughter of the mountain approached and beheld the wonder.
When that divine being with an elephant’s face and a human body was produced from the impurity of his limb,
the Daughter of the Mountain embraced her son with joy.
Then, having smelled him on the crown of his head, Śarva said to Umā:
"O Goddess, even though he has become your son, he cannot exist without a leader."
Because he was born from that [source], the Leader (Vināyaka) shall be known by that name;
he will create thousands of obstacles for the gods and others.
"And all the worlds, O Goddess, both moving and unmoving, shall worship him.
Having spoken thus, he indeed gave [the boon] to his son. (VamP 28.73)
He had as his companion the foremost of the Gaṇas, renowned by the name Ghaṭodara;
likewise, there were the terrible hosts of Mothers, and those spirits who create obstacles.
All of them were bestowed upon the Goddess by the Supreme Lord out of affection;
and the Goddess, seeing her own son, attained supreme joy.
Then she sported with Śambhu on Mount Mandara, which possesses beautiful caves.
O Lord, in this way the goddess Kātyāyanī came to be once again—
she who in the past slew the great Daityas Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Thus has this auspicious speech of yours been told, concerning the origin of Mṛḍānī from the mountain;
it is conducive to heaven, conducive to fame, a destroyer of sins, and a source of vigor for the daughter of the Mountain.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
O best of the twice-born, Kaśyapa had a wife named Danu.
She had three sons who were more powerful than the thousand-eyed Indra.
The eldest was known as Śumbha, another Asura was Niśumbha,
and the third was named Namuci, endowed with great strength.
Hari, grasping the thunderbolt in his hand, desires to slay that Asura, the son of Danu, who is known as Namuci.
Then, as the Lord of the Three Worlds was approaching, Namuci, out of fear of him, entered the chariot of the Sun; consequently, Acyuta was unable [to seize him].
Then Śakra made an agreement with that great-souled one;
O Nārada, he granted him the boon of invulnerability against weapons and missiles.
Then, O Nārada, having realized his invulnerability from both hand-held weapons and missiles,
he abandoned the chariot of the Sun and departed for the netherworld (pātāla).
Even as he was sinking into the ocean water, the lord of the Dānavas beheld an excellent mass of foam; seizing it, he spoke these words: VamP_29.7.1 //
"Let the word spoken by Vāsava, the lord of the gods, be fulfilled:
let this Dānava seize me with his two other hands while I touch him with foam."
He wiped his face, nose, eyes, ears, and so forth as he pleased;
yet Śakra, the Lord, hurled his thunderbolt at him, even though it was invisible.
Because of that, his nose and mouth were shattered; he fell down and died.
And when the appointed time had thus passed, the sin of killing a Brahmin seized Hari.
Having reached that sacred ford and bathed, he was indeed liberated from sin;
thereafter, his two heroic brothers, Sumbha and Niśumbha, became enraged.
Having made a very great effort, they came to harass the gods;
those gods also set forth, placing the thousand-eyed Indra at their head.
Having attacked them, those two Daityas conquered [the gods] along with their armies and followers;
they forcibly seized Indra’s elephant and Yama’s buffalo.
Varuṇa’s jeweled umbrella, the mace of the son of Māruta, and the conch shells,
lotuses, and other treasures were seized by the Dānavas after they had attacked and overwhelmed them.
O Nārada, by those two, the three worlds were brought entirely under their control;
then they came to the surface of the earth and beheld that great asura.
Then they said to Raktabīja, "Who are you?
and he replied, "O Lord, I am a Daitya, the minister of Mahiṣa."
The one renowned as Raktabīja was of great heroism and mighty arms;
his two beautiful and heroic ministers were known as Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
Out of fear of the Goddess, those two mighty-armed ones sank into the water;
as for that powerful Dānava named Mahiṣa who was our lord—
"He has been slain by the Great Goddess on the vast Vindhya mountain.
Of whom are you two the sons, and what are your names as they are heard?
What is your prowess and what is your power? You ought to explain this."
Śumbha and Niśumbha said:
"I am known as Śumbha, the legitimate son of Danu;
this Niśumbha here is my younger brother, the slayer of hosts of enemies."
By him indeed, the gods led by Indra, Rudra, and the Sun,
as well as other heroes who were even more powerful, were assembled and utterly defeated.
"Tell us then, by whom was the Daitya Mahiṣāsura slain?
So that we two, surrounded by our own armies, may slay her."
O Sage, while they were thus offering praise on the bank of the Narmadā,
the two Dānavas, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, emerged from their dwelling in the water.
Then, having approached and taken refuge with Raktabīja, those two best of asuras spoke these gentle words: "Who is this who precedes you?"
And he said to both of them: "That Daitya named Śumbha is the oppressor of the gods;
his younger brother is the second one, Niśumbha."
Relying upon her, that wicked slayer of Mahiṣa, I shall without doubt marry her, who is a jewel among women in the three worlds.
Caṇḍa said:
"You have not spoken correctly; you are not worthy of a jewel, nor is this the proper time.
He who is a lord is worthy of a jewel; therefore, let her be united with Śumbha."
Then he reported to Śumbha and Niśumbha that Kauśikī had once again become as beautiful as before, endowed with exquisite form.
Then Śumbha dispatched his own messenger, the Dānava named Sugrīva,
and a Daitya as well, to the presence of the Goddess dwelling on the Vindhya mountains.
Having gone there and heard those words of the goddess, the great asura Niśumbha, overwhelmed with rage, approached Śumbha and spoke this.
Sugrīva said:
"O leaders of the Daityas, at your word I went this very day to the goddess; I spoke these words to her."
"Just as Śumbha is most renowned even among the Dānavas, he said to you, O highly fortunate one: 'I am the lord of the three worlds.'"
O beautiful one, whatever jewels exist in heaven, upon the surface of the earth, and even in the netherworld (pātāla), all those are always present in my abode.
"O slender-waisted one, you have been described by Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa as a jewel;
therefore, either accept me or my younger brother, Śuṃbha."
And she, smiling, said to me: "Listen, Sugrīva, to my words.
It is the truth, O Lord of the Three Worlds, that Śumbha alone is worthy of the jewels."
"However, O Great Asura, there is a desire in the heart of me, Durvinītā: that he who conquers me in battle shall be my husband."
"And I have said: 'He who shall conquer even the gods and asuras—how could he not conquer you? Therefore, arise, O passionate lady! (VamP 29.37)
Then she said to me: "What can I do, since this desire was formed without due deliberation? Therefore, go and inform Śumbha."
O great asura, having been addressed thus by her, I came into your presence;
she, resembling ten million fires, said, "Having understood this, do what is appropriate."
Pulastya said:
Having heard these words of Sugrīva,
that great asura Sumbha spoke to the Dānava Dhūmralocana, who was standing at a distance.
Śumbha said: "O Dhūmrākṣa, go! That wicked woman, overwhelmed by the pulling of her hair and guilty as she is, seize her like a slave-girl and bring her here quickly."
And whoever shall become her partisan, even if he be possessed of great strength,
he must be slain without hesitation— even if he should be the Grandfather himself.
Thus addressed by Śumbha,
the highly resplendent Dhūmrākṣa, surrounded by six akṣauhiṇīs, rushed toward Mount Vindhya.
Seeing that Durgā there, his vision became confused, and he said:
"Come, come, you fool! O Kauśikī, desire Śumbha as your husband;
otherwise, I shall lead you away by force, overwhelmed as you are by the pulling of your hair."
The Goddess said:
"Indeed, you have been sent here by Śumbha to carry me away by force.
What indeed could a weak woman do in that situation? Do as you wish."
Pulastya said:
Thus addressed by Vibhāvarī, the powerful and heroic Dhūmralocana quickly took up his mace and rushed forward in haste.
As he rushed forward with his mace, Kauśikī reduced him and his army to ashes by a mere *huṃkāra*, just as fire consumes dry fuel.
Then, upon seeing the Dānava reduced to ashes by Kauśikī along with his army, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout this world of mobile and immobile beings.
And Śumbha also heard that great sound uttered;
then he commanded the two powerful great asuras, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
And they went with joy to Ruru, the best among the strong;
and their incomparable army was crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots.
He suddenly arrived where she who was born from the treasure-vessel resided;
then, seeing that enemy force approaching, numbering more than a hundred crores.
With his mane bristling, the lion rushed forward in battle, rending the Dānavas—
some with a blow of his paw and others effortlessly with his mouth.
Having attacked some with his claws, he crushed others with his chest;
they were being slain by the lion dwelling in the mountain cave.
Accompanied by the bhūtas and the attendants of the Goddess, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa took their stand;
seeing their own army in distress, they bit their lips in a quivering rage.
They both rushed toward Durgā like moths into a fire;
seeing those two fierce ones attacking, she was indeed overwhelmed with anger.
The Supreme Goddess formed a three-pronged frown upon her face;
from the surface of the Goddess’s forehead, swiftly curved by that frown, the auspicious Yoginī Kālī emerged with a terrifying countenance. (VamP 29.56)
Taking a skull-topped staff in her hand, she poured out the fierce and terrible collyrium-box;
with her limbs withered yet her body drenched in blood, she bore a garland made from the heads of kings.
In the battle, he cut some with his sword and others with his khaṭvāṅga;
being violently enraged, he utterly destroyed the enemies along with their chariots, horses, and elephants.
O Ambika, when the elephant was released, you hurled back at him a shield, a goad, a mallet, along with a bow and a bell, together with the mechanical device.
Ambikā seizes by the mouth and chews a chariot complete with its wheels and pole, along with its charioteer, horses, and warrior.
One seized him by the hair, another likewise by the neck;
and having trampled another with his foot, he sent him to death.
Then, having seen that army together with its commanders devoured by the Goddess, Ruru fled; but Caṇḍī herself beheld him.
Then he struck the great asura on the head with his khaṭvāṅga;
slain, he fell to the earth like a tree cut at its roots.
Then, seeing him fallen like a sacrificial animal,
Vibhāvarī slit open his sheath from the ear down to the feet.
Taking up her hair-braid, Vimalā bound her matted locks;
one strand did not come loose, so she tore it out and cast it upon the ground.
Having been born, she became exceedingly fierce, with her hair smeared with oil,
bearing her own body half-black and half-white.
She said, "I shall slay one great asura";
she was then given the name by which she became renowned as Caṇḍamārī.
He said, "Go, O blessed one, and bring Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa here;
I myself shall slay them, but you ought to bring them."
Having heard these words of the goddess, she rushed toward those two;
they, afflicted by fear, fled toward the southern direction.
Then those two also, having cast off their garments, ran forward with great speed,
mounting a highly impetuous donkey that resembled Garuḍa.
When those two messengers had departed, Śivā followed right after them;
there she then beheld Pauṇḍra, Mahiṣa, and Masya.
She tore out his serpent-like horn;
grasping it in her very hand, she pursued the Dānava with speed.
Then those two, abandoning the earth, ascended into the sky;
and that great goddess Maheśvarī was carried away with speed by the donkey.
Then he beheld Garuḍa, the lord of serpents, who was seeking to devour him;
seeing Karkoṭaka, his hair stood on end.
Terrified by fear, Garuḍa appeared like a mere lump of flesh,
for the fierce feathers of that bird fell away.
Taking the feathers of the king of birds and likewise the serpent Karkoṭaka,
the goddess pursued Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, who were overcome with fear, with great speed.
And when the two great asuras, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, had arrived before the Goddess,
they were bound by Karkoṭaka himself and, having been bound, he brought them to the Vindhya mountains.
Having presented it to Kauśikī, he took up the formidable quiver,
adorned with the heads of the lords of the Dānavas and with beautiful feathers of Tārkṣya.
Having fashioned an incomparable garland, she offered it to Caṇḍikā;
and she presented the lion’s skin along with the *ghargharā* drum.
And having bound a garland made of the feathers of other bird-kings upon the head of the Lord of Birds,
she herself drank the blood even from among the Dānavas.
The wrathful Durgā, seizing Caṇḍa and the fierce, shaven-headed leader of the Asuras,
made those two great Asuras headless in her anger.
Having made those two serpents her crest-ornament, the goddess Suṣkarevatī went into the presence of Kauśikī together with Mārīca.
Having approached her, she said, "O Goddess, please accept this most excellent crest-jewel;
it was woven from the heads of two Daityas and encircled by the King of Serpents."
Śivā took that crest-jewel and bound it upon the head of Caṇḍā;
she then said to her: "A most dreadful deed has been committed."
"Since you wear this auspicious crest from Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
therefore your fame in the world shall be 'Cāmuṇḍā'."
Having spoken these words, the three-eyed goddess, pleased, addressed her who wore a garland of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa and was clothed in the directions: "Destroy these armies of Khāri."
Thus addressed, she then moved about, destroying the fierce army of the enemy with the tip of her horn and on a very swift donkey, while devouring other asuras.
Then, as those foremost of the Danavas were being struck down by Ambika, Carmamunda, Maya, Simha,
and the hosts of spirits, they took refuge with Shumbha, the bull-like leader.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
"Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa were slain, and the army was put to flight."
He commanded the great asura Raktabīja,
who possessed exceeding power and was surrounded by thirty billion akṣauhiṇīs.
And upon seeing that army of the Daityas rushing toward her,
the Great Goddess Caṇḍikā let out a lion’s roar together with those two.
Then, as the Goddess was crying out, Brahmāṇī emerged from her mouth,
seated upon a celestial chariot drawn by swans, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
In an instant, Kuṇḍalinī became Māheśvarī— three-eyed, mounted upon a bull, bearing a trident, encircled by great serpents, and fierce.
Then, O divine sage, Kaumārī emerged from his throat, together with Barhipatrā and Śaktinī, who have the excellent peacock as their vehicle.
Mounted upon Garuḍa with her two arms, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and sword,
and holding the Śārṅga bow and arrows, Vaiṣṇavī appeared, resplendent in form.
Vārāhī, fierce with great and formidable tusks that scratch the surface of the earth,
has appeared from behind, standing upon the serpent Śeṣa.
With her hand raised holding a vajra-hook, adorned with various ornaments,
Māhendrī was born from the circle of breasts, seated upon the back of a lordly elephant.
Scattering the planets, lunar mansions, and stars with the tossing of her mane,
the most dreadful Narasimhi, armed with claws, sprang forth from his heart.
Beholding that demonic army being struck down by them,
Caṇḍikā, fearless toward her enemies, let out a roar once more;
and hearing that great sound of hers, which filled the three worlds, [the demons were terrified].
The three-eyed Lord of the Gods, wielder of the trident, arrived;
having approached and paid homage to her, he then spoke these words to Ambikā.
"I have indeed arrived at this difficult place; give me your command, what shall I do for you?
At the very moment those words were spoken, a Śivā emerged from the body of the Goddess.
Once born, she said to the Lord of Gods: "Go as an envoy, O Śaṅkara, and speak to Śumbha and Niśumbha: 'If you wish to live... (VamP 30.13).
Therefore go, you of evil conduct, to the seventh netherworld;
let Vāsava obtain heaven, and let the gods be free from affliction.
"Let the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes perform sacrifices now; otherwise, if you desire to fight out of pride in your strength," VamP_30.15.
"Therefore, come without distraction; here I am, ready to destroy her.
Since she had appointed Śiva to the mission as her messenger, O Nārada, [she spoke thus].
Then, from the Great Goddess, Śivadūtī was born.
And they too, having heard the words of Śaṅkara filled with pride,
uttered the sound "huṃ" and all rushed toward where Kātyāyanī stood.
Then, with arrows, spears, excellent *aṅkuśas*, battle-axes, tridents, *bhuśuṇḍis*, *paṭṭiśas*,
sharp darts, and broad iron clubs, the two foremost Daityas rained down upon the Queen of the Gods.
And she too, with arrows discharged from her excellent bow, severed their weapons along with their arms;
then the Great Goddess, whose prowess is fierce in battle, struck down other great asuras with hundreds of arrows.
Mārī struck some with her trident, while Kauśikī felled others with blows from her skull-topped staff;
likewise, Brāhmī rendered other asuras powerless by hurling great torrents of water upon them.
Māheśvarī tore open the chests [of her enemies] with her trident; Vaiṣṇavī burnt others;
Kumārī [struck] with her spear; Aindrī with her thunderbolt; and she in the form of Varāha with her snout and her discus.
Even those torn by claws, the lioness of Aṭṭāṭṭahāsa, the messenger of Rudra, did not spare;
likewise, others were struck by Rudra with his trident, and Vināyaka with his battle-axe.
Thus, struck down by the Goddess in various forms, those lords of the Danus fell upon the earth; being devoured there by spirits, they met their destruction.
Then those great asuras, being struck by the goddesses and agitated by the Mothers—
with disheveled hair and trembling eyes— sought refuge with Raktabīja out of fear.

That Raktabīja, suddenly approaching and seizing a supreme weapon consecrated by the circle of Mothers, began to scatter the hosts of spirits on all sides; with his lips quivering in rage, he entered [the fray].
Seeing him approaching, the Mothers showered the son of Diti with weapons of sharp points;
and whatever drop of blood fell upon the earth, from that very measure another asura was born.
Then, having witnessed that marvel, Kauśikī said to Keśinī:
"O fierce one, drink the blood of the enemy with haste, opening wide your mouth which resembles the submarine fire!"
Thus addressed, that boon-granting Mother indeed opened her mouth wide—fearful and fierce—making her lower lip touch the earth while her upper lip reached the sky; thus stood Carmamuṇḍā.
Then Ambikā, having distressed her enemy by pulling his hair, cast him into her own mouth;
yet even so, she pierced his chest with her trident, and other beings born from the wound fell into her mouth.
Then his blood dried up, and with its depletion he became weak;
him, whose vigor was gone, he cut into a hundred pieces with a wheel adorned with gold.

When that leader of Danu’s army had been slaughtered, those Dānavas wailed most piteously, crying out, "O father! O brother! and saying, "Where are you going? Stay! Come back for a moment!"* 30.31 *The original text contains the vocative particle "he" and the imperative "tiṣṭhasva. I have translated these as "O" and "Stay! respectively to maintain the flow of the English. The phrase "muhūrttam ehi" is translated as "Come back for a moment. I hope this meets your requirements. Let me know if you need further assistance.
Likewise, other Daityas, with their masses of hair disheveled, their armor and ornaments shattered, and stripped naked,
fell upon the surface of the earth and fled toward the great mountain, bewildered by Mṛḍānī.
Beholding that army with its armor, weapons, and ornaments shattered, Niśumbha, the lord of the Dānavas,
his chariot’s wheels and axle likewise broken, approached Mṛḍānī in a fit of rage.
Taking up his sword and brandishing his radiant shield, he gazed upon her form;
then, afflicted by a fever of paralysis and delusion, he became as motionless as a figure painted in a picture.
Seeing him thus paralyzed, the Goddess laughed and spoke these words to the gods in her presence:
"By this valor the gods have been conquered by you; by this strength you now seek to solicit me."
Having heard the words of Kauśikī, the Dānava,
the best among speakers, reflected for a long time and then spoke these words.
O timid one, this delicate body of yours will shatter into a hundred pieces from the mere falling of my sword, like an unbaked clay vessel in water.
Reflecting on this matter, O beautiful one, I do not set my mind upon striking you; therefore, O large-eyed lady, accept me.
Indeed, even Indra would not be able to withstand the fall of my sword;
turn your mind away from battle and become my wife now.
O sage, having heard these words of Niśumbha, the Mistress of Yogins laughed and spoke these words to Niśumbha with profound feeling.
"O hero, I have not been conquered in battle; for I shall never become the wife of anyone.
If you desire me as a wife, then conquer me in combat."
When these words had been spoken, O Nārada, the Dānava raised his sword and then hurled it with great force toward Kauśikī.
As that sword was falling, he cut it along with the shield by means of six arrows adorned with peacock feathers; that was like a marvel.
When his sword along with its scabbard was severed, the great asura seized a mace and rushed toward Kośabhavā,
equal to the wind in speed.
As he was falling, Ambikā swiftly severed both his hands— joined, even, and firm—
with a razor-edged blade attached to her mace in that battle.
While that fierce and terrifying enemy of the gods had not yet fallen,
the Mothers, led by Caṇḍā, were delighted and raised a tumultuous shout of joy.
Then the gods stationed in the sky, led by Śatakratu, cried out "Victory! Be victorious! as they rejoiced once the enemy had been struck down.
Then musical instruments were sounded on all sides by hosts of beings,
and the gods released a rain of flowers toward Kātyāyanī.
O great sage, seeing Niśumbha fallen, Śumbha, out of rage,
mounted his celestial chariot and advanced with noose in hand.
Then, seeing the lord of the Dānavas approaching with his elephant,
he took up four arrows that possessed the luster of the crescent moon.
With two razor-sharp arrows, she simultaneously severed the two feet of the elephant;
then Ambikā, laughing, struck the frontal globes with two more as if in sport.
With his two feet severed, the elephant fell down according to its will,
like the peak of the king of mountains struck by Indra’s thunderbolt.
As Śumbha was about to spring up, having been subdued by him,
Śivā severed his head, adorned with earrings, with an arrow.
With his head severed, the lord of the Daityas fell along with his elephant,
like a great crane together with its buffalo when struck down by Mahāsena.

Having heard that the enemies of the gods had been slain by Mṛḍānī, the gods—led by Indra, Sūrya, the Maruts, Aśvin, and Vasu—approached that excellent mountain, bowing low with humility, and then uttered these words of praise for the Goddess: VamP_30.55.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, O Blessed One, destroyer of sins; salutations to you, shatterer of the pride of the enemies of the gods;
salutations to you, bestower of sovereignty upon Hari and Hara; salutations to you, accomplisher of the work of the enjoyers of the sacrifice."
Homage be to you, the destroyer of the enemies of the thirty-three gods; homage be to you, worshipped at the feet of the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices;
homage be to you, the bringer of destruction to Mahiṣa; homage be to you, praised by Hari, Hara, and Bhāskara.
Homage be to you, who possess eighteen arms; homage be to you, the slayer of Śumbha and Niśumbha.
Homage be to you, the wielder of the trident who removes the suffering of the world; homage be to you, Nārāyaṇī, the bearer of the discus.
Homage be to you, O Vārāhī, who always upholds the earth; homage be to you, O Nārasiṃhī, to whom we bow. Homage be to you, O Nārasiṃhī, to whom we bow;
homage be to you, O Vajradharā, whose banner is the elephant. Homage be to you, O Kaumārī, who are borne by a peacock.
Homage be to you, who are borne by the swan of Brahmā; homage be to you, Mālāvikaṭā of beautiful hair!
Homage be to you, Mālāvikaṭā of beautiful hair!
Homage be to you, who ride upon the back of a donkey; homage be to you, the remover of all afflictions, who pervades the universe!
Homage be to you, O Sovereign of the Universe; protect the universe and utterly destroy the enemies of the twice-born and the gods.
Homage be to you, O Mother of All, O Three-eyed One; homage, homage to you, O Giver of Boons—be gracious!

You are Brahmāṇī, you are Mṛḍānī, with a beautiful peacock for your vehicle, holding a spear in your hand; you are Kumārī, you are Vārāhī with a lovely face, and you are Vaiṣṇavī with Viṣṇu and his bow, Śārṅga.

You are Nārasiṃhī, difficult to behold, with a growling roar; likewise you are Aindrī with the thunderbolt, you are Mārī, and you are the Yoginī who delights in moving through corpses and severed heads, perfected in yoga.

Salutations to you, O three-eyed Goddess! For those who dwell at your feet, bowing their heads day after day in prostration, there is indeed no humiliation nor any inauspiciousness, for they constantly hold in their hands the offerings of hymns and flowers.
Thus praised by the best of the gods, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods laughed and said to the foremost of the gods, siddhas, and great ṛṣis:
"By your grace, I have obtained the most excellent victory over the enemies of the gods at the head of the battle through my crushing power."

"O best of men, those devoted to you who recite this hymn of praise spoken by you shall have their bad dreams destroyed; of this there is no doubt. Let another boon also be chosen according to your desire."
The gods said:
"O you who grant boons to the thirty gods, strive for the welfare of the young brahmins and the cows;
O you whose body is like fire, burn once again those other enemies of the gods."
The Goddess said:
"O gods, I shall once again appear with my face smeared with blood, born from the sweat-drops on the face of Hara;
devoted to the nourishment of the demon Andhāsura, I shall be renowned in the worlds by the name Carcikā."
"Furthermore, having united with Yaśodā in the house of Nanda, I shall slay the supreme enemy of the gods—
Vipracitti, Lavaṇa, and likewise the other two, Śumbha and Niśumbha, who strike with their teeth."
Furthermore, in the Tiṣya age, when the earth shall be devoid of food and afflicted by pestilence within the house of Indra,
I, Śākambharī, shall indeed become manifest in the goddess Amitasatyadhāmā and sustain the gods.
"O gods, for the further destruction of opposing forces and for the protection of the sages in the Vindhya mountains, I shall become a ṛṣi;
having utterly destroyed the Daityas who act with wicked conduct, I shall indeed return once more to the abode of the gods."
O gods, when the great asura Aruṇākṣa comes into being, I shall appear for the benefit of the deities;
having caused his life to perish in the form of a great bee, I will once again reach the third heaven.
Pulastya said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, the boon-granting goddess offered salutations to the foremost of the celestial beings;
then, dismissing all creatures, she ascended into the sky, followed by throngs of Siddhas.
This supreme Purāṇa, the victory of the Goddess, is most sacred and bestows auspiciousness upon men;
it destroys the Rākṣasas, and the Blessed One has declared that this must always be heard by those who are self-restrained.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O observer of noble vows, how was the Krauñca mountain, together with its buffalo, split by Skanda?
O Brahmin of immeasurable luster, tell me this in detail.
Pulastya said: Listen, O Nārada, I shall relate to you this ancient and meritorious story concerning the increase of the fame of Kumāra Kārttikeya.
O Brahmin, because that semen of the wielder of the Pināka bow was drunk by the Fire-god and then spilled, the consumer of oblations became overcome by it and his splendor diminished.
Then he of immeasurable splendor went into the presence of the gods;
and being dispatched by them as well, he quickly went to the world of Brahmā.
As he was going along, the Fire-god saw the goddess Kuṭilā on the path;
seeing her, he said, "O crooked one, this energy is very difficult to restrain."
"Abandoned by Maheśvara, it could consume even the worlds;
therefore, accept this son, for he shall be blessed."
Having thus remembered the supreme resolve made by Agni, that crooked river replied to the Fire-god: "Cast me into the waters. (VamP 31.7)
Then the goddess sustained that energy of Śarva and nourished it;
even the blessed Hutāśana, wandering at will, was roaming about.
Then, for five thousand years, the consumer of oblations (Agni) sustained his flesh,
bones, blood, fat, marrow, semen, and skin.
His body hair, beard, eyes, hair, and so forth—all became golden;
therefore, the Purifier (Pāvaka) is celebrated in the worlds as Hiraṇyaretas (Golden-seeded).
Then, carrying that embryo for five thousand years like a blazing fire, Kuṭilā arrived at the abode of Brahmā.
The Lotus-born One, seeing that great river suffering in distress, asked her: "By whom was this fetus placed within you?"
And she said to Śaṅkara: "O best of beings, that semen which was indeed drunk by Agni was deposited by him today within me, as he was rendered powerless."
O Grandfather, for five thousand years the fetus remained within her while she bore it, and it never fell at any time.
Having heard that, the Blessed One said: "Go to Mount Udaya;
there is a great and formidable forest of reeds there, extending for a hundred yojanas."
O Suśreṇi, cast him right there upon that broad mountain ridge;
at the end of ten thousand years, he will then become a child.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, she, the delight of the mountain, came to the mountain in embodied form; having arrived, she easily gave birth to the embryo.
Having abandoned that child, she suddenly approached Brahmā;
by the power of the mantra, she became composed of water and appeared crooked.
And by the splendor of Śiva, that great forest of reeds became golden;
likewise, the other trees, beasts, and birds dwelling there were transformed.
Then, when ten full centuries of autumns had passed, a lotus-eyed infant was born, radiant like the rising sun.
Lying on his back in a divine forest of reeds,
the Blessed One placed his thumb in his mouth and wept like the king of clouds.
In the meantime, the six highly resplendent goddesses, the Kṛttikās,
while traveling at their own will, beheld the infant situated in the Śara forest.
Filled with compassion, they gathered where Skanda was stationed;
"I first! I first! they cried out for his breast-milk.
Seeing them disputing, he became six-faced;
and out of affection, all the Kṛttikās nurtured that infant.
Being nourished by them, O Sage, that boy attained growth;
he became renowned as Kārttikeya, born as the best among the strong.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, the Lotus-born one said to Pāvaka:
"To what extent has your son Guha grown at this present time?"
Having heard those words and not knowing him to be the son of Hara,
he said to his son, "O Lord of Gods, I do not know which Guha this is."
The Blessed One said to him: "O Lord of the Three Worlds, that energy which was drunk by you in the past has become the three-eyed one, born as an infant in the Śara grove."
Having heard the words of his grandfather, Pāvaka quickly approached, mounted upon a swift ram; Kuṭilā beheld him there.
Then Kuṭilā quickly asked, "O sage, where are you going?
He replied, "To the infant born in the Śara forest for the sake of destroying my sons."
She said, "He is my son," and the Fire-god likewise said, "He is mine.
Then Janārdana, who moves according to his own will, beheld the two of them disputing.
He asked them, "For what reason have you two engaged in this dispute here?
They both replied, "Indeed, for the sake of a son born from the seed of Rudra."
Lord Hari said to them: "Go to that destroyer of Tripura;
whatever the Lord of Gods says, perform that without hesitation."
When Vasudeva had spoken thus, the two crooked-eyed ones approached Hara and said the truth in his presence: "O Nārada, whose son is this? (VamP 31.34).
Having heard those words, Rudra, his mind overflowing with joy, spoke to the Daughter of the Mountain with his hair standing on end, saying, "By good fortune! By good fortune! (VamP 31.35).
Then Ambikā said to Hara: "O Lord, let us go to ask the child; whoever he may take refuge with, he shall become his son."
"So be it," said the Lord whose banner is the bull, and he rose up together with Umā,
Kuṭilā, and the wise Pāvaka.
Having reached Śaravaṇa, those Mothers, whose faces were curved like the fire of Hara,
beheld that infant lying upon the laps of the Kṛttikās.
Then that boy, having respectfully understood their thoughts,
became a yogi of four forms, while that infant himself became six-faced.
The prince Śākha went to Śaṅkara; Viśākha went to Gaurī;
Śākha went to Kuṭilā; and Mahāsena approached Agni.
Then Rudra, filled with joy, as well as Umā and Kuṭilā,
and even Pāvaka, the lord of the gods, attained supreme delight.
Then those Kṛttikās said, "Is the six-faced one the son of Hara?
O Sage, Hara, having understood their intent, spoke these words to them according to the prescribed rite.
By name he shall indeed be Kārttikeya, your son;
however, this imperishable one will become the son of Kuṭilā, known as Kumāra.
"Let him be famous as Skanda, the son of Gaurī;
and by the name Guha, let him be known as my own son."
The son of Hutāśa shall be known as Māhāsena, and the son of Śaravaṇa shall be known as Śāradvata.
In this very way, the great yogi shall attain renown upon the earth;
because he has six faces, the mighty-armed one is celebrated by the name Ṣaṇmukha.
Having spoken thus to the Grandfather, the Blessed One, wielder of the trident, called to mind the deities; they too arrived with great haste.
Having prostrated before the enemy of Kāma (Śiva) and Umā, the daughter of the mountain, and having beheld the Fire-god with joy, as well as Kuṭilā and the Kṛttikās; ||| VamP_31.48 |||
The deities beheld the exceedingly fierce child with six faces, resembling the sun, as if stealing away their very eyes with his own splendor.
Enveloped in wonder, all those best of gods spoke thus:
"O God, the work of the gods has been accomplished by you, as well as by the goddess and by Agni."
Therefore, arise; let us go today to the powerful and imperishable sacred ford at Kurukṣetra on the Sarasvatī, and we shall consecrate the six-faced one.
Let him be the lord of the army; let him slay Mahiṣa, as well as the most terrible Tāraka, O gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras! (VamP 31.52)
"Very well," said Śarva; then the gods, together with Kumāra, rose up and went to Kurukṣetra, which yields great fruit.
Right there, the deities, including Indra, Rudra, Brahmā, and Janārdana,
together with hosts of sages, exerted themselves for the sake of his consecration.
Then Guha, Vyutātman, and the others consecrated him with water from the seven ocean-flowing rivers, which yields great fruit,
and with a thousand forms of excellent medicinal herbs.
As he was consecrated as the commander-in-chief, the prince of divine form,
the lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsarases danced.
Indeed, beholding the consecrated prince, the Daughter of the Mountain took Skanda onto her lap out of affection and smelled him on the head again and again.
Smelling the face of Kārttikeya, wet from his consecration,
the Mountain-born Goddess shone like Aditi, the mother of the gods, once smelled the face of Indra.
Seeing his son thus consecrated, Śarva attained great joy,
as did Pāvaka, the Kṛttikās, and the illustrious Kuṭilā.
Then Hara, having consecrated Guha in the command of his army,
bestowed upon him four Pramathas whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra.
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Lohitākṣa, and the terrible Nandisena;
and the fourth, the chief among the powerful, known as Kumudamālin.
O Nārada, seeing the Gaṇas of Haradatta, all the gods,
led by Brahmā, gave their own respective Pramathas to Skanda.
Viṣṇu bestowed Sthāṇu as a Brahmagaṇa, and he granted three Gaṇas:
Saṃkrama, Vikrama, and the third, Parākrama.
Śakra [bestowed] the *utkeśa* lotus; Ravi, the *daṇḍaka-piṅgala*;
Candra, the *maṇi*; the Aśvins, the *vasumaṇi*; and the two [sons], Vatsa and Nandin.
Jyotirhutāśana gave [him] another [son], Jvalajjihva; likewise, Dhātṛ gave three followers: Kunda, Mukunda, and Kusuma.
Pūṣan gave two very powerful sons, Cakrānucakra and Tvaṣṭṛ, as well as Vedhā, Atisthira, Susthira, Pāṇityaja, and Kālaka.
Svarṇamāla and Ghanāhva, the two best of the Pramathas, were given by Himavat;
likewise, the lofty Vindhya gave Atiśṛṅga as a follower.
Varuṇa gave Suvarcas and Ativarcas; the Ocean gave Saṃgraha and Vigraha; and the Nāgas gave Jaya and Mahājaya.
Ambikā gave him Unmāda and Śuṅkukarṇa, as well as Puṣpadanta;
and Vāyu gave him both Ghasa and Atighasa as his attendants.
The sun indeed gave five attendants to the six-faced one: Parigha, Caṭaka, Bhīma, Dahati, and Dahanau.
Yama gave him six attendants: Pramātha, Unmātha, Kālasena, Mahāmukha, Tālapatra, and Nāḍijaṅgha.
O best of the twice-born, Dhātṛ gave the two lords of the Gaṇas, Suprabha and Sukarman;
and Mitra gave Suvrata and Satyasandha.
Ananta, Śaṅkupīṭha, Nikumbha, Kumuda, Ambuja,
Ekākṣa, Kunaṭī, Cakṣu, Kirīṭin, and Kalaśodara.
Sūcīvaktra, Kokanada, Prahāsa, Priyaka, and Acyuta—
these fifteen groups were indeed given to Guha by the Yakṣas.
Kālakanda was the [son] of Kālindī, Raṇotkaṭa of Narmadā, Siddhayātra of Godāvarī, and Adrikampaka of Tamasā; Sahasrabāhu was the [son] of Sītā, and Sitodara of Vañjulā. 31.75
Likewise, Nanda is the son of Mandākinī, and Priyaṅkara is the son of Vipāśā.
Airāvatī gave a cat with four tusks and sixteen eyes, measuring a span; Gautamī gave a sauśika, as well as a kratha and a krauñca.
Bāhudā gave Śatasīrṣa, as well as Vāha, Gonanda, and Nandika; Bhīmarathī gave Bhīma, and Sarayū gave Vegāri.
Kāśī gave Aṣṭabāhu, and Gaṇḍakī also gave Subāhu;
the great river Citrā gave Citradeva, and Citraratha was given [by the same].
Kuhū gave a blue lotus, Madhūdakā a honey-colored one, Dhūtapāpā a Jambūka lotus, and Veṇā gave a Śvetānana lotus.
And Śrutavarmā gave to Revā, who was as swift as the ocean,
a golden horse with golden eyes for the sake of his power.
Gṛdhrapatrā, Vimalā, Cāruvaktrā, Manoharā,
Dhūtapāpā, Mahārāvā, Karṇā, and Vidrumasaṃnibhā.
Meghavatī gave Suprasāda and Suveṇu to Jiṣṇu;
Viśālā gave Yajñabāhu; and the Sarasvatīs gave the Gaṇas.
Kuṭilā gave her son ten hosts of Śakrabalas:
Karāla, Sitakeśa, Kṛṣṇakeśa, and Jaṭādhara.
Meghanāda, Caturdaṣṭra, Vidyujjihva, Daśānana, Somāpyayana, Ugra, and Devayājina.
The Kṛttikās gave these five to their son: Haṃsāsya, Kuṇḍajaṭhara, Bahugrīva, Hayānana, and Kūrmagrīva.
The sages gave these five to Skanda: Sthāṇujaṅgha, Kumbhavaktra, Lohajaṅgha, Mahānana, and Piṇḍākāra.
The holy site of Pṛthūdaka gave him Nāgajihva, Candrabhāsa, Pāṇikūrma, Śaśīkṣaka, Cāṣavaktra, and Jambūka.
Cakratīrtha, Sucakrākṣa, Makarāśra, Gayāśiras,
and the group named Pañcaśikha— these Kanakhala gave as his own.
Bandhudatta, Vājiśiras, Bāhuśālin, Puṣkara,
Sarva-uñjasa, Māhiṣaka, and Piṅgala were born from Mānasa, just as [the others].
Rudra gave [the cow] Auśanasī; then other Mothers gave [their cows];
Somatīrtha gave Vasudāmā, and Prabhāsa gave Nandinī as well.
Saptasārasvata bestowed Indratīrtha, Viśokā, the Udapāna well, Ghanasvanā, and four wonderful Mothers.
Gītapriyā, Mādhavī, Tīrthanemi, Smitānanā,
Ekacūḍā, Nāgatīrtha, Kurukṣetra, and Palāsadā.
Caraṇapāvana bestowed upon him Brahmayoni, Caṇḍaśilā, Bhadrakālī, Triviṣṭapa, Cauṇḍī, Bhaiṇḍī, and Yogabhaiṇḍī.
Mānasa, the lake of the mind, gave the earth Sopānīyā, Śālikā,
Śakaghaṇṭā, Śatānandā, as well as Ulūkhalamekhalā.
Badarikāśrama gave Padmāvatī and Mādhavī,
as well as the goddess Suṣamā, who was the sole crest-jewel of beauty, and likewise Dhamadhamā.
Kedāra gave [her] the mothers Utkrāthanī, Vedamitrā,
Sunakṣatrā, Kadrulā, Suprabhātā, and Muṅgalā.
Rudramahālaya gave Devamitrā, Citrasenā,
Koṭarā, Ūrdhvaṇī, Śrīmatī, and Bahuputrikā.
Prayāga gave the mothers Palitā and Kamalākṣī,
as well as Sūpalā, Madhukumbhā, Khyāti, and the supreme Dahadahā.
The one who liberates from all sins also gave Khaṭakaṭā, another [goddess],
as well as Saṃtānikā, Vikalikā, Kramā, and Catvaravāsinī.
Jaleśvarī, Kukkuṭikā, Sudāmā, Lohamekhalā, Vapuṣmatī, Utmukākṣī, Kokā by name, Mahāśanī,
Raudrā, Karkaṭikā, and Tuṇḍā— Śvetatīrtha gave these [to him]. (VamP 31.101)
Having seen these beings, the hosts, and the Mothers, the high-souled son of Vinatā gave his own son,
the exceedingly swift peacock, as well as his son Aruṇa, the red-crested one.
Śakti [carried] the fire; the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) the garment; the Preceptor (Bṛhaspati) the staff; she (Umā), being crooked, the water-pot;
Hari the garland; the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva) the banner; and Maghavan (Indra), having placed a necklace upon his neck, [carried] the breast-plate.

Surrounded by his hosts and followed by the Mothers, seated upon his peacock and holding his excellent spear in hand, he was appointed to the command of the army by Bhava; possessing a magnificent form, he shone like the sun.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then Kumāra was consecrated as the commander-in-chief by the gods.
Having prostrated with devotion before Bhava, Girijā, and the pure Pāvaka.
Having bowed her head to the six Kṛttikās and to Kuṭilā as well,
and having paid homage to Brahmā, she spoke these words.
The prince said:
"Homage be to you, O gods! Om, homage be to you, O you whose wealth is asceticism!
By your grace, I shall conquer my enemies, Mahiṣa and Tāraka."
"I am but a child, O deities; I do not know how to say anything.
Please grant me permission now, together with Brahmā."
When these words had been spoken by the high-souled Kumāra,
the gods, their efforts having failed, gazed at his face with tearful eyes.
Rising up out of affection for his son, Śaṅkara also took Prajāpati by the right hand and approached Skanda.
Then Umā said to her son: "Come, come, O slayer of enemies!
Pay homage to the divine feet of Viṣṇu, which are saluted by the worlds."
Then Guha, smiling, said: "O Mother, tell me who this is, for whom such a respectful salutation is performed by people like me?"
When that deed had been performed, his mother spoke these words:
"Indeed, this great-souled one who has the Garuda as his banner shall speak to you."
"However, my lord, your father Śaṅkara told me here that there is indeed no other superior to him, neither myself nor any other embodied beings."
When this had been spoken by Pārvatī, Skanda prostrated before Janārdana and stood with his palms joined in reverence, seeking an order from Acyuta.
Then the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, having performed a rite of benediction for Skanda who stood with palms joined in reverence,
granted him his permission.
Nārada said:
O brahmin-sage, you ought to explain to me that auspicious and meritorious rite which the one whose banner is Garuḍa performed for Śikhidhvaja.
Pulastya said:
Listen to the meritorious rite for securing well-being, which the Blessed Lord Hari proclaimed for the sake of Skanda’s victory and for the slaying of Mahiṣa.
May Brahmā, the lotus-born, and the quality of passion (rajas) grant you well-being;
may Viṣṇu, the unborn whose hands are marked with the discus, bestow well-being upon you.
May Śaṅkara, whose banner is the bull, together with his consort, grant you well-being through devotion;
and may Pāvaka, whose vehicle is the peacock, grant you well-being. (VamP 32.16)
May Divākara grant you well-being; may Soma, along with Bhauṃja, Budha, and Guru, grant you well-being;
may Kāvya always grant you well-being; and may Śanaiścara perform a rite of auspiciousness for you.
May Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras—
may these seven great sages, including Mṛkaṇḍu as the eighth, grant you well-being and constant prosperity.
May the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, the hosts of Sādhyas and Maruts, the fires, the suns, the wielders of the trident, the Maheśvaras,
the Yakṣas, the Piśācas, the Vasus, and the Kinnaras— may all these ever-exerting ones grant you well-being.
May the Nāgas, Suparṇas, rivers, lakes, sacred fords, holy shrines, oceans, the hosts of mighty beings, and the lords of the Gaṇas—ever striving—grant you well-being. (VamP 32.20)

May there be well-being for your two-footed beings and indeed for your four-footed ones; may there be well-being for your many-footed beings, and even for those without feet, may there be freedom from ailment.
May the wielder of the thunderbolt protect the eastern quarter; may the staff-bearer protect the south;
may the noose-wielder protect the west; and may the radiant one protect the north.
Agni [presides] over the southeast; Kubera over the southwest;
Vāyu over the west and north; and Śiva over the northeast as well.
Above is Dhruva, Śiva, and also Purvottarā;
Musatī, Lāṅgalī, Cakrī, and Dhanuṣmān are in the intermediate directions.
May the Boar protect me in the ocean; may the Man-Lion protect me in the fortress;
and may the glorious Mādhava, whose voice is the sound of the Sāmaveda and who is adorned with all creepers, protect me everywhere.
Pulastya said: Thus, having had the rites for success performed, Guha, the foremost wielder of the spear,
prostrated before all the gods and sprang up from the surface of the earth.
Then all those hosts who had been granted by the joyful gods followed Kumāra; they were able to assume any form at will and traveled through the air.
And likewise, all the Mothers rose up into the sky together with the powerful Skanda, desiring to slay the great asuras.
Then, after traveling a very long distance, Skanda said to his attendants:
"O you of great prowess, quickly effect a descent upon the earth!"
Having heard Guha’s words, the Gaṇas descended to the surface of the earth;
falling from nearby toward that region, they let out a terrifying roar.
That roar, having filled the entire earth and the vault of heaven,
entered the netherworld, the abode of the Dānavas, through the opening of the ocean.
Then that [news] was heard by Mahiṣa, and by the wise Tāraka, by Virocana, Jambha, and the asura Kujambha.
Hearing that firm sound, which was like the sudden fall of a thunderbolt, they wondered, "What is this? and quickly went then to Andhaka.
O Nārada, having gathered together with Andhaka himself, those foremost of Dānavas, being greatly agitated, held counsel regarding that sound.
While the Daityas were thus deliberating,
the lord of the Daityas, Pātālaketu, whose face was that of a boar, emerged from the earth and arrived at Rasātala.
Pierced by arrows, pained and trembling again and again, he approached the Asura Andhaka and spoke these dejected words: VamP_32.36.
Pātālaketu said:
"O Lord of Daityas, I went to the hermitage of Gālava;
I began an effort by force to destroy it."
"O King, I do not know that man by whom the arrow was discharged at me, until I enter that hermitage in the form of a boar."
With his collarbone pierced by an arrow, that creature of great speed fled from the hermitage out of fear of him, yet he pursued me from behind.
"O Asura, the supreme sound of a horse's hooves is heard;
'Stay! Stay!'—thus speaks that hero from behind me.
Out of fear of him, I have come to this ocean, the southern sea."
As far as I could see, there were men stationed there in various costumes and forms;
some roared like thunderclouds, while others shouted back in response.
Others said, "We shall surely slay Mahiṣāsura;
we shall cause Tāraka to be killed today," while others spoke thus, full of splendor.
Having heard that, O Lord of Asuras, an even greater terror arose within me;
abandoning the great ocean, I fell down, overwhelmed by fear.
The powerful one leaped into a pit opened in the earth after me,
abandoning his own city of Hiraṇyapura out of fear of that.
"Having arrived in your presence, you ought to show me favor.
Having heard those words, Andhaka spoke these words with a voice like the sound of thunder:
"You should not fear him; O Dānava, I shall protect the truth.
Both Mahiṣa and Tāraka, as well as Bāṇa, the best among the strong—"
Without even announcing it, those heroes— Andhaka, Mahiṣa, and the others—
set out for battle, accompanied by their own retinues, toward the earth.
O Sage, where those hosts of wood-workers raised a great clamor, there the Daityas arrived, equipped with weapons and accompanied by their armies.
Then, seeing the Daityas rushing toward them, the hosts of Kārttikeya suddenly charged forward, as did that fierce circle of Mothers.
Standing at their head, the powerful Sthāṇu, seizing his iron club,
furiously destroyed the enemy host like Rudra destroying the sacrificial animals.
Beholding Mahādeva slaying him, Kalaśodara took up an axe in his hand and struck all the great asuras.
Jvālāmukha, the terrifying one, seizing the asura with his hand, cast him—
along with his chariot, elephant, and horses— into his wide-open mouth.
And Daṇḍaka, filled with rage and spear in hand, uprooted the great asura along with his mount and hurled him into the great ocean.
And Śaṅkukarṇa, bearing a mace and wielding a plow, dragged the Dānavas and crushed them,
like a self-controlled minister who wields a spear subdues a king.
The heroic Puṣpadanta, lord of the Gaṇas, bearing sword and shield,
split the Daityas and Dānavas in two, three, and many ways.
Wherever Piṅgala runs about, raising his staff,
there heaps of corpses of Dānavas are seen.
Whirling his trident, the thousand-eyed leader of the Gaṇas,
that hero, struck down the Asuras along with their horses, chariots, and elephants.
Bhīma, with a rain of terrible rocks, struck down the Asuras as they advanced before him,
just as Indra strikes down great mountains with a shower of thunderbolts.
The fierce and powerful Gaṇa Raudra, whose eyes were like the wheels of a cart and who wore five tufts of hair,
whirled his mallet with great speed and struck down his enemies by force.
With his palm alone, the one of great speed shattered a mountain in battle; he reduced an elephant along with its rider to ashes, as well as a chariot together with its warrior.
O Sage, the powerful Nāḍījaṅgha struck the asuras with his footfalls, fists, and knees, and with stakes equal to thunderbolts.
With his neck like that of a tortoise, he struck down the Daityas along with their mounts by means of his neck, his head, his foot, and his rolling about.
But Piṇḍāraka, who delights in strife, tears apart the Dānavas arrogant in battle with his snout and both horns.
Then that incomparable army, being slaughtered by the lords of the Gaṇas,
fled, as did Mahiṣa and Tāraka, the leader of the Gaṇas.
Being struck by those excellent weapons, the Pramathas, fearing the Dānavas,
surrounded them on all sides and then fought back in great anger.
Then Haṃsāsya struck Mahiṣāsura with a paṭṭiśa;
Ṣoḍaśākṣa struck him with a trident, and Śataśīrṣa with an excellent sword.
Śrutāyudha struck the Daitya on the head with a mace, Viśoka with a club, and Bandhudatta with a trident.
Likewise, though struck by other attendants in battle with spears, javelins, double-edged swords,
and axes, he did not tremble, like Mount Maināka.
Tāraka is slain in battle by Bhadrakālī,
as well as by Ulūkhalā and Ekacūḍā, and he is torn apart by their supreme weapons.
Though being struck by the Pramathas and the Mothers, those two great Asuras did not succumb to agitation; remaining undisturbed, they themselves agitated even the Gaṇas.
Then Mahisha, having quickly defeated the Pramathas with blows from his mace,
rushed toward Kumara, armed with his weapon.
Seeing the buffalo charging toward him, Sucakrākṣa,
filled with rage, raised his discus and blocked the descendant of Danu.
O Brahmin, with their hands marked by the mace and the discus, they then fought against the great chariot-warriors of the Gaṇas and the Asuras— light, wonderful, and skillfully.
Mahiṣa hurled his mace after brandishing it at the Gaṇas,
while Sucakrākṣa cast his own wheel toward the Asura.
Having severed the mace and the sharp-edged discus, he rushed toward Mahiṣa;
then the Daityas cried out loudly, "Alas! Mahiṣa is slain! VamP_32.75.
Hearing that, the swift Bāṇa rushed forward, brandishing a spear;
Raktākṣa struck the discus with five hundred fist-blows.
With five hundred arms, he bound him whose eyes were like beautiful wheels;
yet, though powerful, he was rendered motionless by Bāṇa’s arrow.
Seeing that the chariot with its excellent wheels and axles had indeed been bound by the Asura Bāṇa,
the mighty Makarākṣa, mace in hand, rushed forward.
With his mace, the exceedingly powerful one struck Bāṇa on the head;
then, afflicted by pain, the great Asura released Sucakrākṣa.
And he too, joined with him, was filled with shame, O high-minded one.
Abandoning the battle, he went to Śāligrāma;
Bāṇa, too, struck by Makārākṣa, turned his face away from the fight.
O ascetic who torments the gods, the entire army of the Daityas was shattered.
Then, seeing his own forces broken, the powerful Daitya Tāraka rushed toward the lords of the Gaṇas with sword raised in hand.
Then, by that incomparable sword, those lords of the hosts headed by Haṃsavaktra, along with their mothers, were defeated in battle; afflicted by fear, they sought refuge with Skanda.
Seeing those hosts of Bhaga, the son of Maheśvara beheld Tāraka approaching with his sword;
as soon as he saw him, he pierced him in the heart with a spear, and with his vital organs shattered, he fell to the earth.
When that brother was slain, O great seer, the evil-minded Mahiṣa became broken in spirit and overcome with fear;
abandoning the front of the battle, he fled to the mountain named Dimācala.
When the hero Tāraka had been slain and Mahiṣa had fled to the Himalayas out of fear, Bāṇa,
while Bali was being struck down by Garuḍa for his transgression, entered the formidable ocean out of fear.
Having slain Tāraka at the head of the battle and seizing his spear with great speed,
the prince mounted his peacock adorned with crests and went forth to slay the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Looking back at Śikhaṇḍiketana, who was approaching with a choice spear in his hand,
he abandoned Kailāsa as well as the Himālaya and the Krauñca mountain, and entered into Guha.
The Lord, the son of the wielder of the Pināka bow, though well-disposed, guarded with great effort the Daitya who had entered [the body];
yet, reflecting, "How can I become the slayer of my own kinsman?", he remained there in that state of thought.
Then Puṣkarasaṃbhava, Hara, Murāri, and the Lord of the Devas arrived;
having approached, they said to Mahiṣa, "Shatter him along with his mountain with your spear and accomplish the work of the gods."
Having heard those words, which were both pleasing and true, Kārttikeya laughed at the gods and said:
"How indeed can one kill his own brother, who is the son of his mother’s brother and the grandson of his maternal grandfather?"

This is indeed an ancient sacred tradition (śruti), which the great seers learned in the Vedas sing; and by following the teaching of this supreme [tradition], even those who have committed great sins go to heaven.

A cow, a Brahmin, an elderly person, one whose words are authoritative, a child, a kinsman, and an uncorrupted woman—even if they have committed an offense—must never be killed; likewise, the preceptor and other elders are not to be slain.
Knowing this supreme dharma, O lords of the gods, I would not slay my brother on my mother’s side;
when the Daitya emerges from within the cave, then I shall strike the enemy with my spear.
Having heard the words of Kumāra, O Great Seer, Śakra formed a resolution in his heart and said to Guha:
"You are not wiser than I; for what reason do you speak these words? Listen, for it was previously declared by Hari."
"One should not kill many for the sake of one"—this is the settled conclusion in the scriptures.
One may kill one for the sake of many; by that, one does not become a sinner.
32.95 Having heard this, O Fire-born one, while I was previously established in my vow, I formerly slew Namuci, even though he was my own brother and younger sibling. 32.96 VamP_32.96.
Therefore, for the sake of many, exert your prowess and slay the arrogant Mahiṣāsura with the spear given by Pāvaka.
Having heard the words of Purandara, Kumāra, his eyes bloodshot with rage and trembling, spoke these words to Śatakratu: VamP_32.98.
"O fool, what strength do you have in your arms, even that bodily strength of yours, O slayer of Vṛtra, by which you revile me? Surely you are not a man of sense."
The Thousand-eyed One said to him, "O Guha, I am stronger than you. Guha replied to him, "Come, come! Fight me if you are indeed strong! (VamP 32.100)
Then the powerful Śakra said: "O son of the Kṛttikās, it is known that whoever performs the circumambulation of Krauñca itself more swiftly shall indeed be victorious. (VamP 32.101)
Having heard those words, the swift Skanda cast off his peacock and,
proceeding on foot, went even more rapidly to perform a circumambulation.
Then Śakra, having descended from the king of serpents and circumambulated him with his foot, stood there;
Guha approached and said, "O fool, why have you come to a standstill?"
Indra said to him, "O Kauṭilya, I previously performed a circumambulation to his right; you did not do so before. The prince then spoke to Śakra.
Having previously engaged in mutual dispute,
they both approached and spoke to Maheśa, Brahmā, and Mādhava.
Then Hari said to Skanda: "You ought to question Parvata;
he will tell you what was previously related by the son of Agni when he approached Krauñca:
'By whom was this circumambulation performed first?'"
Having heard those words of Mādhava, the son of Agni approached the Krauñca mountain and asked that peak: "By whom was this circumambulation performed previously?"
Thus addressed, the highly intelligent Krauñca spoke first;
afterwards, Guha, the shatterer of mountain peaks, performed what had been done by Tāyī.
As the Krauñca bird was speaking thus, Kauṭilya, his lower lip quivering with rage,
then pierced him with a spear along with Mahiṣa.
When that son had been slain, the powerful Sunābha, the king of mountains, likewise rushed forward with speed;
meanwhile, Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Śiva, and the Vasus, having seen Mahiṣa killed by Guha, departed for heaven.
Seeing his maternal uncle, the powerful Kumāra, having uprooted a spear, was intent on killing him;
