but he was restrained by Cakradhara, who embraced him with both arms with great force, crying out, "He is my elder!"
Having approached Sunābha, Himācala took [the child] by the hand and led him away elsewhere;
meanwhile, Hari, whose vehicle is the enemy of serpents, swiftly carried Kumāra along with Śikhaṇḍin to heaven.
Then Guha said to Hari, the Lord of the Gods: "O Blessed One, my discrimination has been lost through delusion;
my maternal uncle’s son, my brother, was cast out by me. Therefore, I shall wither away my own body."
Viṣṇu said to him: "Go to Pṛthūdaka, the best of holy places, which is the axe for the tree of sin.
Having bathed in the Oghavatī and beheld Hara with devotion, you shall become equal in splendor to the Sun."
Thus addressed by Hari, the Kumāra approached the sacred ford, beheld Śambhu,
bathed, and having worshipped the gods, he— resplendent like the sun— went to the mountain, the abode of Hara.
Sucakranetra also performed austerities on a great mountain in the wind, subsisting only on air;
while he was thus propitiating the bull-bannered god, Hara became pleased with him and became a granter of boons.

From the god, he chose a boon for the sake of a weapon: "May the Blessed One grant me that peerless discus which can sever the arms of enemies with the hand, just as [Indra] did for Bāṇa. (VamP 32.117)
Śambhu said to him: "Go; this boon has indeed been granted to you, O Discus.
It shall sever that increased strength of Bāṇa’s arms; there is no doubt about this."
When the boon had been granted by the Destroyer of Tripura, Gaṇeśvara approached Skanda;
having prostrated at his feet and paid homage, he joyfully announced the favor of Hara.
Thus has been told by you the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura through the piercing by the spear of the Three-eyed One’s son;
it is the cause of Krauñca’s death, for the sake of those who have sought refuge, a remover of sins, and an increaser of merit.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
He who had been struck by the arrows of the Daityas while they were deliberating—
Tell me, by what arrow was that lord of the sons of Diti pierced?
Pulastya said:

O great sage, there was once a king in the lineage of Raghu, a conqueror of his enemies; he had a high-souled son, a unique jewel among a multitude of virtues, who was heroic, powerful, and irresistible to his foes, yet possessed an equal disposition toward Brahmins, the blind, the wretched, and the miserable.
That great and most illustrious one named Ṛtadhvaja, mounted upon a lordly horse for the sake of Gālava,
swiftly struck Pātālaketu in the back with an arrow resembling a crescent moon.
Nārada said:
For what purpose did that most excellent being accomplish this for Gālava,
by means of which arrow the prince slew the Daitya?
Pulastya said: Long ago, while the sage Gālava was performing austerities, constantly established in his own great hermitage,
Tālaketu, out of folly, fell upon him to create an obstacle to his penance and to shatter his meditative absorption.
He did not wish to waste his ascetic power, for he was indeed capable of reducing him to ashes;
instead, looking toward the sky, he released a long, hot, and most grievous sigh.
Then the excellent horse fell from the sky, and an incorporeal voice spoke:
"This powerful steed could traverse thousands of yojanas in a single day."

Having seized that excellent horse and harnessed it for King Ṛtadhvaja, who had taken up his weapons, the great seer remained as if absorbed in asceticism; then the prince, approaching the Daitya, pierced him with arrows.
"Tell me, O observer of noble vows, by whom was the horse released from the expanse of the sky?
Whose speech has become embodied? My curiosity is great. (VamP 33.9)
Pulastya said:
There was a powerful and illustrious king of the Gandharvas named Viśvavasu, the singer of the great Indra;
he swiftly released the horse within the circle of the earth for the sake of the sacrifice of Ṛtadhvaja.
Nārada said:
For what purpose did the king of the Gandharvas send that one of great speed?
And for what purpose was it sent to King Kuvalayāśva and his son?
Pulastya said:
Among the women of the three worlds, there was a lady endowed with virtuous character and qualities who was the most excellent;
she was a mass of beauty, equal in splendor to the moon, named Madālasā, who was indeed languid with intoxication.
The powerful enemy of the gods saw her sporting beautifully in the Nandana grove;
Pātālaketu then carried off that slender woman, for whom that excellent horse had been given as a prize.
Having slain the Daitya and obtained the fair-limbed maiden, the king’s son remained there;
just as the lord of the gods, Mahendra, was beheld by Śacī, so was the prince beheld by the deer-eyed woman.
Nārada said:
When Mahiṣa and the great Asura Tāraka had thus been slain,
what did the wise son of Hiraṇyākṣa do next?
Pulastya said:
Seeing Tāraka and Mahiṣa slain in battle, the evil-minded Andhaka, the destroyer of the gods' army, became filled with rage.
Then, accompanied by only a small retinue and grasping an iron club in his hand,
he emerged from Pātāla and wandered across the earth.
Then, as he was wandering on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves,
he beheld the auspicious Gaurī, the daughter of the mountain, standing in the midst of her companions.
Then, upon seeing that daughter of the mountain king with her beautiful limbs in the forest, the asura Andhaka was suddenly afflicted by the arrows of desire.
Then the foolish asura, blinded by passion, spoke these words:
"To whom does this beautiful woman belong, whose every limb is lovely, who wanders in the forest? (VamP 33.20)
If she were not indeed a resident of my inner apartments, what would be the use of this fruitless life of mine? (VamP 33.21)
"Since I am not a lover of this slender-waisted woman, fie upon my beauty! What need have I for such enduring form? (VamP 33.22)
He is my kinsman, he is my counselor, he is my brother for the life hereafter—
he who shall unite me with that deer-eyed woman of dark hair.

While the lord of the Daityas was speaking thus, Prahlāda, an ocean of wisdom, covered his ears with both hands, shook his head, and spoke these words: VamP_33.24: "While the lord of the Daityas was speaking thus, Prahlāda, an ocean of wisdom, covered his ears with both hands, shook his head, and spoke these words."
"Do not speak thus, O Lord of Daityas; she is indeed the mother of the world, the wife of Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident and lord of the worlds."
Do not entertain this most wicked thought which instantly destroys a lineage;
let her, who is another's wife, not sink into the netherworld for your sake.
For this is indeed contemptible among the virtuous, and likewise contemptible among the wicked;
let those enemies of yours commit the sin of violating another's wife.

O Lord of the Daityas, you have not heard a certain verse sung by King Gādhi upon seeing his army intent upon the cows of the Brahmins— a verse that is true, wholesome, and beneficial for all the world.

It is better to give up one's life than to take pleasure in slanderous speech; it is better to observe silence than to utter a falsehood. It is better to be impotent than to violate another's wife; it is better to beg for alms than to repeatedly taste the wealth of others.
Hearing Prahlāda’s words, blinded by anger and tormented by passion, he cried out, "This is that mother of my enemies! and rushed forward.
Then the Daityas rushed after him like stones discharged from a machine;
Nandin, the imperishable one with his hand raised in a thunderbolt, forcibly checked them.
Led by Māyātāra, they were warded off and put to flight;
struck by the thunderbolt, they quickly fled in fear toward the ten directions.
Seeing them being tormented in battle by Nandin, the Dānava Andhaka struck Nandin with an iron club and felled him.
Seeing Śailādi fallen and Andhaka likewise running away,
Gaurī assumed a hundred forms out of fear of that evil-minded one.
Then that great lord of the asuras, standing in the midst of the host of goddesses, shone as he moved about,
like a rutting elephant roaming in the forest amidst female elephants with eyes rolling from passion.
He did not recognize her there; who indeed was that daughter of the mountain?
There is no wonder in this, for these four [senses] never perceive anything at all.
One born blind does not see here; one blinded by passion also does not see. One intoxicated by pride does not see; one whose end is stained by greed does not see.
Not seeing Girijā, he is then truly blind, even though he sees her.
Thinking, "I will not strike these young women," that evil-minded one was then repelled by the goddess Śatavārī.
Struck by excellent weapons, he fell to the surface of the earth;
seeing Andhaka fallen, the night, possessing a hundred forms, departed.
Having departed from that place, Ambikā vanished;
and seeing Andhaka fallen, the leaders of the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas [approached].
Making a very great noise, they rushed forward seeking battle;
hearing the sound of those who were charging, the Lord of the Gaṇas stood firm.
Taking up his vajra, the powerful Lord of the Gaṇas was like Maghavan himself.
Having approached and seen Ambikā, he prostrated at her auspicious feet;
and the Goddess, who was his own form, said to them, "Go as you wish."
Dwell upon the surface of the earth here, being honored by men;
and let your dwelling be in gardens and forests.
Having prostrated before Ambikā, go in due order among the lords of the forest, the trees.
Being praised by the Kinnaras, they went to all the various directions;
Andhaka, having regained his senses, no longer saw the Mountain’s Daughter,
and seeing his own army defeated, he then fled toward the netherworld (pātāla).
Then, O Sage, that evil-minded Andhaka, having gone to Pātāla, did not eat by day;
struck by the arrows of Madana and overcome by the power of desire, he could not sleep at night, remembering Gaurī.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
Where indeed had Śaṅkara gone, along with Ambā and Nandin?
He fought against Anadhaka; you should tell this to me.
Pulastya said:
Since he remained in a state of great delusion for a thousand years,
from that time forth he has appeared devoid of luster and with his virility diminished.
Then, beholding his own body devoid of luster, Maheśvara,
the best among the wise, set his mind upon performing penance.
Having undertaken the great vow and consoled Ambikā,
the Lord established Śailādi as her protector and wandered over the surface of the earth.
With his neck adorned by the great mudrā, wearing earrings made of great serpents,
he bears around the region of his waist a girdle fashioned from a great conch shell.
Holding a skull-bowl in his right hand and a water-pot in his left,
he dwelt for a single day at a time, wandering among trees, mountain ridges, and rivers.
Establishing himself in the three worlds, subsisting on roots, then on water,
and then on air, he remained there for nine hundred years in succession.
Then, having placed the betel-roll in his mouth, the ascetic became breathless upon the vast,
delightful, and level rocky surface nourished by the Himalayas.
Then, having split open the skull of the Supreme Lord, that ball of fire,
blazing with flames, descended from the midst of his matted locks onto the surface of the earth.
As the ball fell, the mountain was split open and became level with the earth;
there arose a most excellent and meritorious sacred site (tīrtha), renowned as Kedāra.
Then Hara, whose banner bears the bull, granted a boon to Kedāra,
O Brahmin— a boon that increases merit, destroys sin, and is a means to liberation.
Those self-controlled men who have drunk the water at your sacred ford, VamP_34.12.
Within six months, those who have desisted from cooking for others will certainly bear my own mark within the lotuses of their hearts.
And he shall never have a delight in evil;
his ancestral śrāddha offering shall be inexhaustible for his ancestors—of this there is no doubt.

In this world, the acts of bathing, giving, austerity, as well as fire-oblations, recitations, and so forth, shall become inexhaustible for men; and for those who have died, there shall be no rebirth.
Having reached this sacred ford from Hara, it nourishes the deities;
it purifies men just as Kedāra does, according to the word of the Three-eyed One.
Having granted the boon to Kedāra, Hara departed in haste to bathe in the Kālindī,
the daughter of the Sun, the goddess who destroys all sins.
Having bathed there and become pure, he then went to the Sarasvatī,
which is surrounded by hundreds of holy fords (*tīrtha*), born from the *plakṣa* tree, and destructive of sins.
Then Hara descended to bathe and, submerged in the great waters,
he recited the Gāyatrī known as Drupadā while within the water.
O lover of the Kali age, while Śaṅkara was submerged in the goddess Sarasvatī,
more than a year passed, yet the Lord did not emerge.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, the seven worlds together with their oceans trembled, and the stars fell to the earth along with the constellations.
The gods, led by Śakra, rose from their seats, as did the supreme ṛṣis, muttering the prayer: "May it be well with all the worlds!"
Then, when the worlds were agitated, the gods approached Brahmā;
having seen him, they said, "What is this? The worlds are disturbed and have fallen into doubt."
Padmasambhava said to them: "I do not know the reason for this;
therefore, it is fitting for you to go and see the wielder of the discus and the mace."
Thus addressed by the Grandfather, the gods, led by Śakra and Sureśvara,
placed the Grandfather at their head and went to the abode of Murāri.
Nārada said: "O celestial sage, who was that enemy of the gods? Was he a god, a yakṣa, or a kinnara;
a daitya, a rākṣasa, or perhaps a king? Let this be told."
Pulastya said:
"O divine sage, tell me whether that Murāri was a god, a Yakṣa, or a Kinnara; or perhaps a Daitya, a Rākṣasa, or even a mortal king."
Nārada said: Who was he that is celebrated as Mura? Whose son is he said to be? And how was he slain in battle by Viṣṇu? Tell me that.
Pulastya said:
Listen, for I shall relate this wonderful narrative concerning the slayer of Mura—the gods and demons; it is meritorious and a destroyer of sins.
The legitimate son of Kaśyapa, named Mura, born of the Danu lineage,
beheld in battle the sons of Diti being struck down by the foremost of the gods.
Then, fearing death, he performed austerities for many groups of years and propitiated the all-pervading Lord Brahmā, who is unconquered.
Then the boon-granting deity, being pleased with him, said, "Child, choose a boon. And that Daitya chose this boon from the Grandfather: VamP_34.32.
O Lord, whomever I might touch with the palm of my hand in battle, he,
upon being touched by my hand, would fall from immortality to mortality.
"So be it," said the Blessed One, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds;
thereupon the mighty Mura, endowed with great splendor, went to the mountain of the gods.
O Nārada, having approached, he challenged a god, a yakṣa, or even a kiṃnara; yet no one at all fought as an equal with that Daitya.
Then, having gone to the prosperous Amarāvatī, he summoned Śakra;
however, Purandara did not set his mind on fighting him.
Then, raising his hand, he entered Amarāvatī;
as he was entering, no one dared to stop him.
Having gone to the abode of Śakra, Mura then spoke to Indra:
"O Thousand-eyed One, give us battle; otherwise, abandon heaven."
O Brahmin, having been addressed thus by Mura, Hari-haya then abandoned his sovereignty over heaven and became a wanderer upon the earth.
Then the enemy of Śakra seized the lordly elephant and the thunderbolt;
he, possessed of great splendor, departed together with his wife, the gods, and his son.
Having established his own city on the southern bank of the Kālindī, Muru remained there;
and he, as if established in heaven, enjoyed great pleasures.
And other fierce Dānavas, led by Maya and Tāra,
having reached Mura, rejoice as those of good deeds do in heaven.
Once, that great asura arrived alone upon the surface of the earth, mounted on an elephant, toward the river Sarayū.
On the bank of the Sarayū, he beheld the heroic king named Raghunāman, born of the solar dynasty, consecrated for the performance of a sacrifice.
Approaching him, the Daitya said, "Give me battle;
otherwise, let the sacrifice cease, and you must not worship the gods."
Approaching him, O Brahmin, the wise Vasiṣṭha— the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, possessed of great splendor, and the best among those who perform austerities— spoke.
O Daitya, what is the use of these men you have conquered? Rule over those who remain unconquered;
if you wish to strike him, then restrain Antaka himself.
O great Asura, that powerful one does not carry out your command;
for when he is conquered, consider the entire surface of the earth as already won.
Having heard those words of Vasiṣṭha, that bull among the Danus set out to conquer Dharmarāja, who held his staff in hand.
Hearing that he was approaching and considering him invincible in combat,
Yama mounted his buffalo and went into the presence of Keśava.
Having approached and saluted him, he reported the actions of Mura;
and he said, "Go now, and send me a great asura."
Having heard the words of Vāsudeva, he arrived with great haste;
in the meantime, the Daitya Mura reached the city.
When he had arrived, Yama said to him: "O Lord of the Dānavas, tell me what you wish to do with Mura; speak your word, and I shall carry it out."
Muru said:
"O Yama, you who restrain all creatures, you ought to desist from this;
otherwise, having severed your head today, I shall cast it to the ground."
The King of Dharma said to him, "O Brahmin, if you truly protect me from Mura through your self-restraint,
I shall carry out your word.
Mura said to him, "Tell me, who is your restrainer?"
Having defeated him with this, I shall ward him off; of this there is no doubt.
Yama said to him: "The imperishable Lord Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus and mace, who dwells in Śvetadvīpa—he shall restrain me."
The tiger among the Daityas said to him: "Where does that invincible one dwell?
I myself shall go there, intent on his subjugation."
Yama said to him: "Go to the ocean named Kṣīroda;
there dwells the Blessed Viṣṇu, the lord of the worlds, who pervades the universe."
Having heard those words, Mura said, "I am going to Keśava;
however, you must not restrain human beings from their duty."
He said, "Go for now; I shall exert myself toward victory.
Once the charioteer has controlled [the horses], then engage in battle."
Having spoken these words, Mura went to the Ocean of Milk,
where Janārdana resides in his fourfold form upon the couch of Śeṣa.
Nārada said:
How is it that Viṣṇu, though being one alone, is spoken of as having four forms? Tell me how this is so, both because of his omnipresence and because of his unmanifest nature.
Pulastya said:
O great sage, although the Unmanifest is omnipresent and indeed one alone, it exists here as the Lord of the World in four forms; listen, O Brahmin, to how that is so.
Inconceivable, indescribable, pure, and peaceful,
the supreme state known as Vāsudeva is remembered as the unmanifest lotus with twelve petals.
Nārada said: How is it white? How is it peaceful? How is it inconceivable and beyond reproach?
What are its twelve petals that have been spoken of? Tell those to me.
Pulastya said:
Listen to this supreme secret spoken by Parameṣṭhin;
it was heard by Sanatkumāra, and he related it to me.
Nārada said:
Who is this Sanatkumāra, about whom Brahmā himself spoke?
He also spoke of him to you; tell me of him in due order.
Pulastya said:
Non-violence is the name of Dharma’s wife; from her, O tiger among sages, four sons were born who were investigators of the Yoga-shastra.
The eldest was Sanatkumāra, the second was Sanātana,
the third was named Sanaka, and the fourth was Sanandana.
He saw the knower of Sāṃkhya, the other Kapila, the son of Āsuri,
as well as the excellent Pañcaśikha, who was absorbed in yoga and a treasure-house of asceticism.
Even those who are senior would not bestow the yoga of knowledge upon their juniors;
they abandoned Kapila and others, having rejected the great yoga that is free from pride.
Sanatkumāra approached Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, and inquired about the knowledge of yoga; the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) spoke to him.
Brahmā said:
"O Sādhya, I shall tell it to you if you desire the state of being my son;
for that truth must not be spoken to just anyone, as it is indeed not otherwise."
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Lord of Gods, I am indeed your son; for I am your disciple, O All-pervading One.
There is no difference between a son and a disciple, O Grandfather."
Brahmā said:
"O son of Dharma, there exists a distinction between a disciple and a son regarding the performance of righteous deeds; nevertheless, listen as I explain it."
"He protects from the hell named Punnāman; therefore he is called 'putra' here.
He removes the remaining sins; he is called 'śiṣya'—this is the Vedic revelation."
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Lord, who is this son called 'puṃnāmaka' who rescues one from hell?
From what [remaining] sin does he, as well as the disciple, remove it? Please tell me that."
Brahmā said:
O great sage, this is the supreme Purāṇa, which is always endowed with the limbs of yoga;
likewise, it is formidable yet removes fear for humanity. O Sādhya, listen to this as I speak it to you.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"Approaching the wives of others and serving those who are most sinful [are forbidden]."
Harshness toward all living beings is recorded as the first hell.
Stealing fruit is a great sin, as is wandering about while devoid of fruit and the cutting down of various types of trees; this is recorded as the second hell.

Giving to those who should be avoided, as well as the killing of those who should not be killed and their imprisonment, and disputes arising from the cause of wealth— this is remembered as the third hell.
Causing fear to all sentient beings, destroying prosperity within existence, and causing the loss of one's own dharmas—this is known as the fourth hell. (VamP 35.4)
Killing, treachery toward friends, false accusation,
and eating sweetmeats— these are said to be the five things that are like poison for a king.
The taking of fruits and such, the restraining [of cattle], the destruction of yoga,
and the seizing of vehicles and draft animals— this sixth is declared to be an offense against the king.
Taking the king’s share, being deluded, serving the king’s wife, and acting for the king’s harm in his kingdom—this is remembered as the seventh hell. (VamP 35.7)
Greediness and voracity, which destroy the dharma and wealth already acquired,
are said to be the eighth hell, known as Lālāsaṃkīrṇa.
Living abroad, stealing the Veda, reviling Brāhmaṇas,
and quarreling with kinsmen— these are declared to be the nine acts that ripen men for hell.
The destruction of the conduct of the cultured, hatred toward the cultured, the killing of a child,
the theft of the scriptures, and the destruction of Dharma— these are proclaimed as the ten [sins].
The eleventh hell, which is terrible, characterized by the destruction of the six limbs and the subversion of the sixfold policy,
is declared by the virtuous to be the most supreme [of hells].
Constant enmity toward those who are virtuous, perpetual misconduct, improper conduct, and the lack of refinement—this is remembered as the twelfth [fault]. (VamP 35.12)
The loss of virtue, wealth, and desire; the taking away of liberation;
and the confusion of consciousnesses—this is called the thirteenth [chapter].
That which is miserly, devoid of dharma, that which is to be avoided, and that which causes the burning of fire—
these fourteen types of people are said to be censured as destined for hell.
Ignorance, lack of self-control, impurity, and that which brings about inauspiciousness—these are recorded as the fifteenth; and there are also words that should not be spoken.
Indeed, laziness is the sixteenth, as well as verbal abuse specifically;
and [the offenses include] being a threat to all, and setting fire to dwellings.
Desire for the wives of others is said to lead to hell;
likewise, the absence of envy toward the virtuous is praised, whereas arrogance is censured.
A man joined with these meritorious acts, beginning with *pūrṇa*, will undoubtedly please the God, the Lord of the world, through his progeny. (VamP 35.18)
Delighted by that auspicious creation, he is liberated from sin;
it utterly destroys the terrible hell named Pūyanaraka.
For this reason, a son who accomplishes [one's goals] is called "putra.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the remaining sins.
O best of the twice-born, there is a sequence for the gods, sages, spirits, and especially for humans; and for the ancestors as well, there is oneness in all the Vedas.

Even for one who has attained liberation through the syllable *oṃ*, or who has committed sinful deeds, such as eating fish, committing great sins, or likewise approaching women who should not be approached; [these are purified].

The sale of ghee and other such items, the acceptance of goods from Caṇḍālas and others, the concealment of one's own faults, and the proclaiming of the faults of others are terrible sins. (VamP 35.23)
Miserliness, wickedness of speech, harshness toward others, as well as playing the *ṭāka* drum and playing the *tāla* cymbals— these, by name and by word, are born of unrighteousness.
Cruelty and unrighteousness are said to lead to hell;
yet, even one joined with these sins may please Śaṅkara.
Then, through the complete absorption in knowledge, one shall conquer all remaining evil—
whether it be physical, verbal, mental, or corporeal.
O Dharmaja, whatever has been done by one's father and mother, and whatever has been done by the men one depends upon, as well as by brothers and kinsmen, in that very birth— VamP_35.27.
All that dissolves; such is the rule for both son and disciple. If the opposite occurs, the goal will be contrary, and the sequence of the steps will be reversed.
Therefore, a wise man should treat both his son and his disciple as such;
reflecting on this matter, one sees that a son is superior to a disciple,
for while a disciple saves him from what remains [of his karma], a son saves him from everything.
Pulastya said:
Having heard the words of the Grandfather, the Sādhya, whose wealth is austerity, spoke:
"O God, it is thrice-truly that I am your son; tell me the yoga."
The great yogi said to him, "If your mother and father give you away, then you, my son, shall be my heir. (VamP 35.31)
Sanatkumāra said:
"Regarding this arrangement of heirs which has been mentioned by you, you ought to explain it to me."
Having heard those words spoken by the one whose primary concern was the goal to be accomplished, the venerable Grandfather laughed and said, "Listen, O child Nārada. (VamP 35.33)
Brahmā said: The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the adopted son, the made son,
the son secretly born, and the cast-off son— these six are heirs and kinsmen.
Among these six sons, [the first] performs the funeral rites with rice-balls and wealth;
likewise, he ensures the continuity of the lineage, the family name, the livelihood, and the eternal stability of the clan.

The son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a pregnant bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the son given by himself (svayamdatta), and the Pāraśava— these six are non-heirs and not kinsmen.
Among these people, no talk whatsoever of debts or funeral offerings exists here; they are merely bearers of names, not even recognized as belonging to any lineage or family.
Having heard those words of Brahmā, Sanaka’s elder brother said:
"O Brahmin, you ought to explain to me the distinction among these."
Then the Lord of the Gods said: "Listen, my son, to a distinction:
he who is born of one's own self as a legitimate son is like a reflection of oneself."
If the husband is impotent, insane, or addicted to vice, a wife who,
being herself free from illness, bears a son by his command, that son is indeed a *kṣetraja*.

He who is given by his mother and father is proclaimed as "given" (datta); the best authorities call him who is given by a friend a "friend-given" (mitradatta) son, and such is the "artificial" (kṛtrima) son.
It is not known by whom in the house that son was born;
having been brought in by himself from outside, he is proclaimed as the *apaviddha* (cast-off).

A son born of an unmarried girl is a *kānīna*; one who was conceived before marriage but delivered after is a *sahoḍha*. One obtained for a price is a *krīta* (bought); furthermore, there are two kinds of *punarbhava* (the son of a remarried woman).
O Sage, when a girl who has been given to one man is taken away and bestowed upon another, the son born from her is to be known in the world as a *paunarbhava*, born of a net.
"He who has offered himself during a famine or even in times of calamity is said to be 'self-given' (svayaṃdatta); likewise, another may be so designated for other reasons."
O observer of good vows, the son of a Brāhmaṇa who is born of a Śūdra woman—
whether she has been married or unmarried— is called a Pāraśava.
For this reason, my son, you ought not to give yourself away; go quickly and summon your parents.
Then, at the word of the Lord, he remembered his mother and father;
O Sage, that couple came indeed to see the Sovereign.
Dharma and Ahiṃsā, having prostrated before the Lord of Gods, sat down;
once they were seated and comfortably settled, Sādhyā addressed these words to them.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O dear one, desiring to attain yoga, I urged Brahmā;
he spoke to me for the sake of my son, therefore you ought to grant it."
Thus addressed by their son, the two of them spoke to their grandfather, the master of yoga: "O Lord, this is indeed your own son, our offspring."
"From this day forward, O Brahmin, he shall be your son.
Having said this, the two departed quickly by the very same way they had come.
The Grandfather also spoke to that son Sanatkumāra, who was accomplished and endowed with good conduct, concerning the twelve-petaled yoga.
The syllable Oṃ is situated in the crest-lock (śikhā), and a ram is stationed upon his head;
the month named Vaiśākha is remembered as the first leaf.
Indeed, the syllable *na* situated at the beginning is proclaimed there as Taurus;
the month of Jyeṣṭha is proclaimed as its second petal.
The syllable *mo* represents a pair of arms, and the couple is situated there;
the month named Āṣāḍha is known as the third petal.
The letter *bha* is the pair of eyes, where Cancer is situated;
the month is said to be Śrāvaṇa—this is remembered as the fourth petal.
The letter *ga* is declared to be the heart, and the lion dwells therein;
the month of Bhādra is likewise declared, and it is remembered as the fifth petal.
One should know that the syllable *va* is the armor (*kavaca*); there, a maiden is established.
The month named Āśvayuja is known as the sixth leaf. (VamP 35.59)
The letter *ta*, the collection of weapons, the zodiac sign Libra as its support,
and the month named Kārtika— this is remembered as the seventh leaf.
The letter *vā* is conjoined with the navel, and the scorpion is situated there;
the month named Mārgaśīrṣa is known as the eighth petal.
The letter *su* is said to be the hips, and the archer (Dhanurdhara) resides there;
the month of Pauṣa is declared to be the ninth.
The letter *de* represents the pair of thighs, and the crocodile (*makara*) is also situated here;
the month of Māgha is declared [to correspond], and the tenth petal is thus remembered.
The letter *vā* and the pair of *janu* (the knees) are situated there at the beginning of the pitcher (*kumbha*);
the leaf is said to be *phālguna*, which is the excellent eleventh.
The letter *ya* represents the feet, and it is also the Fish [incarnation]; O Sage, this dwells in Caitra.
This is indeed declared to be the twelfth leaf of Keśava.
Likewise, the Supreme Lord is described as the twelve-spoked wheel, as having six naves and two [flanges], and as the triple manifestation (trivyūha) that is yet a single form.
This form of the God with twelve petals has been described to you;
O best of sages, when this is known, there shall be no further death.
The second [form] is described as abounding in beings, possessing four castes and four faces,
with four arms and noble limbs, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark, and imperishable.
The third is my form as Tamas, the thousand-footed,
thousand-faced, glorious one who brings about the dissolution of all beings.
The fourth is named Rājasa; he is red in color, four-faced, and two-armed, wearing a garland; he is the creator of emanation, the primordial Puruṣa.
O great sage, from the Unmanifest these three manifest beings arise;
from them, Marīci and others, as well as thousands more, were likewise produced.
O best of sages, you have thus described to me that ancient form of the Lord, which increases the nourishment of the intellect;
that four-armed one whom the evil-minded Mura once again encountered because of the words of Kṛtānta.
When he had arrived, the slayer of Madhu said to the sage, "O Asura, for what reason have you come?
He replied, "To fight with you today. The destroyer of the enemies of the gods spoke to him again:
"If you have come here to fight me, why does your heart tremble? It flutters again and again like that of one afflicted by fever; therefore, I will not fight with a coward.
When Madhusūdana had spoken thus, Mura then placed his own hand upon his own heart.
Having repeatedly asked, "How? Where? Whose? he, whose intellect was impaired, caused [the chariot] to fall.
And Hari, with swift and gentle ease, released his discus at that enemy who had struck the lotus;
the gods became free from pain and praised the Lord Padmanābha.
This which was spoken by you has indeed been accomplished through skillful means by the wielder of the sharp discus, the destroyer of the Daitya Mura;
therefore, the Lord Nṛsiṃha attained universal renown as "Murāri" (the Enemy of Mura).
Thus ends the thirty-fifth [chapter] of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then, having approached the abode of Murāri, the gods thereafter—
Having paid homage to the God who is the cause of the world's agitation, they spoke.
Having heard that, the Blessed One said: "Let us go to the temple of Hara;
that great knower will pacify the world, including all things moving and unmoving, which has been thrown into turmoil."
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the gods, led by Śakra,
placed Janārdana at their head and went to Mount Mandara;
yet there they saw neither the god, nor the bull, nor the goddess, nor Nandin.
Seeing the gods shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, beholding them as empty mountains, Viṣṇu of great splendor addressed those of deluded vision.
He said, "Do you not see Maheśa standing before you?
They replied to him, "We do not see the Lord of Devas, the husband of Girijā."
"We do not know the cause by which our vision has indeed been destroyed. To them, the one whose form is the world replied: "You have committed an offense against the God."
The most wicked slayers of embryos, intent only on their own self-interest, were [created];
by that god who wields the trident, Jñāna and Viveka were indeed taken away.
Since you do not see [the deity] even though he stands right before you and you are looking,
therefore, for the sake of purifying the body and for the sake of the divine vision, proceed with diligence.
"O gods, purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance, perform a bath for the Lord;
for the milk-bath, O gods, one should employ one hundred and fifty jars."
Sixty-three jars of curd for the bath, thirty-two for the offering of sacrificial food,
and sixteen jars of pure *pañcagavya* are prescribed.
Eight measures of water are prescribed for the Madana; all those [measures] are doubled for wine.
Then, with one hundred and eight applications of *rocanā*, one should worship the deity.
One should devoutly anoint [the deity] with saffron and sandalwood,
and with *bilva* leaves together with lotuses, as well as with datura and divine sandalwood.
One should likewise worship with mandāra, pārijāta, and atimukta flowers;
one should also incense with aguru, kāleya, and sandalwood.
The Śatarudrīya should be recited according to the word-order (pada) and sequential-order (krama) methods as declared in the Ṛgveda;
when this is done, you shall behold the Lord of Gods, and not by any other means.
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, the gods said to Keśava:
"O Madhusūdana, let the procedure for the *taptakṛcchra* penance be told,
by the performance of which there arises a purification of the body that is valid for all time."
Vāsudeva said:
One should drink warm water for three days, drink warm milk for three days,
drink warm clarified butter for three days, and subsist on air alone for three days.
The wise say that one should drink twelve palas of water, eight palas of milk,
and six palas of clarified butter every single day.
Pulastya said:
When these words had been spoken, the gods, led by Śakra, performed the secret *taptakṛcchra* penance for the purification of their bodies.
Then, when the vow had been performed, the gods were liberated from sin;
freed from sin, they then spoke to Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Gods: *VamP_36.19*
"Tell me, O Lord of the World, O Keśava, where does that Śambhu reside,
whom we shall bathe according to the prescribed rite with an ablution of milk and other substances?"
Then Viṣṇu said to the gods: "Śaṅkara himself remains within my body; do you not see him? And this yoga is firmly established here."
They said to him: "We do not see the Destroyer of Tripura at all from you;
speak the truth, O Lord of the Gods! Where does Maheśāna abide?"
Then that Hari, the imperishable soul, the enemy of Mura, revealed to the gods the supreme sign of Īśvara, who was reclining within the lotus of his own heart.
Thereupon, the gods immediately bathed the eternal, stable, and imperishable Liṅga in succession with milk and other substances.
Having smeared [the image] with gorocanā and fragrant sandalwood paste,
they quickly worshipped the God with bilva leaves and lotuses.
Having offered the supreme medicinal herbs with devotion while burning agallochum incense,
and having recited the names [of the Buddha] one hundred and eight times, they then prostrated themselves.
Thinking thus, these two lords of monkeys, both born from the blinding darkness of the *sattva* element, wondered: "How have they attained the state of yoga?"
Having understood the thought of the gods, the omnipresent Lord assumed a universal form;
he was endowed with all auspicious marks, bore all weapons, and was imperishable.
Together with [his consort], he has three eyes, lotus-earrings made of serpents, matted hair, a staff, and the bull as his banner;
he is accompanied by Mādhava, has serpents for necklaces upon his chest, and his waist region is covered with a yellow deerskin.

O Great Sage, [I see him] with discus and sword in hand, plow and bow in his grasp, and equipped with the Pināka, the trident, and the Ājagava; he possesses matted hair, a skull-topped staff, a skull-bowl, and a bell, and is accompanied by the resonant sound of conchs and ṭaṅkāra-claps.

Upon seeing Hari and Śaṅkara, the gods, led by the one seated upon the lotus (Brahmā), exclaimed, "Salutations to you, the omnipresent and imperishable! and having spoken thus, they offered their obeisance and fixed their minds on a single purpose.
Perceiving that the gods were single-minded, Hari, the lord of the gods,
took hold of them and swiftly rushed toward Kurukṣetra, his own hermitage.
Then they beheld the Lord of Gods, pure in the water and become like a pillar;
having seen him and uttered "Obeisance to Sthāṇu," they all sat down.
Then the Lord of the Gods said: "Come, come! Let a boon be granted;
O Lord of the World, the world is agitated; arise, O you who are dear to guests!"
Then the bull-bannered god heard that sweet voice;
having heard it, the all-pervading and stainless one rose up with speed.
"Homage be to all the gods," Hara said, smiling;
and he was approached by the gods, including Indra, who bowed down with humility.
All the deities said to him: "O Śaṅkara, let this resolve be abandoned!
The three worlds, encompassed by you, have been thrown into agitation because of your great vow."
Then Mahādeva said, "The one of great vows has been abandoned by me.
Thereupon, the gods, joyful and with disciplined minds, went to heaven.
"O Sage, even because of that, the earth—with its oceans, continents, and mountains—trembled.
Thereupon Rudra reflected: 'For what reason has the great earth been shaken?'"
Then, bearing his trident, he wandered all around Kurukṣetra and beheld Uśanas, a treasure-house of asceticism, on the bank of the Oghavatī river.
Then the Lord of the Gods said: "O Brahmin, for what purpose do you perform this penance that causes agitation to the world? Let that be told to me quickly."
Uśanas said:
"O Three-eyed One, he indeed performs great penance out of a desire to propitiate you; he wishes to know the auspicious science of Saṃjīvanī."
Hara said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, I am well-pleased with your well-performed penance;
therefore, you shall truly know the science of restoration to life."
Having obtained the boon, Śukra then desisted from his ascetic penance;
nevertheless, the earth, covered with oceans, mountains, and forests, continued to tremble.
Then the pure Mahādeva went to Saptasārasvata and beheld the ṛṣi named Maṅkaṇaka performing a dance.
In his state of mind, he floated like a child; stretching out his arms, he danced with impetuosity.
Struck by that very force, the earth, together with its mountains, trembled.

Śaṅkara approached him, seized him by the hand, and spoke these words while laughing: "O great seer, what are you meditating upon that you dance? For what reason? Come and tell me; what satisfaction do you find here?"
That Brahmin said: "O best of the twice-born, listen to that by which satisfaction has arisen in me today:
while performing many cycles of austerities for the sake of withering my body, I have spent many years in penance."
Then I beheld here vegetable juice flowing from my hand, arising from a wound;
by that, O best of the twice-born, I am today exceedingly gratified, for with it I, whose self is well-purified, dance.
Śambhu said to him: "O twice-born one, look! Very white ashes have issued from my fingers simply by the act of striking;
yet I feel no joy, for you must surely be negligent."

O great sage, having heard the words of the bull-bannered god and reflected upon them, the sage Maṅkaṇaka then abandoned his dancing; filled with wonder, he bowed low in humility and paid homage at his feet.
Śambhu said to him: "O twice-born one, go to that world of the imperishable Brahmā, which is difficult to attain;
and let this most excellent tirtha on earth be equal in its fruit to Pṛthūdaka."

May there always be the presence right here of the gods, asuras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and kinnaras; may this foremost treasury of Dharma, belonging to Sarasvatī, be the remover of the stains of sin.
Suprabhā, Kāñcanākṣī, Suveṇu, Vimalodakā,
Manoharā, Oghavatī, Viśālā, and Sarasvatī.
These seven Sarasvatīs shall dwell there eternally;
all of them, bestowing great merit, grant the fruit of protecting the Soma.
You too, having installed a most venerable image at Kurukṣetra,
shall go to the highly meritorious world of Brahmā, which is so difficult to attain.
Having been addressed thus by the god Śaṅkara,
that self-controlled one whose wealth is asceticism established his form at Kurukṣetra and departed for the world of Brahmā.
When Maṅkaṇaka had departed, the earth became motionless;
then the pure Śambhu returned to his own abode on Mount Mandara.

This has been told to you, O twice-born one; Śaṅkara had then gone to the mountain to perform austerities, while Dṛṣṭamati approached him in his solitude, having been urged by the Goddess for a certain reason.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said: Having gone to Pātāla, what did the Dānava Andhaka do?
Let it be told what Śaṅkara did even while staying on Mount Mandara.
Pulastya said:
O Brahmin, Andhaka, staying in Pātāla and tormented by the fire of passion, his body trembling with agitation, spoke thus to all the Dānavas: *Vāmana Purāṇa*, Chapter 37, Verse 2.
"He is my friend, he is my kinsman, he is my brother, he is my father—
whosoever shall quickly bring that daughter of the mountain into my presence."
While Andhaka, the lord of the Daityas, who was blinded by passion, was speaking thus, Prahlāda addressed these words with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: VamP_37.4.
O Hero, this daughter of the mountain is your mother according to dharma, and the three-eyed god is your father; hear now the reason for this.
O Dānava, it is said that in former times your father, though childless and ever devoted to righteousness, propitiated Mahādeva for the sake of obtaining a son.
O Dānava, although he was blind, Trilocana became his son; having spoken these words, O Lord, the god granted him a son as he desired one. (VamP 37.7)
O Hiraṇyākṣa, my three eyes were covered by Umā for the sake of sport while I was established in yoga; consequently, there arose a blinding darkness.
And from that darkness was born a being with the roar of a dark cloud;
"O Daitya, seize this son of yours, who is suitable for your purpose."
But when that base man performs wicked deeds loathed by the world, he will even covet the Mother of the Three Worlds.
Or when he shall cause the Brahmin to be slain after having cast [the weapon] at the Asuras,
then I myself will perform the purification of his body.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu departed for his own abode on Mount Mandara;
your father also returned to the netherworld (rasātala), taking you with him.
For this reason, O Mother, Śaileyī shall be yours;
Śambhu, the teacher of the entire world here, is certainly your father.
You too, endowed with asceticism, a knower of the scriptures, and overflowing with virtues—
one such as you should not set your mind upon such an evil intention.
"O crusher of the immortals, this wife of his belongs to one who is the lord of the three worlds, unmanifest, Bhava, saluted by all, and invincible; she is not worthy of you."
Moreover, you are not able to obtain that daughter of the mountain king without first conquering Rudra along with his host; and that desire is difficult to achieve today.
He who could cross the ocean with his two arms, or cast the sun to the ground,
or even uproot Mount Meru— he might conquer the wielder of the trident.
"Or rather, can these tasks be accomplished by men through their own strength?
And yet, Hara cannot be conquered; this truth, this very truth, I have spoken."
O Daitya, have you not heard how the foolish King Daṇḍa, desiring another's wife, met his destruction along with his entire kingdom? (VamP 37.19)
There was a king named Daṇḍa, who possessed abundant forces and vehicles;
that highly resplendent monarch chose a descendant of Bhṛgu for the office of domestic priest.
And the king, devoted to Śukra, performed various sacrifices;
and Śukra had a daughter known by the name Arajā.
Once Śukra went to the Asura Vṛṣaparvan;
honored by him, that best of the Bhṛgus remained there for a long time.
O great Asura, Arajā, whose limbs were most beautiful, remained in her own home serving the fire; then the lord of men arrived there.
He asked, "Where is Śukra? and the attendants replied to him, "The venerable Śukra has gone to officiate as a priest for the son of Danu."
The king asked, "Who is this who stays in the hermitage of Bhārgava?
They replied to him, "O King, it is the daughter of our preceptor, Arajā, who dwells there."
Desiring to see that daughter of Śukra in the hermitage, the mighty-armed joy of the Ikṣvākus entered and then beheld her, free from passion.
Upon seeing her, King Andhakadaṇḍa, tormented by desire and impelled by the power of Fate, was instantly overcome.
Then the powerful king dismissed his servants, brothers, and dearest friends, as well as the disciples of Śukra; he returned alone.
O Dānava, when he arrived, the illustrious daughter of Śukra rose to meet him and,
filled with joy, honored him with the affection due to a brother.
Then the king said to her: "O young girl, refresh me today with the water of your embrace, which shall quench the fire of my desire."
She too said, "O best of kings, do not cause distress;
my father, when afflicted by great anger, could burn even the thirty gods."
"O man of deluded intellect, you are my brother, though you are overwhelmed by misconduct;
according to dharma, I am your sister, and you are the disciple of my father."
He said, "O timid one, Śukra will consume me in due time;
yet the fire of passion, O slender-waisted lady, is burning me this very day."
She said, "O King, wait for a moment;
entreat that very preceptor, and he will undoubtedly grant it to you."
Daṇḍa said: "O fair-limbed one, delay is not permissible for me;
O beautiful one, an obstacle would arise if one acts when the opportunity has passed."
Then Virajā said: "O son of a king, I am not able to give myself to you; for women are not independent."
What is the use of much speaking to you? O lord of men, do not go to destruction through the curse of Śukra, along with your servants, kinsmen, and relatives.
Then the lord of men said: "O fair-limbed one, listen to the deeds of Citrāṅgadā—what occurred in former times during the age of the gods."
The virtuous daughter of Viśvakarṇa was named Citrāṅgadā;
endowed with beauty and youth, she was like a lotus-pond deprived of its lotuses.
Once, that lotus-eyed woman, surrounded by her female companions, went to the great forest named Naimiṣa to bathe.
And as she had descended to bathe, there arrived the wise lord of men,
the son of Sudeva, known by the name Suratha.
And he of beautiful limbs, afflicted by love, beheld that slender-limbed woman.
Seeing him, that maiden spoke these words, consistent with the truth, to her friends:
"This son of a king is being tormented by Love."
"And for my sake, it is fitting that I give away this handsome youth.
Her friends said to her, "O young girl, O beautiful one, you are not being bold enough."
O blameless one, you have no independence here regarding the giving away of yourself;
you have a father who is most righteous and skilled in all arts.
"It is not fitting for you to offer yourself here to the king yourself.
In the meantime, King Suratha, who was truthful and wise, [spoke].
Afflicted by the arrows of Kandarpa, he approached her and said:
"O charming one with intoxicating eyes, you enchant me even with a mere glance."
Struck by the god of love as he approached with a sidelong glance from you,
it behoves you to lie upon me on the bed of your breast.
"If not, Kāma will consume her again and again through excessive gazing;
therefore, that lotus-eyed woman, whose every limb was beautiful, [was consumed] by the King."
Though being restrained by her friends, she gave herself away by her own will;
thus in former times was that king rescued by Tainvi.
"Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, you ought to protect me as well. To him, Arajaskā spoke this reply concerning the matter of his punishment: VamP_37.50.
"Why was this not known by you? Therefore, I shall tell it to you.
Then, by that slender-limbed woman, [the story] of Suratha, the lord of the earth, [was told].
Because she had abandoned her duty out of a desire for femalehood, her father, being slow-witted, cursed her for having given herself away of her own free will. (VamP 37.52)
"Since you have given away your very self, there will indeed be no marriage;
deprived of marriage, you shall certainly not obtain happiness from a husband."

"You shall have neither the fruit of sons nor union with a husband. As soon as the curse was uttered, thirteen years passed away; when her husband had been taken away, she too fell into a state of delusion.
When the king had not yet achieved his purpose, she too fell into a swoon as the lord of men was drawn back thirteen yojanas.
Then her friends sprinkled her with the water of the Sarasvatī;
though being sprinkled with that exceedingly cool water, she [remained] as before.
O mighty-armed one, the daughter of Viśvakarman became like one dead;
perceiving her to be dead, her friends departed in great haste.
Others were busy gathering wood and bringing fire;
and she [the queen] remained there while all of them had gone to the excellent forest.
Regaining consciousness, she of the beautiful limbs looked toward the directions;
yet she did not see her husband, nor her affectionate circle of friends.
With her eyes sparkling,
O lord of men, Kāñcanākṣī fell with force into the waters of the great river Sarasvatī.
O lord of the people, she cast it into the waters of the Gomati, which were curved with waves; and she, having understood what was destined to happen to him through that act, [acted accordingly].
"Surrounded in the great forest, filled with the fear of lions and tigers—
such was the condition of that independent woman as I have heard it."
He said to her: "Daughter, whose daughter are you, appearing like a daughter of the gods?
For what purpose have you come here to this forest where no humans or deer are found?"
Then that slender-waisted woman spoke to the sage exactly as it was;
having heard her, the sage fell into a rage and cursed the craftsmen.
"Since this daughter born of his own body was joined with another by that sinner,
even though she was not given away by her husband, let him therefore become a monkey."
Having spoken thus, that great yogi bathed again according to the prescribed rite,
and after performing the evening twilight devotions, he worshipped Śaṅkara.
Having worshipped Hara, the Lord of the gods of gods, according to the prescribed rite, he said:
"O fair-browed one with beautiful teeth, who yearns for your husband, please come."
Go, O fortunate one, to the auspicious land of Saptagodāvara;
there, having worshipped Maheśāna, the great Hāṭakeśvara.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, while she remains there, the auspicious and renowned daughter of the Daitya Kandaramālin, Devavatī, will arrive.
Likewise, another daughter of the Suhyakas, renowned as Nandayantī,
that ascetic woman will also come there from Añjana;
and similarly, another auspicious one, Vedavatī, the daughter of Parjanya.
O Mahādeva, when the three [rivers] meet in the waters of the Saptagodāvara at the place called Hāṭaka, then you shall attain union.
Having been addressed thus by the sage, the young Citrāṅgadā then departed swiftly from there and went to the Saptagodāvara tīrtha.
Having reached that place, she worshipped the three-eyed Lord of Gods;
devoted to purity, she remained there subsisting on fruits and roots.
That seer, endowed with wisdom, wrote a single verse— a great narrative— in the abode of Śrīkaṇṭha out of a desire to do what was pleasing to her.
There is no one— whether among the gods, the asuras, the yakṣas, mortals, or the night-stalkers—
who could wipe away this suffering of the mother of the young deer by means of his own prowess.
Having spoken thus, that sage departed to behold the omnipresent Lord, the worshipful Master of Puṣkara,
while reflecting upon the river Payoṣṇī, who is praised by hosts of sages and possesses wide eyes.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Daṇḍa said:
"Then Satī lived there with Citrāṅgadā according to her pleasure."
As she remembered the heroic Suratha, a great length of time passed by.
Viśvakarman too, cursed by the sage, was transformed into a monkey;
impelled by destiny, he fell from the peak of Mount Meru to the surface of the earth.
O beautiful one, he dwells near a terrifying forest rich with thickets, beside a lotus-filled river, and at Śākveya, the best of mountains.
There, O lady of beautiful hips, as he ate fruits and roots for a very long time while remaining in that desolate forest, many groups of years passed by.
Once, the tiger among Daityas named Kanda, having received his beloved daughter,
arrived at the famous city known as Devavatī.
And as that fair-faced woman was approaching the grove with her father,
the best of monkeys saw her and seized her by the hand.
Then, O auspicious lady, seeing his daughter seized by the monkey, that Daitya Kandara became enraged and, raising his sword, rushed toward him.
Seeing that lord of the Daityas rushing toward him, the powerful monkey,
together with the lovely-limbed woman, likewise fled to the Himalayas.
And he beheld Mahādeva Śrīkaṇṭha on the bank of the Yamunā,
and nearby, a dense hermitage devoid of sages.
Having established Devavatī in that holy great hermitage,
the monkey indeed bathed in the Kālindī while the Dānava was looking on.
Not knowing that his daughter was dead along with the monkey,
he of great splendor went to his own abode in Pātāla.
And that monkey was carried away by the force of the river goddess Kālindī and led to the region renowned as Śivī, which is filled with auspicious people.
Then, having crossed with speed toward the mountain,
that monkey of great splendor desired to go to where Sulocanā had been left.
Then the monkey, wishing to depart, saw the supreme Guhyaka Añjana approaching together with his daughter Nandayantī.
Seeing her, the illustrious one thought: "This must certainly be Devavatī;
thus my exertion, resulting from plunging into the water, has been in vain."
While he was thus reflecting, he rushed toward the cave of Suṅgada;
out of fear of him, she threw herself into the river Hiraṇvatī.
Seeing his daughter fallen into the waters of the river, the Guhyaka,
overcome with pain and grief, went to Mount Añjana.
There, having undertaken asceticism and observing a vow of silence,
that pure one of great splendor sat for many groups of years.
Though she was carried away by the force of the Hiranyati river,
she was brought with speed to the highly meritorious land of Kosala, which abounds in virtuous people.
And as she went along weeping, she beheld a banyan tree whose body was covered with new shoots, resembling the Lord Śiva with his matted locks.
Seeing that place of vast shade, the lovely-faced woman rested;
having sat down upon a stone slab, she then heard a voice.
There is no man whatsoever who could tell that ascetic how it was that your son hung from the banyan tree.
Having heard those words, articulated with distinct syllables,
she then looked all around— in the horizontal, upward, and downward directions.
O auspicious lady, he saw a five-year-old child standing on the treetop,
his head carefully bound with tawny matted locks.
Upon seeing him speaking thus, Nandayantī became deeply distressed and said: "By whom have you been bound?
Tell me, O child, by which sinner have you been bound?"
He said to her, "O illustrious lady, I am bound by a wicked monkey to this *vaṭa* tree;
thus, by the power of my asceticism, I remain alive."
In that very city called Puronmatta, the god Maheśvara resides;
there dwells my father, Ṛtadhvaja, a mass of ascetic merit.
While that great-souled one was reciting the great yoga-mantra, I was born to him,
accompanied by a swarm of bees and proficient in all the scriptures.
Then my father, having given me a name, spoke to me, O fair-faced one;

Seeing his fourfold army being slaughtered by the lords of the Gaṇas,
Tuhuṇḍa, filled with rage, rushed forward with great speed.
Taking up a terrible iron bar, bound with cloth,
made of silver, and shining exceedingly like the raised banner of Indra, he stood there.
Whirling him about, the powerful one struck down the hosts in battle;
those beginning with Rudra and ending with Skanda were shattered, overcome by fear.
Seeing that army broken, Vināyaka, the Lord of the Gaṇas,
rushed with speed toward Tuhuṇḍa, the bull-like son of Danu.
Seeing Gaṇapati rushing toward him, the evil-minded and mighty Daitya hurled his iron club at Gumba’s back.
O Brahmin, that iron bar, adorned with diamonds, shattered into a hundred pieces upon Vināyaka’s skull-bowl, like a thunderbolt striking the peak of Mount Meru.
Seeing his iron club rendered useless and his kinsman approaching,
Rāhu bound him with the noose of his arms, for he was protecting his maternal uncle.
Having forcibly dragged the Dānava by the arm-noose,
Mahodara struck him on the head with his axe.
Split in two like a piece of wood, he fell to the surface of the earth;
nevertheless, the powerful Rāhu, lord of the Dānavas, did not let go,
and though he made every effort for the sake of release, O Nārada, he was unable to do so.
Then, seeing Vināyaka restrained by Rāhu, the high-souled lord of the Gaṇas named Kuṇḍodara quickly seized a pestle and struck that evil-minded Rāhu.
Then Gaṇeśa, whose banner was a water-jar, pierced Rāhu in the heart with a spear;
Ghaṭodara struck him with a mace, and Sukeśin, the lord of the Rakṣasas, struck him with a sword.
Being struck by those four, Rāhu then released the Lord of the Gaṇas;
as soon as he was released, [the Lord] split his head with a battle-axe.
But when Tuhuṇḍa was struck down and Rāhu turned his face away, the lords of the Gaṇas, desiring to release the poison of their wrath—
resembling five or one fire at the end of an aeon— entered the army of the foremost Danus.
Seeing his own army being bound, the powerful Bali, possessing a speed equal to the wind,
brandished his mace and struck Vināyaka on the forehead, the temples, and the trunk.
He made Kuṇḍodara’s hips shattered, Mahodara’s skull crushed,
Kumbhadhvaja’s joints pulverized, and Ghaṭodara’s thighs split apart at the seams.
Having turned those lords of the Gaṇas away, that most heroic lord of the Asuras, endowed with power,
rushed swiftly to slay the lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Skanda and Viśākha.
Beholding him as he approached—the most excellent among the Gaṇas—the Blessed Maheśvara addressed Śailādi with these words: "Go, O hero; slay the Daityas in battle!"
Thus addressed by the bull-bannered god, the son of Śilāda took up his thunderbolt;
approaching Bali, he struck him on the head, and being utterly bewildered, he fell to the earth.
Perceiving his brother’s son to be utterly bewildered, the powerful Kujambha seized a club;
whirling it with great speed, he, filled with rage, hurled it swiftly at Nandin.
Seizing the club as it came rushing toward him with his hand, the blessed Nandin swiftly struck Kujambha with that very weapon in the battle; deprived of life, he fell to the ground.
Having slain Kujambha with his mace, the hero Nandin struck them down by the hundreds with his thunderbolt;
being thus slaughtered by the leader of the hosts, they indeed sought refuge with Duryodhana.

Beholding the lords of the Daityas struck down by the leader of the Gaṇas with blows from his thunderbolt, Duryodhana brandished a lance as bright as lightning and hurled it at Nandin, crying out, "You are slain!"
As it was falling, Nandin split that lance with his thunderbolt, just as a treacherous man betrays a secret;
seeing the spear thus severed, he then clenched his fist and rushed toward the Gaṇa.
Then Nandi severed his head, which resembled a palm fruit, with his thunderbolt;
struck down, he fell to the ground with force, and the Daityas, terrified, fled in the ten directions.
Then, beholding his own son slain, the elephant approached Nandin;
seizing his bow of fierce velocity, he pierced him with arrows resembling the staff of Yama.
The hosts of the bull-bannered gods, like mountains drenched by torrents from the lord of waters,
were completely covered on all sides by the nets of arrows released by the Asuras, even though they were powerful beings such as Vināyaka and others.
Seeing the Gaṇas turning their backs, Kumāra warded off their spears and arrows with his own;
quickly approaching the enemy and confronting him, he seized him and pierced his heart with a spear.
With his heart pierced by the spear, the elephant fell to the ground;
the enemy host died, and they turned their backs in retreat once more.
Seeing the army of the enemies of the immortals broken, the lords of the Gaṇas became enraged;
placing Nandin at their head, they sought to slay the Dānavas.
Though being struck down by the Pramathas, those powerful Daityas turned their backs;
however, led by Kārttasvara, they returned once more.
Seeing that they had retreated, Nandisena, whose eyes blazed with anger, spoke these words;
and Vyaghrasimha also turned back with great speed.
When that Gaṇapa, with the tip of his spear in hand, had withdrawn,
Kārtasvara then retreated, O Nārada, taking up his mace.
Seeing that great lord of the asuras approaching with the brilliance of fire,
Gama whirled his spear and struck him on the head as he was crying out discordantly in golden tones.
When that [demon] was slain, the hero Turaṅgakaṇṭha,
having brandished his weapon, bound Gaṇeśvara along with Paṭṭiśa and also Nandiṣeṇa.
Seeing Nandisena thus bound, Viśākha, the best among the strong,
approached in a rage with a spear in hand and stood there.
Seeing him, the powerful Ayaḥśiras, the best among the strong, with noose in hand,
engaged Viśākha, who has the cock as his banner, in combat.
Seeing Viśākha indeed held in check by Ayaśiras in battle,
Śākha and Naigameya quickly rushed toward the enemy.
On one side, Śākha pierced the iron-tipped arrows with his power,
while Naigameya quickly rushed toward the enemy.
Being oppressed by the three sons of Śaṅkara, he abandoned the wager;
those lords of the Gaṇas, being watched, quickly reached Śambara.
Having struck the noose with his spear, it was swiftly destroyed by the four sons of Śaṅkara, falling from the sky to the earth like a celestial body.
When his noose had become useless, O celestial sage, Śambara’s eyes grew timid;
he fled in all directions while Kumāra crushed the army.
O great seer, being slaughtered by those hosts of Rudra’s sons and the Dānavas, the army of the Dānavas—
dejected in appearance, its limbs overwhelmed by fear— sought refuge with Śukra, afflicted by terror.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then, having observed his own army being slaughtered by the Pramathas, [he...]
Andhaka, having approached Śukra, spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, relying upon you, we shall subdue the gods, as well as others—the brahmin-sages, gandharvas, suras, and kinnaras—O seer! (VamP 43.2)
Behold this army of his, O Blessed One, which, though protected by me, is being driven away by the Pramathas like a woman without a protector! VamP_43.3.
O Bhārgava, my brothers Kujambha and the others have been slain;
these Pramathas are now indestructible, like the merit obtained from Kurukṣetra.
Therefore, act for our welfare so that we may not be defeated by our enemies,
and you ought to act in such a way that we may conquer our enemies in battle.

Having heard these most wonderful words, Śukra, whose armor was his own darkness, spoke soothingly to the lord of the Dānavas: "O divine sage, this Brahman-sage shall strive for your benefit and shall do what is pleasing to you. (VamP 43.6)
Having spoken these words, the wise sage, pure in his vows, then recited the Saṃjīvanī lore according to the prescribed ritual.
While that knowledge was being repeated, those Dānavas who had been slain first in battle rose up once more, O lords of the Asuras.
While the Daityas, beginning with Kujambha, had arrived for battle, Nandin spoke to Śaṅkara. While they were indeed approaching for combat, Nandin addressed Śaṅkara.
O Mahādeva, listen to my most wonderful words concerning the inconceivable and unbearable restoration to life of those who have died.
Those Daityas who had been slain by the Pramathas on the field of battle were then restored to life once more by Bhārgava through his vidyā.
O Mahādeva, O Īśa, this great deed performed by them in battle has resulted in only a very small depletion of the power of Śukra’s knowledge.
When these words had been spoken by Nandin, the delighter of his lineage,
the Lord replied with affection, [offering] the supreme means for accomplishing his own purpose.
Go, O Gaṇapati, and bring Sukra to my presence;
for once he has arrived, I shall subdue him according to what is appropriate.
Having been addressed thus by Rudra, Nandin, the lord of the Gaṇas,
then approached the army of the Daityas with the desire to seize Śukra.
The powerful and foremost of the Asuras, whose neck was like that of a horse, beheld him and then blocked his path, as a beast in the forest obstructs a lion.
Nandin approached and struck him with a hundred-jointed thunderbolt;
he then fell down unconscious, and Nandin departed in haste.
Then Kujambha, Jambha, Bala, Vṛtra, and Ayaḥśiras—
these five tigers among the Dānavas— rushed toward Nandin.
Likewise, other foremost among the Dānavas, led by Maya and Hlāda,
rushed at the Lord of the Gaṇas in battle with various weapons.
Then the gods, led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), beheld that lord of the hosts being struck down by those of great strength.
Seeing him, the Blessed One spoke to Brahmā and the gods led by Śakra:
"Let assistance be rendered to Śambhu; this is an excellent opportunity."
Having heard the words spoken by the Grandfather, the gods, together with Indra,
then descended with speed upon Śiva’s army from the sky.
The force of those Pramathas as they rushed upon the army shone like the great surge of rivers falling into the vast ocean.
Then, a tumultuous roar arose from both armies,
as terrifying as that of the gods and the Pramathas.
Approaching him at that moment,
the impetuous Nandin seized him and leaped from the chariot onto Bhārgava, like a lion upon a small deer.
Taking him, the leader of the Gaṇas approached Hara;
having struck down all the guards, he then presented Śukra [to him].
The Lord Śarva cast the poet brought there into his mouth;
however, he placed the descendant of Bhṛgu, whose body was covered, within his belly.
Devoured by Śambhu and situated within his belly, that supreme poet,
the sage, then praised the Blessed One with words full of reverence.
Śukra said: Salutations to you, the giver of boons; salutations again and again to Hara, who is endowed with all virtues, to Śaṅkara, the Great Lord, the three-eyed one.
Salutations to you, Jīvana, O Lord of the World, Vṛṣākapi;
salutations to you, Madanāgni, Kālaśatru, and Vāmadeva.
Salutations again and again to Sthāṇu, to Viśvarūpa, to Vāmana, to Sadāgata, to Mahādeva, to Śarva, and to Īśvara.

"O Three-eyed One, Hara, Bhava, Śaṅkara, Lord of Umā, Jīmūtakeśa, Abode of the Auspicious, Dweller in the cremation ground, Smearer with Ashes, Trident-bearer, Lord of Creatures, Lord of Cows, Supreme Being among Men—homage, homage to you!
Thus praised with devotion by the best of poets, Hara was pleased and said, "Choose a boon; I shall grant it to you.
He replied, "O Best of Gods, grant me this boon today: that my emergence indeed be from your own belly."
Then Hara, having closed his eyes, said, "O best of the twice-born, depart this very day.
As soon as he was addressed thus by the Lord, that bull among the Bhārgavas moved within the belly of the god.
Then, as he wandered about, the sage beheld within the very belly of Śambhu the worlds,
oceans, and nether regions, all filled with moving and stationary beings.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the Viśvedevas, as well as the Gaṇas,
Yakṣas, Kiṃpuruṣas and others, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Sages and those beings who can be mastered by humans, as well as beasts, insects, and ants;
trees, shrubs, mountains, creepers, and fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
Those dwelling in vessels and those dwelling in water, the unblinking and the blinking, the four-footed and the two-footed, as well as the stationary and the moving; VamP_43.37 //
Having seen both the unmanifest and the manifest, as well as those with qualities and those without qualities,
Bhārgava wandered about, filled with wonder;
there, a divine year passed for Bhārgava while he remained inactive.
But he did not obtain food, O Brahmin, and consequently the wise one became exhausted.
Seeing himself exhausted and failing to find an exit, the self-controlled sage,
bowing in supplication, sought refuge with Mahādeva.
Śukra said:
O Viśvarūpa, O you of great form, O wearer of the rosary of universal forms,
O thousand-eyed Mahādeva, I have come to you for refuge.
Homage be to you, O Śaṅkara, Śarva, Śambhu, whose thousand eyes, feet, and arms are adorned with serpents! Having seen all the worlds within your belly, I am weary and have come to you for refuge.
When these words had been spoken, the high-souled Śambhu laughed and then spoke these words:
"Come forth, for you are now my son, O moon of the Bhṛgu lineage, by means of my phallus!"
"By the name of Śukra, all beings, both moving and stationary, shall praise you; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One released the semen from his penis, and it emerged.
Having emerged as the moon of the Bhārgava lineage, that high-souled one attained the state of Śukra;
having bowed to Śambhu, he of great luster quickly departed toward the army of the great Asuras.
When the descendant of Bhṛgu had returned, the Dānavas became joyful;
together with the lords of the Gaṇas, they set their minds upon fighting once more.
Then all those lords of the Gaṇas, desiring victory, fought a chaotic battle with those Asuras along with the hosts of the immortals.
Then, O ascetic, as the hosts of Asuras and the deities fought,
a battle of single combats ensued, terrible in form.
Andhaka fought with Nandin, Śaṅkukarṇa with Tvaṣṭṛśiras,
the wise Bali with Kumbhadhvaja, and Virocana with Nandiṣeṇa.
Aśvagrīva fought with Viśākha, Śākha fought with Vṛtra, Bāṇa fought with Naigameya, and Bala, the bull among Rākṣasas, fought [with Skanda].
The leader Mahāvīrya, wielding a battle-axe,
fought in the fray against Tuhuṇḍa, the best of the Rākṣasas, who was filled with rage;
and Duryodhana fought the powerful Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
Hastī fought with Kuṇḍajaṭhara, and Hlāda with Ghaṭodara;
for these were the best among the powerful Dānavas and Pramathas,
O celestial sage, and they fought for six hundred divine years.
Then the powerful great asura named Jambha obstructed Śatakratu, who was approaching with the thunderbolt in his hand.
The lord of the Asuras named Sambhu fought with Brahmā,
and Kujambha fought with the highly powerful Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the Daityas.
In battle, Śālva fought Vivasvat, Triśiras fought Varuṇa,
Dvimūrdhan fought Pavana, Rāhu fought Soma, and Virūpadhṛk fought Mitra.
The eight Vasus, renowned as Dharā and the others,
repelled those eight great archers, the mighty Asuras, in battle.
Sarabha, Śalakṣa, Pāka, Puro, Vipṛthu, Pṛthu,
Vātāpi, and Celvala— these were all warriors who fought with various weapons and missiles.
The great asura Kālanemi alone, fierce in battle, [confronted] all the hosts of the Viśvedevas, led by Viṣvaksena.
The radiant great asura Vidyunmālī, fierce in battle, single-handedly fought against all eleven Rudras.
The two Aśvins, Naraka, Bhāskara, Śambara,
the Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, and the Nivātakavacas and others [were slain].
In this manner, O great sage, thousands of duels were fought by the Pramathas, gods, and Dānavas for sixteen decades of the gods' years.
When the enemies of the immortals were unable to fight with the gods,
they then resorted to illusion and gradually devoured the imperishable ones.
Then the mountain peak became covered by clouds with a luster like those of the rainy season,
yet it was deserted by all the Pramathas as well as by the immortals.
Seeing the mountain plateau empty and the Pramathas and gods being devoured,
the self-controlled Rudra, out of anger, produced Jṛmbhāyikā.
Touched by her, the sons of Danu became sluggish and spoke softly;
making their faces distorted and casting aside their weapons, they yawned.
And as those Dānavas were yawning, the lords of the Gaṇas and the gods quickly emerged, agitated, from the bodies of the Daityas.
Emerging from the Daityas who were like clouds, those supreme immortals,
with eyes like lotus petals, shone like flashes of lightning from the clouds.
O ascetic, when the Gaṇas and the immortals had emerged together,
those high-souled ones, becoming even more enraged, fought once again.
Then the Dānavas were repeatedly defeated in battle, day and night, by the gods together with their hosts, who were protected by Śarva.
Then, when seven hundred and fifty-six years had passed, the three-eyed,
imperishable one with eighteen arms performed his own twilight worship at that time.
Having touched the waters of the Sarasvatī and bathed there according to the prescribed rite, Hara,
his purpose fulfilled and filled with devotion, cast a handful of flowers upon his head.
Then he bowed his head, thereafter performed a circumambulation,
and having worshipped the Sun with the hymn beginning "Hiraṇyagarbha," he recited prayers.
Having properly uttered "Salutation to Tvaṣṭṛ! Salutation be unto you!
the wielder of the trident danced with profound emotion, forcefully brandishing his staff-like arms.
While the Lord of the Gods was dancing, the Gaṇas and the immortals likewise danced,
filled with emotion and imitating the playful movements of Hara.
Having performed the twilight worship and danced as he pleased, the Lord of Gods,
protected by the arms of the Three-eyed One, set out for battle with all the Dānavas.
Then all the hosts of immortals, protected by the three-eyed one’s arms— powerful and free from fear— conquered all the Dānavas.

Seeing his own army defeated and suspecting that he might be invincible, Andhaka summoned Sunda and spoke these words: VamP_43.76: "Seeing his own army defeated and suspecting that he might be invincible, Andhaka summoned Sunda and spoke these words."
"O hero, you are my brother, trusted in all matters. Therefore, I shall speak these words today; having heard them, do what is appropriate. (VamP 43.77)
Difficult to conquer, skilled in battle, and righteous in soul, he dwells within his heart for various reasons— Padmākṣī, the daughter of the mountain.
Therefore, arise; let us go to where she of the lovely smile resides.
There, O Dānava, I shall delude her by assuming the form of Hara.
"O Bhava, become the follower of Bhava as Nandi, the lord of the Gaṇas;
then, having gone there and partaken of that [food], I shall conquer the Pramathas and the gods."
When these words had been spoken, Sunda replied,
"So be it," and Śaṅkara became Andhaka, the progenitor of the mountains.
Then Nandi and Rudra, the commanders of the great hosts of asuras,
having become wounded by blows, reached Mount Mandara.
Taking hold of Sunda’s hand, Andhaka,
the best of asuras, entered the abode of Hara with a mind free from hesitation.
Then the Daughter of the Mountain, seeing Andhaka approaching from afar—
his body concealed by the form of Maheśvara and his skin mangled by blows— [acted].
Then, having seized Sunda who was standing in the form of Śailādi, he entered him.
Seeing this, he spoke to Mālinī, Suyaśas, Vijayā, and Jayā.
"O Jayā, behold the body of the God wounded on my behalf by the enemies, the foremost of the Dānavas; therefore, arise quickly!"
"Bring me aged ghee, *bījikā*, salt, and curd;
