I myself shall effect the healing of the wound of the wielder of the Pināka bow."
"O Suyaśas, quickly perform the healing of your husband's wound!
Having spoken these words, she rose from her excellent seat.
Then, imagining herself to be the bull-bannered god Śiva, she advanced;
having stood before the wielder of the trident, she diligently assumed his form and characteristics.
Then, O Brahmin, she searched for both the bulls standing at her side;
she recognized that the fierce Dānava had concealed his true form through illusion.
Then, O Sage, having understood the goddess’s intention, the asura Andhaka abandoned Sunda and made his retreat, while the daughter of the King of Mountains remained behind.
"Run with speed toward the night, the beloved of Hara!
Run, O Daitya, by the same path along which she has come! (VamP 43.92)
Breaking through the intermediate spaces between the spokes and agitated by leaping with his feet,
as soon as she saw him rushing toward her, Girijā fled in fear.
O bull among sages, having abandoned her home and entered the grove accompanied by her friends, she followed after him there as well, blinded by passion.
Nevertheless, Gaurī did not protect him from the deer with her ascetic power; rather, out of fear of him, she entered the pure white flower of the *śvetārka* tree.
O Sage, Vijarā and the others entered into dissolution within the great thicket;
then, when Pārvatī had vanished, he whose eyes were like golden lotuses appeared once more.
Taking Sunda by the hand,
O best of sages, he returned to his own army when Andhaka had previously departed with his own forces.
Then a great battle commenced between the Pramatha and the Asura;
thereafter, Viṣṇu, the foremost of the hosts of immortals, bearing the discus and the mace, [arrived].
Desiring to do what was pleasing to Śaṅkara, he struck down the army of the Asuras;
the foremost of the Dānavas were pierced through by arrows discharged from the Śārṅga bow.
Janārdana struck some with his mace like dense clouds driven by the winds of the *vṛdhna* verses— five, six, seven, or eight at a time— and others with his discus.
With his sword he cut some down, with his gaze he reduced others to ashes,
and having dragged others away with his plow, he pulverized them with his mace.
Garuḍa struck him with his two wings, with his beak, and with his breast;
he was the Primeval Being, the Ordainer, the Ancient One, and the Great-Grandfather.
Whirling about a vast lotus, he consecrated it with water;
for that water of Brahmā was indeed composed of the essence of all sacred bathing places.
The hosts of Gaṇas and the hosts of immortals numbered more than nine hundred Nāgas;
and the Dānavas were touched by that water which removes all evil.
Seeing Brahmā and Hari slaying the great asuras in battle, [the remaining demons], along with their mounts, went to their destruction like mountains struck by the thunderbolt.
And the powerful Śatakratu, seizing his thunderbolt, rushed forward;
seeing him charging, Bala, the best of the Dānavas, [stood firm].

O Nārada, leaving behind the mace-wielding god [Viṣṇu] and the lotus-born [Brahmā] seated in his celestial chariot, that powerful lord of the Dānavas, invincible to both gods and Dānavas, raised his fist and rushed toward Śakra alone to fight him.

As he was rushing forward, the Lord of the Thirty-three gods, exerting the full strength of his thousand arms, whirled his thunderbolt and hurled it at Bala’s head, crying out: "O fool! You are slain!"
O Sage, although it was his supreme thunderbolt, it shattered into a thousand pieces upon his head;
and Bala, the lord of the gods, fled in fear, turning his back on the battle, O Great Seer.
And Jambha, beholding him with his face turned away, came before him and said: "This is not right.
Stay! You are the king of all that moves and is stationary; flight is not declared to be the duty of a king."
O great sage, having heard Jambha’s words, the thousand-eyed Indra, filled with fear, went quickly to Viṣṇu;
approaching him, he said: "Listen to my words, O Lord; you, Viṣṇu, are my protector, the master of the past and the future."
"Indeed, seeing me weaponless, Jambha threatens me excessively;
O Blessed One, give me a weapon! I have come to you for refuge."
Hari said to Śakra: "Abandoning pride, go now;
entreat Agni for the weapon, and he will undoubtedly give it to you."
Having heard the words of Janārdana, Śakra, swift in his prowess,
went for refuge to Pāvaka and spoke this, O Nārada.
Śakra said:
"O Kṛśānu, my thunderbolt has been shattered into a hundred pieces by his strength;
furthermore, this Jambha is now challenging me. Therefore, give me a weapon."
Pulastya said:
The blessed Fire-god said to him, "O Vāsava,
I am pleased with you because you have abandoned your pride and come to me alone for refuge."
Having uttered this according to his own power and having mentally brought forth the Śakti,
the Blessed One, shining brightly, ascended to heaven and gave [it] to Indra.
Then, taking up that most terrible spear adorned with a hundred bells,
the crusher of enemies advanced against Jambha, desiring to slay him.
Suddenly assailed by that one of exceeding glory,
the Daitya Jambha then became enraged and struck down the lordly elephant.
With the falling of his crushing fist, the elephant, its frontal globes shattered,
fell down like a mountain struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt in ancient times.
As the lordly elephant was falling, the swift Śakra leaped up from him,
abandoned Mount Mandara, and fell to the surface of the earth.
As Hari was falling, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas then said:
"Do not, do not fall today, O Śakra! Stay on the surface of the earth, O Vāsava!"
Having heard their words, the yogin then stood still for a moment and said to them:
"How shall I fight, defenseless as I am, with these enemies?"
The gods and gandharvas said to him: "O Lord of the Earth, do not fall into despair;
mount [your chariot] and fight, and we shall send it forth when the time comes. (VamP 43.124)
Having spoken thus, [he ascended] a vast chariot marked with the svastika,
equipped with a monkey-banner, and yoked to tawny-colored horses.
Led by Viśvāvasu, they sent to Śakra a chariot made of pure gold and adorned with a network of tinkling bells.
Then, seeing that he had arrived deprived of his charioteer, Hari said:
"How shall I fight in battle? How shall I restrain the horses?"
"If someone indeed acts as my charioteer now, then I shall slay the enemies; otherwise, by no means whatsoever."
Then those Gandharvas said to him, "O Lord, we have no charioteer;
you yourself ought to control the horses here."
When this had been said, having abandoned his excellent chariot,
he fell to the surface of the earth, his garlands and garments falling away.
Seeing the thousand-eyed Indra falling— his crown shaking, his hair disheveled, and his weapons and armlets fallen— the earth trembled.
While the earth was trembling, the ascetic woman, Śamīkarṣu’s wife,
said to her husband, "Lord, take the child outside so that you may be at ease."
Having heard the words of Śīlavatī, he asked, "For what reason?
And she replied, "O Lord, please hear what was spoken by the astrologer."
O Best of Sages, whenever this earth trembles, then [the earth] is cast outside;
O Sage, that which is outside becomes double [in size].
Having heard these words at that time, the twice-born man took his young son and,
free from hesitation, quickly cast him onto the surface of the earth outside.
The twice-born man entered again with his wife for the sake of a pair of cows; he was dissuaded [by his son], saying, "The time has passed; there will be a loss of half a muhūrta."
When the divine sage had spoken thus, the impetuous one went outside and beheld two children of equal form standing there.
Having seen him and honored the deity and his wife of wondrous appearance, he said:
"I do not know the truth; tell me that which I ask."
Tell me, what will be the future qualities of this second boy? Speak now of his fortunes and the karma that was previously described for him.
She said, "I will not speak to you today; I shall speak again later, O Lord.
He replied, "Speak to me this very day; otherwise, I will not eat my meal."
She said: "Listen, O Brahmin; I shall speak words that are beneficial.
Regarding what has been asked today by this timid one—why is he called 'Kāru'?"
When these words had been spoken, the boy, though still a child and lacking full consciousness,
went forth to provide assistance to Śakra, being skilled in the art of battle.
As he was thus departing, the Gandharvas, led by Viśvāvasu,
recognizing his purpose, strengthened him with their splendor for the sake of assisting Indra.
Endowed with the splendor of a Gandharva, the infant approached Śakra and said: "Come, come, O Lord of Gods; I shall be your dear charioteer."
Having heard that, Hari said to him: "Whose son are you, child?
And how are you a trainer of horses? A doubt arises within me."
He said: "O Vāsava, know that this earthly abode has arisen from the splendor of Ṛṣi;
it is endowed with the power of Gandharvas and is skilled in the art of riding horses."
Having heard that, Śakra, the Blessed One and best of yogins, ascended into the sky;
and so too did the son of the Brahmin, renowned by the name Mātali.
Then Śakra, the bull among the thirty gods, mounted the chariot,
and Mātali, the son of Śamī, took up the reins.
Then, having reached Mount Mandara, the illustrious one entered the enemy host;
as he was entering, he beheld a great heap of bones fallen there.
The best of gods seized that bow, together with its arrow, which shone with five colors— white, red, black, crimson, and pale yellow.
Then, having mentally paid homage to the gods composed of rajas, sattva, and tamas,
he fixed the arrow upon the strung bow.
Then there issued forth exceedingly fierce arrows feathered with peacock plumes,
marked with the names of Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu, slaughtering the asuras in battle.
O Nārada, with his exceedingly sharp volleys of arrows, he covered the sky, the intermediate directions, the earth, and the cardinal quarters, like the thousand-eyed Indra.
The elephant was pierced, the horse was mangled, and the chariot fell to the earth;
the mahout, afflicted by arrows, instantly sank down and reached the ground.
Struck by Śakra’s arrows, he fell to the ground on foot;
the enemy's army was then mostly deprived of its leaders.
Then, beholding that invincible army struck by Śakra’s arrows,
Kujambha and the asura Jambha both seized two most terrible clubs and rushed toward the imperishable Lord of the Gods.
Beholding them as they were rushing toward him, the Blessed Viṣṇu, with his Sudarśana discus which destroys enemies, swiftly struck Kujambha; lifeless, he fell from his chariot to the earth.
When his brother had been slain by Mādhava, Jambha then fell under the sway of anger;
filled with rage, he rushed at Śakra in battle, like a deer of ruined intellect charging a lion.
Seeing him rushing toward him, the high-souled Śakra cast aside his bow and arrow and seized a spear resembling the staff of Yama;
he hurled that weapon, which had been given by Agni, at his enemy.
Seeing the spear falling with its bell ringing out, he struck it with his mace;
having reduced the mace to ashes in an instant, he swiftly pierced Jambha in the heart.
Pierced in the heart by the spear, that enemy of the gods fell to the earth as if his life-force had departed;
seeing him fallen unconscious upon the ground, the Daityas became terrified and turned away in flight.
When Jambha was slain and the Daitya host was broken, the Gaṇas were delighted and worshipped Hari;
they praised the prowess of Śatakratu, and that destroyer of mountain peaks approached Śarva and stood before him.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
When that army of Daityas had been broken, Śukra then spoke to Andhaka, the lord of the Asuras.
"Come, come, O hero, great asura! Today we shall go to Mount Haras and fight once more."
Andhaka said to him, "O Brahmin, what you have said is not correct;
I shall not withdraw from the battle by citing my own lineage."
Behold, O tiger among the twice-born, my prowess which is exceedingly difficult to withstand;
I shall conquer the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, including Indra and Maheśvara.
Having spoken these words, Andhaka, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa, comforted Śambhu and addressed his charioteer with sweet syllables: "O charioteer! VamP_44.4.
"O one of great strength, drive the chariot toward the enemy host;
meanwhile, I shall slay the army of the Pramathas and the gods with my volleys of arrows."
O Sage, having heard these words of Andhaka, the charioteer then struck the dark-colored, high-velocity horses with his whip.
Though those horses were urged with great effort toward Hara,
they faltered at their haunches and drew that chariot forward only with difficulty.
Carrying the Daitya, even though they were equal to the speed of the wind, the horses reached the army of the Pramathas in more than a year.
Then, bending his bow, he covered the lords of the Gaṇas— the gods including Indra, Upendra, and Maheśvara— with a multitude of arrows.
Seeing the army covered by arrows, the Blessed One Janārdana, the protector of the three worlds who bears the discus and the mace, spoke to the gods.
Viṣṇu said:
"Why do you stand still, O best of gods? Victory will indeed come through the slaying of this one.
Therefore, if you desire victory, let my word be carried out quickly."
Let his swift horses be brought down together with the charioteer;
let the chariot be shattered, and let the enemy be deprived of his vehicle.
"Once he has been deprived of his chariot, Śaṅkara will consume him;
O gods, an enemy must never be neglected, as has been declared by the Preceptor of the Gods."
Thus addressed by Vāsudeva, the Pramathas,
together with the gods, Indra, and the wielder of the discus, exerted their full force.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, Janārdana crushed a thousand horses that resembled clouds with his mace.
From his chariot whose horses had been slain, Skanda seized the charioteer and, with a spear, pierced his heart; he then cast him, lifeless, onto the ground.
The Pramathas, headed by Vināyaka and accompanied by Śakra and the other deities,
those whose wealth is asceticism, swiftly shattered the chariot along with its banner and axle.
Suddenly, that one of great splendor, deprived of his chariot and casting aside his bow,
took up a mace and, full of strength, rushed toward the gods.
Then, having gone eight steps, the lord of the Daityas stood and addressed Mahādeva with words as deep as a thundercloud, providing a reasoned argument.
"O monk, you are accompanied by an army, whereas I am now without a companion;
nevertheless, I shall defeat you—behold my prowess today!"
Having heard those words, Śaṅkara then placed all the hosts of gods, including Indra and accompanied by Brahmā, within his own body.
Having made those Pramathas and the gods abide within his body, Śaṅkara said: "Come, come, O you of contented soul; though I am alone, I remain present here."
Seeing that great marvel— the destruction of the entire host of immortals—
the swift Daitya approached Śaṅkara, taking up his mace.
Seeing him rushing toward him, the Blessed One, the wielder of the trident, abandoned his excellent bull and stood on foot upon the mountain plateau.
And as he was rushing forward with great speed, Bhairava,
assuming a fierce and massive form that terrified the three worlds, pierced him in the chest.
With fangs formidable and resembling ten million suns, clad in the skin of a predator, wearing matted locks,
with serpents for necklaces and a throat as deep as a cave, possessing ten arms and three eyes.
In such a form, the Blessed One— the creator of all beings,
the bestower of auspiciousness, the eternal Śiva— pierced the enemy with his trident.
O great sage, seizing Bhairava despite the pain and even though his chest was pierced, the Dānava roamed for the distance of a krośa with extreme speed.
Then, having somehow steadied himself by his own self with his own self, the Blessed One quickly uprooted the enemy along with his mace using his trident.
The lord of the Daityas also hurled his mace at the head of Hara;
seizing his trident with both hands, the Dānava leapt up.
That great yogin, the support of all and the lord of creatures, remained firm;
yet from the wound inflicted by the falling mace, copious blood flowed forth in four directions.
Arisen from the eastern stream is Bhairava, whose radiance is like fire;
he is renowned as Vidyārāja and is adorned with a garland of lotuses.
Likewise, arising from the southern stream is Bhairava, adorned with corpses,
renowned as Kālarāja, and possessing a luster like black collyrium.
Then Bhairava, arising from the western stream, adorned with leaves and resembling the color of an *atasī* flower, is renowned as Kāmarāja.
Another is Udagdhārābhava, the formidable Bhairava adorned with a trident;
he is renowned as Somarāja and is embellished with a garland of wheels.
Born from the blood of the wounded, Bhairava appeared, adorned with a trident;
he was renowned as Svacchandrarāja, possessing a splendor equal to Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
Born from the blood on the ground was Bhairava, adorned with a trident;
known as Lalitarāja, he possessed a radiance like that of the Saubhāñjana tree.
Thus, O Sage, this Bhairava is said to consist of seven forms;
Vighnarāja is declared as the eighth, and together they are called the "Eight Bhairavas."
Thus, O Brahmin, the great Asura Daitya, impaled upon the trident by the high-souled and formidable wielder of the trident, was held aloft like a parasol.
O Brahmin, from the piercing by the trident, his blood flowed profusely,
by which Mahādeva, possessing seven forms, was drawn down and submerged.
Then a profuse sweat born of exertion broke out on Śaṅkara’s forehead; from that [sweat] was born a maiden drenched in blood.
O Brahmin, from the sweat-drop that fell from Śiva’s face onto the ground,
a young boy was born who resembled a heap of gold.
That child, being exceedingly thirsty, drank the blood of Andhaka;
and the wondrous maiden, having cut [the flesh], licked the blood that had formed.
Then Śaṅkara, whose form was terrifying, the granter of boons in the world, spoke these great words for the sake of her welfare to her, who possessed the radiance of the morning sun.
The gods, sages, ancestors, serpents,
yakṣas, vidyādharas, and even human beings shall worship you, O bringer of auspiciousness.
O Goddess, they shall always praise you with their hands offering heaps of oblations and flowers; for that reason, the auspicious name Carcikā arose, since you were smeared with blood.
Thus addressed by the Giver of Boons, Carcikā— the daughter born after Bhūta, clad in a tiger skin,
and beautiful— wandered everywhere across the earth, having gone to her supreme abode on Mount Haiṅgulatā.
When she had departed, the Giver of Boons granted to Kujja that boon which is the best of all boons:
"O Great-souled One, you shall become the lord of the planets, and the auspicious and inauspicious events of the world shall proceed according to your will."
For a full thousand divine years, the Lord Bhairava Hara, with the fire of his own sun-like eye,
rendered Andhaka’s body completely parched, devoid of blood, and reduced to nothing but skin and bone.
There, purified by Agni, who was born from his eye, that king of the asuras became freed from sin;
thereafter, he became the Lord of many forms, the protector of all beings, both moving and unmoving.
Having recognized him as the Lord of all, the immutable Master, the protector of the three worlds, the bestower of boons, the most excellent,
the primordial one who is bowed to and praised by all the gods and others, Andhaka then composed this hymn of praise.
Andhaka said:
Homage be to you, O Bhairava of terrifying form, protector of the three worlds, wielder of the sharp trident!
O twenty-armed one, wearing a necklace of lordly serpents, three-eyed one, protect me, whose intellect has failed. (VamP 44.52)
Be victorious, O Lord of All, whose form is the universe, whose footstool is worshipped by gods and asuras!
O Bull-bannered One, teacher of the Mother of the Three Worlds, I have come as a frightened seeker for refuge to You, the worthy protector.
O Lord, the gods proclaim you as Śiva; the Siddhas and the great seers call you Hara and Sthāṇu;
the Yakṣas call you Bhīma; and human beings and spirits recognize you as Maheśvara, the sovereign of all beings.
The night-stalkers offer fierce worship; the meritorious ancestors bow, saying "Be [our protector]!
"I am your slave; O Hara, protect me! O Lord of the World, bring about the destruction of my sins! VamP_44.55 //

O Lord, you are the threefold being, the three ages, the threefold dharma, and the triple Puṣkara; O three-eyed one, you whose soul is the triple Aruṇi and the triple destruction—purify me, for I have come to you for refuge.
You have performed the Triṇāciketa rite, you are established in the three steps, you know the six Vedāṅgas, and you are unattached to sense objects;
you are the Lord of the three worlds. Purify me, O Śambhu! I am your servant, terrified and come to you for refuge.
O Śaṅkara, O Lord of the great elements, O Lord of the Mountains, I have committed a great offense against you;
with my mind conquered by Kāma, I propitiate you, bowing down with my head.
"I am sinful, I am a doer of evil deeds, I am evil-natured, and I am born of evil. Save me, O God, O Lord; be the remover of all sins!"
"Do not be angry with me, O Lord of Gods; I have been created such as I am by you, a practitioner of sinful conduct. Be gracious to me, O Īśvara."
You are the creator and the sustainer; you are victory and great victory.
You are the auspicious one, you are the syllable Oṃ, you are the sovereign, the eternal, and the imperishable.
You are Brahmā, the Lord who creates the universe; you are Viṣṇu; you are Maheśvara;
you are Indra; you are the Vaṣaṭ-call; you are Dharma; and you are the supreme among the gods.
You are the subtle, you are the manifest form, you are the unmanifest, and you are the Lord;
by you all this world, both the stationary and the moving, is pervaded.
You are the beginning, the end, and the middle; you are without beginning, the thousand-footed one.
You are victory, the thousand-eyed, the many-eyed, and the mighty-armed.
The all-pervading one within all, the pervasive Haṃsa, the lord of the vital breath, the infallible;
the lord of the gods, the undisturbed Rudra, the lord of creatures, Śiva.

You are the possessor of the three Vedas, one who has conquered anger, one who has overcome his enemies, and one who has mastered his senses; you are Jaya and the wielder of the trident—protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Pulastya said:
O Brahmin, having been thus praised by the lord of the Daityas, Maheśvara,
the three-eyed one, filled with affection, spoke to Hiraṇyākṣa.
"You have attained success, O Lord of the Dānavas; I am well-pleased with you, Andhaka.
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—whatever you desire, with the exception of Ambikā."
Andhaka said:
"Ambikā is my mother, and the Blessed Tryambaka is my father;
I bow at the feet of my mother, for Ambikā is worthy of my veneration."
O Īśāna, if you are the bestower of boons, then let my evil deeds— whether physical, mental, or born of speech— and my ill-considered thoughts, go to destruction.
"O Maheśvara, may this disposition of mine as a Dānava depart;
let my devotion to you remain firm—grant me this boon."
Mahādeva said: "So be it, O Lord of Daityas; may your sin go to destruction.
You are released from your state as a Daitya; become Bhṛṅgī, a leader of my attendants."
Having spoken thus, the Giver of Boons lowered him from the tip of his trident and,
wiping him with his own hand, made Andhaka free from wounds.
Then he summoned the gods, beginning with Brahmā, from his own body;
those great-souled ones emerged, bowing down to the Three-eyed Lord.
Having summoned the joyful Gaṇas and stationed them before him,
he showed Bhṛṅgin [the scene], saying, "This is certainly not Andhaka."
Seeing that enemy, the lord of the Dānavas, his flesh completely withered,
and having attained the leadership of the Gaṇas, they praised the one who has the bull as his banner.
Then the Blessed One, having embraced those deities, said to them:
"Go to your own abodes and enjoy the happiness of the triple heaven."
Let even the thousand-eyed one go to the auspicious Malaya mountain;
having accomplished his purpose there, he may afterwards return to heaven.
Having spoken thus and addressed the thirty gods, he dismissed them;
and having paid homage to Pārvatī and embraced Janārdana,
those gods, released by Maheśvara, departed for the world of the Trakṣis.
Having gone to Mount Malaya and accomplished his task, Mahendra departed for heaven;
and when the foremost gods headed by Śakra had gone, the Blessed One remained silent.
Having honored the hosts as was fitting, he dismissed them;
and the hosts, having beheld Śaṅkara, mounted their respective vehicles.
O Nārada, they went to auspicious worlds of great enjoyments,
where there are cows that grant all desires and trees that yield the fruits of every wish.
When the Pramathas had each returned to their respective abodes, Maheśvara [beheld] rivers flowing with nectar and lakes whose mud was made of milk-rice.
Taking Andhaka by the hand, Sanandana went to Śaila;
after two thousand years, the excellent one returned, taking him with him.
And she beheld the daughter of the mountain seated upon a white *arka* flower;
as soon as she saw him arrive, he was endowed with all auspicious marks.
Having discarded the arka flower and gone out, she summoned those friends;
and being summoned by the Goddess, Jayā and the others arrived there at once.
Surrounded by them, she stood longing for the sight of Hara;
then the three-eyed god, having seen Girijā and having observed the Dānava, [acted].
And out of joy, he embraced Nandin, the son of the Mountain;
then he said, "O Goddess, I have made this Andhaka your servant."
"Behold your own son who has come to prostrate himself, O lady of the lovely smile!
Having spoken thus, [he said: 'O son Andhaka, protect him quickly!'"
"Go for refuge to your mother; she will bring about your welfare.
Thus addressed by the Lord, Nandin and Andhaka, the lord of the Gaṇas, [departed].
Having approached, both of them paid homage at the feet of Ambikā;
and Andhaka also, O great sage, bowing with devotion before Gaurī,
offered a most meritorious hymn of praise that destroys sin and is in harmony with the Vedas.
Andhaka said:

Om! I pay homage to Bhavānī, who is dear to the past and the future, the sustainer of the world, the progenitor, the mother of Skanda, the beloved of Mahādeva, the upholder, the flowing one, consciousness, the mother of the three worlds, the earth, the mother of the gods, the sacrifice, and memory.
I bow to Mṛḍānī—the goddess of compassion, modesty, and supreme splendor; the ever-purifying intellect; the great illusion who destroys the armies of the Daityas;
the beautiful Vaijayantī; Kālarātri; the sister of Govinda; the daughter of the King of Mountains; she who is worshipped by all gods and all beings;
the knowledge Sarasvatī; and the consort of the Three-eyed Lord. Having come for refuge to her who is the worthy refuge, I prostrate, I prostrate to you!
Thus praised by Sāndhaka, the Night-goddess was well-pleased and said:
"O son, I am gratified; choose a most excellent boon."
Bhṛṅgin said:
"O Pārvatī, may my threefold sin be pacified;
likewise, O Ambikā, may I have constant devotion toward the Lord."
Pulastya said:
Then Gaurī said "So be it" to the son of Hiraṇyākṣa;
and he, worshipping Śarva, remained there and became the lord of the Gaṇas.

Thus, in the past, through his own devotion, Maheśvara assumed a terrifying and formidable form with a distorted gaze, and by means of that, he brought about the state of being a *bhṛṅgin* for that best of Dānavas.
O Great Sage, this which has been told to you increases the fame of Hara; it is meritorious, purifying, and bestows auspiciousness.
It should always be recited among the best of the twice-born by one who desires dharma, long life, health, and wealth.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the glorious Vāma Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O bull among brahmins, that which was performed by Mahendra on Mount Malaya—
You have accomplished your own task; you should explain that to me.
Pulastya said:
Listen, O Brahman, to that which was performed by Mahendra on Malaya, the best of mountains, for the benefit of the world as well as for his own welfare.
The followers of Andhāsura, led by Maya and Tāpa,
were defeated by the hosts of gods and became eager to go to Pātāla.
They beheld Mount Malaya, whose caves were inhabited by *siddhas*,
covered with canopies of creepers, and teeming with intoxicated creatures.
The mountain, which was served by the exceedingly cool sandalwood trees inhabited by serpents,
possessed the fragrance of *mādhavī* flowers and was honored by the sages.
Seeing that place of cool shade, those who were exhausted and worn out by their exertions,
led by Maya and Tāra, decided to make it their dwelling.
While they were seated there,
a cool southern breeze, laden with fragrance and providing satisfaction to their vital breaths, blew gently.
And all those great asuras took delight in that very place,
while harboring hatred toward the host of deities who are honored by the world.
Having learned of this, Śaṅkara dispatched Śakra to the Asuras in Malaya;
and on his way, Hari also beheld Gomātṛ on the path.
Having circumambulated her and beheld the radiant mountain,
he saw all the Dānavas, joyful and endowed with enjoyments.
Then the slayer of Bala summoned all the great asuras;
they, remaining unperturbed, responded by scattering heaps of straw.
Standing upon his chariot, O brahmin seer, that woman of wondrous appearance covered those approaching [enemies] with nets of arrows,
just as a cloud covers mountains with rain.
Then Hari, having covered the Dānavas headed by Maya with arrows,
struck Pāka with sharp-pointed shafts fletched with heron feathers.
In that regard, the all-pervading Śakra, the lord of all the immortals, attained the status of Pākaśāsana by means of firm arrows, for he is the subduer of greed through his teaching.
Likewise, with well-feathered arrows, he tore apart another son of the asura Bāṇa named Pura; thereafter, he became Purandara.
Having thus slain the host of Dānavas in battle, the breaker of enclosures (Indra) was victorious;
and that [host], O Brahmin, having been conquered, went down to the netherworld (rasātala).
"For this purpose, O best of sages, the thousand-eyed one was sent to the Malaya mountain by Tryambaka; what else do you wish to hear?"
Nārada said:
For what reason is Hari called the Lord of the Gods and the Destroyer of Guṇas?
O Brahmin, this doubt revolves within my heart.
Pulastya said:
Listen to how Śakra, the destroyer of the mountain [Vṛtra], was celebrated by me; and what that crusher of enemies did after Hiraṇyakaśipu had been slain.
O Nārada, Diti, whose sons had been destroyed, said to Kaśyapa:
"O Lord, you are my protector; grant me a son who shall be the slayer of Śakra."
Then Kaśyapa said to her: "O dark-eyed one, if you shall remain endowed with purity and proper conduct for ten times ten years," VamP_45.21.
"Then, after three divine years, O beloved, you shall give birth to a son who will be the leader of the three worlds and the slayer of his enemies; it shall not be otherwise."
Having been addressed thus by her husband, Diti undertook a vow;
and the sage, having performed the rite of impregnation, departed for the Udaya mountain.
When that best of sages had departed, the thousand-eyed Indra also quickly went to that hermitage and spoke these words to Diti.
"I shall perform service for you, if you so desire," the goddess replied, impelled by her future destiny. (VamP 45.25)
For the sake of her business, Purandara, with a disciplined mind, performed tasks for her such as gathering sacrificial fuel, while watching for a vulnerability like a serpent.
Once, while engaged in asceticism and established in great purity,
that female ascetic bathed her head at the end of a thousand years.
Placing her own head upon her knees with her hair disheveled,
she fell asleep, her feet becoming entwined with the ends of her hair.
O Nārada, knowing that interval of impurity, the thousand-eyed god entered his mother’s womb through the passage of her nostril.
Having entered the belly of the Daitya’s mother, the enraged Purandara beheld a great child with his face turned upward and his hand placed upon his hip.
Then Indra beheld a mass of flesh within his very mouth;
he then grasped it with both hands, and it was like pure crystal.
Then, swelling with rage, Śatakratu began to rub a piece of flesh between his hands; thereupon, it became hard.
The upper half grew upward, and likewise the lower half grew downward;
thus the thunderbolt, consisting of a mass of flesh, came to have a hundred joints.
With that very hundred-jointed thunderbolt, O Brahmin, he cut the embryo of the son of Diti into seven pieces; and it cried out with a discordant sound.
Then Diti woke up and learned of Śakra’s conduct;
she heard the voice of her son as he was weeping, O Nārada.
Śakra also said in a very deep voice, "Do not weep, you fool!
Having spoken thus, he cut each one further into seven pieces.
They were born as the Maruts, the attendants of Śatakratu;
yet, due to their mother’s transgression, they remained unstable even when placed at the forefront.
Then Śakra, holding his thunderbolt, emerged from her womb.
Terrified by the curse, he spoke to Diti with his palms joined in reverence.
"O Teacher, this transgression is not mine, for it was your own son;
since it arose from your own misconduct, O Teacher, you ought not to be angry with me."
Diti said:
"I do not see any fault here; I believe this was ordained by destiny in the past, for even when the time was fully complete, she attained a state of purity."
Pulastya said:
Having spoken thus and personally consoled those children,
O beautiful lady, Diti sent them forth together with the king of the gods.

Thus, O Great Sage, in former times, that Lord Mahendra, afflicted by fear, split even his own uterine brothers while they were still in the womb; therefore, he became renowned as Gotrabhid, the "Splitter of the Womb."
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
Regarding those Maruts whom you have described as the best of the sons of Diti—
By what path did they previously travel? Tell me, [O] Marut-mārga.
O virtuous one, when the previous manvantaras have passed away, who were those who dwelt in the path of the wind? You should explain that to me.
Pulastya said:
Listen; I shall relate to you the origin of the former Maruts, beginning from the Svāyambhuva Manvantara up to this present one.
The son of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu was named Priyavrata;
he had a son named Savana, who was honored throughout the three worlds.
O celestial sage, that king, being childless, passed away to the realm of the departed;
thereupon his wife Sudevā wept, overwhelmed with grief.
Then, embracing her husband, she did not allow him to burn her;
lamenting many times, "O Lord! O Protector!", she was like one who had no protector.
Then an incorporeal voice spoke to her from the sky: "O queen, do not weep here;
if you possess unsurpassed truth, then let this fire be yours together with your husband."
Hearing that voice from the sky, the princess Sudevā said this:
"O bird, I grieve for this king who is childless, and not for myself, though my own fortune is meager."
Then he said: "Do not weep, O long-eyed one; seven sons shall be born to you from this protector of the earth.
Ascend the fire quickly; what has been spoken is the truth, believe it today."
Having been addressed thus by the sky-goer, the young woman placed her father’s worthy garment upon the ground;
then, having approached the fire, that devoted wife entered the flames while meditating upon him.
Then, after a moment, that king, endowed with splendor, rose up together with his wife;
he, able to travel at will, then flew into the sky along with the queen, the daughter of Sunābha.
O Nārada, as that king was traveling along, his queen Rajogā entered the sky;
through divine yoga, he remained suspended in the air together with his wife for five days.

Then, on the sixth day, the king, reflecting that his fertile season should not pass in vain, dallied with the slender maiden according to his desire; subsequently, his semen fell from him into the sky.
O ascetic, at the conclusion of the emission of semen, the king, together with his wife,
went by a divine path to the world of Brahmā.
Then, from that sky, the cloud-colored Śukra descended; the wives of the Seven Sages—Samānā, Nalinī, Vapuṣmatī, Citrā, Viśālā, and Haritālinī—beheld him according to their desire.
Seeing that [fruit] placed upon a lotus, O ascetic, they desired it back,
thinking it was nectar, out of a constant longing for youth.
Then, having bathed according to the rules and having duly worshipped their own husbands,
they were permitted by their husbands to drink the water situated at Puṣkara.
Thinking that semen of the lord of kings to be nectar, they drank it; by the mere drinking of that semen produced from the lord of kings, they— ||| VamP_46.18 ||| —[became pregnant].
Deprived of Brahmanic luster, they became wives of ascetics;
consequently, all those husbands abandoned their wives because they were tainted by fault.
O Sage, they gave birth to seven sons who wept most dreadfully;
by the sound of their crying, the entire world was filled.
Then the Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, arrived;
having approached, he said to the children, "Do not weep, O mighty ones!"
"You shall indeed become known as the Maruts, the wanderers of the sky.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [departed].
Taking them up, the sky-wanderer commanded the Maruts;
they were indeed the Maruts who existed in the interval of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.
O Nārada, listen as I describe the Maruts in the Svārociṣa [manvantara]:
the illustrious Kratudhvaja was the son of Svārociṣa.
O Sage, he had seven sons who were like the seven flames;
those lords of men went to Mount Mahāmeru for the sake of performing austerities.
Then, desiring the station of Indra and seeking to propitiate Brahmā,
the thousand-eyed one named Vipaścit became afflicted with fear.
Nārada, the knower of speech, said to Pūtanā, the foremost of the Apsarases:
"Go, O Pūtanā, to the vast mountain Mahāmeru."
There, O beautiful one, the sons of Kratudhvaja perform great austerities,
for they act in such a way that no obstacle to their penance may arise.
"Act accordingly so that they do not achieve success, O beautiful one.
Thus addressed by Śakra, Pūtanā, who was endowed with great beauty, [responded].
She went quickly to that place where they were performing their austerities;
not far from the hermitage was a river flowing with gentle currents.
All her brothers came together to bathe in that river;
she too, possessed of beautiful limbs, descended into the great river to bathe.
O Sage, when those kings saw her bathed, they were agitated;
and as their semen fell, that water-dweller drank it up.
The beloved wife of Mahāśaṅkha, the chief of the Grāhas, was Śaṅkhinī;
they too, having fallen away from their asceticism, went to rule over the paternal kingdom.
And that apsarā approached Śakra and reported the matter exactly as it was;
then, after a long period of time, she became a crocodile in the form of a conch shell.
The proud woman was pulled up from the great net by the fisherman;
seeing her lying on the ground, that fisherman, who possessed a large conch-shell, [was struck with wonder].
Then, having approached the sons of Kratudhvaja, those high-souled yogins who were masters of yoga made their announcement.
Having led them all to his own palace, he cast them into the city pond;
thereupon, the illustrious Śaṅkhinī gave birth to seven infants.
As soon as her sons were born, she attained the state of liberation;
the children lived in the midst of water, without mother or father.
Then, while those seeking other objects were weeping, the Grandfather arrived and said, "Do not weep, my dear sons; you shall be named Maruts."
"You shall become gods, wandering through the realm of the wind-sphere.
Having spoken thus, he then took all those deities toward [his destination].
Having appointed them to the path of the Maruts, he went to the Vairāja abode;
thus did the Maruts exist during the Svārociṣa interval of Manu.
O ascetic rich in penance, hear now of those who were the supreme Maruts;
in the lineage of Uttama, there was a king who was the lord of Niṣadha.
Renowned as Vapuṣmān, he was like the sun in his physical form;
his son Jyotiṣmān was preeminent in virtue and righteous.
Seeking a son, he performed austerities along the river Mandākinī;
his wife was the beautiful Suśroṇī, the auspicious daughter of Devācārya.
She became the attendant to him who was engaged in the practice of austerity;
she herself gathered fruits, flowers, water, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass.
The lotus-petal-eyed woman performed the worship of guests perfectly;
serving her husband, she became emaciated, her veins showing clearly.
Endowed with splendor and possessed of most beautiful limbs, she was seen by the Seven Sages in the forest;
having thus beheld her, whose every limb was lovely yet emaciated by asceticism.
They asked the reason for her asceticism and that of her husband;
she replied, "This performance of penance by us two is indeed for the sake of a son."
And those seven sages, O Brahmin, became granters of boons to her, saying:
"Go; you shall have seven sons, and there shall be no sorrow for you."
"By the grace of the great seers, you two shall be endowed with virtues.
Having spoken thus, all those great seers departed.
And that royal sage also returned to his city with his wife;
then, after a long period of time had passed, the king’s beloved queen—
That slender-limbed woman conceived a child from that best of kings; then, while his wife was pregnant, that lord of men passed away.
And that devoted wife, desiring to ascend after her husband, was then restrained by the ministers; nevertheless, she did not desist.
Then, having placed her husband upon the funeral pyre, she ascended it as well;
thereupon, O Sage, a piece of flesh fell from the midst of the fire into the water.
Sprinkled with pleasantly cool water, she became divided into seven parts;
they were then born as the Maruts during the interval of the supreme Manu.
I shall now proclaim those Maruts who existed in the past during the interval of Tāmasa, who were fond of song, dance, and sport.
The son of Tāmasa Manu was known as Ṛtadhvaja;
desiring a son, he offered his own flesh and blood into the fire.
"O King, we have heard that Citragu was seeking a son [and offered] bones, hair, body-hair, sinews, marrow, liver, and semen. (VamP 46.58)
Then, immediately after the fall of the seed into the seven flames,
there arose the sound "Do not cast me!"— and that king also died.
Then, from that fire, seven infants resembling its brilliance were born; O Sage, they began to weep.
Having heard their cry, the Blessed One Padmasambhava approached, restrained them, and then made [them] the sons of Maruta.
O Brahmin, those Maruts who were the hosts of deities during the Tāmasa Manvantara,
and those who existed during the Raivata— listen to them as well, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
In the lineage of Raivata, there was a self-controlled king named Ripujit;
he was renowned by the name Ripujit, and it is said that he had no son.
Having propitiated the Sun, the treasury of splendors, through his ascetic penance,
he obtained that maiden Surati and, taking her with him, went home.
O Brahmin, while she was living there in her father’s house, her father died;
overwhelmed by grief, she prepared to cast off her own body.
Then the seven mental-born sages restrained her,
for the hearts of all those whose wealth was asceticism were deeply attached to her.
Unable to endure that suffering, she kindled a fire and entered it;
and those seers, whose minds were thus purified, beheld her.
Seeing her dead, the ṛṣis cried out, "Alas! Alas!
and departed; furthermore, seven sons were born from the blazing fire.
Separated from their mother, they wept;
the Grandfather, the Lord of the World, having restrained them, made them into the hosts of Maruts.
O one whose wealth is austerity, these Maruts were born during the interval of Raivata;
listen, for I shall proclaim them [as they appeared] during the interval of Cākṣuṣa Manu.
There was a practitioner of austerities known as Maṅki, truthful in speech and pure;
he performed great penance at the sacred ford of Saptasārasvata.
To create an obstacle for him, the Tuṣita gods sent forth a woman;
and that beautiful lady, having approached the riverbank, began to disturb him.
Then, as his semen fell into the water of the Saptasarasvatī like a stream from the east, the sage Maṅkaṇaka cursed that foolish woman, saying, "Become a stone! (VamP 46.73).
"Go, you fool! You have obtained the great fruit of this evil deed;
the horse will destroy you in the assembly of the sacrifice. (VamP 46.74)
Having thus pronounced the curse, the illustrious sage then departed for his own hermitage;
from the seven Sarasvatīs, indeed, the seven Maruts were born.
Thus, O great seer, have I told you how the Maruts were born in the past as they pervaded the sky;
by hearing of their birth, there shall indeed be the destruction of sins and a great increase of dharma.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the glorious Vāyu Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
"For this purpose, O beloved of Kali, the Daitya Bali was made king."
Prahlāda was the bestower of mantras, and Śukra was the family priest.
Having learned that Bali, the son of Virocana and a descendant of Diti, had been consecrated,
all the Samayas arrived there, desiring to see him.
Having observed those who had arrived and having honored them in due order, he asked all those born of noble lineage: "What indeed would be most beneficial for me?"
They all said to him: "Listen to this, O crusher of the gods:
that deed which is most conducive to your welfare and likewise beneficial to us."
Your grandfather was the protector of the Dānavas, the heroic Hiraṇyakaśipu; he became Śakra in the three worlds.
Having approached him, Viṣṇu, the best of the gods, assuming the form of a lion,
tore him apart with his claws in the very presence of the lords of the Dānavas.
Likewise, O mighty-armed one, the kingdom of the high-souled Andhaka was taken away by Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, for the sake of those [gods].
Likewise, your paternal uncle Jambha was slain by Śakra,
and Kujambha as well was slaughtered like an animal before your very eyes by Viṣṇu.
Śambhu, Pāka, and your brother Sudarśana—Virocana, your father, has been slain by Mahendra; I shall tell you more.
O Brahmin, having heard that the cattle had been destroyed by Śakra,
the Dānava incited all the great Asuras to make preparations for war.
Some Asuras went forth for battle with the gods on chariots, others on elephants, others on horses, and likewise others as foot soldiers.
The powerful and terrifying general Bali goes at the front,
while Kālanemi follows behind the center of the army.
Leaning upon his left flank, the Śāla tree, whose prowess is renowned,
moves toward the formidable south along with the terrifying one named Tāraka.
O lover of strife, thousands, millions, and hundreds of millions of Dānavas set out for battle against the gods.
Having heard of the exertion of the asuras, Śakra, the lord of the gods, said to the deities:
"Let us go, accompanied by our forces, to fight those Daityas."
Having spoken these words, the powerful lord of the gods,
the Blessed One, mounted his chariot whose horses were driven by Mātali.
When the thousand-eyed Indra had mounted his chariot, the hosts of deities,
each mounting their own respective vehicle, set forth, longing for battle.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and likewise the two Aśvins;
the Vidyādharas, Guhyakas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas.
Likewise, royal sages, perfected beings, and various other creatures gathered together;
some mounted elephants, others chariots, and others horses.
And all of them, O Nārada, having mounted splendid celestial chariots drawn by birds, rushed toward where the army of the Daityas was stationed.
Upon this, Viṣṇu, the best of the gods, mounted and arrived.
When he had arrived, the thousand-eyed Indra, together with all the foremost of the gods, bowed his head in salutation to that imperishable Lord of the three worlds.
Then, at the head of the divine army, Kārttikeya, wielding a mace, marched;
Viṣṇu protected the rear, and the thousand-eyed Indra went in the middle.
O Sage, as the creature moved along,
the powerful Varuṇa followed, supporting himself against its right side, while [the other] supported itself against the left side.
Then the illustrious army of the immortals, protected by Skanda, Indra, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, and Sūrya,
with its multitude of arms raised with various missiles and weapons, assailed the enemy force upon the mountain.
On the delightful and auspicious slope of the Sunrise Mountain,
upon a level rocky surface devoid of trees and birds, a battle between the gods and asuras took place.
O Sage, a fierce clash occurred between those two armies on that best of mountains, like the previous encounter between the monkey and the elephant.
Raising dust from the chariots in the heat of battle, the tawny cloud at the front of the fray resembled a cloud in the sky colored by the twilight, O ascetic.
Then a tumultuous battle ensued in which nothing could be discerned;
however, the constant sound "Cut! Pierce! was heard everywhere.
Then, from the slaughter of the Daityas by the gods,
there arose a fierce stream of blood, consisting of dust and the essence of the self.
When the dust had subsided, the gods and others together with the wise Skanda rushed as one against that great army of the Dānavas.
Protected by the arms of Kumāra, the gods struck down the Dānavas;
and the Daityas, skilled strikers who were guarded by Maya, struck down the gods.
Then, O Nārada, deprived of the taste of the nectar of immortality, those most excellent gods were defeated in battle by the Daityas together with Skanda.
Seeing the gods utterly defeated, the destroyer of foes whose banner bore the son of Vinatā bent his Śārṅga bow and struck them here and there with volleys of arrows.
Being struck by Viṣṇu with his iron-tipped feathered arrows,
those Daityas sought refuge with the great Asura Kālanemi.
O Brahmin, having granted them safety and knowing that Mādhava was invincible, he grew in power like a neglected disease.
Whichever god, yakṣa, or kinnara he touched with his hand,
that one the powerful one would seize and hurl into his wide-open mouth.

Out of fury, the lord of the Dānavas, joined by the sons of Diti, crushed the army of the gods—including Indra, the sun, and the moon—with the force of his hands and the nails of his feet, even though he was devoid of armor;

and when the end arrived, as the fire of Time desired to consume this entire world, its form became such that it was surrounded on all sides—horizontally, above, and below—by wheels radiant like fire.

Seeing that enemy growing ever stronger and exceedingly powerful, all the leaders of the gods and Gandharvas, the Siddhas, Sādhyas, and the chief Aśvins, fled in every direction with eyes trembling from fear;

and the Daityas, their pride overflowing, began to overwhelm Hari—who is worshipped by the hosts of immortals and bears a beautiful crown—with showers of various weapons and missiles, causing his glory to fade.

Having thus observed those Daityas led by Kālanemi, stationed within the cities of Maya and Bala, Viṣṇu—his eyes bloodshot with rage—drew his Śārṅga bow and incessantly pierced their chests with thunderbolt-like arrows. With well-feathered shafts called *nārāca*, he overwhelmed them along with their chariots, elephants, and horses, whose prowess was shaken by his mere glance, just as a cloud covers mountains.

Covered by those arrows—resembling the staff of Death—that had been released from the hands of Hari, and by iron shafts and crescent-headed bolts, the inhabitants of Bāli’s city became terrified and retreated within;
then, having dispatched the lord of the Dānavas, the hundred-faced one, Kālanemi, to the leader of the divine army, Keśava, the protector of the worlds of immeasurable strength, he [Bali] advanced.
Seeing him with his hundred heads raised and mace uplifted, resembling the peak of the king of mountains, Viṣṇu quickly cast aside his Śārṅga bow and seized a discus in his hand.
Then that proud Dānava, having observed him—the cutter of the branches of the Daitya-tree—laughed and spoke to him for a long time with a voice like a thundercloud.

This is that very arrow which terrified the army of Danu’s son; it is the destroyer of Madhu when most enraged, the end-maker of Hiraṇyanetra, and one who delights in worship with flowers—where is this wicked thing going now that it has fallen within the range of my vision?
If this lotus-eyed one now approaches my combat, surely he will not return to his own abode;
with his limbs crushed by my fist and covered in ashes, the gods will behold him with eyes trembling in fear.
Having spoken thus to Madhusūdana, Kālanemi, his lower lip quivering with rage,
hurled his mace at the king of birds, just as Indra hurls the thunderbolt upon a mountain.
Beholding that terrible mace hurled by the arm of the Dānava as it came flying toward him, Viṣṇu cut it down with his discus,
just as one's previously committed karma cuts short the desires of a man in distress.
Having severed the mace and approached the Dānava, he swiftly cut off his two thick arms;
with his two arms lopped off, Kālanemi appeared like another mountain scorched by fire.
Then Mādhava, out of anger, severed his head with his discus and cast it upon the ground,
like a ripe palm fruit.
Thus, with his arms and head gone and his palm tree-like trunk shorn, that headless torso (kabandha), lord of mountains, stood unshakable like Mount Meru in the forest.
O sage, even Vainateya, the best of birds, brought him down to the earth with his beak,
just as Mahendra struck off the arm of Bāhu from the sky to the ground with his thunderbolt when its power was destroyed.
When that protector of the Dānava army had been slain, the Daityas, being hard-pressed by the gods and deprived of their weapons,
armor, shields, and garments, fled in all directions, O Lord of Asuras, save for Bāṇa.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then, when Bāṇa had retreated, the Dānavas quickly [returned] once more.
And the deities, equipped with weapons and eager for battle, withdrew.
Viṣṇu, too, of immeasurable prowess, perceiving that son of Bali to be invincible, addressed all the gods and said: "Fight, free from anxiety!"
Commanded by Viṣṇu, the gods, led by Śakra,
fought with the Dānavas, while Viṣṇu himself vanished from sight.
Knowing that Mādhava had departed, Śukra said to Bali:
"The Murus have been abandoned by Govinda; now, O Bali, may you be victorious!"
Delighted by the words of his family priest, Janārdana departed;
then, taking up his mace, the radiant one rushed toward the army of the gods.
Then Bāṇa, seizing his weapons with his thousand arms,
rushed toward the army of the gods and slaughtered them by the thousands.
O Sage, the powerful Māyā, resorting to various forms,
also fought against the army of the gods.
Vidyujjihva, Praribhadra, Vṛṣaparvan, Śatekṣaṇa,
Vipāka, Vikṣara, and Sainya— they too rushed against the gods.
While the god Janārdana had departed, those gods led by Śakra, being struck down by the sons of Diti,
were for the most part deprived of their preeminence.
All those [demons], led by Bali and Bāṇa and desiring to conquer the three worlds, pursued from behind those gods who had been broken.
Harassed by the Daityas, the gods, including Indra, overcome with fear,
abandoned the triple heaven and fled to the world of Brahmā.
When the gods, including Indra, had thus departed for the world of Brahmā,
Bali became the enjoyer of heaven, together with his sons, brothers, and kinsmen.
O Brahmā, Śakra became the Blessed One; Bali became Bāṇa; Yama became Varuṇa; Maya became Soma; Rāhu became Hlāda; and Hutāśana became [the fire].
Svarbhānu became Sūrya, and Śukra became Bṛhaspati;
those other gods who were appointed as authorities likewise gave birth to enemies of the gods.
At the beginning of the fifth *kali*-age, at the end of the *dvāpara*,
there occurred a most terrible battle between the gods and the asuras, in which even Śakra became powerless.
The seven netherworlds (pātālas) were under his control, as were the three worlds known as Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar; thus Bali was the sovereign of the ten worlds.
He himself dwells in heaven, enjoying pleasures that are very difficult to obtain;
there the Gandharvas, led by Viśvāvasu, wait upon him.
O ascetic devoted to pleasure, the Apsarases, headed by Tilottamā, dance;
and the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and others play musical instruments.
O Brahmin, while enjoying various pleasures, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, remembered Prahlāda, his own grandfather, in his mind.
And that highly devoted asura, being remembered by his grandson,
quickly ascended from Pātāla to the imperishable heaven.
Upon seeing him arrive, Bali abandoned his lion-throne and,
with palms joined in reverence, paid homage at both of his feet.
Having quickly raised up the hero Bali, who had fallen at his feet, Prahlāda embraced him and seated him upon the supreme throne.
Bali said: "O dear father, by your grace the gods have been conquered by me, and the kingdom of Śakra has been seized by me through my own heroism and strength. (VamP 48.23)
Therefore, my dear father, enjoy this sovereignty over the three worlds, which has been won by my prowess, while I stand before you as your servant.
O father, by this much alone may I be endowed with merit:
that I myself am devoted to the worship of your feet and eat the food remaining from your meal.
O best of beings, O Lord, that steadfastness which arises in one who serves his elders does not belong to one merely protecting a kingdom.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having heard those words spoken by Bali,
Prahlāda spoke these words which accomplish the goals of dharma, desire, and wealth.

In the past, I made the kingdom free of thorns; the earth was well-governed, and friends were duly honored. I gave gifts as desired to people and likewise to my own sons; now, established in power, I am a practitioner of yoga.
"O son, that which was taken by me according to the rite has been returned to you again.
Thus, may you always remain devoted to the service of your elders."
Having spoken these words, O Brahmin, he took Bali by the right hand and quickly seated him upon the lion-throne of Śakra.
Seated upon a beautiful lion-throne made of every kind of jewel belonging to Mahendra, the lord of the Daityas shone like Maghavan himself.
Seated there, with his palms joined in reverence and bowing low, he spoke these words to Prahlāda in a voice as deep as a thundercloud: VamP_48.32 //
"O Father, whatever must be done by me while protecting the three worlds for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— may your lordship instruct me in that."
Simultaneously with those words, Śukra said to Prahlāda:
"O mighty-armed one, speak now whatever reply you deem appropriate."
Having heard the words of Bali and Śukra, the Asura Prahlāda, a devotee of the Lord,
spoke these excellent words endowed with righteousness and purpose.
O King, that which is appropriate for the future, that which is beneficial for the world,
and that which constitutes the acquisition of wealth without conflict with dharma— [that is what you should do].
O son, practice that action which follows after all sentient beings, which bears fruit within the realm of desire, and which is conducive to welfare both in this world and the next.
O high-minded one, act in such a way that you shall go today to what is praiseworthy, so that fame may be yours, and that there be no association with infamy.
For this purpose, the best of men desire radiant prosperity,
so that these [beings] may dwell in our home most contentedly.

A man of noble birth who is immersed in calamity, a friend who has been deprived of wealth, an elderly kinsman, a virtuous Brahmin, as well as fame along with renown— [all these are protected by one who maintains his vows]. *Vāmana Purāṇa* 48.40.
Therefore, my son, just as these noble-born ones dwell here while you are established in the kingdom,
so act with your own pure and virtuous conduct that you shall become illustrious in the world.
When the earth is always adorned by Brahmins, supported by Kshatriyas, firmly cultivated,
and characterized by the emergence of those devoted to service, the lords of men attain prosperity here on earth.

Therefore, O best of the twice-born, those lords of men who are joined with the Vedas and the scriptures, O foremost of brahmins, shall find peace for the king through sacrifices and the smoke from the sacrificial fires.

"Let the Brahmins— who are perfected in austerity and study, devoted to officiating at sacrifices and teaching, intent on their own Vedic recitation and sacrifice, generous, and living by the sword— be honored by you in the army, having indeed obtained your permission. (48.44)
O Lord of Daityas, let the Kṣatriyas be those whose duty is the protection of the subjects.
Those accomplished in sacrifice and study shall be givers; those engaged in agriculture shall practice animal husbandry, and courtesans shall live by trade.
O best of Asuras, let the Śūdras always be devoted to serving the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas,
and Vaiśyas, and always carry out your commands.
O Lord of the Daityas, when the social orders abide in their own respective duties, then there is indeed an increase of dharma;
and with the increase of dharma, there is the prosperity of the king.
Therefore, O Bala, you must always ensure that the social classes remain established in their own duties;
for when those duties flourish, your own prosperity follows, and when they decline, your own loss is said to occur.
Having heard these words, the high-souled great lord of the asuras, Bali, became silent;
then Bali spoke these words to the great seer: "I shall do whatever you command."
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Then, O twice-born one, when the gods had departed toward the world of Brahmā...
Bali, always endowed with righteousness, protected the three worlds.
Then Kali, seeing the world endowed with righteousness as it was in the Kṛta age,
sought refuge in Brahmā due to the suppression of his own nature.
Having gone there, he beheld the god accompanied by the deities led by Indra,
illuminating his own realm along with the gods and asuras by means of his own radiance.
Having prostrated before him, Tiṣya then said to Brahmā, the Lord:
"O best of gods, my own nature has been destroyed by Bala."
The Blessed One, the yogi, said to him: "Indeed, he has taken away the very nature of the world, not merely that of you alone, by means of his superior power."
Behold Tiṣya, the lord of the gods, Varuṇa, and the Maruts;
for even Bhāskara has been brought to a state of wretchedness by the power of Bali.
There is no one in the three worlds who can obstruct his action,
except for Hari, who possesses a thousand heads and a thousand feet.
The imperishable one will seize back from Bali the earth, as well as heaven, sovereignty, fortune, and glory, making him a follower of the sphere of the True Dharma.
Thus addressed by the god Brahmā, the imperishable Kali,
seeing Śakra and the others in a state of distress, went to the Vibhītaka forest.
O Nārada, when Kṛta-yuga began, dharma possessed four feet throughout the three worlds and among the four social orders as well.
Austerity, non-violence, truthfulness, purity, restraint of the senses,
compassion, charity, kindness, service, and the performance of sacrifice.
For these indeed exist pervading the entire world;
O Brahmin, even Tiṣya was made powerful by one who is more powerful than the powerful.
For the twice-born castes remained established in their own duties and entered the stages of life,
while the bulls among men always abided by the duty of protecting the subjects.
O Brahmin, while Dharmottara prevails in these three worlds,
the Goddess of Fortune of the three realms, the bestower of boons, has come to you, the lord of the Dānavas.
Upon seeing her approach, who possessed the splendor of the thousand-eyed Indra, Bali asked:
"Who are you? Tell me; for what purpose have you come?"
Having heard those words, Śrī, garlanded with lotuses, said:
"O Bali, listen! I am she who has come to you by force, O Queen."
That god of immeasurable power who wields the discus and the mace has abandoned Maghavan; therefore, I have come here to you.
He created young women endowed with beauty;
she was clad in white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents.
One is mounted upon a white bull, rich in essence, with a white body;
another wears red garments and is adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Mounted upon a red horse, she is red-limbed and indeed characterized by the quality of rajas;
she wears yellow garments, is yellow in complexion, and is adorned with yellow garlands and unguents.
Moving in golden chariots, they have resorted to the quality of darkness (tamas);
they wear blue garments, blue garlands, and are anointed with blue perfumes and unguents.

She who is mounted upon a blue bull is proclaimed as the one consisting of the three qualities (triguṇā). She who is white-clad and white is rich in the quality of purity (sattva) and is seated upon an elephant.
She approached Brahmā, as well as Candra and those who follow Candra;
she was passionate, dressed in red garments, mounted upon a horse, and filled with the menstrual flow.
He gave her to the King of the Gods, as well as to those equal to him—
she who was clad in yellow garments, fortunate, seated upon a chariot, and radiant as gold.
He gave her to Prajāpati, Śukra, and among the Viśas;
she who resembles a woman dressed in blue garments is the fourth, seated upon a bull.
The Brahmins and others describe that Sarasvatī as being white in form, [appearing] to the Dānavas, the Nairṛtas, the Śūdras, and even the Vidyādharas.
In the sacrifice, the Kṣatriyas always praise her together with the Brahmins by means of mantras and other rites; they extol that red-colored goddess as Jayaśrī.
O best of asuras, that illustrious woman was always honored by Indra and Manu;
indeed, the Vaiśyas always [worship] her, who is clothed in yellow garments and possesses limbs of gold.
Thus do the protectors of the people praise Lakṣmī;
likewise, the Śūdras praise her, who has a dark-blue body, with great devotion.
By the name Śrī, she was [given] to him along with the Daityas and Rākṣasas;
thus were those women distributed by that god who wields the discus.
And their essential nature is that inexhaustible treasures abide within them;
likewise, the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, and traditional sayings [reside there].
The sixty-four arts, the white [treasure], and the great lotus treasure are situated there;
as well as pearls, gold, silver, chariots, horses, elephants, and ornaments.
Weapons, missiles, armor, and garments are red; the lotus is known as a treasure (nidhi).
Cows, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, gold, clothing, and lands [are also such treasures].
The herbs and animals have drunk [the essence], and the great sapphire treasure remains;
for all species, a single species is established as the foundation.
The destroyer of others is Nīlā, and the treasure Śaṅkha is situated there;
O Dānava, understand from me as I speak those forms which belong to noble men who are established in these [cities]. VamP_49.35 //
O Lord of the Forest, those men who are endowed with truth and purity, and who delight in sacrifices, gifts, and festivals, come to dwell upon the Great Lotus.
Men who perform sacrifices, those who are fortunate, proud, and self-important, those who give many sacrificial fees,
and those who enjoy pleasures common to all, are said to be dependent on the lotus.

Men who resort to the Mahānīla mountain are characterized by a mixture of truth and falsehood, they are skilled in giving and taking, and their expenditures involve both righteous and unrighteous means.
O Bala, those men who rely on Śaṅkha will be nihilists, devoid of purity, wretched, deprived of enjoyments, and addicted to theft and false speech.
Thus, O Dānava, this decision regarding them has been declared to you.
"I am that woman named Rāgiṇī, the wife of Śrī, who has come to you;
O Lord of the Forest, I have a vow esteemed by the virtuous."
I take refuge in one who is rich in heroism and never in a coward; moreover, there is no one equal to you, nor anyone superior in strength, even throughout the three worlds.
Indeed, by your power and majesty, a firm joy has been produced in me,
since the king of the gods was utterly defeated by you through your prowess in battle.
Therefore, O Dānava, supreme and eternal joy has arisen within me,
having seen your supreme courage, which is superior in strength to all others.
Therefore, O best of Dānavas, I have come here in person to this hero who prides himself on his prowess; it is no wonder in the lineage of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
O King, since such is the deed of you, the newly born lord of the Asuras,
your great-grandfather, the son of Diti, has been surpassed by you.
"By him the three worlds were conquered through valor, though they had been seized by others"— having spoken these words to Bali, the lord of the Dānavas, at that time.
Then Jayashri, moon-faced and auspicious, entered, illuminating [the place];
and when she had entered, the women there became like widows.
Modesty, prosperity, wisdom, fortitude, and fame resort to the powerful;
likewise do splendor, intelligence, diligence, success, learning, policy, and compassion.
Revelation, tradition, fortitude, fame, form, and action accompanied by peace;
as well as nourishment, contentment, and another, desire— these qualities resting upon the quality of goodness (sattva),
all of them, having resorted to Bali, rested at their ease.

Such were the virtues of that eminent Danava, the high-souled Bali: he was of auspicious intellect, self-possessed, a performer of sacrifices, an ascetic, gentle, truthful in speech, a donor, a supporter, and a protector of his own kin.
While the lord of the Dānavas ruled over the triple heaven, no human being was born who was afflicted by hunger, nor one who was filthy or wretched;
rather, even among men, there were those who were ever-luminous, devoted to dharma, self-controlled, and yet enjoyers of sensual pleasures.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
When the sovereignty over the three worlds had passed to the Dānavas, Purandara [acted].
The Lord of Śacī went to the abode of Brahmā together with the gods.
There he beheld the Lord of Gods, Brahmā, born from the lotus,
seated together with the sages and his own father, Kaśyapa.
Then Śakra, together with the hosts of gods,
bowed his head to Brahmā, Kaśyapa, and all those whose wealth was their asceticism.
Indra, together with the gods, spoke to the Grandfather, the Lord of the Devas:
"O Grandfather, my kingdom has been seized by the powerful Bali."
Brahmā said to Śakra: "O Śakra, this fruit of one's own actions is being experienced. Śakra asked: "O Lord, tell me, what evil deed was committed by me?"
Kaśyapa also said to the Lord of the Gods: "The murder of an embryo has been committed by you;
indeed, the fetus from Diti’s womb was forcibly cut into many pieces by you."
The Lord of the Gods said to his father: "O All-pervading One, it was due to the fault of my mother that the embryo underwent excision, for she became impure. (VamP 50.7)
Then Kaśyapa said: "O Bhīṣma, because of his mother's fault he fell into slavery;
thereafter, even as a slave, he was struck down by the thunderbolt."
Having heard those words of Kaśyapa, Śakra said to the Grandfather: "O Lord, tell me the means of atonement for the destruction of my sin."
Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa likewise spoke to the Lord of the Gods—
what was for the welfare of the entire world, and especially for Śakra.
Mādhava, the Supreme Person, holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands;
go to him for refuge, and he will provide for your welfare.
Having heard the words of his elders, the thousand-eyed Indra indeed spoke:
"In what short time can great prosperity be attained?
The deities said to him: "O mortal, in a short time, great prosperity may be achieved."
Thus addressed by Viriñci, by Kaśyapa the son of Marīci,
and likewise by the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, the king of the gods descended with speed to the surface of the earth and stood there.
It is situated to the north of Kāliñjara, likewise to the south of the Himālaya;
it is renowned as being to the east of Suśasthala and stands to the west of the city of Vasu.
Formerly, O best of men, it was here that Gaya performed a horse-sacrifice a hundred times with abundant sacrificial fees;
he performed the human-sacrifice a hundred times, a thousand times, and indeed the Sūrya-sacrifice a thousand times, O lord of men.
Likewise, in ancient times, there was a place difficult to conquer, renowned among gods and asuras and famous as Mahāmedha.
There, the Blessed One, the Enemy of Mura, whose body is unmanifest yet possesses a form of space, made his dwelling;
thus he attained fame as Gadādhara, for he was a sharp axe to the great tree of sin.
In that place, where even the foremost of the twice-born, though devoid of the Vedas and the Shastras, attain equality with the Grandfather (Brahmā);
and where, by worshipping the ancestors but once with single-minded devotion,
men obtain the infinite fruit of the Mahāmedha sacrifice through the grace of the Blessed Lord.
Where the great river, the daughter of the celestial rishi, having come to the snowy mountain under the guise of water,
brought about the supreme destruction of the world's sins through her sight, drinking, and being used as an ointment.
There, Śakra, having approached the wondrous bank of the great river,
established a hermitage for the propitiation of the God and remained there.
Bathing in the morning, sleeping on the ground, eating but one meal a day, and subsisting on alms,
the thousand-eyed Indra performed austerities while praising the god who bears the mace.
As he was thus performing penance, having properly conquered all his senses and being free from desire and anger, a full year passed by.
Then Gadādhara, being pleased, said to Vāsava, "O Nārada, go; I am pleased with you, and you are now freed from sin."
"O Lord of Gods, you shall regain your own kingdom before long;
O Śakra, I shall strive in such a way that your welfare will come to pass."

Having been addressed thus by Gadādhara, he was then dismissed; and after bathing Manoharā, when the Lord had finished his ablutions, the men said to him regarding that sin: "Please grant us your instruction."
He spoke to those Pulindas of terrifying deeds, saying: "O Pulindas, you who have arisen from my sin, dwell indeed within the interval between these two best of mountains, Himavat and Kāliñjara."
Having spoken thus, the king of the gods, freed from sin, followed the praiseworthy chariot of his mother— the abode of Dharma— while being honored by the immortals, Siddhas, and Yakṣas.
Having seen Aditi with her head bowed and her palms joined in reverence, he approached her;
then, having prostrated at her feet which were like the interior of a lotus, he announced his own ascetic practice.
She asked that Lord for the reason, having smelled his head and embraced him with tearful eyes;
and he explained to her his victory in battle over Bali, as well as [the victory] of himself together with the hosts of gods.
Upon hearing this, her limbs overwhelmed with grief, she realized that her son had been defeated by the sons of the Daitya;
filled with sorrow, she went for refuge to Viṣṇu, the primordial, worshipful, and excellent god.
Nārada said: O auspicious one, tell me in which place did the mother of the best of the gods worship Hṛṣīkeśa— the infinite, primordial,
ancient source of all that moves and is stationary?
Pulastya said:
Having observed Śakra dejected and defeated by the leader of the Dānavas, Surāraṇi then,
during the bright fortnight when the sun was situated in the constellation Mṛgaśiras, prepared the oblation for Agni on the seventh day.

50.31–32. Upon seeing that god, the lord of the thirty-three, mounted upon Airāvata in the direction of Indra at the time of great prosperity, she—despairing, her speech restrained, and purified—then approached the lord of the gods for refuge.
Aditi said:

Victory to you, O thief of the calyx of the divine lotus! Victory to you, O axe to the tree of saṃsāra! Victory to you, O fire for the fuel of sin! O you who block the flood of darkness, salutations, salutations unto you!
Homage to you, O Bhāskara of divine form; homage to you, the tilaka of the splendor of the three worlds!
You are the cause of all that is moving and unmoving; O Lord of universal form, protect me.
O Lord of the World, through you, the Protector who pervades the universe, Śakra has recovered his lost kingdom and overcome his enemies; therefore, we have come to you for refuge.
Having spoken thus, she drew the well-honored deity with red sandalwood paste,
worshipped him with *karavīra* flowers, and offered incense of *kaṇa-markabhojya*.
And having offered highly precious food mixed with clarified butter for the benefit of Mahendra, the goddess remained fasting,
observing a fast without food while praising him with a meritorious hymn.

Then, on the second day, having performed her salutations, bathed according to the prescribed rite, and worshipped, she gave gold, grain, sesame, and clarified butter to the twice-born; thereafter, she remained there with a disciplined mind before him.
Then Bhānu, whose flame is ghee, became pleased; emerging from the solar disc and standing before him, he spoke these words.
"O daughter of Dakṣa, by this vow I am well-pleased with you;
through my grace, you shall obtain your difficult-to-attain desire—of this there is no doubt."
"O Goddess, source of the gods, I shall indeed grant the kingdom to your sons;
I will destroy the Dānavas by being born from within your very womb."
O Brahmin, having heard those words of Vāsudeva, the source of the gods spoke again and again to the source of the worlds, trembling repeatedly.
How shall I be able to carry you upon my belly, you who are so difficult to bear,
within whose belly the entire world— both stationary and moving— dwells?
O Lord, who is capable of supporting you? You are the sustainer of the three worlds, within whose belly the seven oceans dwell together with the mountains.
Therefore, O Janārdana, act in such a way that Śakra may become the lord of the gods here, and that no affliction may befall me.
Viṣṇu said:
