"This is true, O illustrious lady; I am difficult to be restrained even by gods and asuras.
Nevertheless, I shall come to be born within your womb, O Goddess."
"O Goddess, by means of yoga I shall support myself, the worlds, the mountains, and you together with Kaśyapa; do not despair, O Mother."
O daughter of Dakṣa, when I am indeed born within your womb,
then the Daityas will undoubtedly become devoid of their splendor.

Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, the Blessed One, the crusher of hosts of enemies, entered her once more; then, with a portion of his own splendor, he entered the womb of the goddess for the sake of Śakra’s welfare.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
While the Mother of the Gods remained pregnant with the one in the form of a dwarf (Vāmana),...
The Asuras became devoid of splendor, just as it was spoken by the Source of the Universe.
Seeing the Asuras deprived of their splendor, Bali, that tiger among the Dānavas, spoke these words to Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas: VamP_51.2 //
Bali said:
"O father, for what reason have the Daityas become devoid of splendor?
Tell me, for you are supremely wise and skilled in discerning the auspicious and the inauspicious."
Pulastya said:
Having heard those words of his grandson, he remained in meditation for a moment, reflecting:
"For what reason is there this loss of splendor, and why is it so extreme?"
Having realized that an unsurpassed fear arising from Vāsudeva had arisen among the Daityas, he, whose soul was absorbed in yoga, reflected: "Where is Viṣṇu stationed at this moment?"
O Nārada, having meditated upon the seven netherworlds (pātālas) below the navel,
the self-controlled one should proceed to travel through the worlds beginning with Bhūr above the navel.
He saw the earth shaped like a lotus, and in its center, Mount Meru, the king of mountains, made of gold and possessed of great miraculous power, appearing in the form of a lotus.
Above that, he saw a great city and likewise eight world-protectors;
their mother was seen by him surrounded by hosts of beasts and birds.
Below that, he beheld the highly meritorious hermitage of the Mother of the Gods, honored by the deities and surrounded by flocks of beasts and birds.
O sage, having seen that mother of the gods, who surpassed all in splendor,
the lord of the Dānavas entered [the cave] to search for Madhusūdana.
Then he beheld the Lord of the World, Mādhava, in the form of a dwarf—
the God who is the most excellent refuge for all those in fear— within the womb of his mother.
Having seen that lotus-eyed one, who bears the conch, discus, and mace,
his form pervaded on all sides by the hosts of both gods and asuras.
Having seen Viṣṇu, who had assumed the form of a dwarf and was the taker of the Daityas' splendor, by means of that very same sequence of yoga, he then returned to his natural state.

Then the highly intelligent Prahlāda, having bowed down to Madhusūdana, spoke these sweet words to Bali, the son of Virocana: VamP_51.14: "Then the highly intelligent Prahlāda, having bowed down to Madhusūdana, spoke these sweet words to Bali, the son of Virocana."
Prahlāda said:
"Listen, I shall tell you everything from which your fear has arisen,
and by what cause, O Lord of Daityas, the Daityas have become devoid of luster."
The gods, including Indra, Rudra, Arka, and Pāvaka, having been conquered by you,
have gone for refuge to the Lord Hari, the sovereign of the three worlds.
Having granted fearlessness to Śakra and the others, the Teacher of the World,
the mighty-armed Hari, descended into the womb of Aditi.
"O Bala, it is my conviction that the strength and splendors have been seized by Vastu;
darkness is not able to endure the rising of the sun. (VamP 51.18)
Pulastya said: Having heard the words of Prahlāda, his lower lip quivering with rage, Bali— impelled by his future karma— then spoke to Prahlāda.
Bali said:
"Father, who is this one named Hari from whom our fear has arisen?
I have hundreds of Daityas here whose strength exceeds that of Vāsudeva."
By whom, in their thousands, the immortals— including Indra, Rudra, Agni, and the Maruts—
were defeated on the field of battle, deprived of heaven, and shorn of their pride.
He by whom the wheel of great speed was dragged from Sūryaratha with force—
that powerful Vipracitti is at the head of my army.
Ayaḥśuṅga, Śiva, Śambhu, Asiloman, Vilomakṛt,
Triśiras, Makarākṣa, Vṛṣaparvan, and Natekṣama.
These and others are powerful and skilled in various weapons;
Viṣṇu does not equal even a sixteenth part of each one of them individually.
Pulastya said:
Having heard these words of his grandson, Prahlāda, overcome with anger, cried out "Fie! Fie! at Bali, who had spoken such insults against Vaikuṇṭha.
Fie on you, O evil-minded one, a heap of sin and a most foolish person!
How is it that your tongue did not fall out as you reviled Hari? (VamP 51.26)
O evil-minded one, you are pitiable and deserving of reproach by the virtuous,
since you, O fool, revile Viṣṇu, the preceptor of the three worlds.
I am to be pitied, there is no doubt, by whom your father was begotten—
you, his son, who have become so harsh and a source of contempt for the gods.
"You surely know this, as do these great Asuras,
that there is no one dear to me other than Janārdana."
Even though you knew Hari to be dearer to me than my own life,
and to be the God who is the Lord of all lords, how could you have reviled him?
Your father is worthy of worship; he, too, has me as his preceptor.
And for me, the Blessed Lord Hari, the preceptor of the world, is worthy of worship.
O fool, the Guru of your Guru is worthy of worship, and he is most worthy of worship by you; O sinner, how is it that you revile one who is worthy of worship, and why have you not fallen downward?
"Those Dānavas have been made pitiable by you through your wicked conduct—
those for whom you, harsh and a reviler of Vāsudeva, are king."
"Since you have reviled Hari, who is worthy of worship and adoration by you,
therefore, O practitioner of sinful deeds, may you suffer the destruction of your kingdom."
"Since there exists nothing dearer to me than Keśava in thought, deed, or word, fall down likewise, deprived of your kingdom! VamP_51.35.
Since nothing else exists apart from or distinct from that, fall down like one who has fallen from the sacrificial butter in the fourteen worlds! VamP_51.36.
For all beings in this world, there is no other ultimate refuge such as you,
who have been fallen from your kingdom, whom we should behold.
Pulastya said: When these words had been uttered, O Brahmin, the powerful Bali then quickly descended from his seat with his palms joined in reverence.
Bowing his head in prostration, he said: "May my teacher show me favor;
for teachers forgive even their young disciples who have committed offenses."
Therefore, O Lord of the Dānavas, it is well that I have been cursed by you;
I fear neither my enemies nor the loss of my kingdom.
"O Lord, it is not at all my suffering that I have been deprived of my kingdom;
rather, because I have committed an offense against you, my suffering is far greater."
Therefore, father, let my offense be forgiven; I am but a child, without a protector, and of very dull wit.
Even when a fault is committed, elders forgive the childish who have come to them in distress.
Pulastya said:
Having been thus addressed, that great-souled one, whose delusion was dispelled and who was a devotee of Hari’s feet,
reflected for a long time upon this wonder and then spoke these sweet words to his grandson.
Prahlāda said:
"O father, by delusion my knowledge and discrimination were obscured,
whereby, though knowing Viṣṇu to be omnipresent, I reviled you."
"O Dānava,
O mighty-armed one, this must surely be you who have entered me, the one who obstructs my discernment."
Therefore, O Lord, you ought not to feel distress regarding the kingdom;
for things that are destined to happen never fail to come to pass.
For the sake of sons, friends, and wife, and for the sake of kingdom, enjoyments, and wealth,
a wise person should not fall into despair regarding income or expenditure.
O Lord of Daityas, just as pleasures and pains arrive according to the dictates of past karma, so must a man endure them.
Seeing the onset of calamities, the self-controlled man should not become despondent;
and having attained vast prosperity, he should not become restless.
The wise do not become deluded when wealth is lost, nor do they rejoice when wealth arrives;
such supreme men are always steadfast in their duties.
Knowing this, O Lord of the Daityas, you ought not to fall into despair under any circumstances; for you are wise, and the learned man does not succumb to despondency.
Furthermore, O mighty-armed one, listen to this other beneficial and highly significant teaching;
having heard it for yourself as well as for others, act accordingly.
Go for refuge to that very Puruṣottama, who is worthy of being sought for protection;
O Lord of Dānavas, he will be your savior from this fear.

Those men on earth who have taken refuge in Hari— the infinite Viṣṇu, without beginning or middle, the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, the Lord Hari, the hand-hold for one fallen into the pit of saṃsāra— truly never become afflicted by fever.
O best of Dānavas, now fix your mind upon him and become his devotee;
this very Janārdana shall bring about your ultimate welfare.
And I, having propitiated the Lord for the sake of pacifying my sins, shall go on a pilgrimage to various sacred sites;
then, freed from sin, I shall go to where Acyuta, the Lord of the World, Nṛsiṃha, resides.
Pulastya said:
Having thus consoled Bali, the high-souled one, having called to mind Viṣṇu, the Lord of Yoga,
and having addressed all the leaders of the Danu host, set out to perform a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O best of Brahmins, which holy places did Prahlāda visit?
You ought to relate to me fully the pilgrimage to the tirthas of Prahlāda.
Pulastya said: Listen, for I shall relate to you the pilgrimage of Prahlāda, which destroys the mire of sin and bestows pure merit.
Having abandoned Meru, the lord of golden mountains, he went to the sacred ford frequented by hosts of immortals—
the famous Mānasa on earth, which bestows auspiciousness, where the Lord of the Gods dwells in the form of a fish.
Having bathed in that excellent tirtha and having satiated the ancestors and the gods,
he worshipped Acyuta, the Lord of the World, accompanied by the Vedas.
Having fasted and further honored the gods, sages, ancestors, and men,
he went to the Kauśikī river to see the sin-destroying tortoise.
Having bathed in that great river, having worshipped the Lord of the Universe,
having fasted and become pure, and having given sacrificial fees to the Brahmins— VamP_52.6.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World who bears the form of a tortoise, he then went to see the Lord known as Kṛṣṇa, who has the face of a horse. There,
having bathed in the Devahrada and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he proceeded.
Having worshipped Hayashirsha, he went to Hastinapura;
there he [saw] the Lord of the World, Govinda, the wielder of the discus.
Having bathed and worshipped according to the prescribed rites, he went to the Yamunā;
having bathed in her, become pure, and offered libations to the ṛṣis, gods, and ancestors,
he beheld Trivikrama, the Lord of the God of Gods and Protector of the World.
Nārada said: Now the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world and the Sovereign, will assume a body for the conquest of the three worlds and effect the binding of Bali.
How then was Trivikrama all-pervading even in former times?
Or whom did Viṣṇu bind? Tell me that.
Pulastya said:
Listen, for I shall tell you about this one who was called Trivikrama—
the time at which he was born and whom he deceived.
There was a son born of Kaśyapa’s own loins, known as Dhundhu,
who arose from the womb of Danu and possessed great strength and prowess.
O Nārada, having propitiated Brahmā, the giver of boons, through his ascetic penance,
that asura requested invincibility against the gods, including Indra.
The Lotus-born One, being well-pleased by his asceticism, granted him that boon;
and the powerful one, having departed, went forth to the celestial realm.
At the beginning of the fourth age (kali-yuga), having defeated the gods along with Indra,
Dhundhu assumed the status of Śakra while Hiraṇyakaśipu was still alive.
At that time, the powerful Hiraṇyakaśipu,
having taken refuge with the Daitya Dhundhu, wandered upon Mount Mandara.
Then the asuras dwell at will in Triviṣṭapa,
while the thirty gods remain in the Brahma-world joined with suffering.
Then, having heard from the immortals dwelling in the Brahma-heaven, Dhundhu, the son of Diti, said:
"O Daitya, let us go to the assembly hall of our elder brother to conquer the thirty gods together with Śakra."

Having heard the words of Dhundhu, the Daityas said: "O Guardian of the World, we have no means by which we may go to the abode of the Grandfather; for this path beyond is exceedingly difficult to traverse."
Beyond this, at a distance of many thousands of yojanas, is the world named Mahas, frequented by great ṛṣis;
for by their mere glance, impelled by their focused vision, the Daityas are consumed as soon as they are looked upon.
Beyond that, at a distance of ten million yojanas, there is indeed a world where the people known as Jana dwell;
O Great Lord of Asuras, even the dust of those Gomātṛs, who cause our destruction, reaches here.
Beyond that, at a distance of sixty million yojanas, is the region named Tapas, frequented by ascetics;
there dwell the foremost of the Sādhyas, for whom the wind of their mere breath is unbearable.

Then, thirty million yojanas further away, there was the abode of the Blessed One named Satyābhidhāna, who possesses the radiance of a thousand suns and bestows boons; he is indeed that one who belongs to you.
Upon hearing the sound of the Vedas, the gods and others rejoice,
while the asuras and those who share their nature undergo contraction.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, do not entertain this thought;
for Dhundhu’s realm, the world of the Vairāja, is always difficult for men to ascend.
Having heard their words, Dhundhu spoke to the Dānavas,
desiring to go to the abode of Brahmā to conquer the lords.
O bulls among the Dānavas, by what action is one led there?
And how did the thousand-eyed Indra arrive there along with the gods?
Questioned by Dhundhu, those lords of the Dānavas spoke these words to their leader:
"We do not know that deed; Śukra undoubtedly knows it."
Having heard the words of the Daityas, Dhundhu questioned the priest of the Daityas, Śukra: "By performing what deed does one attain access to the assembly of Brahmā?"
Then the illustrious preceptor of the Daityas, Kalipriya, related to him the deeds of Śakra, the enemy of Vṛtra, as they had occurred in ancient times.
In former times, Śakra conquered a hundred meritorious Daitya kings in horse-sacrifices; by that merit, he went to the abode of Brahmā.
Having heard those words of Śukra, the powerful lord of the Dānavas formed the highest resolve to perform horse sacrifices. Then,
having taken leave of the preceptor of the Asuras and the most excellent Dānavas, he set forth.
He said, "I shall perform sacrifices with horse-sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees;
therefore, come, let us go to the earth to visit the lords of the land."
"Having conquered the horse-sacrifices that fulfill all desires and qualities,
let the treasures be summoned and let the Guhyakas be commanded."
"Let the sages be invited; let us proceed to the Devikā-ṭaṭa.
For that river is holy, the best of streams, auspicious, and the granter of all success.
Having reached the ancient site, we shall perform sacrifices for the attainment of the Vājins."
Having thus heard the words of the enemy of the gods (Śiva), the priest of the asuras joyfully replied, "So be it," and he dispatched the treasures.
Then Dhundhu was consecrated for the horse sacrifice by Śukra, the lord of the Bhṛgus, at Pāpanāśana, to the east of Devikā.
The members of the assembly and the officiating priests there were also Brahmins of the Bhṛgu lineage;
O Brahmin, with the permission of Śukra, they were the disciples of Śukra who were skilled in trade.
O Sage, there the Asuras, headed by Svarbhānu, were made partakers of the sacrificial offerings by the lord of the Asuras with the consent of Śukra.
Then the sacrifice was commenced and the horse was released;
the illustrious great Asura Asiloma followed after the horse.
Then, O great seer, the earth with its mountains, the quarters, the sky, and the intermediate directions were pervaded by the smoke of the fire;
and because of that fierce odor which reached the heavens, the wind blew even in the world of Brahmā.
Having smelled that fragrance and knowing that Dhundhu was consecrated for the horse sacrifice, the gods, along with Śakra, became despondent;
they then went for refuge to Janārdana, the protector of the world and the supreme resort of the universe.
Having prostrated before the boon-granting god Padmanābha Janārdana, all the hosts of gods spoke with voices faltering from fear: VamP_52.44.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, ultimate refuge of all that moves and is stationary;
O Viṣṇu, destroyer of the distress of the gods, please hear our petition.
The powerful lord of the asuras named Dhundhu, strengthened by boons,
having utterly defeated all the gods, became the great oppressor of the three worlds.
"O Hari, since no one except the god who wields the Pināka bow can protect us from him,
he has grown in power like a neglected disease."
Now, having adopted the counsel of Śukra, he has prepared himself to conquer even those dwelling in the world of Brahmā and has been initiated for the horse sacrifice.
Having performed a hundred sacrifices, that great asura, having gained self-mastery, desires to ascend to the world of Brahmā and even to conquer the gods.
Therefore, O Teacher of the World, consider without delay a means for the destruction of this sacrifice,
by which we may attain perfect peace.
Having heard the words of the gods, the Blessed One Madhusūdana,
the mighty-armed one, granted them fearlessness and immediately dispatched them;
for he had released all the deities after knowing that the great asura was invincible.
He indeed set his mind upon the binding of Dhundhu, whose banner was righteousness;
then the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, assumed the form of a dwarf.
Having cast off his body like a piece of wood into the waters of the Devikā, he remained without support;
with disheveled hair, he sank and rose again for a moment by chance.
Then he was seen by the lord of the Daityas, by other Daityas, and likewise by the sages;
thereupon, O best of Brahmins, they abandoned the sacrificial rites.
Then the members of the assembly, the sacrificer, and the highly powerful officiating priests, being greatly agitated, rushed forward to rescue the Brahmin.
As the dwarf Brahmin was sinking, they all rescued him;
having drawn him out, they all, being well-pleased, asked:
"For what reason have you fallen here? By whom were you cast down? Tell us! (VamP 52.56)
Having heard their words, trembling again and again, he spoke to those led by Dhundhu: "Listen now to the reason for this."
There was a virtuous Brāhmaṇa renowned as Prabhāsa;
he was wise, learned in the meaning of all the Śāstras, and by lineage he belonged to the Vāruṇa clan.
To him two sons were born, dull-witted and deeply distressed;
there, the elder was my brother, and the younger was I.
O Asura, my eldest brother was known as Netrabhāsa;
out of affection, my father gave me the name Gatibhāsa.
O great asura, my father’s dwelling was beautiful, auspicious, endowed with the qualities of heaven, and lovely in form.
Then, after a long time, our father died; having performed his funeral rites, we both returned home.
Then I said to that brother, "Let us divide the house. He replied to me, "There is no share for you at all."
For those who are hunchbacked, dwarfed, or lame; for the impotent, as well as those afflicted with leprosy, the insane, and the blind, no share of the wealth exists.
Only a place for lying down, sitting, and standing, and the act of eating food at their own will—
this much is given to them, for they do not partake in the division of wealth.
When I had spoken thus, he was told by me: "For what reason do I not deserve a share of the wealth from my father's house? By what logic indeed am I not entitled to it? (VamP 52.66)
When these words had been spoken, my brother, filled with rage,
lifted me up and threw me into this river for that reason.
"While I was floating through the middle of this river, the period known as a year passed; yet you have been rescued here by me."
"Who are you gentlemen who have arrived here like affectionate kinsmen?
And who is this long-armed man, resembling Śakra, who has been initiated?"
O you whose wealth is asceticism, endowed with great supernatural powers and exceedingly compassionate toward me, explain all of that to me exactly as it is.
Having heard those words of Vāmana, O Brahmin, the Bhārgavas, the best of the twice-born, spoke thus:
"O Brahmin, we are twice-born and our lineage is indeed Bhārgava."
That great Asura named Dhundhu, possessed of great splendor, was a giver, an enjoyer, and a distributor; he was initiated for the performance of a sacrifice.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, Vāmana, all the Bhārgavas then spoke these words for the sake of Vāmana to the lord of the Daityas.
"O Lord of Daityas, let a magnificent residence be given to him, complete with all furnishings, as well as female servants and various kinds of jewels."
Having heard these words of the twice-born, the lord of the Daityas spoke:
"O best of the twice-born, I shall give you as much wealth as you desire."
"I possess houses, gold, horses, chariots, and elephants; I bestow them upon you today. O Lord, let that which is desired be chosen."
Having heard those words of the lord of the Dānavas, the god Vāmana then spoke these words, which would accomplish his own purpose, to Dhundhu, the lord of the Asuras.
For if even a brother takes away the wealth of one who is incapable [of protecting it],
what other person will not take what has been given to him?
O mighty-armed one, bestow your female and male slaves, servants, house, jewels, and personal belongings upon the capable lords of the twice-born.
"O Lord of Daityas, having observed my own measure and these three steps of mine, grant them; you are not capable of protecting more."

When these words had been spoken by the Great-souled One, the lord of the Daityas laughed and then gave three paces of land to that best of the twice-born, along with his officiating priests, at which time he said, "Do not accept anything else."
Having first observed the three strides given by the illustrious and powerful Lord of the Great Asuras,
the All-pervading One, possessed of infinite power, then assumed the form of Trivikrama in order to leap across them.
Having assumed his form and slain the sons of Diti, he first bowed to the sages and then seized the earth,
together with its mountains, its oceans, and its cities and jewel-mines.

Desiring to reach the beloved of the gods, the Lord, by means of his second stride, swiftly seized the earth with its ancient mountains and the sky adorned with the moon, the sun, and the stars— the dwelling place of the thirty [gods].
When his third stride was not filled, then, out of extreme anger,
the Blessed One Trivikrama, with a body as large as Mount Meru, fell upon the back of that preeminent Danava.
O Nārada, as Vāsudeva descended upon the Dānava,
he solidified a pit in the earth thirty thousand yojanas deep.
Then, having uprooted the Daitya and hurled him with force into that pit,
he filled that chasm by raining down a shower of sand.
Then, by the grace of Vāsudeva, the thousand-eyed Indra attained heaven,
and all the gods obtained the three worlds free from affliction.
The Blessed One, having cast the lord of the Daityas into the sea of sand,
assumed the form of the Yamunā and vanished right there.
Thus, O great sage, in former times Viṣṇu became Vāmana, and he became Trivikrama in order to conquer Dhundhu;
it was there, in that great hermitage endowed with merit, that the son of the lord of the Daityas went.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having bathed in the waters of the Kālindī and having worshipped Trivikrama, [one attains the fruit].
Having observed a fast for one night, he went to the mountain Liṅgabhedaka.
Having bathed there in the pure water and having beheld Bhava with devotion,
he fasted for one night and proceeded to the sacred ford of Kedāra.
Having bathed there and worshipped Īśāna and Mādhava as non-different from one another,
he stayed for seven days and then proceeded to Kubjāmraka.
Then, having bathed at that excellent sacred ford, fasting and with his senses subdued, he worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa and proceeded to Badarikāśrama.
Having stayed there and worshipped Nārāyaṇa with devotion, that wise man then bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī;
at Varāhatīrtha, he beheld Garuḍāsana and, being full of devotion, worshipped him.
Then, having gone to Bhadrakarṇa and beheld Jayeśa, the moon-crested Śiva, he worshipped him and proceeded toward the Vipāśā river.
Having bathed in that [river] and worshipped the God of gods, who is beloved by the twice-born,
he remained fasting on the banks of the Irāvatī and beheld the Supreme Lord.
O best of the twice-born, by propitiating him in Śākala, Purūravas indeed attained supreme beauty and sovereignty that is very difficult to obtain.
And it was by propitiating him that Bhṛgu, though overcome by the disease of leprosy,
attained incomparable health as well as imperishable progeny.
Nārada said:
O best of the twice-born, how did Purūravas, having propitiated Viṣṇu,
cast off his deformity and regain his form along with Śrī?
Pulastya said: Listen, O ascetic, as I shall relate this sin-destroying story, exactly as it occurred in the past, at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga.
O son of Brahmā, there is a land renowned as the Madra country;
it possesses a famous and excellent capital city named Śākala.
In that place, there was a merchant named Sudharma who was established in the business of trade;
he was wealthy, virtuous, an enjoyer of pleasures, and proficient in various sciences.
Once, however, he set out from his own kingdom to go to Surāṣṭra,
accompanied by a great caravan and carrying various wares for sale in the marketplaces.
Then, O lover of strife, as he was traveling on the road through the desert at night, there occurred an unbearable attack by bandits.
Then that merchant, his entire wealth having been stolen and filled with grief,
wandered alone in that desert like a madman, though he was self-controlled.
O Nārada, as he wandered through that forest overcome by suffering,
he beheld the auspicious Śamī tree like his own self, found in a desert.
Seeing that śamī tree devoid of deer, peacocks, and parrots,
he— exhausted and his soul overcome by hunger and thirst— sat down beneath it.
Having slept and rested well, he rose again at midday and then beheld a hungry ghost approaching, surrounded by hundreds of other hungry ghosts.
Then he saw the leader of the departed being carried away by another departed one,
while those who consume the funeral cakes, with coarse bodies, ran ahead.
Then that ghost, having wandered through the forests,
arrived and saw the merchant’s son at the foot of a śamī tree.
Having greeted him with a welcome and addressed one another, they sat comfortably in the shade; the guest, having been asked about his welfare, replied that he was well.
Then he was questioned by the Lord of the Pretas:
"Tell me, O virtuous one, from where have you come, or where will you go? (VamP 53.23)
"And how have you entered this great forest, devoid of beasts and birds? May it be well with you; you ought to tell me everything."
Thus questioned briefly by the lord of the pretas, O Brahmin, the merchant related everything concerning his loss of wealth and departure from his own country.

Having heard that account, the warden of the hungry ghosts, distressed by his suffering, then spoke to the son of Vamī as if to his own kinsman: VamP_53.26: "Having heard that account, the warden of the hungry ghosts, distressed by his suffering, then spoke to the son of Vamī as if to his own kinsman."
Even though things have come to this, O observer of noble vows, you should not grieve;
wealth shall be yours once more, provided that fortune is on your side.
Wealth perishes when fortune is exhausted, yet it arises again during prosperity;
for this body that has been diminished, no further growth can come through mere anxiety.
Having spoken thus and summoned his own servants, he addressed them with these words:
"Today this guest must be honored; he is always my own kinsman. (VamP 53.29)
Now that he has arrived, O pretas, incomparable joy has arisen within me.
While he was speaking thus, a very sturdy new clay vessel,
filled with curd-rice, arrived exactly as desired.
Likewise, a new, very firm,
and full water-jar filled with excellent water appeared and stood before the pretas.
Seeing that he had arrived with food and water, the high-minded one said:
"Rise, O son of a merchant, and perform your daily rites."
Then, having performed their daily rites according to the prescribed rules with water from the water-vessel,
both the merchant and the Lord of the Dead became purified.
Then, having first given curd-rice according to their desire to the merchant’s daughter,
he subsequently offered it to all those *preta*s.
And when everyone had finished eating and had partaken of water as they desired,
the guardian of the pretas immediately thereafter ate excellent food.
O Brahmin, as the hungry ghost was completely satisfied with water, grain, and boiled rice, it vanished from sight while the merchant’s son was looking on.
Then, having seen that most wonderful sight, that wise merchant,
self-controlled and filled with curiosity, questioned the guardian of the hungry ghosts.
O virtuous one, in this desolate forest, from where does the food originate,
and from where comes this water-pot filled with excellent water?
Likewise, these servants of yours have become emaciated due to the armor [you provide],
while you yourself remain radiant, with a somewhat nourished and auspicious body.
Clad in white garments and the protector of many, tell me all this: who are you, and who indeed is this Śamī?
Having heard these words of the merchant’s son, the leader of the pretas related to him his entire ancient history exactly as it had occurred in the past.
"In former times, O Brahmin, I was a learned man in Śākala, the most excellent of cities;
I was renowned as Somaśarman, born from the womb of Bahulā."
I also have a wealthy merchant neighbor who is very prosperous;
he is named Somaśravas, a devotee of Viṣṇu of great renown.
Thus, being miserly, foolish-minded, and evil-willed even though I possessed wealth,
I gave nothing to the twice-born, nor did I eat excellent food myself.
If, through negligence, I eat food mixed with curd, milk, and ghee,
then at night my body is beaten by terrible men.
In the morning, a terrible cholera, like unto death itself, comes upon me;
and no kinsman stays by my side there.
By some means or other, my life has been preserved;
yet, in this way, I remain such a sinner, utterly devoid of compassion.
I shall pass my time by sustaining myself on poor food such as salt from the sea, sesame, oil-cakes, parched grain flour, vegetables, and the like.
In this way, while I remained there, a great length of time passed;
then, in the month of Bhādrapada, there occurred the day known as Śravaṇa-dvādaśī.
Then the world of citizens, preceded by Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, went to the confluence of the Irāvatī and the Naḍvalā to bathe.
On account of my neighbor, I also went there,
having observed a fast on the pure Ekādaśī day and being restrained by my vows.
Then, with water from the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, he filled a new, sturdy water-jar,
wrapped it with cloth, and provided it with an umbrella and sandals.
Even a clay vessel full of sweet curd-rice was given to that eminent Brahmin, who was pure and possessed of the dharma of knowledge.
O son of a merchant, that alone was the gift given by me while living;
for seventy years indeed, nothing else whatsoever was given.
Having died and attained the state of a preta, he indeed gave food to the pretas;
yet these others, who gave no gifts, subsist upon my food.
This is the reason that has been declared: that food which was given by me with water arrives here every single day, even at midday.
"As long as I do not eat, it does not indeed come to exhaustion;
but when I have eaten and drunk, everything becomes invisible."
That parasol which I gave has become this śamī tree;
the two sandals that I gave have become my vehicle as a preta.
O knower of dharma, this speech of mine has been addressed to you, who are of a miserly nature; it concerns the merit of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī, which increases one's merit.
When these words had been spoken, the merchant’s son spoke this speech:
"Father, you should grant me permission for that which must be done by me."
O Nārada, having heard those words of the merchant's son,
the guardian of the dead then spoke these words which brought about the accomplishment of his own purpose.
O high-minded one, I shall fully explain that which must be done by you for my benefit—something that brings welfare both to you and to me. (VamP 53.63)
Having bathed at Gayā, which is frequented by sacred fords, and being endowed with purity,
perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) while uttering my name.
In this regard, O friend, by the offering of funeral cakes, I have been released from the state of a preta; I shall go to the same world as all givers.

Just as this meritorious twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, when conjoined with Wednesday and the Śravaṇa asterism, is remembered as being exceedingly auspicious.
Having spoken thus to the merchant, the King of the Pretas, pure and together with his followers, duly and correctly announced his own names.
Having been placed upon the shoulder of a ghost and deprived of his life,
that merchant indeed reached the beautiful region known as Śūrasena.
Having accumulated much wealth, both high and low, through the application of his own karma and dharma,
he departed for the unsurpassed Gayāśīrṣa.
There, he performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased ancestors in due order,
immediately followed by that for his own paternal forefathers and his heirs.
The one of great intelligence performed the offering of funeral cakes for himself— without sesame seeds— for the sake of great awakening, and likewise for his other kinsmen.
When the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) had been offered in this manner,
those pretas were liberated from their state as spirits and, O twice-born one, they then went to the world of Brahmā.
And that merchant’s son, having observed the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī vow, returned to his own home and met his end.
Having enjoyed exceedingly rare pleasures for a very long time in the world of the Gandharvas,
he attained a human birth and shone as a king in Śākala.
Abiding in the practice of his own dharma and deeds, and devoted to the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī vow, he,
upon meeting the law of time (death), took refuge in the abode of the Guhyakas.
Having dwelt there for a very long time and having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire,
he then reached the world of mortals and became the son of a king.
There too, established in the conduct of a Kṣatriya, self-controlled and devoted to giving and enjoyment,
he conquered hosts of enemies during a cattle-raid and passed away according to the law of time;
having reached the world of Śakra, he was highly honored by all the gods.
Fallen from his state due to the exhaustion of his merit, he became a twice-born man in Śākala;
thereafter, he possessed a formidable appearance and had mastered the meaning of all the scriptures.
O twice-born one, he married the daughter of a brahmin, who was peerless in beauty;
yet that passionate woman held in contempt her husband, even though he was virtuous.
Thinking, "He is deformed," he then became deeply distressed; thereafter, filled with despondency, he went to a great hermitage.
On the bank of the Irāvatī, the illustrious one approached Rūpadhārin;
for he had propitiated that Lord of the World by means of the Nakṣatrapuruṣa rite.
Having attained supreme beauty in that very same birth,
he then became dear to his wife, possessed of enjoyments, and self-controlled;
through his former practice, he became a devotee of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī.
Thus, in former times, that bull among the twice-born, who was of ugly form, became like the very embodiment of the god of love through the grace of the Blessed One; and he became King Purūravas.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O best of the twice-born, [listen] how Purūravas [sought] the Lord, the husband of Śrī.
Tell me how one may worship that [deity] known as the Nakṣatrapuruṣa.
Pulastya said: Listen, O Nārada, as I shall describe the Nakṣatra-puruṣa-vrata— the various limbs of the Divine Being that correspond to the lunar mansions in this world.
The root asterism (Mūla) is the two feet of Viṣṇu; Rohiṇī is remembered as his two shanks;
and the two Aśvinīs are declared to be the two knees of the one who assumes form.
The two Āṣāḍhas, the two of the thighs, the two Phālgunis situated in the private parts,
and the Kṛttikās located at the waist are established as the limbs of Vāsudeva.
The two Proṣṭhapadās are situated at the sides;
Revatī is located in the two flanks; Anurādhā is established in the chest; and Śraviṣṭhā is situated on the back.
Viśākhā is said to be the two arms, and Hasta is the two hands;
Punarvasu is the fingers, and Sārpa (Āśleṣā) is likewise said to be the nails.
Likewise, Jyeṣṭhā is situated in the neck-bones, Śravaṇa is located in the ears, Puṣya is established in the mouth, and Svāti is proclaimed to be the teeth.
The two jaws are said to belong to Varuṇa, and the nose is declared to belong to the Pitṛs;
Mṛgaśīrṣa resides in the eyes, O Rūpadhāriṇī.
Citrā is indeed on his forehead, while Bharaṇī is his head;
Ārdrā is situated in his hair—this is the limb of Hari composed of the lunar mansions.
O Nārada, I shall fully explain the ritual procedure according to its application;
when Hari is worshipped, he grants all desires exactly as they are wished for.
When the moon enters the Mūla asterism on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra,
one should then worship the feet of the Blessed One according to the prescribed rite;
and in the presence of that asterism, one should offer food to the best of Brahmins.
Then, during the conjunction with the Aśvinī asterism, one should worship the knees with devotion;
and for the pregnancy longing, one should offer sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) and, as before, feed the twice-born.
Likewise, a wise man should worship the two thighs with the two Āṣāḍhās;
cool water is prescribed there as the longing (dohada).
During the two Phālgunī constellations, the secret [rite] should be worshipped by the wise;
cow's milk should be offered into the fire, and food should be given to the twice-born.
Under the asterism Kṛttikā, one who has fasted and subdued his senses should worship the hips;
and as a longing offering for Viṣṇu, fragrant flowers and water should be given.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite during the two Bhādrapadās on the sides,
one should give jaggery with a linctus as the pregnancy-longing (dohada) declared by Devakī.
If the *revatī* yoga occurs, there will be two swellings in the womb; the pregnancy longing (*dohada*) consists of mung-bean cakes.
Under *anurādhā*, the abdomen is large, and the longing consists of *ṣaṣṭika* rice.
Likewise, during the *dohada* (craving) for the back under the asterism Śraviṣṭhā, one should give cooked rice with *śāli*;
and during the *dohada* for the two arms under Viśākhā, one should give excellent boiled rice.
Likewise, the two hands are to be worshipped when Hasta is the asterism; barley gruel is prescribed as the longing (dohada).
When Punarvasu occurs, the fingers are to be worshipped, and the patola gourd is the longing for that time.
During the Āśleṣā asterism, having worshipped the nails, one should offer the flesh of a partridge as a dohada;
during Jyeṣṭhā, one should worship the neck and offer sesame-sweets as a dohada.
In the month of Śravaṇa, the two ears are to be worshipped, and curd-rice is the desired offering;
in the month of Puṣya, the face is to be worshipped, and ghee-porridge is the desired offering.
During the conjunction with Svāti, if there is a pregnancy craving for sesame cakes,
they should be given for the pleasure of Keśava, and a meal should be provided for a Brāhmaṇa.
During the conjunction with Śatabhiṣā, one should worship Hanū with great effort;
her longing consists of priyaṅgu, red śāli rice, and honey.
Under the Maghā asterism, the nose is to be worshipped, and honey should be given as a pregnancy longing;
under Mṛgaśiras, the eyes, and deer meat should be given as a pregnancy longing.
During the Citrā yoga, the forehead is to be worshipped and delicious food is desired as a pregnancy-longing;
during the Bharaṇī asterisms, the head is to be worshipped and delicious rice-meat is desired as a pregnancy-longing.
During the conjunction of Ārdrā, the hair should be honored by the learned;
one should devoutly feed Brahmins and satisfy the pregnancy-longing with jaggery and fresh ginger.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World during these conjunctions of lunar mansions, one should,
upon completion, give sacrificial fees and beautiful garments to both a woman and a man.
O wise one, one should present to a Brahmin an umbrella, sandals, a pair of white garments, the seven kinds of grain, gold, and a vessel of ghee.
The twice-born should be honored according to the conjunction with each respective lunar mansion;
for this eternal Puruṣa is considered to be composed of the lunar mansions.
Indeed, the vow known as Nakṣatrapuruṣa is the most excellent of all vows;
it was formerly performed by Bhṛgu and is the destroyer of all sins.
O celestial sage, by worshipping the limbs and minor members of the Teacher of the World,
one is born with beautiful primary and secondary limbs.
Keśava destroys all that sin committed over seven lifetimes, as well as that inherited from one's lineage, and that arising from one's father and mother.
One obtains all auspicious things: supreme physical health, infinite joy of mind, and an exceedingly beautiful form.
O Janārdana, when worshipped, the Nakṣatra-puruṣa bestows sweetness of speech, as well as beauty and whatever else is desired.
O Nārada, having observed the fasts correctly during these lunar mansions in due order,
the highly fortunate Arundhatī attained preeminent renown.
Having fully worshipped Govinda Janārdana, whose body consists of the stars, Āditya obtained a son, Revanta, for the sake of his offspring.
Rambhā attained preeminent beauty, Menakā the sweetness of speech,
the Moon supreme splendor, and King Purūravas sovereignty.

O Brahmin, those by whom Janārdana, who possesses the form of the constellations, was thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite while assuming a physical form, have attained their heart's desire.
This which has been told to you is supremely purifying, auspicious, glorious, and bestowing of beautiful form;
listen now to the supreme ordinance for the man of the lunar mansions, and here to the meritorious pilgrimage.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having reached the holy Irāvatī, that daughter of the sages, [he beheld her].
Having bathed on the eighth day of the month of Caitra, he worshipped Janārdana.
Having performed the merit-bestowing vow of the *nakṣatra-puruṣa*, the pure Prahlāda,
lord of the Dānavas, went to Kurukṣetra.
O Sage, having addressed the Sudarśana Cakratīrtha with the Airāvata mantra, he then bathed there according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Having observed the fast with devotion and having worshipped the one whose banner is the elephant (Garuḍa),
and having performed their purificatory rites, they then went to behold the Man-lion (Viṣṇu).
Having bathed in the Devikā and worshipped Nṛsiṃha,
the Dānava stayed there for one night and then went to Gokarṇa.
Having bathed there and likewise worshipped the Lord Viśvakarman in the east,
the Daitya went to see Kāmeśvara in the eastern part of the western region.
Having bathed there, and having seen and worshipped Śaṅkara,
Prahlāda went to see Puṇḍarīka in the great waters.
Having bathed there, having seen [the deity], and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
and having fully worshipped Puṇḍarīka, he stayed for three days.
Thereafter, having beheld the god Ajita at Viśākhayūpa,
he bathed in the Kṛṣṇatīrtha and dwelt there for three nights, purified.
Then, having seen the Swan at Haṃsapada and having worshipped the Lord,
he went to the Payoṣṇī river to behold the Lord Akhaṇḍa.
Having bathed in the waters of the Payoṣṇī and worshipped the Lord of the Universe in his unbroken form,
the wise man went to the Vitastā to behold Kumārila.
Having bathed there and worshipped the Lord of Gods, who was being propitiated by the Bālakhilyas and Marīcis,
that which was performed there became a destroyer of sins.
There the goddess Surabhi created her auspicious daughter Kapilā for the sake of pleasing the gods and likewise for the welfare of the world.
Having bathed there in the Devahrada and worshipped Śambhu with devotion,
and having consumed curd according to the prescribed rite, he then went to Maṇimanta.
Having bathed there at that excellent sacred ford, the high-minded one beheld Śambhu, Brahmā, and Prajāpati, the lord of the gods.
Having worshipped those gods according to the prescribed rites, O ascetic,
he stayed there for six nights and then went to the Madhunandinī river.
Having bathed in the honey-sweet waters, the preeminent among the Danavas beheld the god Hara bearing the discus,
as well as Govinda with the trident in his arm.
Nārada said:
For what purpose did the Lord Śambhu take up the Sudarśana discus, and likewise Vāsudeva take up the trident? Tell this to me as I ask you.
Pulastya said:
Listen, for I shall relate this ancient tale,
which Viṣṇu formerly narrated to the future Manu.
The great lord of the Asuras named Jalodbhava, of fierce valor, having performed terrible austerities, propitiated Viriñca;
he, being pleased with him, became a granter of boons.
Invincible in the great battle against the gods and asuras, he was incapable of being slain by the immortals even with their own weapons;
yet, by the curses of the Brahman-sages, his desired purpose was frustrated, and his own virtues were stripped away by water and fire.
Such was the power of that preeminent son of Danu; with his fierce form, he wandered the earth afflicting all the gods, great seers, and kings, and brought all their activities to ruin.
Then the immortals dwelling on earth, together with the kings, went to Hari, the Lord and refuge;
and the Blessed One went along with them to the Himalayas, where the three-eyed Hara resides.
Having consulted together regarding the task beneficial to the celestial sages and having resolved upon the destruction of the enemy,
those two lords of the gods, performers of fierce deeds, brought about the reversal of their own weapons.
Then that Dānava, perceiving that the two lords of the gods, Viṣṇu and Śarva— who had arrived desiring to slay him—
were of terrible form and invincible by enemies, entered the waters of the river out of fear.

Knowing that the enemy of the lord of the three heavens had perished, the two lords of the monkeys, their forms concealed, suddenly took up arms and stationed themselves on both banks of the broad river Madhumat, which was exceedingly auspicious.
And the water-born one, having seen that Śaṅkara and Vāsudeva had departed after leaving the water,
looked toward the quarters with eyes distressed by fear and then ascended the Himālaya mountain as his refuge.
Seeing their own enemy roaming upon the peak of the mountain while Viṣṇu and Śambhu looked on,
both Giriśa, bearing the trident and discus, and Viṣṇu rushed forward with speed, armed with their weapons.
Seen by those two supreme among the thirty gods, his body pierced by the discus and the trident,
he fell from the mountain like a stainless star of golden hue falling from the sky.
Thus Viṣṇu held his trident and the three-eyed one [Śiva] his discus for the sake of slaying the enemy;
for it was there that the Vitastā, the destroyer of evil, became cool after falling from the foot of Hara onto the Śiśira mountain.
Having reached that sacred ford and performed worship to Hari and Śaṅkara, the lords of the thirty gods,
he fasted with devotion and went to the Himavat mountain to behold the Lord of the Mountain, who is protected by Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites and having bestowed gifts upon the twice-born,
he went to Bhṛgutuṅga on the celebrated slopes of the Himalayas.

There, the high-souled Lord Śaṅkara, desiring to test the power of his weapon, received from Viṣṇu, the best of gods, the preeminent weapon of the discus, with which he indeed split [the mountain] into three parts.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, [tell me] concerning Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, regarding the three-eyed one."
For what purpose did he give the weapon, the discus, which is honored by the worlds?
Pulastya said:
Listen with an attentive mind to this ancient narrative concerning the granting of the discus, which increases the majesty of Śiva.
There was a preeminent among the twice-born, who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
he was a highly fortunate householder known as Vītamanyu.

He had a highly distinguished wife named Ātreyī, who was esteemed for her virtuous character; she was devoted to her husband, regarded her husband as her very life, and was renowned for her righteous conduct.
To that [wife] of this great seer, who approached her during the proper season,
there was born a glorious son known as Upamanyu.
O tiger among sages, his mother, being in great distress, spoke these words as she nourished him with the liquid made from rice flour, saying, "This is milk."
Not knowing the sweetness of milk, he nevertheless formed the expectation that even the liquid made from rice flour was "milk."
Once, together with his father, he ate very delicious milk-rice at the house of a certain brahmin— a meal that nourished and invigorated his life-force.
Having obtained that incomparable taste of milk,
the young seer did not consume the flour-water given by his mother on the second day.
Then, out of childishness, he wept like a *cātaka* bird seeking water;
his mother, weeping herself, spoke to him with a voice faltering with tears.
While Umāpati, Paśupati, the wielder of the trident, Saṃkara,
and Virūpākṣa remain displeased, how can there be a meal with milk?
If you wish, my son, to enjoy milk that provides immediate nourishment,
then propitiate the Lord of Gods, the three-eyed wielder of the trident.
When that abode of the universe, the bestower of all auspiciousness, is pleased, one attains the state of being made to drink the nectar of immortality; how much more so, then, the enjoyment of milk?
Having heard those words of his mother, the son, free from anger, said:
"Who is this Virūpākṣa who has been mentioned by you as one to be propitiated?"
Then the virtuous Dharma spoke these words to her son, who was rich in righteousness:
"Listen to this one known as Virūpākṣa; I shall tell it to you."
In former times, there was a lord of the great asuras renowned as Śrīdāman; having assailed the entire world, he brought Śrī under his own control.
By that evil-minded one, the three worlds were rendered devoid of splendor;
possessing great strength, he desired to seize the Śrīvatsa mark of Vāsudeva.
Having perceived his wicked intention, Janārdana,
desiring his destruction, approached Maheśvara.
In the meantime, Śambhu, assuming a form of yoga and being the imperishable one,
stood taking recourse to a level ground on a ridge of the Himālaya mountain.
Then, having approached the omnipresent Lord of the World who possesses a thousand heads,
Hari himself worshipped his own self by means of his own self.
For more than a thousand years, he stood on his big toe,
reciting the supreme Brahman, which is to be known by yogins and is devoid of defining characteristics.
Then the gracious Lord, being pleased, granted to Viṣṇu a supreme boon:
the glorious, divine Sudarśana, the discus of radiant energy, which was visible to the eye.
Having given that discus, which resembles the wheel of time and strikes fear into all beings, to the God of gods, Śaṅkara spoke to Viṣṇu.
O Lord of Gods, this Sudarśana, possessing excellent weapons, is the destroyer of all other weapons; it has twelve spokes, six naves, two yokes, and is swift.
These gods of his, the months, and the zodiac signs—six in number—are established as Ṛtus for the sake of protecting the remaining [beings]. They are shaped like spokes.
Agni, Soma, as well as Mitra, Varuṇa, and the Lord of Śacī (Indra),
Indra and Agni, the Viśvedevas, and the Prajāpatis as well.
Then the mighty Hanumān, the god Dhanvantari,
Tapa, and Tapasya— these twelve are established there;
the months beginning with Caitra and ending with Phālguna are established therein.
"O Lord, having thus taken up this excellent weapon, slay the enemy of the gods; do not hesitate.
This [weapon], worshipped by the King of the Immortals, is unfailing; it was held by me and brought into my eyes through the power of asceticism."
Thus addressed by Śambhu, Viṣṇu spoke these words to Bhava:
"O Śambhu, how may I know whether [this] is infallible or indeed futile?"
O Lord, if your wheel is unfailing and unimpeded everywhere, I shall cast it here for the sake of testing you alone; accept it, O Master!
Having heard those words of Vāsudeva, the upholder of the world said:
"If it be so, cast [it] forth with a mind free from hesitation."
Having heard those words of Maheśāna, Viṣṇu,
desiring to test his splendor, swiftly discharged the Sudarśana [discus] toward Śaṅkara.
Having approached the wielder of the trident— the Lord of the Universe, the Lord of Sacrifice, and the officiant of sacrifice— the discus, fallen from the hand of Murāri, split him into three pieces.
Seeing Hara divided into three forms and cut down, the mighty-armed Hari,
his body overwhelmed with shame, became intent on prostration.
Seeing Dāmodara prostrate at his feet,
the glorious Bhava, filled with affection, said again and again:
"O mighty-armed one, this transformation brought about by the rim of the discus is merely natural."
My own nature has not been cut away; it is indeed uncuttable and likewise unburnable.
O Keśava, whatever three portions have been made by this discus,
they will undoubtedly become meritorious.
Hiraṇyākṣa is remembered as the first, Suvarṇākṣa as the second, and Virūpākṣa as the third; these three bestow merit upon men.
Arise and go, O Lord, to slay the oppressor of the immortals;
when Śrīdāman has been killed, O Viṣṇu, the deities will rejoice.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, whose banner bears Garuḍa,
went to the plateau of the celestial mountain and beheld Śrīdāmā.
Seeing that Daitya who destroys the pride of the gods, Hari, the best of deities,
released his discus with great force, saying repeatedly, "You are slain!"
Then, by that discus of unsurpassed prowess, the head of the Daitya was severed;
with his head cut off, he fell from the mountain just like a mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt.
When that enemy of the gods had been slain, Murāri, having propitiated the Lord Virūpanetra and obtained the preeminent discus—
a supreme great weapon— returned, O God, to his abode, the ocean.
Therefore, my son, this Maheśvara, the God of gods, is without form;
if you would worship him, O virtuous one, you shall obtain food consisting of milk.
Having heard those words of his mother, the powerful son, free from resentment,
propitiated Virūpākṣa and obtained food consisting of milk.
Thus was that supreme, most purifying [mantra], which indeed cuts asunder the body of Śarva, spoken by you in the past;
then that great asura approached that best of holy fords for the sake of great merit.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having bathed in that best of holy fords and having beheld the three-eyed Lord, [one attains the fruit].
Having worshipped Suvarṇākṣa, he then proceeded to Naimiṣa.
There, in their midst, are thirty thousand sacred fords that remove all sins:
the Tomtis, the Kāñcanākṣīs, and the Gurudās.
Having bathed in them and worshipped the Lord of Gods, Acyuta, who is clad in yellow garments,
and having also honored the sages dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, [one attains merit].
Then, having worshipped the God of gods, the Lord Īśāna, according to the prescribed rite,
that great asura went to Gayā to behold Gopati.
Having bathed there at Brahmadhvaja and performed a circumambulation of it,
he indeed offered the meritorious funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for his ancestors.
Having bathed there at the well, the self-controlled man, having worshipped the ancestors there,
should also worship Śaṅkara, the Lord of Cows (Śiva), who holds a mace in his hand.
Having likewise bathed at Indratīrtha and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
and having bathed in the waters of the Mahānadī, he arrived at the Sarayū.
Having bathed there at Gopratāra and worshipped the lotus,
and having fasted for one night, he went to the city of Virajā.
Having bathed in the stainless sacred ford and likewise offered rice-balls to his ancestors,
the illustrious one went to behold the unconquered Puruṣottama.
Having beheld that lotus-eyed one, the imperishable and supreme,
the pure one stayed right there for six nights and then proceeded to the southern Mahendra mountain.
There, having seen, saluted, and fully worshipped Śambhu, the best of gods, Hara, who is the Lord of Half-Woman (Ardhanārīśvara), he went to the north to Mahendra after having honored the ancestors.
There, having seen Śambhu, the best of gods, the protector of cows and drinker of Soma, and having bathed at Somatīrtha, he arrived at the Sahya mountain.
Having bathed there in the Mahodakī and having worshipped Vaikuṇṭha with devotion,
and having honored the gods and ancestors, he went to the Pāriyātra mountain.
Having bathed there in the Lāṅgalinī river and worshipped Aparājita,
he went to the region of Kaśeru and beheld Viśvarūpa.
There, Śambhu, the best of gods and knower of yoga, who is highly honored by his hosts,
revealed himself in his universal form (viśvarūpa).
Having bathed there in the waters of Maṅkuṇikā and having worshipped Maheśvara,
Prahlāda went to the fragrant mountain, the Malaya range.
Then, having bathed in the great lake and having worshipped Śaṅkara, he,
whose soul was absorbed in yoga, went to the Vindhya mountains to behold Sadāśiva.
Then, having bathed in the waters of the Vipāśā and worshipped Sadāśiva,
he fasted for three nights and subsequently went to the city of Avantī.
Having bathed there in the waters of the Śiprā and worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion,
he then beheld [the Lord] dwelling in the cremation ground, bearing the form of Mahākāla.
For in that form, Śaṅkara,
having assumed a tamasic form, performs the withdrawal of all beings while remaining self-controlled.
Remaining there, the Lord of the Gods protected the king named Śvetaki by burning Antaka, the one who seizes away all living beings.
There Śarva dwells eternally, exceedingly delighted, together with Umā,
surrounded by many millions of Pramathas and honored by the gods.
Then, having seen that Mahākāla— the ender of the ender of Time, the restrainer of Yama, the death of Death, and one who is wonderfully diverse— VamP_57.23.
Having worshipped Śambhu, the lord of beings and master of the world, who dwells in the cremation ground and bears the trident, he departed toward the Niṣadha country.
Having seen the god Amareśvara there and worshipped him with devotion,
he approached Mahodaya and beheld Hayagrīva.
Then, having bathed at the Aśvatīrtha and beheld the horse-faced one (Hayagrīva),
and having fully worshipped Śrīdhara, he proceeded to the region of Pañcāla.
Then, having seen the son of the Lord of Wealth, Pāñcālika, who was endowed with the qualities of a master, the self-controlled one departed from Prayāga.
Having bathed at the nearby and world-renowned tirtha on the Yamunā,
one should behold Rudra as Vaṭeśvara and Mādhava reclining in yoga.
Having worshipped those two alone with devotion, the great asura then fasted during the month of Māgha and went to Vārāṇasī.
Having circumambulated the city and worshipped Viṣṇu and Śiva at Avimuktaka,
and having observed the swift-moving sun, he then proceeded to Madhuvana.
There, that best of asuras beheld the self-existent god;
having worshipped him, the one of great splendor proceeded to the Puṣkara forest.
Having bathed in all three of those sacred fords and having worshipped the ancestors and the gods,
he also honored Brahmā, who was lotus-eyed and possessed of a fragrant scent.
Then, furthermore, at the world-renowned sacred ford of the Sarasvatī known as Koṭitīrtha, he beheld Rudra, whose banner is the bull, together with ten million Rudras.
The best of the twice-born from Naimiṣa, those from Magadha along with the Saindhavas, those from Dharmāraṇya, those from Pauṣkara, and likewise those from Daṇḍakāraṇya; VamP_57.35 //
The twice-born from Cāmpeya, from Bhārukaccha, and those who dwell on the banks of the Devikā, all arrived there to behold Śaṅkara.
O Sage, ten million ascetics who had attained perfection through austerity and were eager for a vision of Hara spoke thus: "I first! I first! VamP_57.37.
Seeing those great seers agitated yet with their sins burnt away,
Bhava, out of compassion for them alone, assumed ten million forms.
Then all those sages, being delighted, remained there worshipping Maheśvara after each had established his own sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
In this manner, Śambhu became known by the name Rudrakoṭi.
The highly effulgent Prahlāda, devoted and self-controlled, beheld him;
then, having bathed at Koṭitīrtha and offered libations to the Vasus and the ancestors,
and having worshipped Rudrakoṭi, he went to Kurujāṅgala.
He beheld that best of gods, Sthāṇu, Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī,
who was immersed in the waters of the Sarasvatī and honored by the deities.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī and worshipped Sthāṇu with devotion,
and having bathed at the Daśāśvamedha and worshipped the gods and the ancestors;
Having bathed in the Kanyāhrada and purified himself by worshipping the Sahasraliṅga,
he paid homage to his preceptor Śukra and proceeded to Somatīrtha.
Having bathed there and honored the ancestors, and having worshipped Soma with devotion,
the highly illustrious one then went to the abode of Kṣīrikā and performed his ablutions.
Having circumambulated the tree and worshipped Varuṇa, the wise one,
seeing once more the banner of the Kurus, went to the city named Padmā.
There, having honored Mitra and Varuṇa, the two suns worshipped by the world,
the self-controlled one approached Kumāradhārā and beheld his master.
Having bathed at Kapiladhārā, offered libations to and worshipped the ancestors and the gods,
and having beheld and duly honored Skanda, he proceeded to the Narmadā.
Having bathed in that [tirtha] and having worshipped Vāsudeva, the Lord of Śrī,
he went to see the Boar-bearing Mountain, the wielder of the discus.
Having bathed at the holy site of Kokāmukha and worshipped the Upholder of the Earth (Viṣṇu),
he went to Arbuda, the abode of Mahādeva, where there is a golden image three times his size.
Having bathed there in the Nārīhrada and having worshipped Śaṅkara,
he approached Kāliñjara and beheld Nīlakaṇṭha.
Having bathed in the waters of Nīlatīrtha and then worshipped Śiva,
he went to Prabhāsa on the seashore to behold the Lord.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean,
he beheld Someśvara, the Lord of the World, who wears his hair in matted locks.
The moon, the lord of the stars, who was consumed by the curse of Dakṣa and was wasting away,
was nourished by Śaṅkara and by Viṣṇu, who wears matted hair.
Having worshipped those two foremost of gods, he went to Mahālaya;
having worshipped Rudra there, he departed for the Northern Kurus.
Having worshipped Padmanābha there, he went to Saptagodāvara;
having bathed there and worshipped Viśveśa, who is formidable and adored by the three worlds.
Having gone to the Dāruvana forest, the illustrious one beheld a *liṅga*;
having worshipped it and approached the Brāhmaṇī, he bathed and worshipped the Lord of the Thirty Gods.
Having gone to Plakṣāvataraṇa, he worshipped Śrīnivāsa;
and then, having gone to Kuṇḍina, he worshipped [the deity] who bestows complete satisfaction.
Having worshipped Caturbāhu at Śūrpāraka according to the prescribed rites,
he reached the Māgadha forest and beheld the lord of the earth.
Having worshipped that Lord of the Universe, he went to Prajāmukha;
then, having bathed in the great tīrtha and bowed to Vāsudeva, he departed.
Then, having reached the Śoṇa river and worshipped the Lord Skandavarman,
the devoted one next worshipped Mahādeva, known as Haṃsa, at Mahākośī.
Having performed worship, he then went to the excellent Saindhava forest;
there, having worshipped the Lord named Sunetra, the preceptor who bears the conch and the trident,
the mighty-armed one proceeded to Triviṣṭapa.
There he beheld the god Maheśāna, known as Jaṭādhara;
having seen and worshipped him, as well as Hari, he went to the Kanakhala tīrtha.
There, having worshipped Bhadrakālīśa, Vīrabhadra,
and Meghaṅka the lord of wealth, the Dānava then proceeded to Girivraja.
Having worshipped there the god Paśupati, the lord of the world, Maheśvara, he went to Kāmarūpa according to the prescribed rites.
Having worshipped the three-eyed, best of gods, Śaśiprabha, together with Mṛḍānī,
he went to the preeminent sacred ford known as Mahākhya, and there he worshipped Mahādeva.
Then he went to Mount Trikūṭa to see the son of Atri, for that mountain was indeed the refuge of the Wielder of the Discus;
having praised him with devotion, he chanted the supreme, most holy prayer, which grants liberation even to the lord of elephants.

Having stayed there with devotion for three months, subsisting only on roots, fruits, and water, the son of the lord of the Daityas offered gold to the most excellent of Brahmins and departed for the formidable Daṇḍaka forest.
There he beheld the lotus-eyed one, possessing a divine body like a great tree with massive branches, acting as a protector against great beasts of prey.
Beneath it, that highly fortunate Asura remained for three nights,
sleeping on the bare ground while reciting the Sarasvata hymn of praise.
Therefore, the wise Dānava went to see Hari, the best of holy places, who liberates one from all sins and removes every evil.
In his presence, he recited those two hymns that destroy sin,
which the Blessed Lord Janārdana had formerly spoken while in the form of a boar.
Therefore, the lord of the Daityas then went to Śālagrāma, which yields great fruit,
where Viṣṇu is present in all things, both moving and stationary;
there, the powerful one, perceiving Viṣṇu to be omnipresent, took his delight.
O Sage, that great devotee of the Blessed One worshipped the feet of the Lord.
This highly meritorious pilgrimage to the tirthas of Prahlāda, frequented by hosts of sages, has been described to you;
by its recitation, hearing, and touch, men become liberated from sin.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, those mantras which the Dānava Prahlāda recited with devotion—
But tell me those four [deeds], beginning with the liberation of the lordly elephant.
Pulastya said: Listen, O ascetic, I shall tell you these prayers (*japyas*) by which, when they are recited,
heard, or remembered, the destruction of bad dreams occurs.
First, listen to the Liberation of the Lord of Elephants;
immediately after that, the Sārasvata [section], and then the two meritorious hymns that pacify all sins.
The glorious mountain named Trikūṭa, composed of all kinds of jewels,
was the son of Sumeru, the king of mountains, who possesses the radiance of the sun.
With its surface of pure white stone raised up by the crests of the waves of the milk-ocean,
it rose piercing through the sea, frequented by hosts of gods and sages.
Surrounded by Apsarases, the glorious one was crowded with celestial nymphs; he was accompanied by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Pannagas.
Vṛkāgra is resplendent with Vidyādharas accompanied by their wives, as well as self-controlled ascetics,
and with tigers, leopards, and lordly elephants.
With *punnāga*, *karṇikāra*, *bilva*, *āmalaka*, and *pāṭala* trees;
with *cūta*, *nīpa*, and *kadamba*; and with *candana*, *aguru*, and *campaka*.
It was adorned on all sides by *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, as well as by *sarala*, *arjuna*, and *parpaṭa* trees, and by various other kinds of trees.
It was beautified by three broad ridges of exquisite appearance, marked with various minerals and flowing with streams on all sides.
It resounded with deer, monkeys, lions, and ever-intoxicated elephants,
and was filled with the cries of flocks of jīvañjīvaka birds and the calls of cakoras and peacocks.
One of its peaks is golden, which the sun attends;
it is strewn with various flowers and perfumed with various fragrances.
The second peak is made of silver, which the moon frequents;
it resembles pale clouds and is like a mass of frost.
Illuminating the directions with the splendor of diamonds, sapphire, and beryl,
[he ascended] to the third abode of Brahmā, the preeminent and supreme peak.
Neither those who are ungrateful, nor the cruel, nor the nihilists, nor those in this world who have not performed austerities, nor those people who are doers of evil, behold it.
On the back of that mountain was a lake with golden lotuses,
crowded with ducks and adorned with royal swans.
It was adorned with kumuda, utpala, and kahlāra lilies, as well as with puṇḍarīkas; it was further embellished with golden lotuses possessing a hundred petals.
It was surrounded on all sides by shrubs and hollow bamboos, with leaves resembling emeralds and flowers like gold.
In that lake there was a wicked-souled, deformed crocodile dwelling within the water,
an enemy of lordly elephants with squinting eyes.
Then, at one time, the leader of the elephant herd, his face radiant with tusks,
flowing with rut, and desiring water, moved like a walking mountain.
Resembling Airāvata, that elephant, dark as collyrium, with eyes rolling from intoxication, perfumed the mountain with the scent of his rut.
Thirsty and desiring to drink, he descended into that water;
moving gracefully through the forest of lotuses, he wandered in the midst of the herd.
He was seized by that fierce crocodile of unmanifest form,
even as the female elephants watched and cried out piteously.
He is carried away in the lotus grove by an exceedingly powerful crocodile;
bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, his movement has been rendered effortless.
Bound by extremely terrible and firm snares,
the nāga thrashed as best he could and let out great cries of lamentation.
Distressed, devoid of energy, and seized by the performer of terrible deeds,
he fell into extreme calamity and meditated upon Hari in his mind.
But that illustrious and excellent nāga, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa,
then sought refuge in that very god with his whole being.
With a single-minded self, his self subdued by his pure inner soul,
he was devoted to the one whose banner is Garuḍa through the practice of many successive births.
He worshipped no other god besides Mahādeva and Keśava—
the one who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace, and who resembles the foam of churned nectar.

Grasping with the tip of his trunk a supreme golden lotus, the elephant— seeking release from his calamity— uttered a hymn of praise to the primordial god, the unborn and all-pervading Lord of a thousand auspicious names.
The Lord of Elephants said:
Om, salutations to the primordial nature, to the unconquered Great Self;
salutations be to You, the God who is independent and free from desire. *Vāmana Purāṇa* 58.31.
Salutations to the primordial seed, to the one who belongs to the seers, to the impeller;
salutations again and again to the one who is within, the singular, and the unmanifest.
Homage to the secret one, to the hidden one, to the virtuous one who abides in virtue;
homage again and again to the incomparable, the immeasurable, and the peerless.
Homage to Śiva, the peaceful, the free from anxiety, the illustrious;
homage again and again to the eternal, the primordial, the ancient one.
Homage to the God of gods, homage again and again to the Self-nature; homage to the foundation of the world, homage again and again to Govinda.
Homage be to Padmanābha; homage to him who arises from Yoga;
homage to the Lord of the Universe, the divine Śiva, and to Hari.
Homage be to that God, who is devoid of qualities yet the soul of all qualities,
to Nārāyaṇa, the universe itself, the supreme Self of the gods.
Homage again and again to the dwarf who is the cause, to Nārāyaṇa of immeasurable prowess;
homage be to that Puruṣottama, the bearer of the glorious Śārṅga bow, the discus, the sword, and the mace.
Salutation to the Secret One, whose abode is the Vedas, who has a vast belly, the Lion, the destroyer of the Daityas, the four-armed one;
salutation to Acyuta, the best of gods and the giver of boons, who is praised by Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Munis, and the Cāraṇas.

Homage to the ageless one, who is fond of reclining and sitting upon the body of the Lord of Nagas; who resembles cow’s milk, gold, a parrot, and a dark cloud; who is clad in yellow garments; who is the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha; who is the universe itself; and who wears a beautiful crown.

Homage to the supreme one, the giver of boons, the Lord of all, who dwells upon the lotus born from his own navel as the four-faced Brahmā; who has his abode in the glorious ocean of milk; who is adorned with various and wondrous crowns and armlets; and who is the bearer of glory.

Salutation to the excellent one, who is dear to his devotees, whose Sudarśana discus is radiant and bestows boons, whose large and long eyes are like full-blown lotuses, whose prowess is intent on subduing the obstacles of the lords of gods, the Lord of Yoga, and the stainless one. VamP_58.42 //

I pay homage to Mahāvarāha, who is the path to Brahman, the path of the thirty-three gods, the sovereign lord of the worlds, the remover of worldly existence, Nārāyaṇa, and the goal of one’s own welfare.
I take refuge in that God of gods, Nārāyaṇa, the primordial deity and the cause, who is immovable, unmanifest, and of inconceivable form; the ancient Puruṣa who remains at the end of the ages.

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, the Lord of Yoga, whose crown is beautiful and variegated, who is unknowable, the foremost, standing beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), self-born, and most excellent.
I take refuge in that secret of the gods, the eternal Puruṣa whom the great seers declare to be invisible, unmanifest, inconceivable, imperishable, and the primordial Brahman. VamP_58.46.

I approach that eternal Viṣṇu, the Lord who is the ultimate refuge, who is satisfied with unsurpassed qualities, and whom they call the all-pervading Imperishable Brahman; by hearing whom one is liberated from the mouth of death.

I go for refuge to Viṣṇu, Janārdana, the Lord of the gods, who is the effect, the action, and the immeasurable cause; who has golden arms and the excellent lotus-navel; who possesses great strength and is the treasury of the Vedas. VamP_58.48.

I approach Keśava, who wears a diadem, armlets, and a costly golden neck-ornament; whose entire body is adorned with the finest jewels; who is clad in yellow garments variegated with golden patterns; and who bears a garland.

I take refuge in the Lord, the source of existence, the foremost among those who know the Vedas, the best among those whose souls are united in Yoga, and the most eminent among those who know Sāṃkhya;
he who possesses the majesty of the Ādityas, Rudras, Aśvins, and Vasus—the imperishable, self-possessed Master.
I take refuge in the great god Śrīvatsāṅka, the secret of the gods, incomparable,
subtle, immovable, most excellent, and the bestower of fearlessness.
I take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the source of all beings, who is beyond the qualities (nirguṇa),
and the supreme goal of ascetics who are free from attachment.

With devotion, I take refuge in the Blessed One, the presiding lord of all virtues, the imperishable one with lotus-like eyes, the protector who is worthy of refuge, and who is compassionate toward his devotees.
I take refuge in Janārdana, the one who strode across the three worlds, the lord of the three worlds, the great-grandfather of all, the self of yoga, the supreme soul.
I take refuge in the primordial god, the unborn Śambhu, who is both manifest and unmanifest, the eternal Nārāyaṇa, subtler than the subtlest, and beloved of the Brahmins.
Homage to the excellent god, and homage to the all-enduring one;
I take refuge forever in the Lord of the gods of gods, who is more minute than an atom.
Salutation to the one who transcends the world, who is beyond the supreme self; salutation to the thousand-headed, infinite, great-souled one.
The sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas proclaim you alone as the supreme deity, whom all— including Brahmā and the others— regard as their ultimate refuge.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees;
salutations to you, Subrahmaṇya; protect me who have come to you for refuge.
Pulastya said:
Reflecting upon the devotion of that Naga,
Viṣṇu, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, whose manifestations are unfailing, became filled with affection.
Keśava,
the lord of the world, the support of the universe, whose wealth is asceticism, established his presence in that lake while seated upon Garuḍa.
Madhusūdana, whose nature is immeasurable, swiftly rescued from the body of water that lordly elephant seized by the crocodile, as well as that crocodile itself.
Mādhava split the crocodile stationed on land with his discus and liberated the lord of serpents, who had come for refuge, from his bonds.
For that Hūhū, the best of Gandharvas, having become a crocodile due to the curse of Devala,
attained heaven after meeting his death at the hands of Kṛṣṇa.
The elephant, too, touched by Viṣṇu, became a man of divine form;
thus, in that moment of crisis, both the elephant and the best of Gandharvas were simultaneously transformed.
