Then the lotus-eyed Lord of the Gods, who is compassionate toward those who seek refuge, became filled with joy and was duly honored by the two of them.

And then, O tiger among sages, the Blessed One, Madhusūdana, spoke these sweet words to the lordly elephant who had come for refuge: *idaṃ ca bhagavān yogī gajendraṃ śaraṇāgatam / provāca muniśārdūla madhuraṃ madhusūdanaḥ //* VamP_58.67 *//
The Blessed One said:
"He who [saw] me, you, and the lake, as well as the tearing apart of the crocodile,
and the forms of the gulma, kīcaka, and reeds, and of the son of Meru— "
Men who are self-restrained and firm in their resolve will remember the Aśvattha, Bhāskara, Gaṅgā, and the Naimiṣa forest.
Those who, observing pure vows, shall recite this with devotion and listen to it,
their bad dreams will perish and they shall have auspicious dreams.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Dwarf, and Tārkṣya,
as well as the Man-lion and the Lord of Serpents— the cause of both creation and dissolution.
Those men who, having risen at dawn, shall remember these [names],
will be liberated from all sins and attain the meritorious world.
Pulastya said:
Having spoken thus, Hṛṣīkeśa, whose banner bears Garuḍa,
touched the lordly elephant and the Gandharva with his hand.
Then, O brahmin, having assumed a divine form, the lordly elephant, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, went for refuge to Madhusūdana.
Then the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the performer of wondrous deeds, having liberated that best of elephants from the noose of the sinner and from the curse, [released] the crocodile as well.
And being praised by the sages who were devoted to the secrets of the gods,
the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign whose course is difficult to comprehend, departed.
Having witnessed the liberation of the lordly elephant, the gods, led by Śakra,
paid homage to the high-souled Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa.
Having witnessed the liberation of the elephant, the great sages and the celestial bards,
their eyes wide with wonder, offered praises to Janārdana.
Brahmā, the lord of Prajāpati, having witnessed the liberation of Gajendra through the deeds of the Discus-wielder, spoke these words:
The person who, having risen early in the morning, should hear this constantly, shall attain supreme perfection; his bad dreams are destroyed.
O one rich in asceticism, by the narration, recollection, or hearing of the meritorious liberation of Gajendra— which destroys all sins—
one is immediately liberated from sin in this world through that account of Gajendra’s deliverance.
This supreme, most meritorious, and praiseworthy life-story of Murāri is a purifier;
when it is recited, one is released from the bonds of many sins, just as an elephant is freed [from its fetters].

I bow to that unborn, most excellent one, whose navel is a choice lotus; to Nārāyaṇa, the treasure-house of Brahman, the Lord of the gods; to that ancient Puruṣa, the secret of the deities, the Lord of the world, the most excellent one.
Pulastya said:
This supreme hymn among hymns, the praise of Murāri which extols the noble Nāgas, has been told to you;
by reciting, hearing, or likewise reflecting upon it, a person shall obtain the removal of all sins.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
There was once a certain base Kṣatriya, a slanderer and a hater of Brahmins.
A base person, by his very nature, delights in harming others and is devoid of compassion.
By him, the ancestors, gods, and twice-born were utterly cast aside;
when his life was exhausted, he was born as a terrible night-stalker.
Due to that very defect of his own karma, he, the foremost among evildoers,
then adopted a cruel livelihood, especially because of his nature as a *rākṣasa*.
Thus, hundreds of years passed for that man devoted to evil;
due to that very fault of his actions, he found no pleasure in any other way of life.
Whichever being that Rākṣasa of fierce deeds saw, he seized him and devoured him once he had come within the range of his arms.
Thus, as that extremely wicked man continued to commit the slaughter of living beings,
a great length of time passed and his life reached its full maturity.
Once, on the bank of the river, he saw that illustrious man performing austerities,
with his arms raised upward and his senses perfectly restrained.
O Brahmin, by this protection, the storehouse of asceticism has been rendered secure—
a pure and skillful master of yoga who is devoted solely to Vāsudeva.
Viṣṇu stands in the east, bearing the discus; Viṣṇu is in the south, bearing the mace;
Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, is in the west; and Viṣṇu, the bearer of the sword, is in my north.
Hṛṣīkeśa is in the corners, Janārdana in their openings;
Hari in the form of a boar is upon the earth, and Nārasiṃha is in the sky above me.
This stainless Sudarśana wheel, the end of which is sharp, revolves;
its garland of rays is difficult to behold, intended to slay the pretas and night-stalkers.
And this mace, emitting a thousand rays like a blazing fire,
is the destroyer of rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, and ḍākinīs.
And let the twanging of Vāsudeva’s Śārṅga bow utterly destroy my enemies— the tiryaks, humans, kūṣmāṇḍas, pretas, and the rest.
May those who are my enemies, swept away by the blazing moonlight of the sword’s edge,
instantly attain gentleness, like serpents by Garuḍa.
Those who are kūṣmāṇḍas, as well as yakṣas, daityas, and those who roam at night;
the pretas, vināyakas, and cruel beings; humans, jṛmbhakas, and birds—VamP_59.15.
May lions and other beasts, as well as venomous serpents,
all become gentle toward me, struck down by the roar of Viṣṇu’s discus.
Those who rob one of the fluctuations of the mind, those people who steal one's memory, those who take away strength and vigor, and those who destroy one's shadow; VamP_59.17 //
May those who steal enjoyments and those who destroy auspicious marks—
those *kūṣmāṇḍas*— be destroyed, struck down by the roar of Viṣṇu’s discus.
May there be health of the intellect, health of the mind, and likewise health of the senses for me,
through the glorification of Vāsudeva, the God of gods.
May Hari, the destroyer of the demon Jara, be present behind, in front, to the south and north, and in the intermediate corners;
by bowing down to that Janardana—who is worthy of praise, the Lord, infinite, and infallible—one does not suffer.
Just as Hari is the Supreme Brahman, so too is Keśava the very nature of the supreme universe;
by that Truth, may my threefold misfortune perish through the chanting of the name of Acyuta.
Having thus constructed the Viṣṇu-pañjara for the sake of self-protection,
that powerful Rākṣasa nevertheless rushed forward.
Then, while the protection was entrusted to the twice-born, that night-stalker,
his fury dispelled, remained there suddenly for four months.
O celestial sage, as soon as the twice-born’s completion of his meditation was reached and his recitation had concluded, he beheld that night-stalker.
Seeing him wretched, his son’s courage destroyed, fleeing in all directions, and deprived of his splendor, he was overcome with compassion and comforted the night-stalker.
He asked the reason for his arrival, and he explained it exactly as it was:
that he had come to behold his own true nature and to protect the earth from the power of his splendor.
And having explained that various reason to him, the rākṣasa,
despondent with his own deed, said to the brahmin, "Be gracious."
"Through your grace, I desire liberation from my many sins:
I have made many women widows, bereft of sons; and I have brought about the destruction of many innocent beings. (VamP 59.28)
Therefore, through your grace, I desire liberation from this evil;
grant me a teaching of the Dharma sufficient for the pacification of my sin.
"Grant me instruction that leads to the destruction of this evil.
Having heard those words of the rākṣasa, the best of the twice-born [replied]: ||| VamP_59.30 |||
The righteous-souled one spoke these words, which were logical and well-articulated:
"O night-stalker, how has a desire for the path of dharma suddenly arisen in you, who are by nature so cruel? (VamP 59.31)
The Rākṣasa said:
"O Brahmin, I have indeed come to you today, having been forcibly driven away by my duty as a guardian; through association with you, O Brahmin, the highest world-weariness has arisen within me."
I do not know what protection there is for her, nor do I know her ultimate refuge—
that association with whom, having been attained, has brought about supreme world-weariness.
O knower of Dharma, show mercy; bestow compassion upon me.
O Noble One, act in such a way that the removal of my sin may come to pass.
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed in this manner by that Rākṣasa,
the illustrious sage, after reflecting for a very long time, then replied.
The sage said: "That you, being despondent with your own actions, have come to me for instruction—this is indeed fitting; for the cessation of sinful deeds is beneficial."
"I shall not deliver a teaching on Dharma to the Yātudhānas;
O gentle one, ask those twice-born ones who are truly devoted to the sacred word."
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed, while that rākṣasa fell into deep anxiety;
with his senses overwhelmed by worry, he pondered, "How might there be the removal of my sin?"
Even though he was oppressed by hunger, he did not devour living beings;
rather, at every sixth interval of time, he consumed a single creature.
Once, while wandering through a vast forest overcome by hunger, he then saw a celibate student who had arrived there for the purpose of gathering fruit.
Seized by that Rākṣasa, the young sage-ascetic,
despairing of his life, then spoke to the night-stalker with conciliatory words.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O good sir, tell me what must be done and for what reason you have been seized. Speak that, may prosperity be yours; here I am, instruct me."
The Rākṣasa said:
"At this sixth mealtime, you have arrived as food for me, who am hungry—
a man devoid of fortune, exceedingly sinful, merciless, and a hater of the twice-born."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O night-stalker, if you must certainly devour me,
I shall come to you this very day after having offered the fruit to my teacher."
"Having come here for the sake of my preceptor, I have accepted this fruit; it was only after reaching the conclusion of my task that I offered these fruits to him."
Therefore, wait for me right here for just a moment,
until I have informed my teacher and return with the fruit.
The Rākṣasa said:
"O Brahmin, at the sixth mealtime no one has ever come to be seized by me;
even a god might be released—such is my sinful livelihood."
"There is only one cause for your liberation here; listen to it.
I shall release you without a doubt, provided that you perform it."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Rākṣasa, I shall do that which does not cause opposition to my guru, which does not obstruct dharma, and which does not violate my vow."
The Rākṣasa said:
"O Brahmin, by my very nature, and especially due to the defect of my birth,
I have always performed sinful deeds with a mind devoid of discernment."
"From my childhood, my mind has delighted in sins and not in righteous duties.
Tell me that by which I may attain liberation through the exhaustion of those sins."
O twice-born one, having attained this wicked womb, tell me how there may be liberation from those evil deeds committed out of ignorance.
"O son of a twice-born, if you shall relate this to me in its entirety,
then you will certainly obtain liberation from me, who am afflicted by hunger."
If I am not of such a sinful nature, being exceedingly hungry and thirsty at the sixth mealtime, I, cruel-hearted and pitiless, shall devour him.
Pulastya said:
Having been addressed thus by that terrible Rakshasa, the son of the sage fell into deep anxiety, being powerless to respond to him.
Having reflected for a long time, that brahmin, having fallen into a state of supreme doubt, sought refuge in Jātavedas (Fire) for the sake of receiving knowledge.
If fire has been tended by me following the service of my guru,
or if vows have been well-performed, may the seven-flamed one protect me from that [sin].
May the Purifier protect me as I always regard my mother and father with the same reverence as a spiritual preceptor.
Just as I do not disregard my guru in thought, deed, or even in word—
by that truth may the Purifier protect me.
As he was thus making truthful oaths with his mind,
Sarasvatī appeared, commanded by the seven-flamed fire.
She spoke to the son of the twice-born, who was distressed by the Rākṣasa's grasp:
"Do not fear, O son of the twice-born; I shall release you from this peril."
Whatever is for the welfare of this Rākṣasa that resides upon the tip of your tongue, I shall tell you all of that; thereafter, you will attain liberation.

Having spoken thus, Sarasvatī became invisible to that Rākṣasa; she vanished from sight, and the twice-born one spoke to the night-stalker: VamP_59.63: "She has become invisible to that Rākṣasa after he had spoken thus; she has gone out of sight. Then that twice-born man addressed the night-stalker.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Listen to that which is for your own welfare, as well as for other sinners—
that which serves to purify all sins and bestows an accumulation of merit.
Having risen in the morning, it should be recited at midday or even at the end of the day;
without doubt, it should always be recited by those who chant, for it bestows nourishment and peace.
Oṃ! To Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, Janārdana, the Lord of the World—to Him I bow; may He remove my sin.
I bow down to Govinda, the Lord of all that moves and is stationary, who reclines upon Śeṣa; may that supreme deity dispel my sin.
I bow to the supreme Lord of Lakṣmī, who holds the conch, the discus, and the Śārṅga bow, and who wears a garland; may he dispel my sin.
I bow down to Dāmodara, the one of noble eyes, the lotus-eyed Acyuta; may he, who is praised by those worthy of praise, dispel my sin.
I bow down to Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Śauri, Mādhava, Madhusūdana, the supporter of the earth; may he dispel my sin.
I bow to Keśava, whose eyes are like the moon and the sun, the slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin; may that mighty-armed one dispel my sin.
I bow to the Lord of Śrī, who bears the Śrīvatsa on his chest, the bearer of Śrī, the abode of Śrī, the beloved of Śrī; may he dispel my sin.
I have gone for refuge to that Vāsudeva, the imperishable Lord of all beings, whom the ascetics meditate upon as the indefinable.
Having turned the movement of the mind away from all objects of perception,
those who meditate upon Him who is named Vāsudeva— I have gone to Him for refuge.
I have gone for refuge to that Vāsudeva, the Supreme Brahman, who is all-pervading, who exists as all beings, who is the support of all, and the Lord.
I have gone for refuge to that imperishable God, the unmanifest Supreme Self, whom the wise reach upon the exhaustion of their karma.
I have gone for refuge to that which, having entered it, yogins— freed from both merit and demerit— no longer undergo rebirth.
I have gone for refuge to that infallible Lord, who, having become Brahman, creates this entire world together with its gods, asuras, and humans.
I have gone for refuge to Him from whose mouths, while he was in the state of Brahmā, the ancient Lord was born with a body consisting of the four Vedas.
I bow down to the eternal Janārdana, the god who assumes the form of Brahmā, the source of the universe, who is established in the act of creation as the creator.
Having become the Creator, the Yogin remains as the Destroyer of Asuras;
I bow down to that primordial Person, Viṣṇu, Janārdana.
I bow down to that Viṣṇu, the primordial Lord Janārdana, by whom the earth was upheld, the Daityas were slain, and likewise the gods were protected.
I bow down to that eternal Viṣṇu, the Lord of Sacrifice and the source of sacrifice, whom the wise worship with sacrifices as the Person of Sacrifice.
I bow down to that eternal Rudra, the Anta-puruṣa, who destroys those worlds that have become like pathways to the netherworld (pātāla).
I bow to Janārdana, who, having consumed this entire world exactly as it was created, dances as the very self of Rudra.
I bow to that all-pervading God, from whom the gods, asuras, hosts of ancestors, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas have come into being.
All the gods and all the races of men are but portions of that God; I bow down to Him who is omnipresent.
I bow to that omnipresent God, of whom trees, shrubs, and the like, as well as domestic animals, wild beasts, and so forth, are but a single part.
I bow to that all-pervading one, in whom nothing else superior exists, who is the infinite Great Self within whom all things reside, and who dwells in the midst of everything.
Just as fire is hidden within all beings, as it is within wood,
so may Viṣṇu likewise cause all my sin without exception to perish.
Just as everything, including Brahmā and all that is moving and unmoving, is pervaded by Viṣṇu,
so may whatever sin is to be severed by knowledge be destroyed for me.
May auspicious and inauspicious karmas, as well as rajas, sattva, and tamas, and likewise the sin arising from the actions of many lifetimes, be destroyed for me. VamP_59.92.
Whatever sin has been committed by deed, thought, or word during the night, at dawn, at midday and afternoon, or at the two twilights— VamP_59.93.
Whatever unwholesome karma has been committed by me while standing, while walking, or while lying down— whether by body, mind, or speech— VamP_59.94.
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, by those whose minds have been shaken by pride—
may that [sin] quickly go to destruction through the chanting of the names of Vāsudeva.
And that which arises from longing for the wives and wealth of others, from malice, and from the censure of great-souled ones caused by inflicting pain upon others; VamP_59.96.
And whatever there is in food, drink, that which is to be chewed, sucked, or licked—let that dissolve in water like a vessel of salt. (VamP 59.97)
Whatever sin was committed by me in childhood, whatever in youth, whatever in my prime, whatever in the decline of age, and whatever was done in other births; VamP_59.98 //
Through the chanting of the names Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Īśa,
let that [sin] go to dissolution, like a vessel of salt in water.
Salutations again and again, salutations to Viṣṇu, to Vāsudeva, to Hari, to Keśava, to Janārdana, and to Kṛṣṇa; salutations, repeated salutations!
Salutation to the one who will destroy hell, salutation to the slayer of Kaṃsa;
salutation to the destroyer of Ariṣṭa, Keśin, Caṇūra, and the enemy Devaka.
Who else but you will indeed be the deceiver of Bali?
Who else will forcibly destroy the pride of the Haihaya king?
Who else indeed will build a bridge across the ocean?
And who will slay the Ten-necked one, together with his ministers and followers?
"O Madhusūdana, who else but you will find delight in Nanda’s Gokula? O God of gods, who else but you will be the slayer or the subduer of Pralamba, Pūtanā,
and the others?"
In this way, O Jāpini, a man [performs] this supreme Vaiṣṇava dharma, whether through merit,
or through attachment to desired or undesired things, whether knowingly or even unknowingly.
Whatever sin he has committed over the course of seven lifetimes—
whether it be known as a great transgression (mahāpātaka) or likewise a minor transgression (upapātaka)— [is all purified].
And meritorious acts such as the Jajña sacrifice, as well as recitations, fire-offerings, and vows—
these destroy everything for yogins, just as an unbaked clay vessel dissolves in water.
That man who, for a full year, gives sixteen vessels of sesame seeds day after day, and he who recites this [text], both obtain equal merit.
Having attained the unimpaired holy life (brahmacarya) through the remembrance of Hari, one reaches the world of Viṣṇu; this which I have spoken is the truth.
Just as this has been spoken by me in truth— not even a small part of it is false—
so may he release me, whose every limb is terrified by the Rākṣasa.
Pulastya said:
When this had been uttered by him, the brahmin was released by the rākṣasa;
however, against his will, the twice-born one spoke again to that night-stalker.
Brahmā said:
O auspicious one, I have declared to you this hymn to Viṣṇu, the Sārasvata, which destroys all sins, and which Sarasvatī herself uttered.
Sent by the Fire-god and stationed at the tip of my tongue,
she recited this hymn to Viṣṇu, which bestows peace upon all.
"By this very means, worship Keśava, the Lord of the World;
then, when Keśava has been praised, you shall obtain the removal of the curse."
"O Rākṣasa, day and night, with firm devotion, praise Hṛṣīkeśa with this hymn; then you shall be liberated from your sin."
For when praised, he will undoubtedly destroy all evils;
for Hari, when praised with devotion by men, is indeed the remover of all sins.
Pulastya said:
Then, having bowed to that brahmin and propitiated him,
that glorious and self-controlled night-stalker went at that very moment to Śālagrāma for the sake of ascetic penance.
Reciting that very hymn to Sarasvatī day and night,
that night-stalker, becoming devoted to the service of the gods, performed austerities.
Having propitiated Puruṣottama, the Lord of the World, there,
he was liberated from all sins and attained the world of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin, this hymn to Viṣṇu, known as Sārasvata, has been narrated to you;
it was perfectly uttered by Sarasvatī residing within the mouths of the sages.
The man who recites this supreme hymn to Vāsudeva shall obtain liberation from all sins.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
"Salutations be unto you, O Lord of the World; salutations be unto you, O God of gods."
O Vāsudeva, homage be to you; O you of manifold forms, homage be to you!
O One-Horned One, salutations to you; salutations to you, O Vṛṣākapi.
O Abode of Śrī, let there be salutation to you; salutations to you, O Creator of all beings!
O Viṣvaksena, salutations to you; O Nārāyaṇa, let there be salutations to you.
O Dhruvadhvaja, salutations to you; O Satyadhvaja, let there be salutations to you.
Homage to you, O Banner of Sacrifice; homage be to you, O Banner of Dharma.
Homage be to you, O Banner of the Palmyra Tree; homage to you, O Banner of Garuḍa.
O most excellent Viṣṇu, O Vaikuṇṭha, salutations to you, O Supreme Person!
Salutations to Jayanta, Vijaya, Jaya, Ananta, and Parājita!
O you who have performed the whirlpools, O Great Whirlpool, O Mahādeva, homage be to you!
O you who are without beginning, beginning, end, middle, or end, homage to you, O beloved of the lotus-born!
O Purañjaya, salutations to you; O Śatruñjaya, let there be salutations to you;
O Śubhañjaya, let there be salutations to you; O Dhanañjaya, let there be salutations to you.
O you who contain the creation within you, homage to you, O Śuciśravas, Vṛthuśravas!
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha; homage to you, O Padmagarbha!
Homage to you, the lotus-eyed one; homage to you, the dark-eyed one. O you whose navel is time, homage to you; O you of the great navel, homage, homage!
O you whose root is rain, whose root is great, whose dwelling is the root; homage be to you!
O abode of Dharma, abode of water, abode of Śrī; homage be to you!
O Overseer of Dharma, Overseer of Creatures, Overseer of the World, homage, homage!
O Overseer of the Army, homage to you; O Overseer of Time, homage, homage!
O Gadādhara, Śrutidhara, Cakradhārin, and Śrīdhara;
O Vanamālādhara, Hari, O Dharaṇīdhara, salutations to you!
O Ārciṣeṇa, O Mahāsena, homage be to you, O Puruṣṭuta!
O Vahukalpa, O Mahākalpa, homage to you, O Kalpanāmukha!
O you who are the self of all, omnipresent, all-pervading Viriñci, Śvetakeśava,
Nīla, Rakta, Mahānīla, Aniruddha— homage be to you!
O you whose nature consists of the twelvefold time, whose nature is the Sāman, whose nature is the Supreme Self; O Subrahman, whose nature is space and the elements—homage be to you!
O Harikeśa, Mahākeśa, Guḍākeśa, homage be to you!
O Muñjakeśa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Lord of All, let there be peace for my mind!
O you who are subtle, gross, very gross, and very subtle; O bringer of auspiciousness;
wearer of white and yellow garments and blue robes—homage be to you!
O Kuśeśaya, homage be to you; O Sīradhvaja, O slayer of Naraka;
O Govinda, O bringer of joy; O Haṃsa, O lover of the yellow garment!
O Adhokṣaja, salutations to you; O Sīradhvaja, O Janārdana!
Salutations be to you, O Vāmana; salutations to you, O Madhusūdana!
Homage to the thousand-headed one; homage to you whose head is Brahman. Homage to the thousand-eyed one, who has the moon, sun, and fire as his eyes.
And homage to the Atharvaśiras; homage to you whose head is great.
Homage to you, the Eye of Dharma; homage to you, the Great Eye!
Salutation to the one with a thousand feet, whose wrath is manifested through a thousand arms;
salutation to you, the Sacrificial Boar of great form. VamP_60.22.
Salutations to you, the god of all, the self of all, the source of all;
O you whose form is the universe, let there be salutation to you—from whom this entire universe has arisen.
Homage be to you, O Nyagrodha, whose great branches are vast, who are honored by roots and flowers, and who possess trunks, leaves, sprouts, creepers, and tender shoots. VamP_60.24.
O Brahmin, the Brāhmaṇas are your root; the Kṣatriyas are your trunk, extending in all directions; from your navel arose the intermediate space, and from your mind the moon.
The Brāhmaṇas, possessing the sacred fires, issued from his mouth; the Kṣatriyas, bearing staffs and weapons, from his arms;
the Vaiśyas moved forth from his sides; and the Śūdras were born from his feet.
From your eye the sun was born; from your feet the earth; from your two ears the directions;
from your navel the intermediate space arose; and from your mind the moon was born.
From his vital breath (prāṇa) the wind arose; from his desire (kāma) Brahmā, the Grandfather, was born;
from his anger Rudra, the three-eyed one, emerged; and from his head the sky (dyauḥ) evolved.
From your mouth came Indra and Agni; from your impurities arose the animals, and from your body hair the herbs were born. You are Virāj; homage be to you!
O Puṣpahāsa, homage be to you; O Mahāhāsa, homage be to you!
You are the syllable Oṃ, you are Vaṣaṭ, you are Vauṣaṭ, and you are Svadhā and Sudhā.
O Svāhākāra, homage to you; O Hantakāra, let there be homage to you!
O Sarvākāra, Nirākāra, Vedākāra, let there be homage to you!
For you, O God, are composed of the Vedas, as well as composed of all the gods;
you are composed of all sacred fords and likewise composed of all sacrifices.
Salutations to you, O Person of Sacrifice; salutations to you who partakes of the sacrificial portion.
Salutations to you of a thousand streams; salutations to you of a hundred streams.
Salutations to you, whose nature is Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; to the giver of cows and the bestower of immortality; to the giver of gold and the Brahman, and to the giver of everything.

Salutations to you, O Brahma-Isha; salutations to you, O source of Brahma, who assumes the form of Brahman. Salutations be to you, the Supreme Brahman; salutations be to you, the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
You are knowledge, you are the object of knowledge, and you alone are that which is to be known; you are the intellect, you are that which is to be awakened, and you are awakening—homage be to you!
Oṃ, salutations to the Hotṛ, the oblation, the sacrificial offering, that which is being offered, and the carrier of the offering;
to the protector, the purifier, the purified, and that which is to be purified. Oṃ, namaḥ!
You alone are the slayer and the slain, the one who feels shame and the one being shamed;
you are the taker, the leader, and the policy itself; you are the worshipful, the foremost, and the sustainer of the universe.
The *sruva* and *sruk* ladles are your supreme abode; the skull-bowl is the mortar and the fire-drill;
you are the sacrificial vessels, who exist as one, as many, and as threefold.
You are the sacrifice, you are the sacrificer, you are the one to be praised, and you are the officiating priest;
you are the knower, the object of knowledge, and likewise knowledge; you are the object of meditation, the meditator, and the Lord.
You are meditative absorption, yoga, and the yogi; you are the goal, liberation, fortitude, and bliss.
You are the limbs of yoga and the sovereign Lord; you are all-pervading—homage be to you!
You are the Brahman, the Hotṛ, and likewise the Udgātṛ; you are the Sāman, the sacrificial post, and the sacrificial fee.
You are the consecration, you are the sacrificial cake, and you are the animal sacrifice; you are that which carries the animal offering.
He is the secret one, the sustainer, the supreme Śiva, and likewise Nārāyaṇa;
he is the great person, the goal-less, possessing the form of a thousand suns and moons.
O you who possess twelve spokes, six hubs, three layers, and two yokes;
O Kālacakra, Lord of Bhavānī, salutations to you, the Supreme Person!
You are valor, you are prowess, you are Hayagrīva, the Lord of Monkeys;
you are the Lord of Men, the Lord of Brahmā, and the Lord of the Sun—homage be to you!
Horse-faced, possessed of great intelligence, you are Śambhu, Śakra, and the Wind;
you are the embodiment of Mitra and Varuṇa, yet you are formless, sinless, and supreme.
O twice-born one, whose body is the eastern hall (prāgvaṃśa), who is the origin of the elements, the great being, the imperishable;
you are the creator of the heights, the upward-tending, and the one whose seed is drawn up—salutations be to you!
O you who destroy the great sins and likewise the secondary sins,
being powerless against all evils, I have gone to you for refuge.
O Sage, this supreme hymn, which liberates one from all sins,
was formerly recited by Maheśvara in Vārāṇasī.
Having gone before Keśava and bathed in the Sitoda tīrtha,
Rudra then became thus pacified from the power of his sin.
O great sage, the man who, devoted to Viṣṇu, recites this purifying hymn spoken by the destroyer of Tripura,
is freed from sin, becomes one of tranquil form, and is honored by the most renowned and excellent gods.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
O Sage, I shall now declare to you a second hymn that pacifies sin.
By means of which, when correctly studied, evil indeed goes to destruction.
I bow to Matsya, the Lord of Gods, and to Kūrma and Govinda;
I bow to you, Hayaśīrṣa, Bhava, Viṣṇu, and Trivikrama.
I pay homage to Mādhava and Īśāna, who possess the senses and the daughter of Śakra;
I pay homage to Nārāyaṇa, and I pay homage to the one whose seat is Garuḍa.
I bow to the one with upward-pointing hair, the Man-Lion, the bearer of form, whose banner is the boar, the destroyer of desire, the unbroken, who is dear to the Brahmins.
I bow to the unconquered Viśvakarman, to Puṇḍarīka who is dear to the twice-born,
to Haṃsa, to Śambhu, and to Brahmā together with Prajāpati.
I pay homage to the god who holds the trident in his arm, as well as the wielder of the discus;
to Śiva, Viṣṇu, Suvarṇākṣa, Gopati, and the one clad in yellow garments.
I bow to the one who holds a mace in his hand; I bow to the one who reclines upon Kuśa grass;
I bow to the Lord who is half-female, the destroyer of sins.
I bow to Gopāla, Saivakuṇṭha, and Aparājita; I bow to Viśvarūpa, Saugandhi, and Sarvadāśiva.
I bow to Pāñcālika, Hayagrīva, Svayambhuva, and Amareśvara; and to Puṣkarākṣa, Payogandhi, and Keśava.
I saw Mārkaṇḍeya together with Jambuka— the unreleased, the restless, the eldest, the middle one, the tranquil, and the one in darkness.
I pay homage to Padmakiraṇa; I pay homage to Vaḍavāmukha;
I pay homage to Kārttikeya, as well as to Bāhlīka and Śikhin.
I bow to Sthāṇu, the sinless; I bow to the one garlanded with forest flowers;
I bow to the Lord of the plow-bearer; and I bow to the Lord of Śrī.
I bow to the three-eyed one; I bow to the bearer of oblations;
I bow to the one with three golden eyes; I bow to the one adorned by the moon.
I bow to the one who has mastered the three *nāciketa* fires, the Brahman, the Lord; I bow to the moon-crested one, the one with matted hair, the destroyer of all diseases.
I pay homage to the Moon, the Sun, Dhruva, and the mighty Raudra;
I pay homage to Padmanābha, Hiraṇyākṣa, and the imperishable Skanda.
I pay homage to Bhīmahaṃsa and I pay homage to Hāṭakeśvara;
I always pay homage to Haṃsa and I pay homage to Prāmatarpaṇa.
I pay homage to the Lord, the Great Yogin, whose armor is gold;
I pay homage to Śrīnivāsa, and I pay homage to Puruṣottama.
I pay homage to the four-armed one; I pay homage to the lord of the earth;
I pay homage to the Lord of the Forest, the Lord of Creatures, the imperishable Master.
I bow to Śrīkaṇṭha, Vāsudeva, Nīlakaṇṭha, and the one who always bears the staff; I pay homage to the sinless Gaurīśa, the Lord of Nakulī.
I bow to the captivating one with black hair, the wielder of the discus;
I bow to the upholder of glory, the mighty-armed one who is dear to Kuśa.
I bow to Bhūdhara, Chāditagada, Sunetra, Śūlaśaṅkhin,
Bhadrākṣa, Vīrabhadra, and Śaṅkukarṇika.
Salutations to you, the banner of the *vaṣat* call, the Great Lord, Viśvāmitra, and the moon-bright one;
salutations to Upendra, Govinda, and the beloved of the lotus.
I bow to the thousand-headed god who wears a garland of kunda flowers;
I bow to Rudra, the lord of gods, the fire of time, who is clothed in an elephant hide.
I bow to Chāgaleśa, and I bow to the one seated upon the lotus;
I bow to the thousand-eyed Kokanada, and to Hari and Śaṅkara.
I bow to Agastya, Garuḍa, Viṣṇu, Kapila, and Brahmā who is the embodiment of speech; and to Sanātana Brahmā, who is devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
I bow to the King of Dharma, the god whose vehicle is Garuḍa, who is beyond reasoning, four-armed, thousand-rayed, and composed of austerity.
I pay homage to the Great Yogin, who pervades all beings, who is peaceful, stainless, and possesses all characteristics; he is unmanifest and the destroyer of evil.
I bow to the stainless, formless, attribute-less, and pure state;
I seek refuge in the destroyer of sins, the worthy protector.
This supreme and ancient purifier was proclaimed by the great seer Agastya;
it bestows fortune and fame, destroys many sins, and [yields merit] through its recitation, its remembrance, and its hearing.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Now, when Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, had departed on his pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā),...
Virocana’s son, Bali, arrived at Kurukṣetra in order to perform a sacrifice.
At that sacred ford endowed with great dharma, Śukra, the bull among brahmins,
addressed the foremost of the twice-born Bhārgavas.
Hearing that the Bhṛgus were being summoned, the Ātreyas, along with the Gautamas,
Kauśikas, and Aṅgirasas, abandoned Kurujāṅgala.
They proceeded toward the northern direction along the river Śatadrū;
having bathed in the waters of the Śātadrava, they then set out for the Vipāśā.
Perceiving that there too was no pleasure, they bathed, honored the ancestors and the gods,
and departed for the holy Kiraṇā, which flows from the rays of the sun.
Having bathed in that river and worshipped the gods and sages, all the great seers,
after bathing in the highly meritorious Airāvatī, then proceeded toward the goddess Īśvarī.
Having bathed in the waters of the Devikā and the Payoṣṇī,
O Sage, the ascetics, including Ātreya and others, descended to bathe in that auspicious river.
Then, having plunged into it, O best of the twice-born, they beheld their own reflection within the water, which was a source of great wonder.
And as they emerged, their minds were filled with wonder once more;
then all the sages, having bathed, indeed ascended from the water.
O Brahmin, from that place they departed as well, conversing with one another and constantly wondering in amazement, "What is this? VamP_62.10.
Then, from afar, they beheld a vast forest grove,
dark as the throat of Śiva, resounding with the cries of birds.
O Nārada, that best of mountains covered the sky with its exceedingly great height, and it covered the interior of the earth with its spreading matted locks.
The forest shines brilliantly on all sides with blossoming trees of five colors,
like the sky filled with clusters of stars that grant happiness.
Seeing that [lake] covered with lotuses and adorned with white lilies,
and likewise covered with red water-lilies, it was like a forest of lotuses.
They attained incomparable satisfaction and reached supreme joy;
with delighted minds, they entered [the city] like swans entering a great lake.
In the midst of that, O best of sages, they beheld a holy hermitage honored by the world, belonging to the groups of the four world-protectors—
a Dharma-hermitage facing the east and surrounded by palāśa thickets.
O Brahmin, facing westward, there is a land covered with sugarcane fields.
The temple for the fulfillment of desires faces south and is surrounded by groves of plantain and *aśoka* trees;
that for liberation faces north and has the luster of pure crystal.

In the Kṛta age, liberation belongs to the ascetic; in the Tretā interval, desire belongs to the one who exerts himself; at the end of the Dvāpara, the purpose of the stages of life belongs to the ascetic; and at the beginning of the Tiṣya (Kali) age, righteousness belongs to the ascetic.
Having seen those hermitages, the imperishable sages, Ātreya and the others,
took delight right there in that place which was undivided and flooded with water.
The Blessed Viṣṇu, renowned as Akhaṇḍa, the Lord of the World in his fourfold form, was established by Dharmādya and others in the very beginning.
O Nārada, sages who are self-possessed through yoga, deeply learned, and devoted to celibacy, worship him with service, austerity, and the practice of brahmacarya.
Thus those sages dwelt there together in the forest,
having taken refuge on Mount Akhaṇḍa, being then afraid of the Asuras.
Likewise, O Brahmin, other Brahmins— the stone-grinders and those who subsist on rays of light—
having bathed in the waters of the Kālindī, departed facing the south.
Having reached the domain of Avantī and taken refuge in Viṣṇu,
they remained there by the grace of Viṣṇu, a place difficult for even the great asuras to enter.
The Bālakhilyas and others, driven by fear of the Dānava, went away;
remaining celibate students, they took refuge with ten million Rudras and stayed there.
When the Brahmins, Gautama, Aṅgiras, and the others had thus departed,
O Sage, Śukra led all the Bhārgavas to the sacrificial rite.
When the great sacrifice was presided over by the descendants of Bhṛgu, O one of immeasurable luster,
Śukra himself performed the sacrificial initiation for Bali according to the prescribed rites.
The Daitya wore white garments, was adorned with white garlands and unguents,
had a deer-skin draped over his back, and was decorated with peacock feathers.
He sat at the extensive sacrifice, surrounded by the members of the assembly,
including Hayagrīva, Pralamba, and others, led by Maya and Bāṇa.
And his wife was Vindhyāvalī, a daughter of the sages who had been initiated for the sacrificial rite,
the foremost among a thousand women.
In the month of Madhu, Śukra released a white-colored horse with beautiful markings to roam the earth, and Tārakākṣa followed after it.
Thus, when the horse had been released while the sacrificial rite was being performed,
and after three months had passed with the fire being offered oblations, [the horse returned].
While the Daityas were being honored and the sun was situated in the sign of Libra,
the Mother of the Gods gave birth to Mādhava in the form of a dwarf.

O great sage, as soon as he was born, Brahmā, together with the great seers, approached the Blessed One, the Lord Īśa, Nārāyaṇa, the ancient Master of the World, and then uttered a hymn of praise to the All-pervading One.
Homage be to you, O Mādhava, embodiment of pure being; homage be to you, eternal one of universal form!
Homage be to you, the fire that consumes the forest of enemies; homage indeed be to you, the great forest fire of sins!
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe.
Salutations to you, O support of the world; salutations to you, O Supreme Person.
O Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the universe, Lord of the world, wielder of the mace,
clad in yellow garments, beloved of Śrī, Janārdana— salutations be unto you!
You are the savior and the protector, the soul of the universe, all-pervading and imperishable;
you are the sustainer of all, the support of the earth, and the bearer of forms—salutations be unto you!
Prosper, O you who are worshipped by the gods, having increased the entire three worlds!
O Lord of Deities, wipe away the tears of Maghavan.
"You are the Ordainer and the Disposer; you are the Destroyer, O Maheśvara.
O Mahālaya, O Great Yogin, who reclines in Yoga—homage be to you!
Thus praised, Hari, the Lord of the World, the Self of all and the All-pervading, [spoke].
The Blessed One said to me, "O Lord, perform the initiation of Kurūpa."
Then Bharadvāja, the son of Bṛhaspati, possessed of great luster and rich in asceticism, performed for the god the birth-rites and other ceremonies.
Likewise, the Lord, the knower of all scriptures, performed the investiture of the sacred thread;
thereafter, everyone, filled with joy, bestowed boons one after another in due order.
Pulaha gave the sacred thread, and I gave two white garments;
Kumbhayoni gave a deer-skin, and Bharadvāja gave a girdle.
Marīci, the son of Brahmā, gave him a staff made of *pālāśa* wood;
Vāruṇi gave him a rosary of seeds; and Aṅgiras gave him a garment of *kauśya* grass.
King Raghu gave an umbrella, Nṛga gave a pair of sandals,
and Bṛhaspati, of great splendor, gave a water-pot to Viṣṇu.
Having thus had the initiation ceremony performed, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings,
studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches while being praised by the sages.
O Sage, from Bharadvāja of the lineage of Aṅgiras, he received the Sāmaveda of great resonance,
which was joined with great narratives and accompanied by the Gandharvas.
Within a single month, the Blessed One, that great ocean of wisdom and learning,
became proficient in the Vedas for the sake of engaging in the worldly ways of conduct.
Having attained mastery in all the scriptures, the imperishable and undecaying Lord spoke these words to Bharadvāja, the best of brahmins: VamP_62.51.

The venerable Vāmana said: "O Brahmin, I am going; give me leave. To Kurukṣetra, the place of great prosperity, I go, for there the meritorious horse-sacrifice of the lord of the Daityas is being performed."
Behold the splendors pervading the surface of the earth—
those portions of myself that are ever present there, increasing merit. Therefore, I declare that Bali has gone to Kurukṣetra.
Bharadvāja said:
"Stay or go as you wish; I do not command you.
We shall go to the sacrifice of Bali, O Viṣṇu; do not cause us distress."
"O Lord, tell me that which I ask of you:
O All-pervading One, Supreme among Men, in which specific places do you always maintain your presence? Speak, for I wish to know this according to the truth."
Vāmana said:
"Listen, O Guru, I shall tell you in which various most meritorious places I dwell, assuming many forms."
O Bharadvāja, the earth, the vault of heaven, the netherworld, the oceans, the sky, all the directions, the mountains, and the clouds are pervaded by my incarnations, which are suited to me.

Those who are celestial and those who are terrestrial, those who move through water and sky, the stationary and the moving, along with Indra, the Sun, and the Moon, as well as Yama, the Vasus, Varuṇa, and all the guardians of the quarters;

from Brahmā down to the smallest stationary beings, honored by the twice-born and the birds—whether they possess form or are formless—all of them are born of me, endowed with many diverse qualities, for the purpose of filling the earth.
For these are the foremost ones, worshipped by gods, siddhas, and dānavas, and likewise present upon the surface of the earth;
O best of the twice-born, merely by seeing them or by chanting their names, sin goes to its destruction instantly.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The first great form, that of the Fish, was established in the Mānasa lake."
It brings about the destruction of all evils through chanting, touching, and other such means.
There is another presence of the Kūrma [incarnation] at Kośikī, which destroys sins;
Hayaśīrṣa is in Kṛṣṇāṃśa, and Govinda is in Hastināpura.
There, one should worship Trivikrama at Kālindī, the omnipresent Lord Bhava at Liṅgabhedaka,
Mādhava at Kedāra, and Śauri with joyful hair at Kubjāmra.
One should worship Nārāyaṇa at Badarī, Garuḍāsana in Vārāha,
Jayeśa at Bhadrakarṇa, and Dvijapriya on the Vipāśā.
One should worship Rūpadhara in Irāvatī, Kurudhvaja in Kurukṣetra,
Nṛsiṃha in Kṛtaśauca, and Viśvakarman in Gokarṇa.
In the east, one should worship Kāmapāla; Puṇḍarīka in the great waters;
Ajita at Viśākhayūpa; and likewise Haṃsa at Haṃsapada.
One should worship Akhaṇḍa on the Payoṣṇī, Kumārila on the Vitastā,
Śambhu on Mount Maṇimat, and Prajāpati at Brahmaṇya.
O best of sages, know that Viṣṇu, bearing the discus and having the trident in his arm, resides on the medicinal peaks of the Himalayas at the Madhunadī river.
On Bhṛgutuṅga he is Suvarṇāśra; in Naimiṣa, Pītavāsas;
at Gayā, the divine Lord Gopati, who holds a mace in his hand.
He is the Lord of the three worlds, the bestower of boons, as the Kuśeśaya at Gopratāra;
he is the Lord who is half-female on the auspicious Māhendra mountain and on Mount Dabhina.
Gopāla is eternally in the north; Somapīthin is on Mount Mahendra; Vaikuṇṭha is on the Sahya mountain; and Aparājita is on the Pāriyātra mountain.
In the region of Kaśeru, he is Deveśa; in the Malaya mountains, Viśvarūpa, whose wealth is austerity; and at the foot of the Vindhya range, Sadāśiva.
O Brahman-sage, Viṣṇu is established in the region of Avanati, the Lord of the Immortals (Indra) among the Niṣadhas, and Pāñcālika is situated among the Pāñcālas.
One should worship Hayagrīva at Mahodaya, Yogaśāyin at Prayāga,
Svayaṃbhū at Madhuvana, and Ayogandhi at Puṣkara.
In the very same way, O best of Brahmins, Keśava is in Vārāṇasī;
Avimuktaka is right here, and Lolaka is likewise celebrated in this very place.
In Padmā is Padmakiraṇa; in the ocean is Vaḍavāsukha;
in Kumāradhāra is Bāhlīśa, and Kārttikeya is in Barhiṇa.
The people dwelling in Diṣkindhā call me Ajeśa, Śambhu, Anagha, Sthāṇu in Kurujāṅgala, and Vanamālī.
The hero mounted upon Kuvalaya, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his noble body— the Lord of Śrī on the banks of the Narmadā.
In Māhiṣmatī he is Trinayana, and in that very place he is Hutāśana;
in Arbuda he is Trisauparṇa, and on Mount Sūkara he is Kṣmādhara.
O Brahman-sage, Triṇāciketa is at Prabhāsa, Kapardī is likewise there,
and the third, Śaśiśekhara, is renowned in this very place as well.
O Sage, the triad consisting of the moon at its rising, the sun, and Dhruva is situated on Hemakūṭa; and Hiraṇyākṣa and Skanda are on Śaravaṇa.
O best of sages, Rudra is remembered as Mahālaya in the northern Kurus,
while Padmanābha is the bestower of all happiness.
O Brahmin, Hāṭakeśvara is renowned at Saptagodāvara;
likewise, Mahāhaṃsa is there, and Vaṭeśvara is at Prayāga.
At Śoṇa he saw Rukmakavaca; at Kuṇḍina, Ghrāṇatarpaṇa;
at Bhillīvana, Mahāyoga; and among the Mādras, Puruṣottama.
O best of the twice-born, one should worship Viśva at Plakṣāvataraṇa,
Śrīnivāsa at Śūrpāraka, and Sudhāpati in Magadhā.
At Girivraja he is Paśupati; on the banks of the Yamunā he is Śrīkaṇṭha;
and he is celebrated as Vanaspati, dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest.
One should worship Nīlakaṇṭha at Kāliñjara, the supreme Śambhu on the Sarayū,
and the destroyer of all sins, Haṃsayukta, at Mahākośī.
One should worship Śarva at Gokarṇa in the south, Vāsudeva at Prajāmukha,
Mahāśairī on the peak of the Vindhya mountains, and Madhusūdana at Kaṇṭhā.
O Brahmin, one should worship the Lord Cakrapāṇi on the peak of Trikūṭa,
Hṛṣīkeśa at Lauhadaṇḍa, and Manohara in Kosala.
Mahābāhu in Surāṣṭra, Yaśodhara in Navarāṣṭra,
Bhūdhara by the Devakā river, and Kuśapriya in Mahodā.
He saw Chāditagada at the Gomatī river, Śaṅkhin at Śaṅkhoddhāra,
Sunetra in the Saindhava forest, and Śūra stationed in Śūrapura.
They know Rudra to be in the Haraṇvatī, Vīrabhadra in Triviṣṭapa,
Śaṅkukarṇa in Bhīmā, and Bhīma in the Śāla forest.
And Viśvāmitra spoke of Maheśa, whose banner is the bull, on Kailāsa; and of him who possesses the luster of the moon on Mahilāśaila and in Kāmarūpa.
In Balabhī he is Gomitra; in Kaṭāha, Paṅkajapriya;
in Siṃhaladvīpa, Upendra; and in the land called Śakra, Kundamālin.
And in the netherworld (rasātala), O sage, there is the famous thousand-headed Kālāgnirudra,
and likewise another there, Kṛttivāsas.
On Sutala is Kūrmamacala; on Vitala is Paṅkajāsanam;
on Mahātala is the one renowned as Guru; and on Chāgala is Deveśa Chāgaleśvara.
Thus he is renowned as the Lord with a thousand feet, a thousand arms,
and a thousand eyes, who dragged down the Dānavas with his mace.
In Pātāla, he is Hariśaṅkara, the lord of yogins;
on the surface of the earth, he is Kokanada; and upon the ground, he is Cakrapāṇi.
In Bhuvarloka he saw Garuḍa, and in Svarloka the imperishable Viṣṇu;
likewise, in Maharloka he saw Agastya, and Kapila residing in Janaloka.
O Brahmin, in the world of heat (Tapoloka), the entirety of the Vedic word, joined with truth, is established;
and in the seventh world, that of Brahmā (Brahmaloka), Brahmā himself is established.
Likewise, in the Śaiva [tradition] it is eternal, and in the Vaiṣṇava it is the Supreme Brahman;
it is beyond reasoning, without support, devoid of space, and composed of austerity.
In Jambudvīpa he is Caturbāhu; in Kuśadvīpa, Kuśeśaya;
and in Plakṣadvīpa, O best of sages, he is renowned as Garuḍavāhana.
Likewise, Padmanābha resides on Krauñca; on Śālmala is Vṛṣabhadhvaja;
Sahasrāṃśu is stationed on Śāka; and Dharmarāj resides on Puṣkara.
Likewise, O Brahman-sage, I am stationed at Śālagrāma upon the earth;
I pervade everything from the waters to the dry land, among both moving beings and the immobile.
O Brahmin, these meritorious abodes of mine are ancient and eternal;
they bestow righteousness here, possess great power, are worthy of being proclaimed, and destroy all sins.
Through the chanting of her name, through remembrance, through seeing, and even through touching the deity,
gods, humans, and the Sādhyas alike obtain dharma, artha, kāma, and even final liberation.
"These abodes of mine here, consisting of asceticism, have been offered to you.
Arise, O Brahmin; I am going to the sacrifice of the great Asura for the benefit of the gods."
Pulastya said:
Having thus spoken these words to the great sage Bharadvāja, the high-souled Viṣṇu,
whose movements are characterized by graceful sport, departed from that king of mountains and went indeed to Kurujāṅgala.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said: [Chapter Sixty-four of the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa] Pulastya said:
Then, as Vāsudeva approached, the earth trembled and the mountains shook;
the oceans were agitated. Pulastya said:
Then, as Vāsudeva approached, the earth trembled and the mountains shook.
The oceans were agitated and the constellation of stars in the sky shone with its course reversed, O Great Sage.
The sacrifice has fallen into great agitation; I do not know what the slayer of Madhu will do to me.
Just as I have been consumed by Maheśvara, will Vāsudeva not utterly incinerate me?

Out of fear of the All-pervading Lord, the sacrificial fires do not accept even those portions offered with devotion by the best of the twice-born, consisting of oblations made with *ṛc* and *sāman* mantras during the sacrificial canopy.
Having seen those portents of terrible form, the lord of the Dānavas prostrated with palms joined in reverence and questioned Uśanas Śukra.
"O Teacher, for what reason has the earth, together with its mountains, trembled like a plantain tree struck by the wind?
And why do the sacrificial fires here not accept their well-offered portions, as if they were possessed by demons?"
"O Teacher, why are the oceans agitated? Why do the bears no longer roam in the sky as before?
Why are the quarters of the world overwhelmed by darkness? Tell me today, by whose fault has this come to pass?"
Pulastya said:
Having heard those words spoken by the son of Virocana,
and having understood the underlying cause, Śukra then addressed these words to Bali.
Śukra said:
Listen, O Lord of Daityas, as to why these [gods] do not indeed accept their shares belonging to the Asuras;
for Vāsudeva surely comes here even to the oblations offered with mantras into the sacrificial fire.
O Lord of the Daityas, unable to endure the pressure of his footsteps, the earth with its mountains trembled;
as she shook, O son of Diti, the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, overflowed its shores today.
Pulastya said:
Having heard the words of Śukra, Bali spoke to Bhārgava regarding that which is righteous, truthful, beneficial, and impelled by every kind of vigor.
Bali said:

"O Blessed One, now that Vāsudeva has arrived, tell me the truth regarding dharma, kama, and artha; what should be done, and what should be given—jewels, gold, land, elephants, horses, or the like? What should be said to the enemy of Mura—is it for my own benefit or for his? O auspicious-toothed one, speak truly and beneficially to me as I stand ready to act; I shall do exactly that and nothing else."
Pulastya said:
Having heard those words concerning the boon uttered by the lord of the Daityas, Nārada, the knower of the past and the future, reflected and spoke, O Bhārgava.
For the sake of those lords of the asuras who, though they partake in sacrifices, have been excluded from the path seen in the Vedas;
for the sake of those gods who, while eating at the sacrifice, hold the authority of the Vedas outside [that path]—for their sake, Hari approaches.
"Why do you ask me what task is to be done for him who has arrived at the sacrifice with the Daityas?
For not even a blade of grass, nor land, gold, or anything else, is to be given as a fee at the sacrifice, O Lord."

O All-pervading Lord, such conciliation would likewise be useless; for who indeed would be able to grant you a boon, when within your belly the lords of the earth, the intermediate space, heaven, and the subterranean realms dwell eternally?

Bali said: "O Bhārgava, I have never spoken such words, nor do I lack anything, yet I cannot bring myself to give even when the Lord of the World, Janārdana, who has fallen from his proper conduct, comes as a petitioner— how could I do so?"
And thus, O Lord, this verse is heard from the virtuous as they speak:
"One who desires prosperity should cultivate a state of goodness toward Brahmins alone;
for it is seen to be so, and that is the truth, O best of Brahmins. (VamP 64.17)
Through the force of past habituation, actions of speech, body, and mind clearly manifest for human beings here, even when they have entered another womb.
Or rather, O best of the twice-born, have you not heard the ancient tale concerning the son of a silkworm-keeper that occurred long ago on Mount Malaya?
Śukra said:
"O mighty-armed one, tell me the ancient and meritorious story concerning the daughter of the silkworm; for my curiosity is great."
Bali said:
Listen, O scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage; I shall relate this true story that occurred during a sacrifice, for it is bound to my former practice.
O Brahmin, the son of the sage Mudgala, who had reached the further shore of theoretical and practical knowledge and was devoted to austerity, was known as Kośakāra.
He had a virtuous and righteous daughter, beloved by name,
who was the daughter of Vātsyāyana, chaste, of pious character, and devoted to her husband.
To her was born a son who was by nature dull-witted; like one mute he did not speak, and like one blind he did not see. (VamP 64.24)
On the sixth day, the brahmin woman, considering her newborn son to be dull-witted, mute, and sightless, cast him out at the door of her house.
Then there approached a wicked-natured Rākṣasī,
a child-stealer named Sūrpākṣī by name, carrying her own emaciated infant.
There, having abandoned her own son, she took hold of the son of the twice-born;
taking him with her, she then went to the interior of a Śāla tree on the mountain to eat.
Then, seeing her returned, her husband Ghaṭodara, who was blind, replied: "My dear, what have you brought back?"
She said, "O Lord of the Rākṣasas, having placed my own infant in the house of a silkworm-cultivating brahmin, I brought back your son, O Master."
He said, "O blessed lady, you have not acted auspiciously.
Then that great wise lord of the twice-born, being provoked to anger, will curse you.
"Therefore, O beautiful one, quickly abandon this man of terrible form and swiftly bring the son of someone else."
Having been addressed in this manner, that fierce Rākṣasī, who moves at will,
sprang up into the sky and arrived there in haste.
And that son of the Rākṣasa, once cast outside the house,
O Brahmin, cried out with a piercing voice as he thrust his thumb into his mouth.
Having heard the crying after a long time, that most virtuous woman said to her husband:
"O best of sages, see for yourself; your son is making a sound."
Then that ascetic woman, terrified, emerged from the middle of the house;
and that best of brahmins also beheld that infant.
Endowed with color, form, and other qualities just like his own son,
the silkworm then laughed and spoke to his beloved wife.
"Having entered this most righteous being, you must now become manifest.
Surely some handsome man has taken his place upon the earth in order to deceive us."
Having spoken these words, the minister, having drawn lines upon the earth with his hand holding *kuśa* grass, bound that son of the Rākṣasa with mantras.
In the meantime, Sūrpākṣī arrived and, having become invisible, cast the Brahmin boy onto the ground far from the house.
As soon as it was thrown, the silkworm-keeper caught his own son;
but that rākṣasī, having approached, was unable to seize her own son.
Wandering here and there, she approached her husband and related everything that had happened, including the loss of her own two sons.
O Brahmin, when she had thus been transformed into a Rākṣasī, that high-souled Brāhmaṇa presented the impetuous child to his wife.
And that son of his was given by his father to Kapilā with her calf,
having been excessively provided with curds, milk, and sugarcane juice.
The two boys grew and reached the age of seven;
their father gave them the names Niśākara and Divākara.
That brahmin performed, in due order, the initiation ceremony for the vows of Naiśācarin, Divākīrti, and Niśākīrti, his own sons.
Once the initiation ceremony was performed, we have heard that Divākara studied the Veda,
whereas Niśākara, due to his dullness, did not study it.
His kinsmen, his parents— both mother and father— and likewise his brother and preceptor,
as well as those people who dwelt in Malaya, all censured him.
Then he was thrown by his angry father into a waterless well,
and a massive stone was indeed placed upon him as a cover.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, when he had thus been thrown into the well and some time had passed,
his mother came to that well which was covered by a stone slab.
Then, O Bhārgava, when ten years had passed,
his mother went to that well which was filled with stones and where he lay blind.
Seeing the well completely covered by a rock as large as a mountain, she spoke aloud:
"By whom has this rock been placed over the well?"
Having heard those words of his mother from within the well, Niśākara said:
"This stone upon the well has been given to me by my father."
Terrified, she asked, "Who are you, standing within the well with such a wondrous voice? He replied, "I am your son, known as Niśākara."
She said: "My son is renowned by the name Divākara;
indeed, I have no son named Niśākara. (VamP 64.54)
And he related his mother’s former deeds in their entirety;
having heard them, that fair-complexioned woman lifted up the stone and entered her own abode.
Having emerged from the well, O Blessed One, he prostrated at his mother's feet;
she, seeing her son who was worthy of herself, [beheld] her own offspring.
Then that most virtuous woman, taking her son and approaching her husband,
related all of those actions performed by her son.
Then that brahmin asked: "O father, what is the reason for this?
Why did you not speak before? I have a great curiosity."
Having heard those words, the wise son spoke these extraordinary words to his mother and father, that best of brahmins, who was like a silkworm in its cocoon.
"Listen, dear father, to the reason why I have resorted to silence,
why I have become dull-witted, O sinless one, and likewise why my own eyes have become blind."
"O Brahmin, formerly I was born in the family of Vṛndāraka as the son of Vṛṣākapi, produced from the womb of Mālā."
Then my father taught me the scriptures that bestow virtue, wealth, and pleasure,
as well as the supreme scripture of liberation, O dear one, along with the histories and the Vedas.
Therefore, my dear father, though I was a man of great knowledge and skilled in the higher and lower truths,
I became blinded by pride and devoted myself to evil deeds.
From pride the elephant was born; by him, boldness was destroyed.
Discernment met its end, and he fell into a state of folly.
Furthermore, due to my state of delusion, I became devoted to evil;
my mind was always set upon the wives of others and the wealth of others.
"Because I violated another's wife and because I seized the wealth of others,
I died by hanging and went to the Raurava hell."
Therefore, when a thousand years had passed and that sin remained as a residue to be experienced,
I was born as a sinful hunter of deer, a lord of beasts, in the forest.
O dear one, while remaining in the state of a tiger, he was bound and placed in a cage by the powerful lord of men,
and led away to his own city.
While he was bound, confined in a cage, and possessed by the state of a tiger,
the treatises on dharma, artha, and kāma appeared to him from all sides.
Then, at one time, that tiger among kings, mace in hand and clad in a single garment, went out from the city.
His wife, named Jitā, was peerless in beauty upon the earth;
when her lover had departed, she came into my presence.
Upon seeing her, the god of love grew within me due to my former practice;
and just as the treatises on dharma prescribe, so did I speak to her.
"O princess, auspicious one, endowed with fresh youth,
you steal my heart, O timid one, just as the cuckoo does with its song."
Having heard my words, that slender-waisted woman said:
"O tiger, how indeed shall there be a union in love between us two?"
Then, O dear one, I said to the slender-waisted princess:
"Open the door today; I shall emerge quickly."
She also said this: "During the day, people watch this tiger;
at night we shall open [the door], and then we will enjoy ourselves as we please."
I indeed said to her: "I am not capable of further delay;
therefore, open the door and release me from my bonds."
Then, O Sage, that thick row opened the door;
once the door was opened, I emerged from the row and went outside.
Indeed, the snares, fetters, and other bonds were forcibly severed by me;
and that wife of the king was seized by me, desiring to sport with her.
Then I was seen by the king’s servants of incomparable prowess;
with weapons in hand, they surrounded me on all sides.
Struck by great nooses, chains, and mallets,
and being beaten, I cried out, "Do not, do not harm me, you agitated ones!"
Having heard my words and recognizing him as a night-stalker,
O ascetic, they bound him firmly to a tree and slew him.
And having gone to hell due to consorting with another's wife,
I was released at the end of a thousand years and born as a white donkey.
In the house of the Brahmin Agniveśya, who had many wives, all branches of knowledge appeared there as well; from that, they manifested to me.
I was respectfully made into a garden-tree by the wives of the twice-born;
once, the wife of that brahmin was from Navarāṣṭra.
Vimati, known by that name, desired to go to her father’s house;
her husband said to her, "Go, having mounted a white donkey."
"You must return within a month; you must not stay beyond that time.
Having been addressed thus by her husband, that slender woman mounted me.
Then, O Sage, having been released from her bonds, she departed in haste;
then, on the way, that slender woman indeed descended from my back.
Seeing her, beautiful in form, having entered the river to bathe in her own natural state with wet garments and all her limbs and ornaments intact, I rushed toward her.
And as I was pursued by him, I quickly fell to the surface of the earth;
O dear father, I fell upon her, being extremely distressed.
Delighted by his master’s command,
O Brahmin, that man, following him, raised his staff and rushed toward me with great haste.
Out of fear of that, O Sage, he abandoned her and fled toward the south; then, as he rushed forward swiftly, his bit and bridle fell away.
I became stuck in a bamboo thicket that was difficult to escape and fatal to life;
while clinging there for six nights, my life came to an end.
I went once more to hell, but from there I was released as a parrot;
likewise, I was captured in the great forest by a wicked Śabara.
Having been cast into a cage, he was sold to a merchant’s son for rice;
by him, too, he was placed near the young women in the excellent inner apartments.
It was established that one who knows the science of grammar is indeed a destroyer of faults;
therein, those young women [served] the unrighteous with boiled rice, water, fruits, and so forth.
O father, day after day they nourished him with various foods and pomegranate fruits;
once, that dark-complexioned woman with lotus-petal eyes and full breasts— VamP_64.97 —
Then, opening the cage, he saw the auspicious beloved of the merchant's son, who had beautiful hips and a slender waist, and was named Candrāvalī.
The woman of beautiful limbs and lovely smiles grasped me with her two hands; then that woman of lovely smiles placed me upon her two full breasts.
Then, leaping about, I formed the intention to sport with her; thereupon, as I was leaping, I became entangled like a monkey in a snare at that necklace.
Bound and joined with evil, I died immediately thereafter; once again, being of wicked mind, I have fallen into a terrible hell.
And because of that, I indeed attained the state of a bull in a settlement of Caṇḍālas;
and once, having yoked me to his cart, he [set out] for his own mistress.
Having placed [the child] upon it, the one of great splendor resolved to go to the forest;
then that Caṇḍāla went before him, while he himself followed behind.
Hearing her singing as she went, my senses became distressed; looking back when questioned, I was bewildered and leaped away.
I fell to the ground from that axle due to my momentary lapse;
though I was still firmly bound by the yoke, I then met my death.
Furthermore, I was submerged in hell for even ten hundred years;
therefore, I have been born in your house, remembering my previous birth.
I remember all those very same births in their proper sequence;
and due to my former practice, both the scriptures and this bondage have come back to me.
Therefore, having gained this realization, I shall by no means commit any evil deeds—
whether through thought, action, or speech— that are terrible in form.
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, whether it be Vedic recitation, livelihood through the sciences,
bondage, or even death— it arises through previous habituation.
O Sage, when a person remembers his former birth, O dear one, he then [seeks] the forest for the increase of virtue and the destruction of sins; therefore,
you should establish this son of yours, Divākīrti, in the duties of a householder.
Therefore, O Sage, I shall go to the forest to increase my merit and destroy my evil;
you, however, should employ this son of yours, Divākīrti, in the duties of a householder.
Bali said:

Having spoken thus, O great sage, that maker of the night (the Moon) then bowed to his parents and went to the holy abode of Murāri, the famous and primordial Badarikāśrama, which is worthy of praise.
Thus, for a man who delights in former practice, acts such as giving and study come naturally;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, I tell you that I indeed practiced these in the past.

O Great Sage, O Protector, charity, austerity, and study were formerly considered the means for achieving dharma and artha; however, theft, arson, and even the various forms of knowledge became causes of great sin for those who lacked self-restraint. (VamP 64.114)
Pulastya said:
Having spoken thus to Śukra, his own preceptor and master,
the powerful lord of the Daityas then remained absorbed in meditation upon Nārāyaṇa, the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who holds the discus, mace, and sword in his hands.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
In the meantime, the Blessed One arrived in the form of a dwarf.
Having approached the sacrificial enclosure, he spoke these words aloud:
In this sacrifice, the Vedas of the ascetics, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, abide in embodied form;
the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is the most excellent of rites, and likewise, O Lord of Daityas, you are the foremost among those who perform long sacrificial sessions (*satra*).
Having heard these words, the self-controlled lord of the Dānavas approached,
carrying an offering vessel with its contents, to where the god was stationed.
Then, having worshipped the Lord of the gods with offerings such as the *arghya*, the Asura,
together with the sage Bharadvāja, led him into the sacrificial enclosure.
As soon as the Lord of Gods had entered, [the king], having honored him with prostrations, said:
"O Blessed One, speak; what may I give to you, O giver of honor?"
Then the imperishable and best of gods, having laughed for a very long time and looking toward Bharadvāja, spoke to the king of the Daityas.
My preceptor has a preceptor who maintains the sacred fire;
he does not maintain the Jātavedas on land belonging to another.
For that purpose, O King of the Dānavas, I entreat you:
O King, grant me three paces of ground measured by the span of my own body.
Having heard the words of Surārī, and having looked at his wife and his son Bāṇa, Bali spoke these words: VamP_65.9 //
"O beloved, this dwarf is not only small in stature according to the measure;
for he begs for three paces out of both folly and even intelligence."

Generally, for men of small intellect who have been excluded by those of great majesty, wealth and other such things are not bestowed in abundance; indeed, as in this world, there is no great effort on the part of Viṣṇu [to grant them these].
Fate does not grant anything to one whose fortune has turned away;
yet he who now begs me, a giver, for three paces of land—VamP_65.12.
Having spoken these words, the high-souled son of Danu then spoke again to Hari:
"O Viṣṇu, ask for elephants, horses, land, female slaves, gold, or whatever else you desire."
"O Viṣṇu, you are the beggar and I am the giver, the Lord of the World;
how could there not be shame for both the giver and the beggar regarding these three steps?"
"Whether it be Rasātala, or the earth, or Bhuvarloka, or even Svarga— heaven—
whichever among these places you desire, ask for it, O Vāmana."
Vāmana said:
"Let elephants, horses, land, gold, and so forth be given to those who desire them;
but as for me, O King, I am desirous of only this much—grant me three paces of ground."
When these words had been spoken by Vāmana, the great asura Bali took up a golden pitcher and offered three steps of ground to Viṣṇu.
When his hand fell into the water, he indeed assumed a divine form—
multiform and consisting of the universe— for the purpose of traversing the three worlds.
From his two feet came the earth, from his calves the sky, O you who are worshipped by the three worlds;
from the pair of his knees came truth and austerity, and from his thighs came Meru and Mandara.
The Viśvedevas reside in the region of the hips; the Maruts are located in the head of the bladder;
Manmatha is situated in the penis; and Prajāpati is in the two testicles.
The seven oceans are in his two flanks, and the worlds are in his belly;
the rivers are in his three folds, and the sacrifices reside within his stomach.
All rites, such as sacrifices and charitable works, are established therein;
the Vasu deities reside upon its back, and the Rudras preside over its two shoulders.
His arms are all the directions, and the eight Vasus are said to be in his hands;
Brahmā resides in his heart, and the thunderbolt is in the bones of his chest.
Śrīsamudrā is in the middle of the chest, and Candramas is situated in the mind; Aditi, the mother of the gods, is in the neck, and the Vidyās are stationed in her bracelets.
In their mouths, the Brahmins possess the fires; their lips are the purificatory rites;
and their teeth are the scriptures endowed with purity, which deal with virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
Lakṣmī resides upon his forehead; the two Aśvins are in his two ears;
Mātariśvan (the Wind) dwells in his breath; and the Maruts are in all his joints.
All the well-spoken hymns are the ten tongues; the goddess Sarasvatī is the tongue;
the moon and sun are the two eyes; and the Kṛttikās and other stars are situated in the eyelashes.
King Dhruva sat upon the crest-lock of the God of gods;
the stars arose from his pores, and the great sages from his body hairs.
Having become identical with everything through his qualities, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings,
gradually withdrew the world, including all that is mobile and immobile, in a single step.
As he of the great form strode across the earth,
his right breast became the moon and his left breast became the sun;
as he stepped upon his navel, the sun and moon were on his left and right sides.
Then, by the second sequence, Svar, Mahar, Jana, and Tapas were traversed;
with half of that half again, the Vairāja realm was reached, and the sky was filled by the middle [of the third].
Then, O Brahmin, the blazing Bṛhadviṣṇu,
having struck the interior of the cosmic egg in the sky, departed into the darkness.
As his all-pervading foot spread forth, the shell was forcibly split;
then, meeting Viṣṇu’s foot, the Kuṭilā became crooked.
O Sage, she came to be known by the name Viṣṇupadī;
likewise, the ascetics worshipped her as Suranadī.
And when the third step was not yet completed, the omnipresent Lord [remained there].
Approaching Bali with his lower lip slightly quivering, he said:
"O Lord of Daityas, in due course a terrible bondage shall come upon you.
Fulfill that condition for me; otherwise, O sir, accept your imprisonment."
Having heard those words of Murāri, Bāṇa, the son of Bali, laughed and then addressed these reasoned words to the lord of the immortals.
Bāṇa said:

O Lord of the World, having made the earth so very small— reducing it to only six worlds beginning with Svāyambhuva— why do you now demand such a vast tribute, which you previously made so extensive for us?
O Lord, this assembly of friends, together with all the intermediate worlds that were created by you today, has indeed been bestowed by our father;
why then is he bound today by such a verbal trick?
Since it is impossible for you to fulfill even this much, how could that lord of the Daityas expand upon it?
O Murāri, you alone are capable of honoring him; be gracious and do not command me to imprisonment.
O Lord, you yourself have declared in the Śruti that giving to a worthy recipient bestows happiness;
O wielder of the discus, all of this is seen to be complete when the place is most meritorious, the recipient is excellent, and the time is right.
Generosity is the ground; you, the God of gods who have conquered the self, are the worthy recipient for the granting of all desires;
the time is the conjunction of Jyeṣṭhāmūla; and the moon is the famous sacred place of Kurukṣetra.
Or rather, how could the Lord be instructed by those like us who are devoid of wisdom, regarding what is good or even what is bad?
For He Himself is the original author of the Vedas, and He exists pervading the entire world, both the existent and the non-existent.
Having yourself set the limit, you asked for only three paces of land;
why then, O you who are honored by the three worlds for your beauty, do you not accept the three worlds?
There is no wonder here that the entire world and even the three steps were not fully traversed by you today;
O Lord of the World, you are capable of leaping over them all at once, yet you have performed this sport.
O Mādhava, O Padmanābha, O Viṣṇu, having yourself rendered the earth devoid of authoritative rulers, you do not bind Bali; he is not far off, for a lord does whatever he desires.
Pulastya said:
When these words had been spoken by Bāṇa, the son of Bali,
the Blessed Lord Janārdana, the primordial creator, spoke these words.
Trivikrama said:
"O son of Bali, listen now to my reasoned reply to those words which you have just spoken."
"O King, your father was previously told by me: 'Give me three paces according to measure'; that has now been fulfilled."
Does not your father Bali, O Asura, know my authority,
by which he fearlessly offered me three steps of infinite extent?
"Truly, I shall traverse the worlds beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ both gradually and all at once;
these three steps were taken for the benefit of Bali as well."
"Therefore, O son of Bala, because a great amount of water was given by your father into my hand,
his lifespan shall endure for an entire kalpa."
O Bāṇa, when the Manvantara of Śrāddhadeva has passed and the Sāvarṇika period has arrived,
Bali shall become Indra.
Having thus addressed Bāṇa, the son of Bali, the divine Trivikrama approached Bali and spoke these words in sweet syllables.
The Blessed One said:
"O King, because of the fulfillment of your sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), go to the great fruit;
dwell there in the netherworld named Sutala, free from all affliction."
Bali said: "O Lord, while I dwell in Sutala, from what source shall my imperishable enjoyments come,
by which I may live free from affliction?"
Trivikrama said:
"O Lord of Daityas, I shall now describe to you in their entirety those highly precious enjoyments that shall belong to you while you reside in Sutala."
Gifts given without the prescribed rites, funeral offerings made to those who are not learned in the Vedas,
and likewise Vedic studies performed by those who do not observe their vows— these shall yield fruit for you.
Likewise, after the great festival of Śakra has concluded, there shall be another meritorious festival for you called Dvārapratipadā.
There, those tigers among men— joyful, well-nourished, and well-adorned—
will diligently strive to honor you with offerings of flowers and lamps.
There, a most excellent festival shall take place day and night, delightful to joyful people;
just as it is now in your kingdom, so too shall that Kaumudī festival be.
Having spoken thus and dismissed the Lord of the Daityas along with his wife to Sutala,
