the slayer of Madhu took the sacrifice and departed swiftly to that place frequented by hosts of gods and celestial beings.
Having bestowed heaven upon Maghavan and having made the gods partakers of the sacrificial portions,
O great seer, the Lord of the Universe vanished even as the lords of the Mura-demons were looking on.
When Vāsudeva, the Creator, had gone to heaven, Śālva, with a great army of asuras,
constructed the city known as Saubha and then roamed at will through the sky.
But the high-souled Maya, having constructed the triple city made of gold, copper, and iron— which provided unsurpassed happiness—
resided there together with Tārakākṣa and Vaidyuta, accompanied by his servants and wives.
When heaven had been seized by the god, Bala bound, and the netherworld occupied, Baṇa,
having established a well-guarded city on earth named Śoṇita, dwelt there together with the lords of the Dānavas.
Thus, in the past, Bali was bound by Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus, who had assumed the form of a dwarf for the sake of pleasing Śakra,
for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose, and for the welfare of the best of Brahmins, the cows, and the twice-born.
O Great Sage, you have narrated the meritorious, pure, and sin-destroying manifestation of Vāmana;
upon hearing, remembering, or reciting it, evil is utterly destroyed and merit is attained. (VamP 65.67)
Thus has been told to you the manifestation of the imperishable Bali, whose fame is meritorious, and his binding;
and whatever else you desire to hear, O Brahmin, let it be spoken, for I shall relate it to you in its entirety.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"I have heard how Bali was bound by the high-souled Blessed One."
However, there is something else that must be asked; having heard it, tell it to me today.
"O father, tell me where has that Viṣṇu, the soul of all, gone— he who, having given the celestial realm to the king of the gods, vanished from sight?"
And while staying within the earthen vessel, what did the lord of the Daityas do?
Tell me that; O brahmin-sage, you should explain to me what his activity was.
Pulastya said:
Having made himself invisible to the abode of the gods, Vāmana became non-Vāmana;
mounting the eater of serpents (Garuḍa), he went to the dwelling of Brahmā.
Knowing that Vāsudeva was approaching, the imperishable Brahmā,
whose seat is the lotus, rose up and out of affection embraced him.

Having embraced and honored Hari according to the prescribed rites with worship and other offerings, the Creator asked: "Why have you come here after such a long time? Then the Lord of the World replied: "A great task has been accomplished by me."
For the sake of the gods' share of the sacrifice, the Self-Existent One performed the binding of Bali.
Having heard those words, the Grandfather, with a joyful mind, said, "How? How? You ought to show yourself to me."
When these words had been spoken, the Blessed One, whose banner is Garuḍa,
swiftly manifested that form which embodies all the gods.
Having seen that lotus-eyed one, who was ten thousand yojanas in extent and likewise in height,
the Unborn One then bowed down before him.
Then, having prostrated for a very long time and exclaimed, "Excellent!
Excellent!", the lotus-born Brahmā, his mind devoted to Bhakti, uttered a hymn of praise to Mahādeva.

Oṃ, salutations to you, O God of gods, Vāsudeva, One-horned One, Many-formed One, Vṛṣākapi, Creator of beings, Bull among gods and demons, Destroyer of gods and demons, Yellow-robed One, Abode of Śrī, End-maker of the works of Asuras, Immeasurable Creator, Kapila, Mahākapila,
Viṣvaksena, Nārāyaṇa. (5)

O Dhruvadhvaja, Satyadhvaja, Khaḍgadhvaja, Tāladhvaja; O Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣottama, Vareṇya, Viṣṇu, Aparājita; O Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, Kṛtāvarta, Mahādeva; O Anādi, Ananta, Ādyāntamadhyanidhana, Purañjaya, Dhanañjaya, Śuciśrava, Pṛśnigarbha. (10)
O you whose navel is like a lotus, O you with eyes as broad as lotuses, O Lord of Śrī, O Viṣṇu, O Root of all, O Abode of the Root, O Abode of Dharma, O Dwelling of Dharma,

O Overseer of Dharma, O Overseer of Subjects, O Wielder of the Mace, O Wielder of Śrī, O Wielder of the Vedas, O Wielder of the Forest Garland, O Wielder of Lakṣmī, O Wielder of the Earth, O You whose name is Padmanābha. (15)

O Viriñci, O Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, O Mahāsena, O Commander of the Army, O Much-Praised One, O You of many aeons, O Great Aeon, O Face of all aeons, O Aniruddha, O All-pervading, O Soul of All, O Twelve-fold One, O Solar-Souled, O Lunar-Souled, O Time-Souled, O Ether-Souled, O Elemental-Souled (20),
O Essence-Souled, O Supreme Self, O Eternal One, O Muñjakeśa, O Harikeśa, O Guḍākeśa, O Keśava, O Blue One, O Subtle One, O Gross One!

O yellow, red, and white one; O you whose dwelling is white; O lover of red garments; O bringer of joy; O abode of affection; O swan; O blue-clad one; O you whose banner is the plow; O abode of all worlds; (25) O lotus-dweller; O Adhokṣaja; O Govinda; O Janārdana; O Madhusūdana; O Vāmana—salutations to you!

You have a thousand heads; you have a thousand eyes; you have a thousand feet. You are the Lotus; you are the Great Puruṣa; you have a thousand arms; you have a thousand forms. The gods call you the Thousand-faced; homage to you! Oṃ, homage to you, O Lord of all the gods, source of the universe, universal self, universal form, origin of the universe! From you this entire universe has come into being.

The Brāhmaṇas arose from your mouths, the Kṣatriyas were born from your arms, the Vaiśyas emerged from your pair of thighs, and the Śūdras from your lotus-feet. From your navel the intermediate space was born; Indra and Agni from your face; the Sun from your eye; the Moon from your mind; I myself am born from your grace; Tryambaka from your anger; Mātariśvan (the Wind) was born from your breath; and the sky was born from your head.

From your hearing the quarters arose, and from your movement this earth came into being; from the emergence of your hearing the quarters were born of you, the Self-existent One, and the stars were born of your splendor.
All forms, both embodied and formless, have emerged from you.
Therefore, you are the soul of the universe. Oṃ! You are the one whose smile is like a flower; you are the Great Laughter; you are the Supreme; you are the syllable Oṃ; you are the Vaṣaṭ-call.

"You are the utterance *svāhā*, you are the utterance *vauṣaṭ*, you are the utterance *svadhā*; you consist of the Vedas, you consist of sacred fords (*tīrtha*), you consist of the sacrificer, you consist of the sacrifice; you are the sustainer of all, you are the enjoyer of the sacrifice, you are the sustainer of the pure, you are the giver of *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *svarṇa*, cattle, and immortality.

Oṃ! You are the origin of Brahmā, you consist of Brahmā, you are the sacrifice, you are the desire for knowledge, you are that which is to be known, you are the support of the sacrifice, you are the Great Fish, you are the Great Army, you are the Great Head."

(50) "You are the man-lion; you are the Hotṛ; you are the one to whom oblations are offered; you are the one to be invoked; you are the one being invoked; you are the horse-sacrifice; you are the Potṛ; you are the purifier; you are the pure; you are the one worthy of worship; you are the giver; you are the one being slain;

you are the one being carried away; you are the carrier—Om! You are policy; you are the leader; you are the foremost; you are the abode of all; you are the auspicious egg; you are the firm; you are the fire from the two kindling woods—(55)"

You are meditation; you are the object of meditation; you are that which is to be known; you are knowledge; you are the knower; you are the sacrificer; you are the giver; you are the Infinite; you are the one to be beheld;

you are Brahman; you are the Hotṛ priest; you are the Udgātṛ priest; you are the goal of those who possess a goal; you are the knowledge of the wise; you are the yoga of the yogis; you are the liberation of those seeking liberation; you are the prosperity of the prosperous; you are the one to be grasped; you are the protector; you are the Supreme. (60)
You are Soma, you are Sūrya, you are Dīkṣā, you are Dakṣiṇā, you are Nara, you are Trinayana, you are Mahānayana, you are born from Āditya,

you are the supreme among gods, you are pure, you are Śukra, you are Nabhas, you are Nabhasya, you are Food, you are Strength, you are Might, you are Powerful, you are Heat, you are the Season of Heat, you are Sweetness. (65)
You are Mādhava; you are Time; you are the transition; you are valor; you are prowess; you are Aśvagrīva; you are Mahāmedha;

you are Śaṅkara; you are Hariśvara; you are Śambhu; you are Brahmeśa; you are Sūrya; you are Mitra and Varuṇa; you are Prāgvaṃśakāya; you are the origin of beings; you are the Great Element; you are the upward-acting one; you are the agent. (70)
"You are the liberator from all sins; you are Trivikrama. Oṃ, salutations to you!
Thus praised by Padmaveṇa and by the ascetics, Viṣṇu, the performer of wondrous deeds, spoke. Pulastya said: [Thus was he praised].
He spoke to the god, his great-grandfather: "Choose a boon, O you whose conduct is of pure essence!"
Filled with affection, the Grandfather said to him: "O Lord, O Murāri, grant me this boon today:
remain here in my abode in this very form of yours, which is so holy and beautiful."
When the best of gods had thus chosen [him], the Lord, whose self is imperishable, granted him the boon saying,
"So be it," and remained there in the form of a dwarf, being worshipped in the abode of the Self-born One.
There, throngs of apsarases dance, and the singers of the Lord of the Gods sing songs;
the vidyādharas play the sounds of musical instruments, while the hosts of gods, asuras, and siddhas offer praise.
Then, having propitiated the Lord, the Grandfather, the sovereign of the gods— his impurities washed away and purified—
took beautiful flowers from his abode in heaven and performed worship to Viṣṇu.

In heaven, he was indeed a thousand *yojanas* in height according to the measure of Viṣṇu; there, O great seer, Śakra himself performed for him a worship equal in merit to that of the Self-born. This which the blessed, high-souled Trivikrama did for the benefit of the gods has been told to you;
now hear, O Brahmin, what the son of Diti, dwelling in the netherworld, did, which I shall tell you today.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having gone to Rasātala, which was adorned with highly precious gems, the Daitya—
He indeed caused the city to have staircases made of pure crystal.
In its center is a very extensive palace with a vajra-terrace;
its door is set within a lattice of pearls, fashioned by Viśvakarman.
There he dwelt, enjoying various divine and human pleasures;
his beloved wife was named Vindhyāvalī, who was the foremost among a thousand young women and adorned with virtuous character. (67.3)
O Sage, the immensely radiant son of Virocana took his pleasure with her.
While the Daitya, addicted to enjoyments, was dwelling in Sutala,
the Sudarśana [discus], which robs the Daityas of their splendor, arrived in Pātāla.
When the discus had entered Pātāla, the city of the Dānavas,
a great tumultuous roar arose, resembling the agitation of the ocean.
Hearing that great sound, Bali drew his sword; and the bull among the Asuras asked, "Ah! What is this? thus.
Then Vindhyāvalī, the lawful wife of pure vows, having sheathed her sword in its scabbard, spoke to her husband while consoling him.
"O Lord of Daityas, this wheel of the high-souled Vāmana, which brings about the destruction of the circle of the Daityas, is worthy of worship.
Having spoken thus, the lady of beautiful limbs departed, carrying the vessel of offerings.
Then, O Sage, Viṣṇu’s thousand-spoked discus, the Sudarśana, arrived. Thereupon, the lord of the asuras, bowing with palms joined in reverence,
duly worshipped the discus and uttered this hymn of praise.
Bali said:
I bow to the discus of Hari, which tears asunder the hosts of Daityas;
it possesses a thousand rays, a thousand splendors, a thousand spokes, and is perfectly stainless.
I pay homage to the discus of Hari, in whose nave is the Grandfather (Brahmā),
at whose tip is Śarva holding the trident, and at the base of whose spokes are the great mountains.
Within his spokes are stationed the gods, together with Indra, the Sun, and Agni;
within his speed abide Vāyu, Āpa, Agni, Earth, and Space.
On its outer edges are clouds, lightning, bears, and stars;
and on its exterior are the sages, such as the Bālakhilyas and others.
I worship that supreme weapon of Vāsudeva with devotion,
so that whatever sin of mine arises from the body, from speech, or even from the mind may be destroyed.
O Sudarśana, the discus of Viṣṇu with blazing rays,
burn away that sin of mine which has arisen from my lineage, as well as that inherited from my father and mother.
Take that away from me swiftly; salutations to you, O wielder of infallible weapons!
May my mental anxieties perish, and may my physical ailments go to their destruction.
O Discus, by the chanting of your name, may all evil go to its end.
Having spoken thus, the wise one then paid homage with devotion.
Remembering the lotus-eyed one, the destroyer of all sins.
O Sage, having rendered the Asuras devoid of splendor by means of the discus worshipped by Bali,
he then emerged from Pātāla during the southern equinox.
When Sudarśana had departed, Bali fell into a state of distress;
having reached the height of calamity, he called to mind his own grandfather.
And that lord of the Dānavas, having been summoned and arrived at Sutala,
stood there with great splendor, holding a vessel of offerings, as Bali beheld him.
Having worshipped the Lord, the father of his father, according to the prescribed rites, O Brahmin, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words:
"O Father, you have been remembered by me with a deeply dejected heart; therefore, O Father, tell me that which is beneficial, wholesome, and the highest good for me."
67.23 What indeed, O father, is the duty for a man living in this world of transmigration,
by the performance of which no bondage arises for him?
For men of small intelligence who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra—
You should explain to me what that boat would be for crossing over.
Pulastya said:
Having heard these words from his grandson, the lord of the Dānavas reflected and spoke these words regarding that which is the supreme good in this worldly existence.
Prahlāda said:
"Excellent, O tiger among Dānavas, that such a thought has arisen in you!
I shall now declare what is for your benefit, as well as for the benefit of these others, O Bala."
For men who have entered the ocean of existence, who are struck by the winds of the pairs of opposites, who are oppressed by the burden of protecting sons, daughters, and wives,
and who are sinking without a raft in the waters of treacherous sense-objects, Viṣṇu alone is the boat that serves as their refuge.
Those wise ones who have taken refuge in Hari— the infinite, without beginning or middle, Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the gods, the giver of auspiciousness, the most excellent,
the pure one whose gait is like that of the king of birds, the Lord whose abode is the lotus— do not enter the domain of the King of Dharma.
Having seen his own servant with noose in hand, Yama indeed speaks into his ear:
Avoid those who have taken refuge in Madhusūdana; for I am the lord of other men, but certainly not of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Likewise, another thing was said by that best of men, Ikṣvāku, who was surely filled with devotion:
"Those men on earth who are devotees of Viṣṇu become beyond the domain of Yama."
That is a true tongue which praises Hari; that is a true mind which is offered to Him;
and those alone are praiseworthy hands which perform His worship.
Surely those two hands are not called the sprouts at the tips of tree branches,
since they are unable to worship the pair of Hari’s lotus feet.
Surely that is a lotus-root in his throat, or perhaps an epiglottis;
or it is some other disease—it is not a tongue which does not speak the virtues of Hari. (VamP 67.34)
That man who does not worship the lotus feet of Viṣṇu with devotion is to be pitied by his kinsmen; though living, he is as good as dead.
Those men who are constantly devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva are not to be mourned even when dead; this truth, the absolute truth, has been spoken by me.
Whatever is physical or mental, born of speech, formed or formless, moving or stationary,
visible, tangible, or invisible— all that has Keśava as its essence.
For by him who has worshipped the Blessed One Trivikrama in his fourfold form, the worlds— including the gods and the Dānavas— have undoubtedly been worshipped.
Just as the jewels of the ocean are innumerable, my son,
so too are the virtues of the divine Wheel-turner truly incalculable.

Those who take refuge in the Lord of Śrī— the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence, the bestower of boons, whose banner bears the king of birds, and who holds in his hands the conch, the discus, the lotus, and the bow— they do not fall again into the pit of saṃsāra.
Those in whose minds Govinda dwells constantly, O Balarāma,
do not suffer humiliation, nor do they tremble before death.
Those who have taken refuge in the divine Viṣṇu, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, as their supreme resort—
neither shall they dwell in the realm of Yama, nor shall they be inhabitants of hell.
O tiger among the Dānavas, those brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and scriptures do not attain that goal which those devoted to Viṣṇu reach.
O tiger among Daityas, the destination that awaits those slain in the great battle is surpassed by the even higher destination reached by the best of men who are devotees of Viṣṇu.
O Daitya, that destination which belongs to those of virtuous character, those of sattvic nature, and the high-souled ones, is said to belong likewise to those who serve the Blessed Lord.
Devoted to him and with no other thought in their minds, his devotees enter that great-souled Vāsudeva, who dwells in all abodes, who is subtle, and whose form is unmanifest.
Those pure and high-souled ones who, with undivided minds and devotion, pay homage to Keśava, become themselves like sacred fords.
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, drinking,
or eating, he who constantly meditates upon Nārāyaṇa— Vaikuṇṭha, who wields the sword and the axe and utterly severs the bonds of worldly existence— is none other than a partaker of merit.
Having prostrated according to the rule, he shall not be born again in saṃsāra;
dwelling eternally in the sacred fields, he of immeasurable luster remains sporting there.
Seated within all bodies, he is not bound by actions—
those for whom Viṣṇu is dear at the end of their lives are always dear to Viṣṇu.
Those who are devoted to Him and have Him as their supreme goal are never born again;
whoever meditates upon Dāmodara or worships Him with devotion and humility [is likewise liberated].
O Lord of the Dānavas,
those who rise at dawn and with devotion remember Madhusūdana,
praise him, or even listen to his praises, do not sink into this mire of saṃsāra; they cross over all difficulties.
Those whose minds rejoice after drinking the nectar of Hari’s words with the pure vessels of their ears, they cross over all difficulties.
Those who possess unwavering devotion to Him who holds the discus and mace in His hands go certainly to that place where Hari, the Lord of Yoga, resides.
That supreme goal which belongs to the devotees intent upon the work of Viṣṇu cannot be attained even in a thousand births, nor by means of austerities.
What is the use of muttered prayers or mantras for him, what is the use of austerities or stages of life,
if he lacks supreme devotion to Madhusūdana at all times?
Vain are the sacrifices, vain are the Vedas, vain is the gift, and vain is the sacred learning;
vain too are austerity and fame for one who hates Madhusūdana.
What need has he for many other mantras, who possesses devotion to Janārdana?
The mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" is the accomplisher of all goals.
Viṣṇu alone is the refuge of women; how could there be defeat for those in whose hearts Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus, resides?
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa— the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, the most excellent, the bestower of boons, and the Lord— one should perform all ritual actions.
O great Asura, the *viṣṭis*, the *vyatipātas*, and whatever other calamities arise from ill fortune— all these indeed perish through the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Thousands of crores of sacred fords and hundreds of crores of sacred fords are not worth even a sixteenth part of a prostration made to Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever sacred fords and holy shrines exist upon the earth,
one attains them all by chanting the names of Viṣṇu.
Neither those who observe vows nor those who practice austerities attain those worlds which are reached by men who are solely intent on offering salutations to Kṛṣṇa.
Even he who, devoted to another deity, worships Keśava with false devotion,
goes to the great abode of the virtuous who have performed meritorious deeds.
Whatever fruit is obtained by worshipping Hṛṣīkeśa with constancy,
that fruit is never attained even by men who have performed well-practiced austerities.
Those of great intelligence who remember Padmanābha at the three junctions of the day obtain the fruit of fasting; there is no doubt about this.
Constantly worship Hari with actions seen in the scriptures;
through His grace, O Bala, you shall attain supreme and eternal perfection.
Fix your mind on him, be devoted to him, sacrifice to him, and bow down to him;
by taking refuge in that Lord of Gods alone, O son, you shall attain happiness.
Indeed, those best of men dwelling on earth who remember day after day Hari—the primordial, infinite, undecaying, and immutable;
the all-pervading, bestower of auspiciousness, consisting of Brahman, and ancient—they go to the eternal and imperishable abode of Viṣṇu.
Those men who, having transcended passion and knowing what is higher and lower, constantly remember Nārāyaṇa, the preceptor of the gods—
they cross to the further shore of the waters of the ocean of saṃsāra like royal swans with washed-clean white wings.
Those who constantly meditate upon the Imperishable Lord, who is stainless and whose eyes are as long as the petals of a preeminent lotus—
by that meditation, their afflictions and sins being destroyed, they shall never again drink the milk from a mother’s breast.
Those who glorify the Giver of Boons, whose lotus-navel is supreme, who holds in his hands the conch, the lotus, the discus, the excellent bow, the mace, and the sword,
and who is known as the bee at the lotus-face of Lakṣmī— they surely go to the abode of the Slayer of Madhu.
Those people who, devoted with faith, hear the Primal Lord being glorified,
become freed from sin and happy, like those satiated by consuming nectar.

Therefore, meditation, recollection, or the chanting of the names of the virtuous who recite them, as well as listening to the names of Viṣṇu, should be performed by faithful men; for the gods praise that as equal to formal worship.
He who does not worship Keśava, the Lord, with external and internal faculties free from agitation,
using flowers, leaves, water, sprouts, and the like, is surely robbed by the thief of fate.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Bali said:
"Everything has been told by you regarding how one should propitiate Janārdana."
You ought to tell me here what destination is attained in this world.
By what form of worship does delight arise for the God?
What gifts are praised for the gratification of the Teacher of the World?
On which lunar day (tithi) should rites such as fasting be performed for great success?
Which meritorious acts are praised as being truly conducive to the gratification of Viṣṇu?
O Lord of Daityas, you ought to tell me here in its entirety whatever else is to be done by those who are joyful in form and free from indolence.
Prahlāda said:
"The sages have declared that those gifts which are given by the faithful and devoted to Bala, dedicated to Janārdana, are inexhaustible."
Those very lunar days (tithis) are praised, on which a man, having worshipped the Lord of the World and becoming one whose mind is fixed on Him and absorbed in Him, should observe a fast.
When the best of the twice-born are honored, Janārdana is honored;
those fools who hate them will certainly go to hell.
A man devoted to Viṣṇu should worship those Brāhmaṇas with devotion;
for Hari spoke thus in the past: "The Brāhmaṇas are my own body."
A Brāhmaṇa is not to be despised, whether he be learned or unlearned;
for he is a divine form of Viṣṇu, and therefore a person should worship him.
And those very flowers, O great Asura, are praised which possess the proper color as well as flavor and fragrance.
I shall now specifically describe the flowers, the lunar days (tithis),
and the commendable gifts that are pleasing to Mādhava. These include the *jātī*, *śatāhvā*, *sumanā*, *kunda*, and *bahupuṭa*.
And the bāṇa, the campaka, the aśoka, the karavīra, and the yūthikā.
The pāribhadra, the pāṭalā, the bakula, the giriśālinī, the tilaka, the japā flower, and also the yellow nāgara; VamP_68.13.
For these are the most excellent flowers for the worship of Acyuta;
likewise, other fragrant flowers are suitable, with the exception of the ketakī.
The leaf of the bilva, the leaf of the śamī, the leaf of the bhṛṅga, the leaf of the mṛgāṅka,
the leaf of the tamāla, and the leaf of the āmalakī are recommended for the worship of Keśava.
Furthermore, those plants whose flowers are praised for the worship of Acyuta,
their sprouts, shoots, and leaves should also be used in the ritual of Hari’s worship; likewise, one may worship with the young shoots of creepers and with sacred grass.
And with various water-born forms, such as lotuses, blue water-lilies, and the like.
O Bala, one should worship the lords of the forest with pure, smooth sprouts washed in water,
as well as with the tips of dūrvā grass shoots.
One should diligently anoint [the image] with sandalwood, saffron,
as well as with uśīra, padmaka, kālīyaka, and other such substances.
The incense known as mahiṣa, kaṇa, dāru, silhaka, agallochum (sāgaru), white sugar, conch-shell, and nutmeg are indeed beloved by Śrīśa.
Barley, wheat, and rice, as well as sesame, mung beans, and the like, along with black gram and paddy— all these, when consecrated with oblations, are dear to Hari.
O sinless one, gifts of cows, gifts of land,
and gifts of clothing, food, and gold are purifying and lead to the pleasure of the Slayer of Madhu.
O giver of gifts, in the month of Māgha, sesame seeds and a cow made of sesame should be given,
as well as fuel and other such items, for the sake of pleasing Mādhava.
In the month of Phālguna, rice, mung beans, clothing, black antelope skins, and so forth,
should be given by the best of men for the purpose of pleasing Govinda.
In the month of Caitra, variegated garments, beds,
and seats should then be given to Brahmins for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu.
In the month of Vaiśākha, fragrant perfumes and garlands should indeed be given;
they should be offered to the foremost of the twice-born for the satisfaction of Madhusūdana.
A water-pot, a water-cow, a palm-leaf fan, and excellent sandalwood should always be given by the virtuous for the sake of pleasing Trivikrama.
A pair of sandals, an umbrella, salt, myrobalan,
and other such items should be given with devotion in the month of Āṣāḍha for the pleasure of Vāmana.
Clarified butter, jars of milk, and cows yielding clarified butter should be given by a wise person in the month of Śrāvaṇa for the pleasure of Śrīdhara.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should offer milk-rice with honey and clarified butter,
as well as salt and rice with jaggery, for the purpose of pleasing Hṛṣīkeśa.
In the month of Āśvayuja, men should give sesame seeds, a horse, a bull, curd, copper, iron, and so forth, for the sake of pleasing Padmanābha.
In the month of Kārttika, a person should offer silver, gold, lamps, jewels, pearls, and so forth, for the sake of pleasing Dāmodara.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, men should give donkeys, camels, mules, elephants, vehicles, draft animals, goats, and sheep for the pleasure of Keśava.
Palaces, cities, and the like, as well as houses and garments,
should be given with devotion in the month of Pauṣa for the sake of pleasing Nārāyaṇa.
For the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama, female and male servants, ornaments, and food endowed with the six flavors should be offered at all times.
Whatever is most beloved, or whatever pure thing exists in the house,
that very thing should be given for the sake of pleasing the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
He who causes a temple to be built for Keśava shall indeed conquer eternal, meritorious worlds;
by giving gardens filled with flowers and fruits, he enjoys praiseworthy pleasures according to his desire.
The builder of a temple for Viṣṇu shall, together with himself, deliver eight generations of his lineage before his grandfather.
And these verses, O Daitya, the *yogins* among the ancestors sing before Jyāmagha,
the ascetic lion of the Yadus.
"Will there be someone in our family who will become a devotee of Viṣṇu—
one who builds a temple for Hari and observes the vow of silence?"
Moreover, may a righteous-souled one be born in our lineage who will, out of devotion, perform the smearing of Viṣṇu’s abode and its sweeping.
May one born in our lineage offer a lamp, flowers, and unguents to the God of gods at the temple of Keśava.
Whether one is burdened by a great sin (mahāpātaka), a sin (pātaka), or a minor sin (upapātaka),
the painter of a temple of Viṣṇu becomes liberated from all evil.
Having thus heard the words of the ancestors, that best of kings built a sanctuary upon the earth and smeared the demon Khya with [the remains].
Devoted to the worship of Keśava, he [adorned the image] with the manifestations of Keśava’s opulence,
using various modifications of minerals and paintings of five colors.
O Balarāma, he himself duly offered lamps filled with fragrant oil and ghee in the temple of Vāsudeva.
Victory banners of various colors, dyed with mahārajana,
madder, and the nine primary hues, were fixed upon white pāṭalika trees.
There were various delightful groves, rich in flowers and abounding in fruit,
covered with creepers and tender shoots, and surrounded by *devadāru* trees.
And they were made to be placed upon great couches by skillful people, supervised by experienced stewards and supported by sturdy craftsmen skilled in working with jewels.
In those [houses], ascetics, celibate students, those learned in the Vedas, those endowed with knowledge, and the poor, the blind, the infirm, and others are constantly honored.
Having acted in this manner, that king Jyāmagha, full of faith and having conquered his senses, went to the abode of Viṣṇu; so we have heard.
O tiger among men, even today people who desire to conquer the world of Viṣṇu travel along that very path established by Jyāmagha.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should have a temple built for Hari;
worship Him with diligence, as well as the highly learned Brahmins—
especially those who are devoted to the Purāṇas, pure, and dedicated to virtuous conduct.
With garments, ornaments, jewels, cows, land, gold, and other such things,
satisfy the Lord who wields the discus whenever you have the means to do so.
Thus, for you who are now devoted to the yoga of action, Murāri will surely be the bestower of auspiciousness today.
Men do not falter when they have taken refuge in the Infinite, the Unfallen, the Lord of the World, and the All-pervading One, relying upon His strength.
Pulastya said:
Having spoken these words of truth and unsurpassed excellence to Vairocana, the lord of Diti, being honored by him, attained liberation; his desires fulfilled, he was a devotee at the feet of Hari.
When that joyful grandfather of Bali had departed, the palace shone with the hue of the moon;
then Keśava, the most excellent of the architects of Mahendra, caused it to be made even more magnificent.
Together with his wife, the high-souled one personally performed the acts of sweeping and smearing in the temple,
and he offered an incomparable oblation of barley, sugar, and other items to the Slayer of Madhu.
The long-eyed Vindhyāvalī herself offered lamps in the temple of Viṣṇu;
and the wise king caused the recitation of righteous songs and the listening to the Purāṇas by the most excellent of Brahmins who were experts in those texts.
The high-souled Janārdana, the Lord of the World with a divine form, stood there for the protection of Bali— that foremost of Asuras who was thus situated upon the righteous path.
Grasping a mace that shone like ten thousand suns and striking down the wicked leaders of the enemy hosts,
he stood at the gate and did not grant entrance to the powerful man within the house protected by the wall.
While Dhātṛ stood at the gate as a guardian and Nārāyaṇa, who is delightful in all his virtues,
remained there, he worshipped Hari, the Lord and foremost of divine sages, within the palace.
Thus did Bali, the king of the asuras, remain, worshipping the lotus feet of Hari;
he constantly remembered the words spoken by Hari, for those words had become for him a goad of discipline.
And as he remembered the auspicious, truthful, and beneficial words of his preceptor—the grandfather who was equal to Indra—the heroic king of the Daityas recited this verse: "VamP_68.64"

Those who act upon the words of the elders—even after first hearing harsh speech—and who later find delight in their affectionate words, pure as fresh butter, they rejoice; there is no doubt about this. (VamP 68.65)
For one bitten by the serpent of misfortune who is always devoid of mantra, the words of the elders and medicinal herbs surely render him free from poison. (VamP 68.66)

When a man drinks the nectar of the words of the elders and acts in accordance with what they have said, what satisfaction could possibly arise from drinking the Soma juice that compares to it? (VamP 68.67)

Those who have fallen into transgression and for whom there are no elders to act as teachers are to be pitied; though they live here in this world, they are equal to the dead, like withered trees in a forest.
For those seized by the crocodiles of calamity, there may be elders but no wise men;
for those who have no deliverers, peace is truly not to be found.
For those submerged in the blazing fire and being carried away by the waves of calamity,
there is surely no way at all to cross over without the words of the elders.
Therefore, whoever listens to the words of the elders and acts upon them attains immediate success, just as Bali, the son of Virocana, did.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
"O Nārada, this most meritorious Purāṇa has indeed been recounted by me to you."
And having heard this, one endowed with supreme renown and devotion to Viṣṇu attains his abode.
Just as sins are purified by plunging into the waters of the Gaṅgā,
so too is the destruction of misdeeds brought about by listening to the Purāṇas.
No diseases arise for him, nor any poison resulting from malevolent spells,
O Brahmin, in his body or his family, who hears this account of Vāmana.
He who constantly hears [this] according to the rule with devotion, worshipping and bowing down to Viṣṇu,
becomes cleansed of sin and attains the entire fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees.
A man or a woman who, being pure, hears even a single quarter-verse of this gift of gold, land, horses, cattle, and chariots, becomes the most meritorious on earth.

(69.5) This merit is equal to that which the Brahmins declare comes from bathing in the most holy waters of the Gaṅgā, or at Naimiṣa and Puṣkara, or at Kokāmukha, or by reaching Prayāga and bathing during the month of Māgha. (69.6)

Having obtained that fruit, O Nārada, he shall go to the supreme abode with a single-minded focus while glorifying Vāmana; this which I have told you today bestows the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

O Great Seer, whatever complete and great happiness a man may obtain upon reaching the world of the gods, which is attainable even in the world of mortals, he attains that through hearing this Sautrāmaṇī; of this I have no doubt.
Whatever fruit may arise from the gift of jewels, and whatever from the eclipses of the sun and moon by Rāhu,
and the fruit of giving food as it has been described when given to an eminent Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and is hungry— [all that is attained by this].
The fruit that the gods proclaim for one who always strives to nourish his wife and children when they are oppressed by famine,
who is devoted to the gods, fire, Brahmins, and sages, and who serves his parents and his eldest brother with a spirit of harmony—
the same fruit he obtains from reciting this.
They say the fourteenth is the foremost Vāmana, by hearing which the accumulation of sins goes to destruction;
I have no doubt in this matter, O Nārada, that even great sins perish quickly.
O Brahmin, through reciting it, hearing it, or even causing someone else to hear it,
all sins are destroyed for the eternal joy of Vāmana.

This supreme secret has been told to you; it must not be spoken to one devoid of devotion to Hari, nor to a twice-born man who delights in censuring others, who is skilled in deceit, and whose being is filled with the sins of sophistry.
"Salutations, salutations to the dwarf who is the cause"— the twice-born who constantly and with discipline utters this,
to him Viṣṇu, worshipped by the gods, grants the state of liberation.
One should bestow cows, land, gold, and ornaments upon the reciter;
one must not practice stinginess with wealth, for doing so destroys the merit of the hearing.
O Brahmin, reciting and listening to this at the three junctions of the day destroys all sins;
it is free from envy and bestows all prosperity.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter in the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa;
thus the glorious Vāmana Purāṇa is completed.
